Impact: If public trust collapses due to a shelter-in-place reversal, uncontrolled evacuation of 50,000–200,000 outer-zone residents could begin within 2–4 hours of a Scenario Beta order, creating gridlock on I-15, I-90 and US-191 that prevents the organized Zone One evacuation of the 35,000 park visitors and strands medical transport. Additionally, reduced compliance with time-banded departure instructions or shelter assignments would increase the unplanned vehicle load on evacuation corridors by 20–40%, consuming an additional 4–6 hours of corridor throughput.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Develop and pre-authorize a 'Adaptive Messaging Protocol' that explains the rationale for phased evacuation orders: initial shelter-in-place is based on current (low) eruption probability; Scenario Beta escalation will be triggered by specific USGS indicators (published in advance); outer-zone residents should monitor official channels daily and expect possible reversal if indicators cross thresholds. Deliver this protocol to media outlets, emergency management offices, and community leaders in Zone One communities (Bozeman, Gardiner, West Yellowstone, Cody) 60 days before T+0, so that the public understands the escalation logic. At T+0 hours, rebroadcast the protocol on IPAWS, local radio and TV to reinforce the message. If a Scenario Beta trigger fires, issue a separate messaging campaign explaining the new indicator values and stating that the previous shelter-in-place order is superseded, effective immediately. Conduct a messaging credibility exercise with local government and media 60 days before T+0 to test message clarity and anticipate public-response scenarios.

Risk 13 - Financial / Procurement & Contracting

Procurement and contracting lead times for emergency supplies (bottled water, N95 respirators, generator fuel, buses, tents) are not addressed. The plan assumes water convoys can be 'mobilized within 12 hours,' but sourcing, loading and dispatching a convoy of 20–40 water trucks requires coordination with suppliers, transportation contractors, and state agencies. If contracts are not pre-positioned or suppliers are not pre-authorized, delays of 24–48 hours are typical for emergency procurements.

Impact: A 24-hour delay in water-convoy dispatch means the convoy does not arrive at Bozeman or Idaho Falls until T+36 hours (instead of T+12 hours), during which shelter occupancy could reach 15,000–20,000 people. Water shortages affecting thousands of evacuees for 24+ hours increase risk of dehydration, medication non-compliance, and secondary health emergencies. Similar delays in N95 respirator resupply could leave shelters and hospitals without adequate stock within 48 hours. Estimated impact: 1,000–3,000 evacuees experience 12–24 hours without adequate water; additional 20–50 respiratory distress cases.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Execute pre-event contracts with bottled-water suppliers, N95 respirator manufacturers, generator-fuel wholesalers, and charter-bus operators 60 days before T+0, with explicit 'surge-mobilization' clauses requiring 12-hour dispatch of supplies upon verbal activation by the forward command. Identify alternative suppliers (e.g., water distributors in Pocatello, ID and Butte, MT; N95 suppliers in Salt Lake City and Denver) and list them in a standby-supplier roster. Pre-authorize payment via emergency FEMA contract vehicles so that suppliers can charge supplies immediately without normal competitive-bidding delays. Establish a procurement checkpoint at the forward command element tasked with tracking all inbound supply shipments and alerting the incident commander if any convoy is delayed >4 hours beyond dispatch.

Risk 14 - Technical / Electric Grid Resilience

The plan identifies grid failure due to ash-induced flashovers as a contingency and directs generator fuel to hospitals and communications centers, but does not specify which transmission lines are at highest risk, which substations have single points of failure, or how voltage regulation and protective relays will behave under ashfall. Regional power utilities (Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power, Idaho Power) operate interconnected transmission networks that could experience cascading failures if multiple substations are hit by ash-induced flashovers simultaneously.

Impact: If a major transmission line fails and backup protection systems malfunction due to ash, a regional blackout affecting 100,000+ people could occur within 2–4 hours of ashfall onset, well before generator fuel can reach all facilities. A multi-hour regional blackout would affect water pumping and treatment, fuel convoys' refrigeration and communication equipment, ambulance dispatch centers, and shelter HVAC systems. Estimated impact: 4–8 hour regional blackout affecting 50,000–100,000+ people; 5–10 additional deaths in hospitals and care facilities due to loss of ventilator and life-support power.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: Coordinate with Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power 60 days before T+0 to identify critical transmission lines, substations and protective relays in the evacuation-corridor and shelter-area zones. Request pre-deployment of mobile generator units and voltage-regulation equipment at the two largest substations serving Bozeman and Idaho Falls. Establish a 24/7 utility-operations hotline from the forward command to the regional dispatch centers so that the incident commander can track grid status and request emergency load shedding or localized de-energization to prevent cascading failures. Conduct a grid-failure scenario exercise with utility operators 30 days before T+0, testing manual switchover procedures and the adequacy of generator fuel at critical facilities.

Risk 15 - Operational / Landslide & Road Engineering

The South Entrance (US-89/191/287) is currently landslide-blocked, and the plan does not specify the debris volume, ground conditions or timeline for a single-lane clearance or bypass. Engineering assessment of the slide is not described. Secondary slides and hydrothermal explosions could further damage the North Entrance (US-89) and the Grand Loop Road during the evacuation window, adding to the blockage load.

Impact: If the South Entrance clearance attempt fails or takes >12 hours, the plan loses a potential third exit route and relies entirely on US-191/US-20 (west) and US-89 (north). This concentration adds 20–40% additional load to the two surviving corridors, extending evacuation time from 6 hours to 8–10 hours and increasing the overlap with ashfall onset. If a secondary explosion damages the North Entrance during the evacuation peak, that corridor could be reduced to one lane for 2–4 hours, creating a bottleneck that delays 2,000–4,000 vehicles.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Conduct a pre-event geotechnical survey of the South Entrance landslide and the Grand Loop Road 60 days before T+0, using ground-penetrating radar and aerial drones to assess debris volume, slope stability and secondary slide risk. Develop a time-boxed single-lane clearance plan (max 4-hour work window) and a longer-term bypass-route plan, with pre-positioned heavy equipment and a clear abort trigger (e.g., renewed seismic activity M>4.0). Deploy a geotechnical monitoring team at the North Entrance and Grand Loop Road sections starting at T-12 hours to detect incipient slope movement and trigger temporary traffic closures before collapse. Establish a 'loss-of-exit' contingency: if the South Entrance or North Entrance becomes impassable and cannot be restored within 6 hours, the forward command will issue a shelter-in-place order for any vehicles still in the south or north sections of the park and redirect them to the nearest surviving exit (US-191/US-20 west or US-89 north) via the safest park roads available.

Risk 16 - Operational / Visitor Transport & Special Needs

The plan does not specify transport arrangements for disabled visitors, elderly visitors in lodges, or families with children who may have mobility or medical constraints. A mandatory private-vehicle evacuation assumes all visitors have access to a functioning vehicle; the ~5–10% of visitors who arrived via tour bus, without a personal vehicle, or with mobility aids may face delays in accessing contraflow lanes or may be left behind if buses are not pre-allocated and staffed.

Impact: If 1,500–3,500 mobility-constrained or vehicle-less visitors cannot board evacuation shuttles within the first 2 hours, they may become trapped in lodges or at trailheads. Emergency extraction of such populations by helicopter is not feasible if airspace is closed or ashfall is heavy. These visitors could become casualties or stranded, requiring secondary rescue operations after the main evacuation window. Estimated impact: 200–500 stranded or delayed evacuees; 5–20 requiring rescue or hospital care due to exertion or medical decompensation.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Coordinate with Xanterra Parks and Resorts and other concessioners 60 days before T+0 to identify all mobility-constrained guests and pre-arrange dedicated evacuation buses (1–2 buses per major lodge) staffed with attendants trained in mobility assistance. At T-12 hours, confirm occupancy of all lodges and tour groups via concessioner manifests, and designate a 'priority-transport' staging area at each lodge where mobility-constrained guests gather first, ahead of general traffic. Pre-authorize a secondary evacuation protocol: if any lodge or group cannot evacuate within the first 3 hours, notify the forward command, which will dispatch helicopter support (if available) or a ground-based rescue team from the National Guard. Pre-stage medical supplies and attendants at the priority-staging areas to manage any acute medical events during the evacuation wait.

Risk 17 - Regulatory & Inter-agency Coordination

FAA authority over airspace grounding (ZLC and ZSE) is not explicitly coordinated with the Unified Command's decision-making. The plan states that a VEI-6 eruption will trigger grounding of ZLC and ZSE airspace, but the FAA operates independently and may not immediately coordinate grounding with the incident commander's needs for medevac, surveillance or emergency airlift. Conversely, the incident commander may want exceptions for medevac that the FAA blocks due to ash-concentration forecasts.

Impact: Delays in grounding coordination could result in one or more aircraft encountering ash and suffering engine damage within the first 2–4 hours of ashfall, adding a secondary emergency response load and reducing public trust in the warning system. Alternatively, rigid FAA grounding without any medevac exceptions could deny hospitals access to helicopter transport for critical patients, delaying some transfers by 4–6 hours and causing preventable deaths. Estimated impact: 1–3 aircraft-ash encounters; 2–5 critical patients unable to access helicopter medevac within the first 24 hours.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: Establish a pre-event coordination protocol with the FAA Regional Flight Service Stations (Salt Lake City and Seattle centers) and the air-operations offices at mountain airports (Gallatin County, Jackson Hole, Billings) at least 60 days before T+0. Define an explicit trigger for airspace grounding (e.g., USGS detection of VEI-6 magma signatures, NOAA forecast of ash concentration >100 µg/m³ in flight corridors) and pre-authorize a narrow set of medevac and survey flight corridors below ash-concentration thresholds. Establish a 24/7 aviation-operations liaison at the forward command element with direct phone lines to the FAA regional desk and the military (Malmstrom AFB, Montana) to coordinate real-time flight requests and ash-model updates. Pre-authorize helicopter fuel caches at forward airfields (Gallatin County, Jackson Hole, Billings) to enable rapid deployment of medevac sorties if airspace restrictions are lifted temporarily.

Risk summary

This is a high-stakes, multi-state government evacuation plan for a VEI-6+ volcanic event at Yellowstone Caldera with a 72-hour decision window and 40% eruption probability. The plan aims to evacuate ~35,000 tourists and 800 staff from the park interior (Zone Zero) within 6 hours and expand to 100 km radius communities (Zone One) within 24 hours. The three most critical risks are: (1) single-point road chokepoints on narrow, ash-exposed mountain corridors (US-191, US-89) with no bypass capacity if a breakdown, rockfall, or secondary slide occurs during peak evacuation; (2) cascading communications and command failures as cell towers collapse from ash and tremors, leaving drivers and responders unable to receive route updates, and the cross-jurisdiction authority transfer between NPS and three state governors creating command gaps; (3) shelter and hospital capacity collapse under Scenario Beta (VEI-7) expansion to 500 km radius, which would exceed all pre-staged supplies, road throughput and facility capacity, yet the trigger is pre-authorized without a defined secondary-stage evacuation plan. These three risks are tightly coupled: communication failure undermines the contraflow operation, command gaps delay the escalation decision, and inadequate shelter capacity forces uncontrolled shadow evacuation that saturates the very corridors the plan depends on. Mitigation relies on execution discipline, real-time asset positioning, and a credible second-stage plan for Scenario Beta that does not yet exist.

Make Assumptions

Question 1 - What funding source and budget ceiling cover pre-positioned supplies, contracts and surge operations across FEMA, NPS and the three states?

Assumptions: Assumption: Funding comes from a federal emergency declaration (Stafford Act) plus pre-event contract vehicles, with an initial surge envelope of about USD 150-250 million (estimate), reimbursed through FEMA procedures. Justification: large multi-state responses typically draw on declaration-based cost-sharing.

Assessments: Title: Financial Feasibility Assessment Description: Evaluates funding availability and speed of access. Details: Risk: procurement delays of 24-48 hours (estimate) without pre-awarded contracts. Mitigation: pre-event surge contracts for water, N95, fuel and buses, with verbal activation. Opportunity: FEMA contract vehicles remove competitive-bidding delay. Track burn rate in USD hourly at the forward command; hold a 20% contingency (proposed) for Scenario Beta.

Question 2 - Which milestones and decision gates must be met within the 72-hour window, including the T+6 evacuation and the T+12 water convoy deadlines?

Assumptions: Assumption: Project starts at Month 0 (2026-10-14) with preparation as the first activity. Milestones: Zone Zero cleared by T+6 hours, Zone One by T+24 hours, water convoys dispatched by T+12 hours (user constraints), and shelter selection at T+6 from the plume forecast. Justification: matches the phased structure of the plan.

Assessments: Title: Timeline Feasibility Assessment Description: Tests whether phase deadlines are achievable. Details: Risk: ashfall and gridlock may stretch the 12-hour convoy to 18-30 hours (estimate). Mitigation: pre-stage depots before T+0, reserved convoy lane, hourly gate reviews. Opportunity: a three-exit design (including East Entrance) shortens clearance. Hard abort triggers for southern clearance work keep the schedule from slipping.

Question 3 - What numbers of rangers, highway patrol, National Guard, tow crews, buses and medical staff are available for traffic control, sweeps and perimeters?

Assumptions: Assumption: About 100-150 NPS rangers (estimate), supplemented by Montana, Wyoming and Idaho highway patrol and Guard units, staff the control points; relief depth is 1.5 responders per post (proposed). Justification: 8-hour shifts need that ratio for continuous coverage.

Assessments: Title: Resource Adequacy Assessment Description: Compares staffing demand with likely availability. Details: Risk: all ranger hours consumed during T+2 to T+8, leaving no relief. Mitigation: request out-of-region Guard and a 30-50 person standby reserve (proposed), tier posts by criticality. Count responder N95s separately from the 100,000 civilian stock (user constraint). Opportunity: concessioner buses raise people per vehicle.

Question 4 - What legal authorities and agreements govern the NPS-to-state handoff, FEMA Region 8/10 coordination, FAA grounding and interstate mutual aid?

Assumptions: Assumption: Authority transfers at defined roadside checkpoints under a written protocol, backed by governor MOUs and EMAC mutual aid; Idaho coordination runs through a FEMA Region 10 liaison at the Denver RRCC. Justification: standard Unified Command practice.

Assessments: Title: Governance Assessment Description: Reviews command clarity and legal basis. Details: Risk: authority gaps mid-corridor delay reroutes by 15-45 minutes (estimate). Mitigation: Boundary Coordination Officer at the forward element, pre-signed MOUs, pre-authorized state reroute powers. FAA grounding needs a liaison at the Unified Command. Benefit: pre-agreed authority removes turf disputes and speeds the pre-authorized Scenario Beta order.

Question 5 - What are the principal life-safety hazards (chokepoint failure, secondary slides, ash exposure, hospital power loss, stranded backcountry visitors) and the abort criteria for each?

Assumptions: Assumption: Principal hazards are corridor blockage in Gallatin Canyon, secondary slides at the South Entrance, backcountry stragglers, and hospital power loss. Abort criteria are seismic-based (e.g. renewed M4.0+ activity, proposed threshold) and blockage lasting over 45 minutes (proposed) triggers diversion.

Assessments: Title: Safety and Risk Assessment Description: Prioritizes hazards by severity and likelihood. Details: Highest: single-point corridor failure (high/high). Mitigation: pre-placed tow and rockfall teams at chokepoints, geotechnical monitoring, diversion rule. Crew safety: time-boxed clearance with abort triggers. Medical: 72-hour fuel reserves at receiving hospitals. Maintain a risk register with owners and review each shift.

Question 6 - How will ashfall, contaminated reservoirs and air quality affect shelter siting, water supply and respirator demand?

Assumptions: Assumption: Ash footprint forecasts are uncertain by tens of kilometers (estimate), so shelters are chosen at T+6 with ranked upwind backups, open reservoirs are isolated before ash, and N95 demand may exceed 100,000 (user constraint) within days.

Assessments: Title: Environmental Impact Assessment Description: Evaluates ash, water and air-quality effects on operations. Details: Risk: shelters in heavier ash require relocating 10,000+ people (estimate). Mitigation: real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensors, backup sites 50+ km upwind (proposed), supplemental N95 stock at Billings or Salt Lake City, reservoir isolation. Note N95s clog quickly in heavy ash, so replacement cycles must be planned. Opportunity: USGS/NOAA plume updates refine siting.

Question 7 - Which stakeholders (governors, local officials, concessioners, utilities, hospitals, international visitors, outer-zone residents) must be engaged, and how?

Assumptions: Assumption: Engagement runs through the Unified Command liaison cell: governors via MOUs, concessioners such as Xanterra for lodge manifests and buses, utilities for grid coordination, and consular and multilingual channels for foreign visitors.

Assessments: Title: Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Description: Maps who must be aligned and the risk of non-compliance. Details: Risk: conflicting shelter-in-place and evacuation orders cut corridor throughput 20-40% (estimate). Mitigation: unified messaging protocol, published USGS triggers, joint exercises. Non-English visitors may be a large share of the 35,000, so pre-produced multilingual alerts are needed. Opportunity: trusted local radio sustains credibility if escalation reverses earlier guidance.

Question 8 - What communications, traffic management, logistics tracking and power systems must keep working under ash and tremor, and what are the fallbacks?

Assumptions: Assumption: Layers are IPAWS/WEA/NOAA Weather Radio, Guard signal bridging, satellite terminals, highway advisory radio, variable message signs and printed route cards; priority generator fuel goes to hospitals and comms centers.

Assessments: Title: Operational Systems Assessment Description: Tests resilience of comms, power and logistics tracking. Details: Risk: cell network failure leaves 10-20% of drivers on unintended routes (estimate). Mitigation: deploy repeaters and satellite phones to control points before ash, pre-recorded HAR messages, printed cards. Fuel tiering protects hospitals, comms and shelter kitchens. Test systems in ash-simulation exercises before the window. Use one shared common operating picture across NPS, states and Guard.

Distill Assumptions

  • Funding comes from a Stafford Act declaration with a USD 150-250 million surge envelope (estimate).
  • Pre-awarded surge contracts for water, N95, fuel and buses avoid 24-48 hour procurement delays (estimate).
  • Project starts Month 0 (2026-10-14) with preparation first; Zone Zero cleared by T+6 hours, Zone One by T+24.
  • Water convoys dispatch from Salt Lake City by T+12 hours; shelters selected at T+6 from plume forecast.
  • The 72-hour window carries a 40% probability of VEI-6+ eruption (user constraint).
  • About 35,000 tourists and 800 staff exit via contraflow on US-191, US-20, US-89 to I-90.
  • East Entrance toward Cody on US-14/16/20 adds a third exit, with fixed district-to-gate assignments.
  • Staffing is 100-150 NPS rangers (estimate) plus state patrol and Guard, with 1.5 relief per post (proposed).
  • A 30-50 person standby reserve and out-of-region Guard are requested; responder N95s counted separately.
  • Authority transfers at roadside checkpoints under written protocol, governor MOUs and EMAC mutual aid.
  • Unified Command sits at Denver RRCC with a forward element in Bozeman or Livingston, plus Region 10 liaison.
  • Pre-authorized USGS trigger matrix lets Unified Command order the VEI-7 500 km expansion without further approval.
  • Corridor blockage over 45 minutes (proposed) or renewed M4.0+ activity (proposed) triggers diversion or abort.
  • Comms rely on IPAWS/WEA, NOAA Weather Radio, Guard signal bridging, satellites, highway advisory radio and printed cards.
  • ZLC and ZSE airspace is grounded indefinitely; FAA liaison sits at the Unified Command.
  • Shelters at Bozeman and Idaho Falls are not safe from ash; ranked backups 50+ km upwind (proposed).
  • N95 pre-staging covers 100,000 people (user constraint), but demand may exceed it and masks clog quickly.
  • Open reservoirs are isolated before ashfall; fuel priority goes to hospitals, comms centers and shelter kitchens.
  • National Guard enforces the exclusion perimeter and prevents looting while supporting logistics.
  • Concessioners such as Xanterra supply lodge manifests and buses; multilingual alerts reach foreign visitors.
  • Shelter-in-place and evacuation orders conflict risk cutting corridor throughput 20-40% (estimate).

Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Government emergency management and disaster response planning, with focus on multi-jurisdiction civil protection operations, evacuation logistics, and life-safety decision-making under extreme time pressure and uncertainty.

Domain-specific considerations

  • Evacuation throughput and contraflow engineering under cascading hazards (ash, tremor, secondary slides) with hard time constraints and single-point failures
  • Cross-jurisdiction command authority and decision-making speed during rapid escalation from 100 km to 500 km radius with conflicting state and federal mandates
  • Communications resilience and public trust messaging when digital networks fail and escalation orders reverse earlier guidance
  • Resource sustainability and responder protection across 72-96 hour continuous operations with fatigue, respiratory exposure and equipment degradation under ashfall
  • Shelter capacity and life-support logistics for dynamic population (35,000 to potentially millions) with uncertain ash footprint and supply-chain fragility
  • Scenario Beta secondary-stage planning: absent defined second-stage shelters, host-community coordination, and capacity for 500 km radius evacuation creates cascade-failure risk if trigger fires

Issue 1 - Missing Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Plan and Capacity Analysis

The plan pre-authorizes a VEI-7 trigger that will order immediate 500 km radius evacuation, potentially affecting 100,000 to 500,000+ people across Montana, Wyoming, Idaho and Colorado. However, no second-stage shelter hubs, host-community coordination, onward transport routes, or supply-staging depots are defined. The stated 'shelter-siting strategy' applies only to Bozeman and Idaho Falls (100 km radius), which become overwhelmed within hours if Scenario Beta expands the evacuation. This absence creates a vacuum: once the trigger fires, evacuees and residents have no published destinations, leading to chaotic, uncontrolled flight on all routes away from Yellowstone. This directly undermines the core evacuation plan.

Recommendation: Develop and pre-authorize a written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan by Month -2, specifying: (1) five to ten ranked secondary shelter hubs (e.g., Salt Lake City metro, Billings, Denver, Cheyenne, Boise) with capacity estimates and pre-signed MOUs with host communities; (2) tiered public messaging that differentiates shelter-in-place zones (250–500 km, self-supplied residents), time-banded zones (100–250 km, shelters pre-assigned by county), and organized evacuation (Zone One); (3) bus fleets and rail corridors moving evacuees from primary shelters to secondary hubs, using lateral routes away from I-90; (4) supply-estimation models for 100,000–500,000 additional people, with food, water, medical stock pre-positioned at secondary hubs before Month 0 (2026-10-14). Conduct a joint multi-state Scenario Beta exercise 30 days before the eruption window, testing messaging, routing and secondary-hub readiness. Assign ownership of each secondary hub to a named state/county emergency manager, with quarterly coordination calls before the event.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: Scenario Beta affects 50,000–100,000 additional evacuees outside the 100 km radius. If no secondary plan exists and uncontrolled evacuation saturates I-15, I-80 and I-90, the delay to organized Zone One evacuation is estimated at 4–8 hours, reducing overall corridor throughput by 30–50% and extending the overlap between peak evacuation and ashfall arrival. Cost of secondary-hub pre-positioning and planning (estimated USD 20–40 million) is a fraction of the surge envelope (USD 150–250 million estimate); failure to execute costs an additional USD 100–200 million in emergency response and 5–20 preventable deaths in stranded populations.

Issue 2 - Responder Exposure Limits and Relief Rotation Regime Undefined: Staffing Depth Insufficient for 72-Hour Operations

The plan lists 'Responder Exposure Limits and Relief Rotation Regime' as a secondary decision but does not specify shift lengths, withdrawal thresholds, or how many relief personnel exist. Assumption of 100–150 NPS rangers (estimate), 1.5 relief per post (proposed), and no explicit responder N95 count creates a staffing gap: at peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 hours), all ranger hours are consumed with zero relief depth. If strict exposure limits are applied (e.g., 6-hour shifts with 2-hour rest before 18-hour withdrawal), the coverage available at traffic-control and perimeter checkpoints during the evacuation peak may fall below 50%, causing throughput loss and enabling unauthorized entries or looting. Conversely, loose limits expose rangers to respiratory injury and entrapment, degrading the force just when ashfall intensifies.

Recommendation: Define concrete responder exposure limits in writing by Month -1: rangers and highway patrol work maximum 6-hour shifts at ash-exposed locations (contraflow points, perimeters, comms sites) before mandatory 2-hour rest with N95 replacement; all responders withdraw completely after 18 consecutive hours of duty. Count responder N95 respirators separately from the civilian stock (100,000 user constraint), with a minimum 50% surge buffer for replacement cycles (estimated 150,000–200,000 total responder+civilian stock). Pre-stage a 30–50 person standby reserve from outside the region (Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, Idaho Department of Lands) at a logistics depot outside the ash zone, ready to deploy within 4 hours if coverage falls below 50% at any checkpoint. Pre-authorize the forward command to request additional National Guard from Fort Carson without needing supervisory approval. Conduct a shift-rotation exercise at a control point 30 days before the window, testing relief logistics, N95 replacement cycles and fatigue protocols under simulated ashfall.

Sensitivity: Baseline staffing: 100–150 rangers at 1.5 relief ratio covers 100–150 positions with continuous staffing. If exposure limits reduce effective working time to 50% (6-hour shifts with 12-hour rest), available staffing drops to 50–75 people, creating gaps at 30–50% of positions. Each uncovered checkpoint reduces corridor throughput by ~5–10% (estimate), so understaffing adds 2–4 hours to total evacuation time and strands 500–2,000 vehicles in ash exposure. Cost of a 30–50 person standby reserve (estimated USD 3–5 million over 72 hours) prevents a 2–4 hour evacuation delay worth USD 50–100 million in indirect costs (medical, rescue, stranded-vehicle recovery).

Issue 3 - Ashfall Footprint Uncertainty and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Strategy Lack Real-Time Monitoring and Relocation Protocols

The plan states shelters will be 'selected at T+6 hours from the forecast wind and plume model,' assuming the forecast is accurate. However, ashfall from a VEI-6 eruption has never been directly observed in North America; volcanic ash grain-size distribution, settling rates and regional wind variability could shift the modeled footprint by 100+ km. Additionally, the plan pre-stages 100,000 N95 masks (user constraint) based on a model estimate; if ashfall is 2–3 times heavier than forecast, this stock lasts only 12–24 hours instead of 72 hours. Finally, the plan does not specify real-time ash and air-quality monitoring at shelter sites or a trigger to relocate evacuees if actual ashfall exceeds forecast. This creates a scenario in which 10,000–15,000 evacuees are sheltered in zones of moderate to heavy ashfall, requiring emergency relocation within 6–12 hours and exposing them to respiratory distress.

Recommendation: Establish continuous ashfall and air-quality monitoring at the forward command and all three shelter sites using real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensors and visual ash-depth markers, updated hourly starting at T-12 hours. At T+6 hours when final shelter locations are selected, update the selection based on the latest wind and plume forecast from NOAA and USGS, not the T+0 forecast. Maintain a ranked second and third shelter backup for each primary site, located 50+ km upwind (confirmed daily from the latest wind forecast) so a rapid relocation order can be issued within 4 hours if ashfall exceeds model predictions. Pre-stage a supplemental 100,000 N95 masks at a secondary distribution hub (e.g., Billings or Salt Lake City) with a standing agreement for daily air or ground transport to primary shelters if ash consumption exceeds 20% of stock per day. Conduct an air-quality monitoring exercise with NOAA and USGS 30 days before the window, testing real-time forecast updates, sensor accuracy and relocation-decision protocols.

Sensitivity: Baseline model assumption: ashfall matches forecast within a 20 km margin, stock lasts 72 hours. If actual ashfall shifts 50+ km from forecast or doubles in intensity, shelter relocation is needed within 6–12 hours. Cost of relocating 10,000–15,000 evacuees (estimated USD 5–10 million in additional buses, intake processing and medical) is high, but failure to relocate results in 500–2,000 evacuees developing respiratory distress within 24 hours, with 5–10 preventable deaths. Pre-positioned backup shelters and supplemental N95 stock (estimated USD 10–15 million) avoid both costs.

Issue 4 - Egress Corridor Chokepoint Vulnerability: Gallatin Canyon and Gardiner Single-Point Failures Lack Viable Bypass and Rapid-Clearance Capacity

The plan's three egress corridors (US-191/US-20 via Gallatin Canyon, US-89 via Gardiner, US-14/16/20 via Cody) depend on narrow, two-lane mountain passes with minimal shoulders, documented rockfall and secondary-slide hazard, and no pre-surveyed bypass routes. Gallatin Canyon is especially critical: a single breakdown, rockslide, or tremor-induced slide could block the entire contraflow and strand 500–2,000 vehicles within 30 minutes. The plan lists 'pre-positioned tow and rescue assets at chokepoints' but does not specify the number of crews, equipment staging, or hard decision rules for diversion if clearance exceeds 45 minutes. The South Entrance remains landslide-blocked, eliminating a potential third southern exit that could relieve the north and west corridors.

Recommendation: Pre-position at least two mobile heavy-equipment teams (wreckers, debris chippers, spotters) at Mammoth or Spanish Creek by Month -1, with 72-hour fuel and supplies, tasked to reach any Gallatin Canyon blockage within 15 minutes of dispatch. Establish live geotechnical monitoring along Gallatin Canyon, US-89 near Gardiner and Grand Loop Road using motion sensors or drones at identified slide-prone zones, with automatic alerts to the forward command if incipient movement is detected. Conduct a geotechnical survey of the South Entrance landslide 60 days before the window; develop a time-boxed (4-hour maximum) single-lane clearance plan and a longer-term bypass-route plan, with hard abort triggers tied to seismic activity (M>4.0 renewed swarm, proposed threshold). Issue a written 'loss-of-exit' contingency: if any primary corridor becomes impassable for more than 45 minutes (proposed threshold) and cannot be restored, the forward command will trigger overflow diversion to the nearest surviving exit and issue a shelter-in-place order for vehicles still in that sector. Test the tow-team mobilization and diversion protocol during a full-scale exercise 30 days before the window.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: corridors remain passable with only routine debris clearing, or blockages are resolved within 30–45 minutes. If a major blockage occurs and persists for 2–4 hours, estimated impact is 5,000–8,000 stranded vehicles in one corridor, adding 2–4 hours to peak evacuation time and increasing the overlap with ashfall onset by 20–30%. Cost of pre-positioned tow equipment and crews (estimated USD 2–3 million) prevents a cascading 4-hour delay worth USD 50–100 million in indirect emergency response costs and 10–20 additional respiratory-distress casualties.

Issue 5 - Cross-Jurisdiction Authority Transfer and Command Gaps: NPS-to-State Handoff and FEMA Region 8/10 Seams Lack Explicit Protocols and Real-Time Coordination

The plan specifies authority transfer 'at the park boundary under written protocol,' with NPS incident commander handing responsibility to state governors at defined checkpoints. However, contraflow traffic does not stop at jurisdictional lines; drivers cross from NPS to state control mid-queue, creating a window where no single authority owns traffic-reroute or shelter-assignment decisions. Additionally, Idaho falls under FEMA Region 10 (Seattle) while Montana and Wyoming fall under Region 8 (Denver). The plan names only the Denver RRCC, leaving Region 10 mutual aid (Boise and Pocatello resources) uncoordinated and potentially delayed by 1–2 hours. Furthermore, the plan does not specify written MOUs with the three governors confirming their acceptance of NPS incident command authority or their agreement to enforce unified messaging, creating risk of conflicting evacuation orders if local pressure favors shelter-in-place.

Recommendation: Establish a dedicated Boundary Coordination Officer role, co-located at the forward command element (Bozeman or Livingston), with real-time voice and data links to the NPS incident commander and the designated state highway patrol and National Guard commanders on both sides of the boundary. Issue a written protocol specifying that the boundary officer controls traffic reroutes and initial shelter assignments during the corridor crossing, and that NPS care ends at a specific roadside checkpoint (e.g., Mammoth Checkpoint or Gallatin County line) where state custody formally begins. Pre-authorize state on-scene commanders to issue temporary reroutes without requesting park ranger approval, reducing decision latency. Add an explicit FEMA Region 10 liaison call at T+0 hours from the Denver RRCC, with pre-agreed mutual aid arrangements (e.g., Boise and Pocatello fuel, water and medical resources) documented in a signed MOU 60 days before the window. Obtain written pre-event confirmation from the governors of Montana, Wyoming and Idaho confirming their authorization of the Unified Command's evacuation orders for Zone One and any Scenario Beta expansion, and their commitment to enforce unified public messaging. Conduct a multi-state command-authority exercise 60 days before the window, testing the boundary handoff, Region 8/10 coordination and governor-to-FEMA hotline under simulated escalation scenarios.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: authority transfer occurs smoothly with no decision latency or jurisdictional conflict. If authority gaps delay reroutes or shelter assignments by 15–45 minutes (estimate), one instance cascades into a backup affecting 500–1,000 vehicles, adding 1–2 hours to peak evacuation. If FEMA Region 10 mutual aid is not pre-authorized, water and fuel convoys from Boise or Pocatello are delayed 1–2 hours, leaving shelters 12–24 hours without adequate supply. Cost of pre-event MOUs and one multi-state exercise (estimated USD 0.5–1 million) prevents a 1–2 hour evacuation delay and supply shortage worth USD 50–100 million in indirect costs.

Issue 6 - Communications Layer Fragility Under Cascading Failures: Ash-Induced Cell-Network Collapse and Tremor Damage Leave IPAWS and Bridge Systems Untested Under Actual Conditions

The plan relies on IPAWS and Wireless Emergency Alerts as the primary public channel, with National Guard signal bridging as the fallback for responder coordination at gateway towns. However, ash-induced flashovers on transmission lines, tremor damage to cell towers, and silicate-ash clogging of repeater fans could collapse the local network faster than signal units can deploy. The plan does not specify the number of Guard signal units available, their staging locations, fuel and equipment pre-positioning, or testing protocols under simulated ashfall. Additionally, printed route cards and highway advisory radio (HAR) are mentioned as fallbacks but are not pre-produced or validated for clarity and multilingual comprehension. Finally, the plan assumes 'National Guard signal bridging' restores responder radios 'at gateway towns,' but does not specify which towns, how many radio channels are needed, or how interoperability among NPS, state patrol and Guard nets is verified before the event.

Recommendation: Deploy National Guard signal corps teams with satellite phones, portable repeaters, and generator fuel to each contraflow control point and the forward command element (Bozeman/Livingston) at T-12 hours, before ashfall onset. Pre-stage printed route cards and windshield placards at all park entrance stations and lodges by Month -1, with simple instructions ('North Exit: Follow US-89 to Gardiner, then I-90 to Livingston') in English and the five most common visitor languages (Spanish, Japanese, German, Mandarin, French), including shelter addresses and contact numbers. Activate all available highway advisory radio stations and variable message signs along US-191, US-20, US-89 and I-90 with pre-recorded messages updated hourly from the forward command. Specify that Guard signal teams will establish redundant radio nets at West Yellowstone, Gardiner, Cody, Bozeman, Idaho Falls and Livingston, with formal interoperability testing 30 days before the window (on-air checks across all agencies, frequency coordination, call signs and protocol). Test satellite and portable-repeater systems in ash-simulation exercises at each control point 30 days before the window, measuring ashfall effects on radio propagation, equipment overheating and operator visibility.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: IPAWS and WEA function for the first 4–6 hours, giving drivers time to depart; Guard signal bridging restores responder coordination within 2–4 hours of deployment. If cell network fails within 1–2 hours (early ashfall or transmission-line damage) and Guard signal units are delayed in deployment, an estimated 10–20% of drivers take unintended routes, adding 1–3 hours to some transit times. Loss of responder-coordination for 30 minutes to 2 hours delays 5–10% of ambulance and hospital patient transfers. Cost of signal units, satellites, repeaters and fuel (estimated USD 5–10 million) prevents a 1–3 hour evacuation delay and routing chaos worth USD 100–200 million in indirect costs and 10–20 additional casualties.

Issue 7 - International and Non-English-Speaking Visitor Notification: Language Access and Mobility-Assistance Gaps Leave 10,000–15,000 Vulnerable Visitors Unaccounted For

The plan lists 'International Visitor, Language, and Access-Needs Notification Pathways' as a low-priority decision, stating only that concessioner and consular networks should carry instructions. However, Yellowstone hosted ~4 million visitors in 2023, with approximately 40% from outside the USA. During peak season, non-English speakers could comprise 30–40% of the 35,000 visitors in the park at any time (estimate), meaning 10,000–15,000 evacuees may not understand English-language IPAWS alerts or ranger announcements. Additionally, the plan does not specify how visitors arriving via tour buses, without personal vehicles, or with mobility aids (elderly, disabled, families with young children) will access contraflow lanes or priority evacuation shuttles. Visitors without vehicles and unclear evacuation instructions could delay departure, cluster at wrong shelters, or become stranded if buses are not pre-allocated and staffed.

Recommendation: Pre-produce IPAWS messages, radio broadcasts and digital alerts in the five most common visitor languages (Spanish, Japanese, German, Mandarin, French) by Month -1, with simple, phased messages ('Evacuate now,' 'Follow US-89 North,' 'Go to Shelter at [address]'). Coordinate with concessioner Xanterra Parks and Resorts to pre-arrange multilingual briefings for all guest rooms, tour buses and visitor centers at T-0 hours. Pre-identify 20–50 multilingual volunteers from major tour operators and position them at major lodges and campgrounds by T-0, with translation materials and communication devices. Establish a dedicated shuttle-bus evacuation plan for tour groups and lodge-based visitors by Month -1, pre-assigning 4–6 buses per major lodge (estimated 20–30 buses total) with pre-briefed drivers and attendants trained in mobility assistance. At T-12 hours, confirm lodge occupancy via concessioner manifests and create 'priority-transport' staging areas at each lodge for mobility-constrained guests, with medical supplies and attendants pre-positioned to manage acute events. Pre-authorize a secondary protocol: if any lodge cannot evacuate within 3 hours, notify the forward command, which will dispatch helicopter support (if available) or ground rescue teams from the National Guard.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: English-language alerts and visual traffic cues reach 90% of visitors; 10% (3,500 people) experience 1–2 hour delays due to language or mobility barriers. If multilingual alerts are absent and mobility assistance is not pre-arranged, this proportion could rise to 30–40% (10,000–15,000 people), adding 2–4 hours to some evacuee transit times and stranding 50–200 people. Cost of pre-produced multilingual materials, volunteer coordination and dedicated shuttle buses (estimated USD 2–3 million) prevents a 2–4 hour evacuation delay and 5–15 preventable stranding incidents.

Issue 8 - Hospital and Utility Power Grid Failure: No Explicit Fuel Pre-Positioning Timeline, Multi-Hour Generator Startup Failures, and Cascade-Failure Risk Under Simultaneous Ashfall on Multiple Substations

The plan identifies grid failure as a contingency and directs fuel priority to hospitals and communications centers, but does not specify which hospitals are critical receivers, fuel pre-positioning timeline, or how many hospitals have adequate on-site reserves. Regional hospitals typically have 24–48-hour generator fuel on hand; a simultaneous power loss across multiple substations due to ash-induced flashovers could occur within 4–8 hours of ashfall, faster than fuel convoys can deliver from distant depots (Rock Springs, WY is 200+ miles away estimate). Additionally, hospitals often have single fueling ports and outdated generators with startup failures during high-stress events; a 4-hour outage before generator fuel arrives could force cancellation of 10–20 surgeries and loss of ventilator support if manual bagging fails. Finally, the plan does not coordinate with regional power utilities (Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power, Idaho Power) to identify critical transmission lines, substations with single-point failures, or protective relay behavior under ashfall.

Recommendation: Pre-position 72-hour diesel and propane fuel reserves at the three largest receiving hospitals (Bozeman Deaconess Medical Center, Livingston HealthCare, Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center) by Month -1, confirming tank capacity and fueling-port adequacy with each facility. Establish fuel-delivery contracts with local vendors (e.g., Yellowstone Energy, Basin Fuel) requiring priority dispatch and arrival within 2 hours of a fuel request during the event. Conduct a hospital-power-failure and generator-startup exercise at each facility 30 days before the window, testing manual generator startup procedures, fuel-transfer protocols, load-shedding protocols and backup surgical equipment under simulated ashfall. Coordinate with Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power 60 days before the window to identify critical transmission lines, substations and protective relays in the evacuation and shelter zones. Request pre-deployment of mobile generator units and voltage-regulation equipment at the two largest substations serving Bozeman and Idaho Falls. Establish a 24/7 utility-operations hotline from the forward command to each regional dispatch center so the incident commander can track grid status and request emergency load shedding or localized de-energization to prevent cascading failures. Pre-authorize helicopter fuel caches at forward airfields (Gallatin County, Jackson Hole, Billings) to enable rapid delivery of fuel or emergency medical supplies to isolated hospitals if ground routes are blocked.

Sensitivity: Baseline assumption: power is lost at 1–2 hospitals within 4–6 hours of ashfall; fuel convoys arrive within 6–8 hours. If simultaneous flashovers damage multiple substations and fuel is delayed 12+ hours, an estimated 4–6 hour outage could prevent 10–20 surgeries and cause 5–10 preventable patient deaths due to ventilator support loss. Cost of pre-positioned fuel reserves and utility coordination (estimated USD 5–10 million) prevents a multi-hospital crisis worth USD 50–100 million in emergency response and patient casualties.

Review conclusion

This plan is operationally ambitious and addresses core evacuation logistics (corridors, command, communications) effectively. However, three critical gaps threaten success: (1) the pre-authorized Scenario Beta VEI-7 trigger lacks a defined secondary-stage plan, leaving 100,000–500,000 additional evacuees without destinations and risking chaotic shadow evacuation that strands Zone One visitors; (2) responder staffing for 72-hour operations is underspecified (no concrete shift limits, relief depth or separate N95 count), risking coverage gaps at traffic and perimeter checkpoints during the evacuation peak; (3) ashfall forecasts and shelter siting are static, lacking real-time monitoring and relocation protocols when actual ashfall diverges from model predictions. These three issues are tightly coupled: inadequate Scenario Beta planning drives uncontrolled shadow evacuation that saturates corridors already threatened by single-point chokepoints; responder fatigue degrades traffic control during that chaos; and incorrect shelter siting forces emergency relocations during the same peak period. Immediate actions: (1) develop and pre-authorize Scenario Beta secondary-stage destinations and messaging by Month -2; (2) define responder exposure limits, relief staffing (30–50 person standby reserve) and separate N95 counts by Month -1; (3) establish continuous ashfall monitoring at shelters and pre-authorize 4-hour relocation protocols by Month -1. These actions cost an estimated USD 30–60 million but prevent a cascading 4–8 hour evacuation delay and 20–50 preventable deaths, with benefit-cost ratio >10:1.

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Vendor collusion on bottled-water and N95 respirator supply contracts: suppliers inflate prices during the surge, or coordinate bids to exclude competitors, knowing FEMA contract vehicles bypass competitive bidding. Mitigation: pre-audit all surge-contract pricing against historical benchmarks; rotate vendors across regional hubs; require transparent cost breakdowns in invoices.
  • Diversion of pre-positioned fuel and N95 stocks at forward depots (Bozeman, Billings, Idaho Falls): staff or contractors resell critical supplies on the black market instead of routing them to hospitals and shelters, motivated by scarcity pricing during the event. Mitigation: weekly inventory audits at each depot starting T-48 hours; chain-of-custody tags on all pallets; surprise physical counts at T+6 and T+24 hours.
  • Favoritism in shelter-site selection and contract awards: forward-command staff steer shelter locations to facilities or contractors with personal or financial ties, reducing suitability and increasing cost. Mitigation: document the T+6 shelter-siting decision with NOAA/USGS wind-forecast data and PM10 sensor readings; disclose declared conflicts of interest for all siting committee members; third-party review of site selection rationale by Month 2 (2026-12-14).
  • Kickbacks or side deals in bus and ambulance dispatch contracts: contractors assign vehicles to private evacuees or commercial operations not authorized by the Unified Command, delaying public transportation and diverting fuel. Mitigation: GPS tracking and log audit of all contracted vehicles; reconcile vehicle-hours invoiced against dispatch logs; spot-check random routes to confirm actual evacuee transport.
  • Abuse of authority in perimeter and re-entry control: National Guard personnel or contractors allow unauthorized entries into the exclusion zone in exchange for bribes or favors, enabling looting or unauthorized resource extraction. Mitigation: checkpoint video surveillance; roster verification of all personnel at perimeter gates; weekly independent audits of entry logs versus authorized-access lists.
  • Misuse of FEMA contract vehicles for non-emergency purposes: personnel use pre-positioned water trucks, buses or fuel tankers for unauthorized tasks (personal transport, commercial operations) before or after the event window, reducing availability and integrity. Mitigation: pre-event equipment inventory with photos; GPS tracking active from T-0 to T+72; post-event mileage and fuel-consumption audits; certification of only-evacuation-related use.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Budget misuse in pre-event readiness spending: USD 47.5–87 million (estimate) allocated to responder reserves, N95 stocks, tow teams and MOUs is not tracked against actual deliverables; some funds are spent on lower-priority items (e.g., office supplies, training tangential to evacuation) instead of critical capabilities (e.g., backup shelter facilities, supplemental water). Mitigation: detailed line-item budget tracking; monthly burn-rate reviews from Month -2 through Month 0 (2026-10-14); earned-value audits linking spending to deliverable completion (e.g., signed MOUs, trained responders).
  • Double-spending on shelter facilities: both federal funds and state/local contributions are committed to the same shelter site (Bozeman, Idaho Falls) without coordination, creating duplicate costs or inadequate cost-sharing agreements. The plan does not clarify federal vs. state funding responsibility. Mitigation: written cost-sharing agreements by Month 1 (2026-11-14); monthly reconciliation of all facility invoices across funding sources; audit trail showing which entity paid for each service.
  • Inefficient allocation of responder hours: traffic-control rangers are deployed to low-priority checkpoint positions while backcountry sweeps and perimeter patrols remain under-staffed, consuming 100–150 ranger hours on non-critical tasks during the T+2 to T+8 peak when all hours are scarce. Mitigation: pre-event staffing plan assigning rangers to positions by priority (evacuation corridors tier 1, backcountry sweeps tier 2, perimeters tier 3); shift logs audited weekly to verify adherence.
  • Procurement delays and emergency cost overruns: surge contracts lack binding 12-hour dispatch clauses, leading to 24–48 hour (estimate) delays and forcing emergency procurement at premium pricing (estimated additional USD 10–20 million for expedited water and fuel). Mitigation: contract language audits by legal counsel 60 days before Month 0 (2026-10-14); written dispatch timelines with liquidated-damages clauses; daily burn-rate tracking against the USD 40 million contingency reserve.
  • Misallocation of communication equipment and operator hours: Guard signal teams are deployed to all 6 gateway towns (Livingston, Bozeman, West Yellowstone, Gardiner, Cody, Idaho Falls) without prioritization, consuming fuel and operator fatigue on secondary locations while primary contraflow points (Gallatin Canyon, North Entrance) lack continuous coverage. Mitigation: priority-ranking of signal-team locations by traffic volume and ashfall exposure; weekly operator fatigue audits; real-time signal-quality metrics recorded at each site.
  • Unauthorized use of pre-positioned supplies for non-evacuation purposes: N95 masks or water pre-staged at shelters are used for other medical or municipal operations before T+0, reducing the available stock for evacuees. Mitigation: seal all pre-positioned supplies at T-48 hours; custody logs with daily verification signatures; forensic inventory counts at T+0 and T+24 to detect depletion.

Audit - Procedures

  • Pre-event readiness audit (Months 1–0): quarterly reviews of all pre-positioned supplies (water, N95, fuel, tow equipment) at forward depots and receiving hospitals, including inventory counts, expiration dates, equipment functionality tests and cost reconciliation against budgets. Document deviations and corrective actions in a readiness log reviewed by the Unified Command.
  • Real-time operational audit of surge contracts and procurement (T+0 to T+72 hours): daily burn-rate tracking against the USD 200 million envelope; invoice audits confirming unit prices, quantities and delivery timelines match contract terms; spot-check 10% of supply deliveries for quality and quantity. Assign a dedicated procurement-compliance officer at the forward command.
  • Post-event contract and vendor reconciliation audit (Month 1 = 2026-11-14): audit all surge contracts within 30 days of closeout, verifying actual deliveries, pricing compliance, dispatch-time adherence and any change-order justifications; identify and recover any overbillings or unauthorized extras; publish summary findings to the Unified Command.
  • Asset tracking and custody audit (T+0 to T+72 hours and Month 1 = 2026-11-14 after-action): GPS tracking on all FEMA contract vehicles and fuel tankers; weekly vehicle-hours reconciliation against dispatch logs; mileage and fuel-consumption audits post-event to certify evacuation-only use; investigate any discrepancies >5% of expected usage.
  • Responder staffing and exposure audit (T+0 to T+72 hours): daily shift logs for all traffic-control, perimeter and backcountry-sweep personnel, recording hours worked, location, exposure conditions and relief cycles; monthly analysis comparing actual deployment to priority staffing plan; audit for compliance with 6-hour shift and 18-hour withdrawal limits.
  • Shelter capacity and relocation audit (T+6 to T+72 hours): daily census counts at Bozeman, Idaho Falls and any third/backup shelters; reconciliation of arrivals, departures and on-site population against expected inflow; if relocation is triggered, document decision drivers (PM10 readings, wind forecast), execution timeline and outcomes. Post-event review of shelter-siting effectiveness.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Unified Command common operating picture (T+0 to T+72 hours): a shared digital dashboard accessible to all primary stakeholders (NPS, states, FEMA Regions 8 and 10, Guard commands) displaying real-time status of evacuation progress (cumulative exit counts by gate and time), shelter occupancy, supply deliveries (water, fuel, N95), responder status (staffed vs. uncovered positions), and communications outages. Updated hourly and published daily to state emergency management offices.
  • Published USGS eruption-trigger matrix and escalation decision log (Month -1 and T+0 to T+72): explicit, written threshold values for USGS indicators (uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux) that trigger Scenario Beta expansion to 500 km radius; posted to the Unified Command website and distributed to media, governors' offices and Zone One communities. Document each decision to issue or withhold the 500 km order, with the date, trigger values at that moment, and the Unified Command authorized signature.
  • Post-event after-action report and audited financial summary (Month 2 = 2026-12-14): detailed summary of phase-by-phase execution, including actual vs. planned throughput, supply deliveries, responder hours and any corrective actions; full accounting of all expenditures by line item, identifying budget variances >10% with explanations; lessons learned and recommendations for future events. Distribute to FEMA, governors and the public.
  • Shelter-siting decision documentation and public notice (T+6 hours): written record of the shelter-site selection process, including the wind and plume forecasts used, PM10 sensor readings at candidate sites, and the rationale for each primary and backup choice; published to Zone One residents and evacuees upon notification of their assigned shelter.
  • Responder exposure and fatigue logs, summarized monthly (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-14 to 2026-11-14): aggregate analysis of all shift logs showing median and maximum hours worked, relief-cycle compliance rates and any exposure-limit violations; identify any personnel who worked beyond 18 consecutive hours and require post-event health screening. Publish summary compliance rate (e.g., '98% of all shifts compliant with 6-hour limit') in the after-action report.
  • Incident-specific audit reports for high-value decisions (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-14 to 2026-12-14): independent audits of the three most-critical cost and outcome drivers—shelter relocations (if any), Scenario Beta secondary-hub designation (if triggered), and hospital/utility power and supply contingencies. Each audit published with findings and recommendations accessible to the Unified Command and state officials.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Unified Command (UC) – Strategic Oversight Board

Rationale for Inclusion: A 72-hour window with 40% eruption probability (user constraint) and multi-state jurisdiction requires a single, pre-authorized strategic authority over zone expansion, escalation triggers, and inter-agency resource requests. The UC sits at FEMA Region VIII RRCC Denver and must coordinate Regions 8 and 10, three state governors, NPS, and the FAA to avoid authority gaps and command paralysis. Its primary role is authorizing the pre-written Scenario Beta VEI-7 trigger and issuing the 500 km evacuation order within 30 minutes of detection.

Responsibilities:

  • Activate the Unified Command at T+0 and authorize contraflow and initial evacuation orders
  • Monitor USGS eruption indicators and authorize Scenario Beta 500 km expansion under the pre-written trigger matrix within 30 min of threshold crossing
  • Authorize authority transfer at park boundaries and resolve any NPS-to-governor jurisdiction disputes in real time
  • Approve shelter-siting decisions at T+6 h based on NOAA/USGS plume forecast and PM10 sensor data
  • Allocate emergency resources across multi-state response and approve any critical supply-chain reroutes
  • Issue and maintain public messaging on evacuation zones, shelter assignments and escalation triggers to sustain credibility

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Seat the Unified Command with federal, state and NPS representatives at FEMA Region VIII RRCC Denver by T+0
  • Activate FEMA Region 10 liaison and confirm region-to-region communication links
  • Publish the pre-authorized USGS trigger matrix to media and Zone One communities at T+0
  • Establish a 24/7 shared common operating picture (digital dashboard) tracking evacuation progress, supply deliveries and responder status, updated hourly
  • Conduct verbal pre-authorization calls with MT, WY and ID governors confirming Zone One and Scenario Beta orders by T+6 h

Membership:

  • FEMA Region VIII Incident Commander (chair)
  • FEMA Region 10 liaison (Region 10 authority, Idaho coordination)
  • NPS Incident Commander or delegated senior NPS official
  • Montana State Emergency Manager and Governor's designee
  • Wyoming State Emergency Manager and Governor's designee
  • Idaho State Emergency Manager and Governor's designee
  • USGS lead volcanologist (ex officio, eruption monitoring and trigger authority)
  • NOAA forecast lead (ex officio, ashfall and air-quality authority)

Decision Rights: The UC authorizes all strategic decisions with multi-state or federal implications: (1) evacuation zone expansion (Zone Zero to One to Beta); (2) authority transfer and boundary handoffs; (3) shelter-siting and relocation orders; (4) resource allocation above the operational management threshold (USD 10 million per decision, proposed); (5) any messaging reversal or escalation signal to the public. Decisions requiring consensus; in the event of tie or disagreement, the FEMA Region VIII IC has final authority, with a documented dissent from the disagreeing state recorded for accountability.

Decision Mechanism: The UC meets in continuous session (at least hourly briefings) during the 72-hour window and stands up as needed thereafter. Decisions on evacuation expansion and shelter siting are made by real-time consensus on the shared common operating picture, with decision triggers defined in the pre-written matrix (USGS indicators and PM10 thresholds). Tie-breaker: FEMA Region VIII IC, with one veto override right per state governor (may be used once to block a decision; once used, majority rule prevails thereafter). All decisions documented in real time in the shared log.

Meeting Cadence: Continuous operation during the 72-hour window (Month 0 = 2026-10-14, T+0 to T+72 h); hourly formal briefings at T+0, T+2, T+6, T+12, T+24, T+36, T+48, T+60, T+72 h, plus ad hoc calls on trigger events (Scenario Beta, shelter relocation, authority disputes). Post-window: weekly calls from Month 1 (2026-11-14) through Month 3 (2027-01-14 to 2027-01-14) to finalize MOUs, plan exercises and review after-action items.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Current evacuation progress: cumulative exit counts by gate and time, zone-clearance status against T+6 and T+24 h gates
  • USGS eruption indicators and proximity to Scenario Beta trigger thresholds; ashfall forecast and PM10 readings at all shelter sites
  • Supply deliveries: water convoy status, N95 distribution, fuel inventory at hospitals and comms centers
  • Authority and jurisdictional issues: boundary handoff execution, state reroute compliance, any NPS-governor conflicts
  • Responder status: staffed vs. uncovered posts, fatigue reports, any exposure-limit breaches or relief shortfalls
  • Communications status: IPAWS/WEA delivery, Guard signal bridging coverage, any digital-network degradation

Escalation Path: The UC is the apex strategic authority for the evacuation response. Disagreements among members (states vs. federal, or state vs. state) are resolved by UC consensus; if consensus fails, the FEMA Region VIII IC decision prevails with documented dissent. Constitutional or legal challenges to the evacuation order (e.g., governor refuses to enforce a UC-issued relocation directive) are escalated to the U.S. Attorney's Office (Colorado District) and the White House Chief of Staff via the FEMA Regional Administrator. Resource allocation disputes exceeding the USD 10 million threshold or requiring supplemental declaration authority are escalated to the FEMA Deputy Administrator in Washington.

2. Forward Unified Command Element (FUCE) – Operational Management & Incident Control

Rationale for Inclusion: The Denver RRCC is 250+ km from the evacuation corridors (US-191, US-89, I-90), creating a decision latency of 2-4 hours for reroute orders and real-time resource dispatch. The FUCE co-locates the incident command team at Livingston or Bozeman, MT, within sight of the contraflow corridors and shelter sites, enabling rapid reroute directives, supply-chain troubleshooting and real-time response to corridor blockages or ashfall shifts. The FUCE operates under authority delegated by the UC and reports status hourly to the UC dashboard.

Responsibilities:

  • Execute contraflow traffic management on US-191, US-20, US-89 and I-90, authorize reroutes and diversion rules within the T+6 h clearance window
  • Dispatch tow and rockfall-clearance teams to corridor chokepoints, enforce the 45-minute blockage-diversion threshold (proposed), and manage loss-of-exit contingencies
  • Activate Guard signal teams and communications infrastructure at each control point; maintain hourly updates to the UC common operating picture
  • Monitor real-time PM10 and ashfall depth at all shelter sites; trigger shelter-relocation decisions within 4 h if exceedance is detected (proposed threshold)
  • Manage water convoy dispatch from Salt Lake City, authorize priority-lane allocation and track arrival times against the T+12 h and T+24 h targets
  • Coordinate with state highway patrol and National Guard commanders at each state boundary to enforce the authority-transfer protocol and prevent jurisdictional disputes

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the FUCE at Livingston, MT (or alternate Bozeman) by T+0, with direct communication links to the UC in Denver and to all state EOCs
  • Deploy Guard signal teams, satellite phones and repeaters to all control points and shelters by T+1 h (proposed threshold)
  • Position tow and rockfall-clearance teams at Mammoth and Spanish Creek by T+0
  • Activate real-time PM10 monitoring at the forward element and every shelter site by T+0
  • Confirm concessioner lodge manifests and bus availability for priority evacuation at each facility by T+0
  • Brief state on-scene commanders at West Yellowstone, Gardiner and Cody on authority-transfer protocols and pre-authorized reroute powers by T+0

Membership:

  • Operations Section Chief (FUCE incident commander, delegates from FEMA and NPS, chair)
  • Logistics Section Chief (water, fuel, N95 supply tracking)
  • Planning Section Chief (common operating picture, USGS indicator tracking, Scenario Beta readiness)
  • Safety Officer (responder exposure limits, N95 replacement cycles, fatigue monitoring)
  • Boundary Coordination Officer (NPS-to-state authority transfer, reroute approvals at each gate)
  • Guard Signal Officer (communications status and redundancy management)
  • NOAA/USGS liaison (real-time plume forecast and PM10 sensor updates)

Decision Rights: The FUCE makes all operational decisions within the pre-authorized rules: (1) reroute orders and traffic-control post assignments (within total of 100-150 rangers and Guard personnel, proposed); (2) tow-team dispatch and the 45-minute blockage-diversion trigger; (3) water convoy priority and reserved-lane allocation on I-15; (4) shelter-relocation orders if PM10 exceeds thresholds (proposed); (5) responder shift assignments and relief activation. Decisions below the USD 10 million threshold do not require UC approval. Any decision that conflicts with an active UC order or requires deviation from the pre-written trigger matrix must escalate to the UC within 15 minutes.

Decision Mechanism: The FUCE operates on a continuous real-time basis, making decisions as conditions change (blockages, ashfall, supply delays). Standing orders and pre-authorized thresholds guide decisions without waiting for UC approval. Example: if Gallatin Canyon blockage lasts >45 minutes, overflow is automatically diverted to US-89 without FUCE debate. If PM10 exceeds 100 ug/m3 at Bozeman shelter, a backup-site relocation analysis is triggered within 30 minutes and a relocation order (if suitability threshold is met) is issued within 4 h. Tie-breaker: Operations Section Chief, with a dissent flag to the UC if the decision creates new risk.

Meeting Cadence: Continuous operation and real-time decision-making during the 72-hour window (T+0 to T+72 h). Formal briefing calls to the UC at T+0, T+2, T+6, T+12, T+24, T+36, T+48, T+60, T+72 h. Internal FUCE section briefings every 2 hours during peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h) to synchronize logistics, planning and communications. After-action reviews during Months 1-3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Real-time evacuation status: cumulative vehicle counts at each gate, queue length and flow rate (vehicles/h), ETA for 98% clearance
  • Corridor blockage and tow status: any incidents detected, clearance time estimates, overflow-diversion decisions and their impact on other gates
  • Water and supply convoy tracking: departure time from Salt Lake City, current location, ETA at shelters, any delays or route changes
  • Ashfall and PM10 readings: real-time sensor data at each shelter, forecast updates from NOAA, any triggers for relocation analysis
  • Responder status: staffed positions, uncovered posts, fatigue and exposure-limit breaches, relief-team deployment status
  • Communications: signal-team coverage, any outages, IPAWS delivery success rate, driver feedback on message clarity

Escalation Path: Operational decisions stay within the FUCE unless they violate pre-authorized thresholds or conflict with UC orders. Any request for additional Guard personnel, change to the pre-written trigger matrix, or decision to revise public messaging escalates to the UC. Resource requests exceeding available stock (e.g., need for additional N95 from the supplemental reserve at Billings) escalate to the Unified Command Logistics Officer. Responder casualties or critical incidents escalate immediately to the UC and to the responsible state's emergency manager.

3. Escalation & Scenario Beta Decision Cell – Specialized Advisory (Volcanology & Triggering Authority)

Rationale for Inclusion: The 72-hour window carries a 40% VEI-6+ eruption probability and a pre-authorized VEI-7 trigger matrix that authorizes the UC to order a 500 km radius evacuation immediately without further deliberation. However, the scientific indicators (USGS uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux) that define the trigger must be continuously monitored and interpreted in real time, requiring dedicated expert authority separate from operational command. This cell owns the trigger-matrix refinement, indicator interpretation, and the real-time decision to declare that the threshold has been crossed. The cell's recommendation is binding on the UC unless the UC explicitly overrides it (a rare event, since the matrix is pre-authorized).

Responsibilities:

  • Refine the USGS trigger-matrix indicator thresholds (uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux, magma-depth models) by T+3 h using pre-event USGS data and the latest volcano-monitoring techniques
  • Monitor USGS real-time feeds (seismic networks, GPS, gas sensors) continuously during the 72-hour window and maintain a live status of each indicator relative to the trigger threshold
  • Issue a formal Escalation Readiness Assessment every 6 hours during the 72-hour window, stating the current distance from the Scenario Beta trigger and the estimated time to trigger if current trends continue
  • Declare the trigger crossed (or not) within 15 min of any indicator crossing the pre-written threshold, with a written statement of which indicator crossed and by how much
  • Provide technical guidance to the UC on any ambiguous or marginal trigger events (e.g., an indicator that crosses threshold but then retreats) and recommend whether to order Scenario Beta or hold status
  • Coordinate with NOAA on ashfall dispersion forecasts and provide updated wind-direction and ash-extent estimates every 6 hours to support shelter-siting and Scenario Beta planning

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Convene the Decision Cell at T+0, with USGS and NOAA leads, to review the pre-written trigger matrix and agree on final indicator thresholds by T+3 h
  • Establish real-time data feeds from USGS seismic, GPS and gas networks to the cell's monitoring station at the FUCE (Livingston or Bozeman) by T+1 h
  • Brief the UC on the refined trigger matrix and the cell's readiness to monitor at T+3 h
  • Create a visual status dashboard (displayed at the FUCE) showing current values of each indicator, the trigger threshold, and the distance from the threshold in real time
  • Prepare a written decision template and a dissent log so that any trigger-crossing declaration is documented with full traceability and any disagreement among cell members is recorded

Membership:

  • USGS Volcano Disaster Assistance Program lead (chair, eruption monitoring and indicator interpretation)
  • USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory seismologist (seismic swarm interpretation)
  • USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory modeler (magma ascent and VEI estimation)
  • NOAA Forecast lead (ashfall dispersion, wind shifts)
  • UC Liaison (FEMA or NPS representative to relay cell decisions to the UC)

Decision Rights: The cell's role is scientific interpretation and trigger declaration, not policy or resource decisions. The cell declares whether the pre-written trigger threshold has been crossed. This declaration is binding on the UC (the UC does not second-guess the scientific finding), unless the UC explicitly overrides it on policy grounds (e.g., national-security concerns). The cell does not have authority to modify the trigger matrix after T+3 h; any matrix changes must be approved by the UC. The cell's recommendation on marginal triggers is advisory; the UC makes the final call to order Scenario Beta.

Decision Mechanism: Real-time monitoring of USGS feeds and automated alerts when an indicator approaches the threshold (within 20% of the trigger value). When any indicator crosses the threshold, the cell convenes immediately (within 5 min) to verify the data and declare the crossing. If data are ambiguous or disputed among cell members, a simple majority vote determines the declaration (two out of three USGS leads vote); if still disputed, the USGS Disaster Assistance Program lead has final authority. The UC is notified within 15 min of any threshold crossing or declaration.

Meeting Cadence: Continuous real-time monitoring during the 72-hour window. Formal briefings to the UC every 6 hours (T+0, T+6, T+12, T+18, T+24, T+30, T+36, T+42, T+48, T+54, T+60, T+66, T+72). Ad hoc calls whenever an indicator crosses 80% of the trigger threshold (a warning). Post-window: joint after-action review with the UC and state emergency managers by Month 2 (2026-12-14).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Current status of each USGS indicator: uplift rate (cm/h), seismic magnitude and frequency, gas flux (SO2, CO2), and magma-depth estimates relative to the trigger thresholds
  • Ashfall forecast: NOAA 72-hour wind and plume model; projected ash concentration (ug/m3) at each shelter site and Zone One community
  • Indicator trends: are current values stable, accelerating, or retreating; estimated time to trigger if acceleration continues
  • Any data anomalies or instrument failures affecting indicator reliability; recommendations for data-quality assurance
  • Scenario Beta readiness: are the secondary hubs (Denver, Cheyenne) pre-authorized and ready; are bus fleets and rail corridors confirmed

Escalation Path: The cell's trigger declaration goes directly to the UC via the UC Liaison and the shared common operating picture. If the cell declares trigger crossing and the UC does not order Scenario Beta within 30 min, the cell has the right to escalate the non-response to the White House Situation Room via the FEMA Regional Administrator. Conversely, if the UC orders Scenario Beta without a cell trigger declaration, this is logged as a policy override and reported in the post-event after-action review.

4. Responder Health & Fatigue Management Board – Specialized Advisory (Occupational Safety & Exposure Limits)

Rationale for Inclusion: The 72-hour evacuation window requires continuous staffing of traffic-control checkpoints, perimeter gates and backcountry sweeps by rangers, highway patrol and Guard personnel exposed to ashfall, tremor hazards and heat stress. A formal board with authority to enforce exposure limits and manage relief cycles protects responders from entrapment and respiratory injury while maintaining staffing continuity. The board monitors shift logs, triggers relief rotation, and has the power to withdraw responders from ash-exposed posts if limits are breached, directly affecting traffic throughput and evacuation speed. This board is necessary to balance responder safety against the evacuation deadline.

Responsibilities:

  • Define and enforce responder exposure limits: max 6-hour shifts at ash-exposed posts, mandatory 2-hour rest with N95 replacement, full withdrawal after 18 consecutive hours (proposed thresholds); document all shift assignments and monitor compliance in real time
  • Monitor responder health status: track N95 mask inventory and replacement, manage respiratory-exposure symptoms (coughing, shortness of breath) and refer affected personnel for medical evaluation; maintain a confidential responder-health log
  • Activate relief rotation and standby reserves: when staffing at any checkpoint falls below 50% (proposed threshold) due to exposure limits or fatigue, trigger deployment of the 30–50 person out-of-region standby reserve within 4 h
