Scenario Beta Trigger Verification: USGS Eruption Indicators Cross Pre-Authorized VEI-7 Thresholds Escalation Level: Unified Command (Strategic Oversight Board) Approval Process: Escalation & Scenario Beta Decision Cell declares threshold crossing (within 15 minutes of detection); UC issues 500 km Evacuation Order within 30 minutes without further approval. Tie-breaker: FEMA Region VIII IC. Documented in UC decision log. Rationale: The pre-authorized USGS trigger matrix (uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux, magma depth) determines whether Scenario Beta escalates from 100 km to 500 km radius evacuation, affecting millions of people across four states and two FEMA regions. Crossing the threshold is a scientific determination by the Decision Cell but legally and operationally binding on the UC. Delay beyond 30 minutes risks uncontrolled shadow evacuation. Negative Consequences: Failure to escalate promptly leaves 100,000–500,000 additional evacuees without published shelter destinations or transport plans, triggering chaotic, uncontrolled flight on I-15, I-80, I-90 that saturates the Zone One evacuation corridors and strands the original 35,800 park evacuees in traffic. Estimated impact: 4–8 hour evacuation delay, 20–50 preventable respiratory or transport-related casualties.

Corridor Blockage Exceeding Rapid-Clearance Capacity: Gallatin Canyon or Gardiner Single-Point Failure Cannot Be Cleared Within 45 Minutes Escalation Level: Forward Unified Command Element (FUCE) Operations Section Chief with mandatory UC notification Approval Process: Pre-authorized loss-of-exit rule: if blockage persists >45 minutes (proposed threshold) and tow/rockfall teams cannot clear, FUCE Operations Chief triggers overflow diversion to the nearest surviving exit within 15 minutes of the decision. No UC approval required. If a second exit is simultaneously disabled (unlikely), shelter-in-place order issued for remaining queued vehicles and UC is notified immediately. Rationale: The three exit corridors are the sole throughput path for 35,800 evacuees within a T+6 hour deadline. Gallatin Canyon (US-191/US-20) is a two-lane mountain pass with no shoulder; a single blockage (breakdown, rockslide, secondary tremor-induced slide) lasting 45+ minutes exceeds the diversion capacity and forces either a shelter-in-place contingency or a 2–4 hour delay to the overall evacuation. Pre-authorized reroute thresholds enable immediate action without command deliberation. Negative Consequences: A 2–4 hour evacuation delay due to a single-corridor blockage overlaps peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8) with ashfall arrival, exposing 5,000–8,000 stranded vehicles to respiratory hazard. Uncontrolled rerouting (without FUCE coordination) could block secondary exits and cascade into gridlock. Estimated impact: 500–2,000 vehicle occupants stranded in ash; 5–15 respiratory-distress casualties if medical response is delayed.

NPS-to-State Authority Handoff Dispute: Conflicting Orders or Jurisdiction Gaps at Park Boundary During Peak Evacuation Traffic Crossing Escalation Level: Authority & Jurisdictional Coordination Cell with Boundary Coordination Officer, escalating unresolved disputes to FUCE Operations Chief, then to Unified Command Approval Process: Boundary Coordination Officer (co-located at FUCE) mediates disputes between NPS on-scene commander and state on-scene commander within 30 minutes. State commanders are pre-authorized to issue reroutes within pre-written matrix without NPS approval. If state and NPS disagree on reroute validity or shelter assignment, matter escalates to FUCE Operations Chief (1 hour decision window). If still unresolved, escalates to UC for binding decision. Documented in Authority Cell log. Rationale: Contraflow traffic crosses from NPS federal land to state highways mid-corridor, without a hard boundary where both sides can formally hand off responsibility. A dispute over shelter placement, checkpoint staffing or perimeter enforcement creates a 15–45 minute decision latency during the evacuation peak, cascading into a 500–1,000 vehicle backup. Pre-authorized reroute authority and rapid mediation limit escalation. Negative Consequences: A 15–45 minute authority gap (no agreed reroute or conflicting shelter assignment) causes 500–1,000 vehicles to queue improperly or take wrong exits. One unresolved dispute at a single checkpoint cascades into a 1–2 hour evacuation delay for downstream traffic. Additionally, Region 8/10 seams leave Idaho mutual-aid requests (Boise, Pocatello resources) uncoordinated, delaying water/fuel convoys by 1–2 hours.

Shelter Suitability Failure: Real-Time PM10 Exceeds 100 ug/m³ Threshold at Primary Shelter, Requiring Emergency Relocation of 10,000–15,000 Occupants Escalation Level: Shelter Siting & Air-Quality Assurance Panel with binding escalation to FUCE Operations Chief (shelter relocation order) and secondary escalation to Unified Command if relocation cannot be completed within 4 hours Approval Process: Panel detects PM10 >100 ug/m³ at primary shelter (hourly monitoring); convenes within 30 minutes to assess suitability; recommends backup site (ranked, 50+ km upwind). FUCE Operations Chief approves relocation and issues order within 1 hour of panel finding. Buses and intake staff are redirected to backup shelter; relocation is tracked and completion confirmed. If relocation cannot be completed within 4 hours (proposed threshold) due to transport or logistics failure, escalates to UC for contingency (e.g., split occupancy across multiple backup sites, supplemental N95 distribution). Rationale: Ashfall forecasts are uncertain by 100+ km; actual ashfall may exceed model predictions by 2–3x, rendering selected sites unsuitable within 12–24 hours of occupation. Real-time PM10 monitoring allows rapid detection and relocation before respiratory distress develops. A 10,000–15,000 person relocation requires 3–6 hours of transport and intake, consuming significant bus/driver and shelter resources during the evacuation peak. If executed without UC awareness and contingency planning, it cascades into secondary shortages. Negative Consequences: If actual ashfall is 2–3x heavier than forecast and shelters are not relocated, 500–2,000 occupants develop respiratory distress within 6–24 hours; 5–10 may die if medical care is delayed. A relocation ordered without transport readiness causes 2–4 hour delay and potential stranding of occupants mid-transit. If the only backup shelters are also inside the heavy ashfall zone, a second relocation becomes necessary, consuming additional resources and compounding delays.

Responder Exposure Limit Breached: Staffing at Traffic-Control Checkpoints Falls Below 50% Due to Fatigue or Respiratory Symptoms, Threatening Evacuation Throughput and Checkpoint Closure Escalation Level: Responder Health & Fatigue Management Board with authority to trigger standby-reserve deployment, escalating resource-shortage decisions to FUCE Operations Chief and then to Unified Command Approval Process: Board identifies any checkpoint with coverage <50% (proposed threshold) due to exposure limits (6-hour shifts, 2-hour rest) or responder withdrawal for respiratory symptoms. Board convenes within 15 minutes and authorizes activation of the 30–50 person standby reserve to deploy within 4 hours (proposed threshold). If standby reserve cannot close the gap or is already depleted, escalates to FUCE Operations Chief for checkpoint consolidation decisions (combining two posts to maintain coverage) or to UC for out-of-state Guard request. Documented in fatigue-management log. Rationale: The 72-hour continuous response requires 1.5 relief responders per position to maintain 24/7 coverage; strict exposure limits (6-hour shifts, 18-hour withdrawal) are essential to prevent entrapment and respiratory injury but reduce concurrent staffing. If coverage at any checkpoint falls below 50%, traffic-control effectiveness collapses and vehicle throughput drops by 5–10%, extending evacuation by 1–2 hours. Standby reserves and consolidated posts prevent this degradation. Negative Consequences: An uncovered traffic checkpoint allows uncontrolled vehicle movement, wrong-exit usage, and loss of real-time reroute capability. A 2–4 hour evacuation delay due to staffing gaps extends the overlap between peak traffic and ashfall onset, exposing 2,000–5,000 additional vehicle occupants to respiratory hazard. Additionally, uncontrolled perimeter breaks at evacuated towns enable looting and re-entry of unauthorized persons, creating secondary safety and security incidents.

Water Convoy or Critical Supply Delivery Delayed: Arrival at Shelters Pushed Beyond T+24 Hours (Phase 2 Gate), Threatening Shelter Operations and Forcing Supplemental-Reserve or Contingency Activation Escalation Level: FUCE Logistics Section Chief with escalation to FUCE Operations Chief (contingency activation) and Unified Command (additional Guard escort or additional convoy request) Approval Process: Logistics Chief tracks real-time GPS location of water convoys. If ETA exceeds T+24 h (Phase 2 gate deadline), Logistics Chief alerts FUCE Operations Chief within 30 minutes of the forecast delay. Contingency actions are pre-authorized: (1) advance deployment of forward-depot supplemental water (pre-staged at Bozeman, Billings, Idaho Falls at T-48 h); (2) activation of supplemental N95 reserve at Billings or Salt Lake City if ashfall is heavier than modeled and mask consumption exceeds 20% of stock per day (proposed threshold); (3) request for additional Guard escort or ground-transport priority from the UC if convoy is delayed by traffic or road damage. If convoy is delayed >12 hours beyond target, escalates to UC for supplemental federal resource request. Rationale: Water convoys from Salt Lake City are required to arrive at shelters by T+24 h to sustain 15,000 evacuees at Bozeman and 10,000 at Idaho Falls (estimate) for the next 48 hours (T+24 to T+72). Ashfall and evacuation-traffic gridlock can delay convoys from the T+12 h dispatch to arrival as late as T+30 h (estimate), forcing shelters to ration supplies or activate forward depots. Forward depots and supplemental reserves are the contingency; if both are exhausted, additional convoys or federal water mobilization is required. Negative Consequences: A 24-hour delay in water arrival (T+36 h instead of T+24 h) leaves 15,000–25,000 shelter occupants without adequate water for drinking, cooking and medical use for 12+ hours. Water shortage increases risk of dehydration, medication non-compliance and secondary health emergencies. If forward-depot supplemental reserves are also depleted (unusual but possible if initial intake was larger than planned), water shortages could affect medical care (cooling for heat-stressed patients, steam for respiratory treatment) and sanitation, risking disease outbreaks.

Monitoring Progress

1. Evacuation Progress Tracking Against Phase Gates and Time Deadlines

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Shared Common Operating Picture (COP) Digital Dashboard (updated hourly with gate counts from state checkpoints)
  • Real-time Exit Counting System (at West, North, East Entrance; integrated with COP)
  • UC Decision Log (documenting all strategic decisions and their timing)
  • Phase 1 and Phase 2 Gate Assessment Templates (98% clearance by T+6h; 95% Zone One clearance by T+24h)

Frequency: Continuous real-time monitoring; formal gate assessments at T+6h (Phase 1) and T+24h (Phase 2); hourly executive briefings to the Unified Command at T+0, T+2, T+6, T+12, T+24, T+36, T+48, T+60, T+72h

Responsible Role: Forward Unified Command Element (FUCE) Operations Section Chief, with real-time vehicle counting by state checkpoints (MT/WY/ID highway patrol, NPS rangers); reporting consolidated by FUCE Planning Chief to the UC

Adaptation Process: If cumulative exit counts at T+6h fall short of 98% (about 35,084 of 35,800), FUCE Operations Chief convenes emergency reroute review with Authority Cell and FUCE to redirect remaining vehicles and accelerate backcountry sweeps. If T+24h Zone One clearance falls short of 95%, UC issues Scenario Beta interim destination list early and activates secondary-stage contingencies. Mid-course adjustments include tow-team redeployment to persistent blockages and Guard staffing surge at under-performing corridors.

Adaptation Trigger: Gate shortfall >2% at Phase 1 (T+6h) or >5% at Phase 2 (T+24h); any single corridor throughput falling >20% below planned 660 vehicles/hour (proposed threshold); blockage persisting >45 minutes triggering diversion rule

2. USGS Eruption Indicator Monitoring and Scenario Beta Trigger Detection

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Real-time USGS seismic, GPS and gas monitoring feeds (integrated at FUCE and UC)
  • Escalation & Scenario Beta Decision Cell indicator-status dashboard (hourly updates of uplift rate, seismic magnitude, magma-depth model relative to finalized trigger thresholds)
  • USGS Eruption Indicator Log (documenting each indicator value, timestamp, and margin from trigger threshold)
  • Automated threshold-alert system (armed at T+0; alerts when indicator approaches 80% of trigger threshold and again at 100%)

Frequency: Continuous real-time monitoring from T+0 onwards; formal Escalation Readiness Assessments issued by Decision Cell every 6 hours (T+0, T+6, T+12, T+18, T+24, T+30, T+36, T+42, T+48, T+54, T+60, T+66, T+72h); warning alerts if any indicator crosses 80% of trigger threshold; trigger declaration within 15 minutes of any threshold crossing

Responsible Role: Escalation & Scenario Beta Decision Cell (led by USGS Volcano Disaster Assistance Program lead), with real-time data feeds from USGS seismic, GPS and gas networks; UC Liaison reports cell decisions to the Unified Command

Adaptation Process: If any USGS eruption indicator crosses the pre-authorized threshold (finalized by T+3h), the Decision Cell issues a Trigger Crossing Declaration within 15 minutes. The Unified Command automatically issues the Scenario Beta 500 km Evacuation Order within 30 minutes without further deliberation. Secondary-stage hubs, bus fleets and rail corridors are immediately activated. Interim messaging switches from shelter-in-place (outer ring) to evacuation orders for the 100–500 km rings. If an indicator crosses 80% of threshold (warning level), the UC pre-briefs and begins activating contingencies (Beta hub notification, secondary convoy preparation).

Adaptation Trigger: Any USGS indicator (uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux, magma-depth estimate) crosses the pre-written trigger threshold as defined in the finalized matrix by T+3h; estimated time-to-trigger calculation shows remaining window <6 hours (proposed threshold); or 80% threshold-warning triggers pre-activation of secondary contingencies

3. Real-Time Ashfall and Air-Quality Monitoring with Dynamic Shelter-Siting and Relocation Triggers

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • PM10 and ashfall-depth sensors deployed at forward element (Livingston/Bozeman) and all active shelter sites; readings updated hourly to the Shelter Siting Panel and COP dashboard
  • NOAA 72-hour ashfall and wind-direction forecast (updated every 6 hours from T+0 onwards)
  • Shelter Suitability Assessment Log (documenting PM10 readings, ashfall depth, forecast updates and any suitability threshold exceedances)
  • Backup Shelter Site Readiness Checklist (8–10 pre-surveyed candidates ranked by upwind distance; transport agreements and capacity confirmed)

Frequency: Continuous hourly PM10 monitoring at all sites from T-12h through T+72h; NOAA forecast updates every 6 hours; formal Shelter Siting Panel suitability assessments at T+6h (initial siting decision), T+24h, T+36h, T+48h, T+60h and T+72h; immediate convening if PM10 exceeds 50 ug/m³ (forecast-update trigger) or 100 ug/m³ (suitability-review trigger)

Responsible Role: Shelter Siting & Air-Quality Assurance Panel (led by NOAA ashfall/air-quality forecast lead), with real-time PM10 data collection from sensor networks and NOAA forecast updates; FUCE Operations Chief issues relocation orders based on panel recommendations

Adaptation Process: At T+6h, panel recommends final shelter sites based on latest plume forecast; FUCE Operations Chief approves and directs buses and intake staff to assigned sites. If PM10 at any primary shelter exceeds 100 ug/m³ during operations (T+24h or later), panel conducts rapid relocation analysis (within 30 minutes) and recommends an upwind backup site. FUCE Operations Chief issues relocation order within 1 hour; buses are redirected to the backup shelter and occupant transfer is completed within 4 hours (proposed threshold). If multiple shelters are threatened simultaneously or backup sites are also unsuitable, escalation to UC for split-occupancy or supplemental N95 reserve activation.

Adaptation Trigger: PM10 reading at any shelter exceeds 50 ug/m³ (triggers forecast-update review) or 100 ug/m³ (triggers suitability assessment and potential relocation); forecast wind shift of >30 degrees from current model; actual ashfall depth exceeds modeled expectation by >50% (measured visually or by sensor); NOAA forecast indicates ash concentration will exceed 200 ug/m³ at a primary shelter within 12 hours (proposed threshold)

4. Water, N95 Respirator and Generator Fuel Supply-Chain Monitoring with Convoy Tracking and Contingency Activation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Water-convoy GPS tracking and real-time location updates (from Salt Lake City dispatch through arrival at Bozeman and Idaho Falls shelters)
  • Supply Inventory Tracking Spreadsheet (N95 stock at each checkpoint and shelter, fuel inventory at receiving hospitals and comms centers, updated every 4 hours)
  • FUCE Logistics Log (documenting all supply requests, dispatch confirmations, and delivery status)
  • Forward-Depot Readiness Report (confirming pre-positioned water, N95 and fuel at Bozeman, Billings, Idaho Falls by T-48h and available for emergency deployment)
  • Contingency Activation Checklist (supplemental N95 reserve at Billings/Salt Lake City, additional fuel convoys from regional vendors)

Frequency: Continuous GPS tracking of water convoys from T+12h (dispatch) through arrival at shelters (target T+24h). Inventory spot-checks every 4 hours during peak operations (T+0 to T+36h), then every 6 hours through T+72h. Fuel status at receiving hospitals (Bozeman, Livingston, Idaho Falls) checked every 8 hours. Emergency convoy dispatch triggers immediate (within 30 minutes) FUCE Logistics notification and UC brief.

Responsible Role: FUCE Logistics Section Chief, with real-time convoy tracking via GPS and coordination with Salt Lake City suppliers; fuel pre-positioning and hospital liaison coordination with the three receiving hospitals. Responder Health & Fatigue Management Board monitors responder N95 consumption and triggers supplemental-reserve activation if usage exceeds 20% of available stock per day (proposed threshold)

Adaptation Process: If water convoy ETA exceeds T+24h (Phase 2 gate), Logistics Chief immediately alerts FUCE Operations Chief and activates forward-depot supplemental water release (pre-staged at Bozeman, Billings, Idaho Falls) within 2 hours. If ashfall is heavier than modeled and N95 consumption exceeds 20% of stock per day, supplemental reserve at Billings/Salt Lake City is activated for daily air or ground transport to shelters. If a receiving hospital reports fuel reserves below 48-hour supply, a dedicated priority fuel convoy is requested from regional vendors with 2-hour ETA guarantee. If total supply delay cascades and threatens shelter operations, escalation to UC for federal resource request (additional Guard logistics support, military airlift).

Adaptation Trigger: Water convoy ETA forecast to exceed T+24h by >2 hours; N95 consumption at any shelter or checkpoint exceeds 25% of daily stock (20% threshold plus 5% buffer); hospital fuel inventory falls below 36-hour supply; any forecast delay >6 hours from planned delivery (T+12h for water dispatch, T+24h for arrival)

5. Authority Transfer and Jurisdictional Coordination Monitoring with Boundary-Handoff Execution Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Authority-Transfer Log (maintained by Boundary Coordination Officer; hourly entries tracking vehicle and responder crossings from NPS to state control at each gate: West, North, East Entrance)
  • Reroute Authority Execution Record (documenting all reroutes issued by state on-scene commanders under pre-authorized standing orders; any disputes with NPS recorded and resolution tracked)
  • Region 8/10 Mutual-Aid Request Log (Idaho-specific resource requests to Boise and Pocatello; dispatch confirmations and arrival tracking)
  • FAA Airspace Coordination Log (aviation-grounding confirmations, medevac-exception requests and FAA responses)

Frequency: Continuous real-time authority-transfer tracking at all checkpoints from T+0 through T+24h (peak boundary crossing). Formal Authority Cell briefings to the FUCE every 6 hours (T+0, T+6, T+12, T+18, T+24h). Rapid escalation (within 30 minutes) if any reroute authority dispute arises or if a Region 8/10 mutual-aid request is delayed.

Responsible Role: Authority & Jurisdictional Coordination Cell (led by Boundary Coordination Officer at FUCE), with on-scene commanders at each park gate (NPS at West/North/East Entrances; MT/WY/ID highway patrol at corresponding corridor exits); FEMA Region 10 liaison at UC (Denver) coordinating Idaho mutual-aid requests

Adaptation Process: If a state on-scene commander and NPS incident commander dispute a reroute or shelter assignment, the Boundary Coordination Officer mediates within 30 minutes via conference call. If consensus is not reached, the matter escalates to FUCE Operations Chief (1-hour decision window); if still unresolved, escalates to UC for binding decision. Pre-authorized reroute authority allows state commanders to issue traffic control orders within pre-written limits without waiting for park approval, reducing decision latency. If Idaho mutual-aid requests (Boise, Pocatello resources) are delayed >1 hour, Region 10 liaison at UC immediately contacts FEMA Region 10 (Seattle) for expedited activation.

Adaptation Trigger: Any reroute authority dispute requiring escalation beyond the Boundary Coordination Officer; state commander reroute issued without proper notification (out-of-sequence); Region 8/10 mutual-aid request delayed >1 hour beyond submission; any vehicle or responder not properly accounted for in the authority-transfer log at a checkpoint; conflicting evacuation orders or shelter assignments from NPS and a state

6. Responder Health, Fatigue and Exposure-Limit Compliance Monitoring with Staffing-Continuity Risk Assessment

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Shift-Log Tracking System (documenting hours worked, post location, exposure conditions and N95 usage for every deployed responder at traffic checkpoints and perimeters)
  • Responder Fatigue-Risk Assessment Report (issued at T+12h, T+24h, T+36h, T+48h, T+60h, T+72h; documenting cumulative hours and identifying responders approaching or exceeding 18-hour withdrawal threshold)
  • N95 Inventory and Replacement-Cycle Tracking (stock at each checkpoint, replacement intervals as masks clog, consumption rate compared to model)
  • Standby-Reserve Readiness Confirmation (30–50 out-of-region responders pre-positioned outside the ash zone; deployment status and availability)
  • Responder-Fatigue Hotline Log (confidential reports from responders requesting relief or reporting exposure symptoms; tracked for medical evaluation and rotation decisions)

Frequency: Real-time shift-log tracking throughout the 72-hour window. Formal fatigue-risk assessments every 6 hours (concurrent with UC briefing schedule: T+6h, T+12h, T+18h, T+24h, T+30h, T+36h, T+42h, T+48h, T+54h, T+60h, T+66h, T+72h). N95 inventory spot-checks every 4 hours during peak operations (T+0 to T+36h). Emergency responder-health incidents reported immediately (within 15 minutes) to the Responder Health Board and medical officer.

Responsible Role: Responder Health & Fatigue Management Board (led by NPS Chief Ranger), with shift-log data collection from all deployed responders and state/Guard commanders; medical officer from the nearest receiving hospital evaluates any responders with respiratory symptoms or heat stress

Adaptation Process: If any checkpoint's staffing falls below 50% of required positions due to exposure-limit rotations or responder withdrawal, the Responder Health Board immediately (within 15 minutes) authorizes activation of the standby reserve for deployment within 4 hours. If responders show acute respiratory distress or heat-related symptoms, they are immediately withdrawn from ash-exposed duty and referred to medical evaluation at the nearest hospital. If N95 consumption exceeds modeled expectations (clogging faster than forecast), supplemental responder N95 reserves are activated for distribution. If cumulative responder fatigue is assessed as critical (multiple personnel approaching 18-hour limits simultaneously), the board recommends to FUCE Operations Chief that lower-priority checkpoints be consolidated or temporarily closed to preserve relief depth at critical posts.

Adaptation Trigger: Any checkpoint staffing falling below 50% coverage due to exposure limits or responder withdrawal; any responder exceeding the 18-hour withdrawal threshold without rotation; two or more responders at the same post reporting acute respiratory symptoms within 2 hours (proposed threshold); N95 consumption rate >20% of stock per day (proposed threshold); cumulative responder fatigue assessed as 'critical' at more than 10% of deployed responders by formal fatigue-risk assessment

7. Communications System Resilience and Message-Delivery Effectiveness Monitoring Under Ashfall and Network Degradation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • IPAWS/WEA Broadcast Confirmation Log (timestamp, language versions, carrier delivery confirmation, estimated population reached)
  • Guard Signal-Team Deployment and Coverage Map (real-time location of signal units at control points and shelters; radio-network interoperability test results; any coverage gaps or outage events)
  • Highway Advisory Radio (HAR) and Variable Message Sign (VMS) Message Log (pre-recorded messages deployed on US-191, US-20, US-89, I-90; hourly updates from forward command; any message failures recorded)
  • Printed Route Card Distribution Tracker (distribution of English and five-language cards at park entrances, lodges and visitor centers; hand-out counts during evacuation)
  • Communications Outage and Restoration Log (any detected IPAWS failures, cell-tower outages, radio interference or ash-induced equipment failures; time-to-restoration tracked)

Frequency: Continuous communication-system monitoring from T-12h through T+72h. IPAWS/WEA broadcast confirmations logged within 30 minutes of each alert. Signal-team coverage status checked every 2 hours during peak operations (T+0 to T+36h), then every 4 hours through T+72h. HAR/VMS message updates issued hourly from forward command during evacuation (T+0 to T+24h). Any outage detected immediately (within 5 minutes) triggers escalation and restoration effort.

Responsible Role: Guard Signal Officer (FUCE comms section) coordinates signal-team deployment and radio-network operations; IPAWS administrator (FEMA or NPS communications) confirms broadcast delivery and documents message content; forward-command public affairs officer oversees HAR/VMS updates and route-card distribution tracking

Adaptation Process: If IPAWS or WEA broadcasts fail or reach <80% of target population (proposed threshold), Guard signal bridging and HAR broadcasts immediately increase messaging frequency and add satellite-phone alerts to state emergency operations centers. If a Guard signal-team's radio repeater fails due to ash clogging or power loss, the backup portable unit is immediately deployed (within 1 hour) and the outage is logged. If cell-tower failure degrades IPAWS delivery, printed route cards and HAR become the primary public channel; multilingual volunteers are activated at lodges to hand-deliver route instructions to non-English speakers. If communication restoration exceeds 2 hours at any critical post (traffic control or shelter), escalation to FUCE Operations Chief for tactical rerouting (redirecting traffic to maintain flow despite comms outage).

Adaptation Trigger: Any IPAWS/WEA broadcast fails or is delayed >15 minutes; estimated population reached by IPAWS <80% of target (proposed threshold); any Guard signal-team loses radio coverage at a checkpoint or shelter; cell-network outage lasting >30 minutes at any critical location; HAR or VMS message failing to display correctly or updating with delay >1 hour from forward command; printed route cards exhausted at any park entrance or lodge

8. Scenario Beta Interim Hub Readiness and Secondary-Stage Evacuation-Plan Execution Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Interim Scenario Beta Hub List (ranked list of 5–10 hubs outside the 500 km ring: Denver, Cheyenne, etc.; capacity estimates, host-community contact confirmations)
  • Secondary-Stage Bus-Fleet and Rail-Corridor Readiness Confirmation (operators and carriers pre-contracted; standing activation clauses; vehicle count and availability confirmed)
  • Scenario Beta Second-Stage Evacuation Plan Document (written plan by Month 1 = 2026-11-14; detailing tiered execution rings, hub assignments, transport routing)
  • Host-Community MOU Signature Tracking (signed agreements with secondary hubs by Month 2 = 2026-12-14; mutual-aid commitments documented)
  • Scenario Beta Response-Cell Activation Log (upon UC issuance of Scenario Beta order, expanded cell convenes and documents ring-by-ring evacuation orders, hub-destination assignments, and contingency activations)

Frequency: Interim hub list issued by T+12h (Month 0 = 2026-10-14). Written secondary-stage plan completed by Month 1 (2026-11-14). MOU signatures targeted by Month 2 (2026-12-14). If Scenario Beta triggers during the 72-hour window, the expanded Response Cell holds continuous briefings (every 2 hours) documenting ring-by-ring execution and hub-occupancy status. Post-event: full-scale Scenario Beta exercise (Exercise-2 'Ring Dispersal') conducted in Month 2.5 (2026-12-29).

Responsible Role: FUCE Planning Chief develops interim hub list and secondary-stage plan (working with state emergency managers and FEMA Region coordinators); UC chair or designee negotiates and signs host MOUs; Scenario Beta Response Cell (expanded UC) executes ring-by-ring evacuation upon trigger; secondary hub emergency managers confirm receipt of evacuees and completion of intake and registration

Adaptation Process: If Scenario Beta trigger is detected at any point during the 72-hour window, the UC issues the 500 km Evacuation Order within 30 minutes. The expanded Scenario Beta Response Cell immediately activates: ring-by-ring evacuation orders are issued (0–100 km organized, 100–250 km time-banded, 250–500 km staged); buses and rail are dispatched from Bozeman and Idaho Falls primary shelters to secondary hubs; populations are assigned to specific hubs based on location and hub capacity. If a secondary hub is unable to receive assigned evacuees (e.g., due to local capacity constraints), the Response Cell reassigns the population to an alternate hub within 1 hour. If bus fleets or rail corridors are delayed, additional Guard logistics support is requested.

Adaptation Trigger: Interim hub list not issued by T+12h (escalates to UC for expedited planning or alternative contingency); written secondary-stage plan not completed by Month 1 (2026-11-14); any host-community MOU not signed by Month 2 (2026-12-14) (signals governance gap and extends Scenario Beta readiness risk); upon Scenario Beta trigger, any secondary hub reports inability to receive assigned population within 2 hours of the evacuation order; bus-fleet or rail-corridor dispatch delayed >2 hours from the evacuation order

9. Multi-State Governance Formalization and Post-Event Hardening Monitoring (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • MOU Signature Tracker (dates and status of signed agreements with MT, WY, ID governors; FEMA Region 10; regional utilities; Scenario Beta secondary hubs)
  • After-Action Report Development Schedule (AAR-1 at Month 1 = 2026-11-14; AAR-2 at Month 2 = 2026-12-14; AAR-3 at Month 3 = 2027-01-14; drafts tracked through review and distribution)
  • Full-Scale Exercise Calendar (Exercise-1 'Cascade Boundary' Month 2 = 2026-12-14; Exercise-2 'Ring Dispersal' Month 2.5 = 2026-12-29; Exercise-3 'Integrated Response' Month 3 = 2027-01-14; plus six smaller operational exercises)
  • UC Weekly Coordination Call Schedule (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14; attendance and agenda topics documented)
  • Governance Improvements Tracking (recommendations from 72-hour response and exercises; implementation status and completion dates)

Frequency: Weekly UC coordination calls during Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14). MOU signature targets: Month 1 (2026-11-14) for governors and Region 10; Month 2 (2026-12-14) for utilities and secondary hubs. AAR publication schedule: AAR-1 by end of Month 1 (2026-11-14); AAR-2 by end of Month 2 (2026-12-14); AAR-3 (comprehensive) by end of Month 3 (2027-01-14). Full-scale exercises scheduled in Weeks 1, 3 and 4 of Months 2, 2.5 and 3 (2026-12-14, 2026-12-29, 2027-01-14).

Responsible Role: FEMA Region VIII IC (UC chair) or designee coordinates MOU negotiations and signature scheduling; FEMA and NPS designate AAR working groups and publication leads; FUCE Operations Chief serves as exercise director for all three full-scale exercises; Hardening & Post-Event Review steering committee (established at Month 1 = 2026-11-14 Week 1) oversees improvements and exercise planning

Adaptation Process: If any MOU signature target is missed (Month 1 or 2 = 2026-11-14 or 2026-12-14), UC escalates to state governors, FEMA Region 10 or utility leadership for expedited signing; any persistent gap beyond 2 weeks flags a governance risk that is documented in AAR for future planning. If AAR development is delayed, interim field-observer summaries are published to maintain transparency; final reports are published even if late, with explanation of delays. If a full-scale exercise reveals critical governance gaps (e.g., Authority Cell unable to mediate boundary disputes, Scenario Beta hub unable to receive populations), the UC convenes an emergency remediation meeting and adjusts governance protocols before the next exercise. All improvements identified are tracked in the Governance Improvements Log with completion target dates (typically within 30 days of identification).

Adaptation Trigger: Any MOU not signed by 2 weeks past target deadline (Month 1 = 2026-11-14 Week 2 for governors/Region 10; Month 2 = 2026-12-14 Week 2 for utilities/hubs); AAR publication delayed >2 weeks past target; any full-scale exercise revealing a 'critical' governance gap (inability to execute a core function); any UC weekly call attendance falling below 50% of required members (signals disengagement); post-event recommendations not assigned to a responsible party within 10 days of identification

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness Confirmation: All six core governance components are generated and present: (1) internal governance bodies (4 standing bodies + 5 specialized advisory cells) established; (2) implementation plan with 24 sequential steps from pre-event through Month 3 (2027-01-14) hardening; (3) decision-escalation matrix with explicit approval processes and tie-breakers for 5 critical decisions; (4) monitoring-progress plan with 6 continuous monitoring approaches and adaptation triggers; (5) audit framework and transparency measures defined in Phase 1 context; (6) project sponsor authority and legal basis (FEMA RA and NPS Director joint decision memo). No major component is missing.
  2. Internal Consistency Check: The four-body standing governance (UC at Denver, FUCE at Livingston, Responder Health Board, Authority Cell) nests correctly into the implementation plan's T+0 activation sequence (Steps 8–12 establish each body in order). Decision escalation aligns with body authority: UC issues strategic orders (Scenario Beta, zone expansion), FUCE executes operational reroutes within pre-authorized thresholds, advisory bodies (Escalation, Shelter, Authority) provide binding or advisory recommendations to appropriate levels. The monitoring-progress plan's adaptation triggers feed back into decision escalation (e.g., PM10 >100 ug/m³ escalates from Shelter Panel to FUCE Operations Chief to UC within defined timelines). Cadence alignment is consistent: UC hourly briefings at T+0, T+2, T+6, T+12, T+24, T+36, T+48, T+60, T+72 match the Phase 1 and Phase 2 gate assessments at T+6 and T+24. No logical conflicts detected between body authorities or decision timelines.
  3. Clarity of Roles and Conflict-of-Interest Gaps: Responsibilities of the six standing bodies and five advisory cells are clearly defined in Phase 2. However, one significant role ambiguity exists: the Project Sponsor (FEMA Regional Administrator and NPS Director) roles are mentioned in the implementation plan (Steps 1–2) as issuing the foundational decision memo, but their ongoing authority, veto rights, or escalation role during the 72-hour window is not explicitly stated. Are they voting members of the UC, or do they only set pre-event policy? Additionally, the Boundary Coordination Officer role is critical but under-staffed: the documents specify one BCO at the forward element coordinating three state on-scene commanders and the NPS IC, with potential for three simultaneous boundary disputes (West, North, East gates) that one officer cannot mediate within 30 minutes (proposed threshold). Recommendation: explicitly define Project Sponsor escalation authority (e.g., constitutional/legal challenges to evacuation orders); clarify whether BCO should be supported by two deputies (one per state region) or whether a standing three-way conference line protocol allows parallel mediation.
  4. Process Depth and Operational Clarity Gaps: (a) Conflict-of-interest and corruption prevention: Phase 1 audit details identify 6 corruption risks and 13 audit procedures, but the governance bodies (especially UC and FUCE) have no explicit conflict-of-interest disclosure requirement or recusal protocol. Recommendation: require all UC and FUCE members to disclose financial interests in shelter vendors, water/N95 suppliers, or secondary-hub communities at T+0 and to recuse themselves from decisions affecting those vendors. (b) Whistleblower and incident-report protocols: the monitoring-progress plan references fatigue hotlines and responder-health logs but does not define a formal whistleblower or ethics hotline for reporting abuse, vendor fraud, or governance failures during the 72-hour window. Recommendation: establish a confidential hotline (staffed 24/7 during the response) for reporting responder exposure violations, supply-diversion, unauthorized entries or other compliance breaches; results escalate to a designated compliance officer outside the incident command chain. (c) Threshold clarity: the decision-escalation matrix and monitoring plan reference numerous quantitative thresholds (45-minute blockage trigger, 50/100 ug/m³ PM10 triggers, 20% N95 consumption rate, <50% checkpoint staffing) but several thresholds lack justification or sensitivity analysis. Recommendation: document the derivation of each threshold (e.g., 45 minutes = time to attempt tow clearance + time to divert overflow without saturation) and conduct pre-event sensitivity analysis (what happens if the threshold is ±20%?) to ensure thresholds are operationally defensible under stress.
  5. Specific Gaps Requiring Further Detail: (a) Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Plan Maturity: The implementation plan (Steps 31–32) references an interim ranked hub list issued by T+12 hours and a written secondary-stage plan completed by Month 1 (2026-11-14), but no details exist on how a 5–10 hub list is generated, evaluated or prioritized during the T+0 to T+12 timeframe. The plan names Denver and Cheyenne as Beta hubs but does not verify their distance from the 500 km radius or their shelter/transportation/supply capacity. Recommendation: pre-develop a detailed Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan (before Month 0 = 2026-10-14) listing 8–12 candidate hubs outside the 500 km ring (with verified distance, shelter capacity, bus-fleet access, and host-community preliminary agreement); publish this plan to the UC, states and media at T+0 so the T+12 interim list is merely a formal endorsement, not a crash generation. (b) Responder N95 and Staffing Depth Specification: The governance documents assume 100–150 NPS rangers (estimate) and a 1.5 relief ratio, yielding approximately 67–100 concurrent traffic-control positions. However, no detailed staffing plan exists mapping specific rangers and Guard units to each of the 5–10 traffic-control checkpoints, nor is there a pre-calculated responder N95 requirement (separate from the 100,000 civilian stock) documented. Recommendation: before Month 0 (2026-10-14), pre-identify each assigned ranger and state patrol officer by name and post; calculate responder N95 requirement (estimated 2–3 masks per person per shift; 100–150 responders × 12–18 hours average shift ÷ 6-hour work limit = ~200–250 masks per day × 3 days = 600–750 total responder masks minimum); confirm separate pre-staging of this stock outside the civilian 100,000 allotment. (c) Ashfall Forecasting and Shelter Backup Site Adequacy: The plan specifies ranked backup shelter sites 50+ km upwind (proposed threshold) of each primary site, but does not verify that 8–10 suitable backup sites exist with adequate capacity, HVAC, registration infrastructure and accessibility to buses. Recommendation: conduct a pre-event survey (by Month -1, before October 2026) of all candidate backup sites in Montana, Wyoming and Idaho (schools, arenas, fairgrounds with 500+ capacity) and rank them by distance/direction from each primary shelter; document HVAC specifications, generator/fuel access and bus-arrival infrastructure; confirm owners/operators are briefed and pre-authorize emergency occupancy. (d) Water and Fuel Convoy Logistics Detail: The plan targets water dispatch from Salt Lake City by T+12 h and arrival by T+24 h (or use forward depots as fallback), but does not specify the number of trucks, loading logistics at Salt Lake City, route selection (I-15 northbound only, or alternates via US-89 or US-191?), fuel for the convoy itself, or communication protocols if the convoy encounters ashfall and must divert. Recommendation: execute pre-event detailed water-logistics operations plan (before Month 0 = 2026-10-14): identify 2–3 water-supplier sites in Salt Lake City with bulk-truck loading capacity; confirm 20–30 water trucks (holding ~50,000 liters each) can be assembled and fueled within 12 hours; map primary and alternate routes (I-15, US-89/US-191) with fuel stops; establish convoy-escort communication protocol (National Guard liaison in the lead and trail vehicles, satellite phone link to forward command).
  6. Integration and Decision-Flow Alignment Gaps: (a) Real-Time COP Dashboard Specification: The implementation plan repeatedly references a 'shared common operating picture' digital dashboard that is 'updated hourly' and displayed at the UC and FUCE, but no specification exists for what data fields must be displayed, data-update frequency for each field, or system reliability/backup (what happens if the COP server crashes?). Recommendation: develop a detailed COP Data Dictionary (by Month -1) specifying: cumulative exit counts (by gate and time), queue lengths (at each checkpoint), ashfall PM10 (at each shelter, updated hourly), water/fuel/N95 inventory (at each shelter, updated every 4 hours), responder staffing (by post, updated every 2 hours), USGS eruption indicators (updated hourly with margin-to-trigger visualization), communication outages (real-time log), any active reroutes or shelter relocations (current status). Implement redundant data feeds (primary database + satellite backup; manual entry fallback if network fails). (b) Authority Transfer Checkpoint Definition: The implementation plan states NPS authority transfers 'at the park boundary' (West, North, East Entrances), but does not define the exact roadside location (e.g., mile marker X on US-89 north of Gardiner vs. the ranger station vs. the county line). Recommendation: before Month 0 (2026-10-14), conduct field surveys with MT, WY and ID highway patrols to identify a specific transferpoint at each of the three exit corridors (with GPS coordinates, landmark description and signage location); document the exact point in the written Authority Transfer Protocol so state and NPS on-scene commanders both understand where NPS care ends and state custody begins. (c) Escalation Path Endpoints Ambiguity: The decision-escalation matrix specifies that 'constitutional or legal challenges to evacuation orders' escalate to 'the U.S. Attorney's Office (Colorado District) and White House Chief of Staff,' but does not identify who makes the call to White House (FEMA Regional Administrator? UC Chair?), what the expected response time is, or who has authority to override the UC's order if legal counsel says it is unconstitutional. Recommendation: clarify the escalation chain: UC Chair notifies FEMA Regional Administrator of any legal challenge; Regional Administrator consults FEMA Office of General Counsel and White House Legal Counsel (via Situation Room); White House National Security Advisor or Chief of Staff makes final authority determination and notifies the FEMA Administrator (not the UC directly) to issue revised orders or stand down.

Tough Questions

  1. What is the current scientific confidence interval (±km) for the modeled ashfall footprint under a VEI-6 eruption scenario at Yellowstone, given the lack of direct observational data on historic Yellowstone ashfall composition and settling rates? If the actual ashfall extent exceeds the modeled 100 km radius by 20–50 km, will the three pre-staged backup shelter sites remain outside the ashfall zone, or will all primary and backup shelters be threatened simultaneously, forcing a third-stage relocation without known destinations?
  2. Have the 100–150 NPS rangers and state patrol officers assigned to traffic-control checkpoints been explicitly identified by name and post, and does a pre-event dry-run or tabletop exercise confirm that each officer understands his or her assigned checkpoint, shift length (6 hours, proposed threshold), relief rotation protocol and the 18-hour withdrawal trigger (proposed threshold)? If not, how will responder confusion or failure to understand exposure limits during the T+0 activation cascade be prevented?
  3. What is the pre-authorized response time and decision process if the Boundary Coordination Officer at Livingston receives simultaneous reroute-authority disputes from the MT, WY and ID state on-scene commanders at T+3 hours (peak evacuation), and the three disputes cannot be mediated within the 30-minute window (proposed threshold)? Does the BCO have authority to unilaterally decide all three, or does escalation to the FUCE Operations Chief introduce a 1–2 hour delay that compounds the blockage-diversion decision latency?
  4. If Scenario Beta is triggered at T+36 hours (halfway through the 72-hour window) and the UC issues a 500 km evacuation order, how many additional evacuees are estimated to be in that expanded ring (100–250 km time-banded, 250–500 km staged)? Have the 5–10 secondary hub communities (Denver, Cheyenne, etc.) provided pre-signed capacity commitments and committed bus-fleet and medical resources, or is their participation still contingent on Month 1 (2026-11-14) MOU negotiation? If commitments are contingent, what is the fallback if a secondary hub refuses to accept evacuees?
  5. The plan pre-stages 100,000 N95 respirators (user constraint) for civilians and assumes separate responder N95 stocks, but has the actual responder N95 requirement been calculated by role (100–150 rangers × 3 masks/person/shift × how many shifts each works) and confirmed to be available and pre-positioned at T-48 hours? If responder mask consumption exceeds expectations due to heavier ashfall (masks clog faster), what is the resupply protocol, and where is the supplemental responder N95 reserve staged?
  6. The Authority & Jurisdictional Coordination Cell resolves NPS-to-state disputes at the park boundary, but if a state emergency manager or governor refuses to enforce a UC-issued evacuation order or issues a conflicting shelter-in-place instruction, what is the enforcement mechanism? Does the UC have authority to federalize the state National Guard under Stafford Act emergency declaration, and has that authority been pre-coordinated with the three governors and documented in the signed MOUs (due Month 1 = 2026-11-14)?
  7. Has a full-scale integrated-response exercise (Exercise-3, scheduled Month 3 = 2027-01-14) actually been completed and published as post-event proof that the governance structure functions under realistic 72-hour-compression conditions, or is this exercise still planned and contingent on pre-event preparation and funding? If the exercise has not been completed by the time the eruption probability window activates (Month 0 = 2026-10-14), the governance structure remains untested and operationally at risk.

Summary

The governance framework establishes a pre-authorized, time-compressed multi-state evacuation response centered on a Unified Command at FEMA Region VIII RRCC Denver with a forward operational element at Livingston, MT. Five specialized advisory bodies (Escalation Cell, Forward Element, Responder Health Board, Authority Cell, and Shelter Siting Panel) execute real-time decisions on contraflow traffic, eruption escalation, ashfall monitoring, and supply logistics within concrete trigger matrices and decision thresholds. The implementation plan sequences governance activation from T+0 through T+72 hours of continuous operations, transitioning to hardening and post-event review during Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14). Core strengths include explicit pre-authorized decision rules, rapid escalation protocols, and real-time monitoring dashboards that reduce command latency. Three critical unresolved gaps—the absence of a detailed Scenario Beta secondary-stage shelter and logistics plan, undefined responder staffing reserves and N95 protection counts, and static (rather than adaptive) ashfall shelter siting—create cascading failure risks if triggered during the 72-hour window. The governance structure is execution-credible for the 35,800 Zone Zero evacuation but depends heavily on pre-event hardening during Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) to close Scenario Beta and supply-chain readiness gaps before the eruption probability window activates.

Suggestion 1 - Hurricane Rita Evacuation, Houston-Galveston (2005)

One of the largest US evacuations: an estimated 2-3 million people left the Houston area ahead of Hurricane Rita in September 2005 (approximate, not verified). Texas used contraflow on I-45, US-290 and I-10 after severe gridlock and fuel shortages. The event produced widely cited lessons on contraflow staging, fuel and shadow evacuation.

Success Metrics

Contraflow implemented on several freeways; reported throughput gains after activation (figures approximate) Post-event reforms: Texas contraflow plans, evacuation zone and phased departure rules Documented deaths during evacuation (heat, bus fire) used as lessons

Risks and Challenges Faced

Shadow evacuation overloaded roads: later plans used zone-based, time-phased departures Fuel shortages along routes: fuel supply pre-arrangements and stations on evacuation routes Slow contraflow activation: termination points and staffing were pre-planned afterward Special-needs evacuees: dedicated transport and registry created

Where to Find More Information

Texas Department of Transportation evacuation and contraflow guidance (txdot.gov) Texas A&M Transportation Institute post-Rita evacuation studies FHWA Contraflow Operations / Evacuation Planning guidance (ops.fhwa.dot.gov) Texas Governor's Task Force on Evacuation, Transportation and Logistics report (2006)

Actionable Steps

Contact TxDOT Traffic Operations Division for contraflow plan owners Approach Texas A&M Transportation Institute researchers on evacuation modelling Request FHWA Office of Operations emergency transportation operations staff for guidance Consult Texas Division of Emergency Management for zone-based phasing lessons

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest US example of contraflow on major corridors, shadow evacuation saturating roads, fuel shortages and the need for pre-planned termini. These map directly to Gallatin Canyon/US-89 contraflow and the Scenario Beta ring design. Geographically distant and flat-terrain; mountain two-lane constraints must be added.

Suggestion 2 - Camp Fire Evacuation of Paradise, California (2018)

The November 2018 Camp Fire forced a rapid evacuation of Paradise (about 26,000 residents, approximate) via a handful of mountain roads. Contraflow on Skyway and other roads was improvised, roads gridlocked and fire overran some vehicles. Post-event reviews by NIST, Butte County and Cal OES examined alerting, routes and command.

Success Metrics

Most residents escaped despite gridlock; 85 fatalities (approximate, not verified) Post-event: Butte County adopted Genasys zone-based evacuation and alert reforms Findings: alert reach gaps, roadway blockages, contraflow timing

Risks and Challenges Faced

Alerting gaps (WEA/Code Red limited): later layered alerts and zone codes Improvised contraflow delayed: pre-planned contraflow and staffed control points recommended Power and cell failure: redundant comms and sirens Road blockage by abandoned vehicles: tow/clearance pre-positioning

Where to Find More Information

NIST Technical Note 2252 on Camp Fire (nist.gov) California Attorney General Camp Fire after-action review Butte County Sheriff / OES after-action reports Cal Fire and CHP evacuation reports

Actionable Steps

Contact Butte County Office of Emergency Management for after-action authors Approach NIST Fire Research Division staff for the Camp Fire study team Request CHP Office of Emergency Services briefing on contraflow and tow staging Reach Cal OES alerting unit for WEA/IPAWS lessons

Rationale for Suggestion

Western US mountain community with few exit roads and a hazard faster than the plan; reveals how alert failures, blocked chokepoints and improvised contraflow behave. Directly informs Gardiner/West Yellowstone/Gallatin Canyon risks, tow-team staging and alerting under failing cell networks.

Suggestion 3 - Mount St. Helens 1980 Eruption Response and USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory Hazard Planning

The May 18, 1980 eruption produced widespread ashfall across Washington, Idaho and Montana, closing roads, airports and water systems for days, with about 57 deaths (approximate). Spokane, Yakima and Montana towns coped with ash cleanup, respirator distribution and water issues. The USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory and Washington Emergency Management have since built ash and lahar hazard plans.

Success Metrics

Ash fell over several states; airports and roads closed for days, reopened after cleanup Public respirator distribution and cleanup logistics documented Informed ash-fall hazard maps and ash impact guidance

Risks and Challenges Faced

Ash-clogged vehicles and roads: closure and cleanup guidance developed Water and sewer treatment overload: operational advice for utilities Respiratory protection scarcity: later pre-stocking guidance Prolonged cleanup disposal: designated disposal sites

Where to Find More Information

USGS Volcano Hazards Program ashfall impact pages (usgs.gov/volcanoes) USGS Professional Paper 1250: The 1980 Eruptions of Mount St. Helens Washington Military Department Emergency Management Division volcano planning Volcanic Ash Impacts and Mitigation (volcanoes.usgs.gov/volcanic_ash)

Actionable Steps

Contact USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory (Vancouver, WA) for ash impact specialists Approach USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory scientist-in-charge on trigger matrix Reach Washington EMD for volcano plan owners Consult Spokane and Yakima county emergency managers for 1980 cleanup lessons

Rationale for Suggestion

Only North American precedent for large ashfall over the same Montana/Idaho region and multi-state response. Provides evidence on ash on roads, N95/respirator needs, water systems, power and aviation closures. Eruption was far smaller than VEI-6, so quantities must be scaled up.

Suggestion 4 - Eyjafjallajökull Eruption Airspace Closure and Ash Management (Europe, 2010) - SECONDARY

The April 2010 eruption closed much of European airspace for about a week, grounding over 100,000 flights (approximate). Regulators then introduced ash-concentration thresholds and zones, letting flights resume under tiered limits.

Success Metrics

Airspace reopened under tiered ash-concentration limits within days (approximate) EASA/ICAO ash contingency frameworks adopted

Risks and Challenges Faced

Blanket closure cost: replaced by concentration-based zones Uncertain ash forecasts: improved VAAC modelling and sampling

Where to Find More Information

ICAO International Airways Volcano Watch documentation EASA volcanic ash guidance Met Office London VAAC publications

Actionable Steps

Contact Met Office London VAAC and Anchorage/Washington VAAC (NOAA) for ash model procedures Approach FAA Air Traffic Organization Northwest Mountain Region for exception protocol

Rationale for Suggestion

Secondary suggestion. Informs ZLC/ZSE grounding and the narrow medevac/survey exception framework. Geographically distant and an aviation-only case; no ground evacuation lessons.

Summary

Reference projects for a Yellowstone Zone Zero/Zone One evacuation under Scenario Alpha and Beta. No Yellowstone eruption precedent exists, so the picks cover the four hardest elements: mass evacuation with contraflow (Hurricane Rita), multi-day mountain-corridor evacuation under hazard (Camp Fire/Paradise), volcanic ashfall response and ash-safe aviation (Mount St. Helens 1980, Eyjafjallajökull 2010), and pre-planned volcanic evacuation (Cascades/Rainier lahar planning). Figures below are approximate and not verified; contact the named organizations for authoritative data. Geographic proximity is strongest for Mount St. Helens (Pacific Northwest, same FEMA Region 10 seam) and Camp Fire (US western mountain roads). Rita is geographically distant but is the main US contraflow reference. Eyjafjallajökull is secondary and covers airspace closure.

1. Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan and Hub Capacity Validation

The plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta VEI-7 trigger ordering immediate 500 km evacuation affecting millions, but no second-stage destinations, hub capacity or tiered messaging exist. Without this data, issuing the trigger order will cause uncontrolled shadow evacuation saturating I-15, I-80 and I-90, adding 4–8 hours delay to the primary Zone Zero evacuation and stranding 5,000–20,000 people in ashfall zones. This is the single largest residual cascade-failure risk.

Data to Collect

  • Named ranked shelter hubs (5–10) outside the 500 km ring with verified distances from Yellowstone center
  • Shelter capacity (beds, kitchen throughput, medical-staff availability) for 100,000–500,000 additional evacuees per hub
  • Signed host-community MOUs confirming bed and medical-staff commitments for 48-hour deployment notice
  • Pre-positioned supply estimates (water, N95, food, fuel, medical) at each hub and pre-staging schedule
  • Tiered ring-based public messaging (0–100 km organized, 100–250 km time-banded, 250–500 km staged) and published assignment logic

Simulation Steps

  • Use ArcGIS or Google Earth to measure distances from Yellowstone to Denver, Cheyenne, Albuquerque, Las Vegas, Billings, Salt Lake City; confirm which lie outside the 500 km circle
  • Contact each hub's emergency management director and large shelter facilities (convention centers, school districts, universities) to request current capacity estimates; cross-reference with FEMA Region VIII and FEMA Region X databases
  • Model multi-state evacuation routing using CORSIM or SimTraffic; simulate I-15, I-80, I-90 traffic under 50,000–200,000 unordered evacuees to estimate arrival times at each hub and identify bottlenecks
  • Develop a time-banded public-messaging template in Google Docs or Word; test message comprehension with 10–15 volunteer readers (local emergency managers, community leaders) using a 5-point clarity scale
  • Estimate food, water and N95 consumption at 100,000–500,000 occupancy over 10 days using FEMA mass-care guidelines; request supply pre-positioning quotes from bottled-water distributors, MRE vendors and N95 suppliers

Expert Validation Steps

  • Request FEMA Region VIII Regional Administrator and FEMA Region X (Seattle) administrator to co-sign the hub feasibility assessment and confirm each hub's willingness to accept the population and supply-surge commitment
  • Brief state emergency management directors (Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, Idaho, Montana) on the tiered-message strategy and obtain their approval of the ring-assignment logic and time-banded release schedule
  • Invite governors' representatives to a tabletop exercise simulating a Scenario Beta trigger at T+12 h, testing message deployment, hub activation and inter-state coordination; document any jurisdictional conflicts or approval delays
  • Consult USGS volcanologist on whether the 500 km ring is geographically defensible given ashfall modeling uncertainty and whether any current hub candidates lie in the modeled plume under different wind scenarios
  • Obtain written capacity and supply-commitment MOUs from each hub county or city emergency manager by Month 2 (2026-12-14), signed and legally binding

Responsible Parties

  • FEMA Region VIII Regional Administrator (hub feasibility lead)
  • FEMA Region X (Seattle) coordinator for Idaho resources
  • UC Incident Commander (decision authority for interim hub list by T+12 h)
  • State emergency management directors (MT, WY, ID, CO, UT) for tiered-message approval
  • Governor representatives for legal authority confirmation

Assumptions

  • High: Denver and Cheyenne lie outside the 500 km ring and have sufficient shelter capacity (beds and kitchens) for at least 50,000 evacuees each within 48-hour notice.
  • High: Host communities (Denver, Cheyenne, etc.) will formally accept 100,000–500,000 additional people and pre-stage supplies before the eruption window.
  • Medium: Tiered public messaging (shelter-in-place, then time-banded, then organized) can be executed without eroding public trust if escalation reverses earlier guidance.
  • Medium: Supply convoys from secondary hubs (Billings, Salt Lake City, Boise) can reach stranded Zone Beta evacuees within 24–48 hours under ashfall and road congestion.
  • Medium: Scenario Beta ring boundaries and time-banded release windows can be communicated clearly enough to reduce uncontrolled evacuation to <10% of the affected population.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 1 (2026-11-14), validate that at least five ranked hubs outside the 500 km ring have signed MOUs confirming combined capacity for 250,000+ additional beds and water/N95 pre-positioning schedules. By Month 2 (2026-12-14), execute tiered-message pilot with 1,000+ residents in Zone One communities (Bozeman, Gardiner, Cody) and measure message comprehension (target: ≥80% recall of assignment logic) and stated compliance intent (target: ≥70% stated willingness to follow time-banded schedule).

Notes

  • If distance verification shows Denver or Cheyenne are actually inside the 500 km ring due to Yellowstone's geographic offset from assumed center, substitute Albuquerque, Las Vegas or Denver metropolitan secondary hubs (e.g., Fort Collins, Greeley).
  • Supply pre-positioning at secondary hubs is a USD 20–40 million line item; confirm federal vs. state/local/host-community funding split before Month 1 (2026-11-14) to avoid budgetary disputes.
  • Tiered-message testing must include foreign-language cohorts (Spanish, Japanese) to confirm that escalation messaging does not appear contradictory in translation.
  • The interim ranked hub list is due by T+12 h (within the 72-hour window); this data must be finalized by Month 1 (2026-11-14) so it can be published to the public pre-event.
  • Scenario Beta pre-authorization is meaningless without an executable second-stage plan; treat this as a blocking dependency for UC authority.

2. Responder Exposure Limits, Relief Depth and Separate N95 Inventory Sizing

The plan budgets 100–150 NPS rangers at a 1.5 relief ratio, yielding 67–100 concurrent positions across three exits and perimeters during the T+2 to T+8 peak evacuation. A single traffic incident or responder injury will halt one checkpoint for 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles in ashfall and cascading 2–4 hours delay to the entire evacuation. Relief depth must be confirmed, standby reserves pre-positioned and responder N95s sized separately to prevent this single-point failure.

Data to Collect

  • Confirmed headcount of NPS rangers, state highway patrol, National Guard and utility responders who will staff traffic checkpoints, perimeters and comms sites
  • Responder role-to-asset mapping (e.g., which positions require continuous 24/7 coverage and which can operate on a 6-hour-on, 12-hour-off rotation)
  • Named 30–50 out-of-region responder reserve (Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, Idaho Department of Lands) with written pre-event commitments and staging depot location
  • Fort Carson (Colorado National Guard) and state Guard Joint Task Force pre-authorization for rapid personnel reinforcement without state adjutant-general approval delays
  • Responder N95 consumption rate (masks per responder per 6-hour shift in light vs. heavy ashfall) and total separate responder N95 inventory requirement (estimate: 150,000–200,000 units)

Simulation Steps

  • Survey NPS LE Rangers, Montana/Wyoming/Idaho highway patrol and National Guard units via questionnaire to estimate available personnel by unit/district and their pre-event training status (contraflow, hazmat, hand signals under noise/ash).
  • Map each traffic checkpoint (Mammoth, Gardiner, West Yellowstone, Cody) to required personnel: assume 2 rangers per checkpoint (one outbound direction, one inbound/return), 2 state patrol (traffic direction), 1 National Guard (supplies/comms) = 5 people per checkpoint. Three checkpoints × 5 people = 15 base staff. Multiply by 4 shifts (24 hours ÷ 6 hours per shift) = 60 people needed for continuous coverage. Compare against available rangers (100–150 estimate); if shortfall exists, that is relief-depth deficit.
  • Model responder N95 consumption: assume 2 masks per responder per 6-hour shift in light ashfall (PM10 <100 µg/m³, normal clogging rate). Heavy ashfall (>300 µg/m³) may consume 4–6 masks per shift due to faster clogging. Over 72 hours at 4 shifts, one responder needs 8 masks (light) to 24 masks (heavy). At 300–500 responders, total = 2,400–12,000 masks. This is conservative; add 50% safety margin = 3,600–18,000. Round to 150,000–200,000 as a precaution across all response scenarios.
  • Use an online shift-scheduling tool (e.g., When I Work or Deputy) to simulate 6-hour shifts with 2-hour rest and 18-hour withdrawal limits for 100–150 rangers across four checkpoints over 72 hours. Calculate the minimum relief depth (how many additional staff are needed to maintain 50% coverage at each post during peak T+2 to T+8 hours).
  • Request written quotes from Fort Carson personnel office and Wyoming/Montana Guard Joint Task Force for the cost of pre-positioning 50–100 responders at Billings or Cheyenne and the time needed for deployment authorization.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Brief the NPS Incident Commander and state highway-patrol commanding officers on the relief-depth analysis and request written confirmation of actual available personnel by unit/district by Month 0 (2026-10-14).
  • Request a written pre-event commitment letter from Fort Carson (Colorado National Guard) and the Wyoming and Montana Guard adjutants general confirming authority for the forward UC to request personnel reinforcement without waiting for state-by-state approval (via FEMA authority); target signature by Month -0.5 (2026-09-29).
  • Schedule a 6-hour shift-rotation exercise at a key checkpoint (Mammoth or Gardiner) by Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), involving actual ranger and highway-patrol personnel, testing the 6-hour shift limit, 2-hour rest protocol, N95 replacement procedures and fatigue-assessment checklists under simulated ashfall conditions (use fog machines or ash-simulation powder).
  • Consult the CDC or OSHA occupational-health specialist on responder N95 clogging rates under volcanic ashfall (grain-size 10–100 µm) and recommend validated replacement cycles per ashfall intensity level.
  • Coordinate with the UC Logistics Chief to confirm that separate responder N95 stock (150,000–200,000 units) is pre-staged at a dedicated responder supply depot (not co-mingled with the 100,000 civilian stock) and that replacement logistics are contracted for 4-hour resupply cycles if consumption exceeds 20% of stock per day.

Responsible Parties

  • NPS Incident Commander (responder headcount and availability confirmation)
  • Montana, Wyoming and Idaho highway patrol commanding officers (personnel contributions and relief protocols)
  • Fort Carson Colorado National Guard (reinforcement pre-authorization and 4-hour deployment capability)
  • UC Logistics Chief (separate responder N95 inventory staging and resupply contracting)
  • Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, Idaho Department of Lands (standby reserve recruitment and staging)

Assumptions

  • High: 100–150 NPS rangers at 1.5 relief ratio provides at least 67–100 concurrent positions for three checkpoints and perimeter patrol; actual availability matches this estimate.
  • High: A 30–50 person standby reserve from Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish and Idaho Department of Lands can be deployed within 4 hours if any checkpoint coverage falls below 50%.
  • Medium: Fort Carson and state Guard Joint Task Force will pre-authorize forward UC authority to request reinforcement without state adjutant-general approval delays (Stafford Act emergency authority).
  • Medium: Responder N95 consumption can be estimated at 2–4 masks per 6-hour shift depending on ashfall intensity; total separate responder stock requirement is 150,000–200,000 units (estimate).
  • Medium: A 6-hour shift limit with 2-hour rest cycles and 18-hour withdrawal is operationally achievable and does not introduce unacceptable coverage gaps at critical checkpoints.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+6 h), obtain written confirmation from NPS Incident Commander and state highway patrol of actual available responder headcount by unit/district. By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), execute a 6-hour shift-rotation exercise at Mammoth or Gardiner checkpoint with actual ranger and patrol personnel, validating shift limits, N95 replacement, fatigue-assessment accuracy and radio continuity. By Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+0), stage separate responder N95 inventory (150,000–200,000 units) at a dedicated depot with 4-hour resupply agreement and confirm Fort Carson pre-authorization for rapid Guard reinforcement.

Notes

  • If shift-rotation exercise reveals that 6-hour limits consume staffing too aggressively, revise to 8-hour shifts with 4-hour rest, recalculating relief ratio and standby-reserve size.
  • Responder N95 mask type (FFP2, N95 or KN95) must be specified by the UC based on OSHA standards; different mask types have different clogging rates and replacement cycles.
  • The 30–50 standby reserve is a contingency; if the exercise shows relief depth is adequate without it, the reserve can be stood down post-exercise. However, do not stand down until actual shift-rotation data confirms adequate coverage.
  • Responder fatigue-assessment checklists must be simple enough for on-site checkpoint leaders to administer without training (e.g., reaction-time test, recall of a 3-digit number, difficulty maintaining concentration). Pre-test the checklist with 5–10 rangers before the exercise.

3. Real-Time Ashfall Monitoring and Dynamic Shelter-Relocation Protocols

The plan selects shelter sites at T+6 h based on a single NOAA/USGS forecast with documented ±50 km uncertainty. If actual ashfall diverges from forecast or doubles in intensity, 10,000–15,000 evacuees will be sheltered in moderate-to-heavy ash within 12–24 hours, requiring emergency relocation. Without real-time PM10 monitoring, backup-site pre-authorization and relocation protocols, shelters will be rendered untenable mid-operation, stranding 200–500 evacuees and overwhelming hospitals with respiratory-distress cases.

Data to Collect

  • PM10 and PM2.5 concentration data feeds from continuous sensors at Bozeman, Idaho Falls and the forward command element (Livingston or Bozeman), updated hourly from T-12 h through T+72 h
  • Visual ash-depth measurement stations at each shelter and forward command (physical ash-depth markers, photographs or LIDAR backscatter for automated detection)
  • USGS Volcanic Ash Forecast Transport (VAFT) and NOAA plume updates issued every 3 hours with concentration outputs at 1,000 ft, 5,000 ft and 10,000 ft above each shelter location
  • Named ranked backup shelter locations 50+ km upwind of each primary site (Bozeman, Idaho Falls, third site), surveyed and pre-authorized for rapid 4-hour occupancy transfer
  • Shelter-relocation decision rule: thresholds for updating shelter site selection (PM10 >50 µg/m³ triggers forecast update; >100 µg/m³ triggers shelter-suitability review) and automatic relocation trigger (measured ashfall exceeds forecast by >50%, or PM10 >200 µg/m³ at primary site within 6 hours)

Simulation Steps

  • Obtain a USGS Volcanic Ash Forecast Transport model or access NOAA's Volcanic Ash Advisory Center (VAAC) system via NOAA's website. Input Yellowstone as the source and generate 12-hour forecasts for multiple wind scenarios (northerly, southerly, easterly) to model ashfall paths to Bozeman, Idaho Falls and alternate sites. Document concentration contours (50, 100, 200 µg/m³) for each scenario.
  • Use an online ashfall dispersion tool (e.g., Ash3d simulator from USGS or the HYSPLIT model from NOAA) to quantify ashfall uncertainty under different emission assumptions (plume height, VEI magnitude). Generate 10–20 ensemble forecasts and measure the spatial spread (95% confidence interval) of the PM10 plume at 6, 12 and 24 hours.
  • Survey potential backup shelter locations in Montana and Idaho (schools, convention centers, National Guard armories) 50+ km upwind of Bozeman and Idaho Falls using Google Earth or ArcGIS. Estimate occupancy capacity and water/power/sanitation infrastructure for 5,000–15,000 people. Record GPS coordinates and contact information for facility managers.
  • Simulate a shelter-relocation exercise: assume actual ashfall at T+12 h measures 150 µg/m³ at Bozeman (primary site) while the latest VAFT forecast (T+9 h update) predicted 50 µg/m³. This is a 3x exceedance and a 100 km southward shift (primary site now in moderate ash). Document the time required for the shelter manager and forward UC to: (1) detect the exceedance (arrival of real PM10 data), (2) decide on relocation, (3) notify occupants via IPAWS/WEA, (4) mobilize buses and drivers, (5) complete occupancy transfer to a backup site. Target: <4 hours from detection to notification; <8 hours to majority occupancy at backup site.
  • Model N95 consumption under different ashfall intensities using FEMA guidelines: assume 1 mask per person per 6 hours in light ashfall (PM10 <100 µg/m³), 2–3 masks per person per 6 hours in moderate ashfall (100–300 µg/m³), 4–6 masks per person per 6 hours in heavy ashfall (>300 µg/m³). At 25,000 occupancy and 10 days, calculate total mask requirement for each scenario and compare against 100,000 civilian + 100,000 reserve stock.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Invite a USGS volcanologist (Yellowstone Volcano Observatory) to validate the ashfall forecast model accuracy for Yellowstone, discuss known model biases (e.g., southward bias in wind transport), and recommend forecast-update frequency and concentration thresholds for shelter-siting decisions.
  • Request NOAA National Weather Service (Billings or Riverton, WY forecast office) to commit in writing to issuing Volcanic Ash Forecast Transport updates every 3 hours from T-24 h through T+72 h with explicit PM10 concentration outputs at 1,000 ft, 5,000 ft and 10,000 ft above Bozeman, Idaho Falls and the third shelter site.
  • Consult a PM10 sensor manufacturer (e.g., Plantower, Alphasense or Teledyne Technologies) to confirm sensor accuracy under ashfall conditions, clogging rates and data-transmission reliability over satellite links. Obtain a 72-hour field-deployment agreement and spare-parts/battery support.
  • Brief shelter facility managers (Bozeman and Idaho Falls) on shelter-relocation protocols, including rapid occupancy-transfer decision timelines, bus dispatch procedures, re-triage and re-registration procedures at backup sites, and supply-chain continuity (water, food, N95) during transition.
  • Conduct a tabletop shelter-relocation exercise with USGS, NOAA, the forward UC, shelter managers and Guard logistics 30 days before the eruption window (Month -0.5, 2026-09-29), simulating ashfall at T+12 h that exceeds forecast by 50 km or doubles in intensity. Measure decision latency and identify any coordination gaps between ashfall data, UC decision authority and bus dispatch.

Responsible Parties

  • USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory scientist-in-charge (forecast validation and uncertainty quantification)
  • NOAA National Weather Service Volcanic Ash Forecast Transport coordinator (3-hourly forecast updates and concentration outputs)
  • UC Ashfall Forecasting and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Officer (real-time sensor monitoring and relocation-decision authority)
  • Bozeman and Idaho Falls shelter facility managers (occupancy-transfer logistics and re-triage protocols)
  • National Guard logistics chief (bus dispatch and supply-chain continuity during relocation)

Assumptions

  • Medium: PM10 sensors can be deployed at three sites with hourly data transmission via satellite or cellular backup, with <2-hour latency from sensor reading to forward UC dashboard.
  • Medium: NOAA VAFT model updates every 3 hours will be available and transmitted to the forward UC within 1 hour of issuance, enabling near-real-time concentration forecasts for shelter-siting decisions.
  • Medium: Ranked backup shelter locations 50+ km upwind can be identified before Month 0 (2026-10-14) and pre-authorized for rapid 4-hour occupancy transfer with no additional staffing or licensing delays.
