  • High: A 4-hour shelter-relocation decision-to-notification timeline is achievable; actual bus dispatch and occupancy transfer may require 6–12 hours (estimate), stranding evacuees temporarily.
  • Medium: N95 consumption under heavy ashfall (>300 µg/m³) can be modeled reliably using FEMA guidelines; actual consumption may exceed estimates by 2–3x if masks clog faster than anticipated (estimate).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), deploy PM10/PM2.5 sensors at Bozeman, Idaho Falls and forward command with confirmed 4-hour data-transmission capability. By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), obtain signed NOAA commitment for 3-hourly VAFT updates with concentration outputs at three shelter elevations. By Month 1 (2026-11-14), complete survey and pre-authorization of at least three ranked backup shelter locations per primary site. By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), execute a tabletop shelter-relocation exercise and measure decision latency from PM10 exceedance detection to UC relocation order (<2 h target).

Notes

  • PM10 sensor accuracy under ashfall is critical; if sensors show >20% variance vs. official NOAA/USGS estimates, the relocation-decision credibility will be questioned. Include sensor cross-calibration with USGS equipment in the deployment protocol.
  • Ashfall forecast uncertainty of ±50 km means shelter siting is inherently probabilistic. Consider a ranking system: primary site (50–70% confidence), backup 1 (20–30% confidence), backup 2 (<10% confidence) based on ensemble forecast spread.
  • The 4-hour relocation decision rule assumes buses, drivers and pre-authorization are ready at T+0. If buses are consumed in primary evacuation, relocation will be delayed 6–12 hours. Pre-stage additional buses (estimate: 20–30 buses reserved for relocation) at forward command.
  • Backup shelter occupancy-transfer logistics (re-triage, re-registration, food service startup) are complex and time-intensive. Conduct a dry-run relocation with 500–1,000 volunteer evacuees 30 days before the eruption window to validate 8-hour transfer timelines.

4. Water Supply Chain Validation: Dispatch Timeline, Forward-Depot Pre-Positioning and Ashfall-Impact Testing

The plan targets water arrival at shelters by T+24 h, but estimates realistic delivery time as T+18–30 h. Without forward-depot pre-positioning, shelters must ration water for the first 18–24 hours, risking dehydration in 10,000–20,000 evacuees. Municipal water sources become ash-contaminated within 4–6 hours and are unsafe without treatment. This data collection validates the water supply chain from source through shelter intake and identifies contingency backup sources (groundwater, tanker fills) to ensure T+24 h water availability without relying solely on distant convoys.

Data to Collect

  • Realistic convoy travel time from Salt Lake City to Bozeman and Idaho Falls shelters under ashfall visibility reduction (estimate: 18–30 hours, not 12 hours) and evacuation-traffic congestion (estimate: 25–40% I-15 saturation by Hour 8–12)
  • Forward-depot water pre-positioning schedule and capacity: 200,000–300,000 liters at Bozeman and 100,000–150,000 liters at Idaho Falls by T+0, with 4-hour resupply contracts from three backup suppliers (Salt Lake City, Pocatello, Butte)
  • Identified water sources and treatment timelines for municipal contamination response: settling time, filtration requirements, turbidity thresholds for continued use at Bozeman and Idaho Falls water districts
  • Backup groundwater or tanker-fill stations (e.g., wells, springs, potable-water storage tanks) at Bozeman and Livingston with pre-tested pump/hose interfaces and 24-hour operator availability
  • Validated water-consumption model: 1.43 million liters for 35,800 shelter occupants at 4 L/person/day over 10 days; breakdown by category (drinking, cooking, hygiene, medical) and contingency for increased demand under stress or medical surge

Simulation Steps

  • Conduct a realistic convoy-routing exercise from Salt Lake City (3 distribution centers: Culligan, USA Water, Nestlé Waters) to Bozeman and Idaho Falls under simulated ashfall and evacuation traffic. Assume: (1) ashfall reduces I-15 visibility to 50–100 meters, safe speed 10 mph (not 60 mph); (2) evacuation traffic saturation at 25–40% on I-15 northbound by Hour 8–12, delaying non-priority traffic; (3) ashfall-dust contaminates vehicle windows and air filters, requiring frequent stops for cleaning. Measure actual travel times using a Google Maps simulation with traffic-layer data and manual speed reductions. Expected outcome: 18–30 hours (not 12 hours).
  • Contact Bozeman and Idaho Falls water districts (Gallatin County, Bonneville County public utilities) to request water-system emergency-response plans: settlement basins, filtration capacity, turbidity thresholds for ash-contaminated municipal water. Simulate 500–1,000 µm/kg ashfall ash-particle concentration at 100 µm grain size and model settling time (estimate 24–48 hours for 90% particle removal). Quantify how long municipal water is non-potable and at what ashfall level.
  • Identify and survey groundwater or alternative-water sources within 50 miles of shelters (wells, storage tanks, potable-water distribution depots). Use USGS water-resource databases and contact local water-district operators. Measure depth to water table, pump capacity, power requirements and hose/interface compatibility with shelter filling systems.
  • Obtain operational quotes from three water-supply vendors (e.g., basin Water, Great Lakes Water, United Water) for 12-hour and 24-hour dispatch of bottled-water convoys (2,000–3,000 gallons per truck × 10–15 trucks = 20,000–45,000 gallons per trip) from Salt Lake City, Pocatello and Butte. Document lead-time, cost, minimum order size and surge-rate pricing.
  • Model water consumption at 35,800 shelter occupants under baseline and stress scenarios: baseline 4 L/person/day (drinking 1.5, cooking 1, hygiene 1, laundry 0.5) = 143,200 L/day. Stress scenario (diarrheal disease, heavy ash contamination requiring frequent handwashing): 6 L/person/day = 214,800 L/day. Over 10 days: 1.43–2.15 million liters. Cross-check with FEMA mass-care guidelines (typically 5 gallons/person/day = 19 L/person/day for all uses, higher than the baseline estimate). Adjust upward to 2 million liters as contingency.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Request Montana-Dakota Utilities, Idaho Power and Bozeman/Idaho Falls water-district general managers to brief the UC on water-system ashfall impact and emergency-isolation protocols (e.g., intake isolation, bypass to standby storage) during volcanic ashfall.
  • Consult a water-treatment engineer (EPA or state water-resource specialist) on ash-particle concentration thresholds that render municipal water non-potable and on acceptable settling/filtration timelines and costs to restore potability.
  • Contact USGS National Water-Quality Assessment Program or a regional hydrogeologist to validate groundwater survival likelihood (ashfall does not typically contaminate groundwater aquifers, though surface intakes may be affected; confirm for Bozeman and Idaho Falls hydrologic settings).
  • Arrange a site visit with Bozeman and Idaho Falls public-works departments to verify water-system infrastructure drawings, intake locations, treatment-plant capacity and emergency-isolation capability. Confirm that emergency shutdown and bypass-to-storage procedures are feasible within 2–4 hours of ashfall onset.
  • Execute a water-convoy exercise from Salt Lake City to Bozeman 30 days before the eruption window, driving under fog-machine ashfall simulation (visibility reduced to 50–100 meters, require safety vest fluorescence and headlight clarity checks), measuring actual travel time and driver fatigue effects. Target: 18–30 hour arrival time, document any mechanical or fueling delays.

Responsible Parties

  • Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director (forward-depot pre-positioning and resupply contracts)
  • Bozeman and Idaho Falls public-works directors (water-system emergency protocols and municipal-water contamination response)
  • Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power operations managers (grid-failure planning and emergency load shedding if water-pumping loses power)
  • USGS National Water-Quality Assessment Program or state hydrogeologist (groundwater vulnerability assessment)
  • Water-supply vendors (Salt Lake City, Pocatello, Butte bottled-water distributors for surge-rate and 12-hour dispatch contracts)

Assumptions

  • High: Realistic convoy travel time from Salt Lake City to Bozeman/Idaho Falls under ashfall and evacuation traffic is 18–30 hours (not 12 hours), requiring forward-depot pre-positioning to meet T+24 h shelter-supply targets.
  • High: Forward-depot pre-positioning of 200,000–300,000 liters at Bozeman and 100,000–150,000 liters at Idaho Falls by T+0 is feasible and contracts for 4-hour resupply from backup suppliers (Pocatello, Butte) are executable.
  • Medium: Municipal water systems at Bozeman and Idaho Falls can be isolated or shut down within 2–4 hours of ashfall onset and diverted to alternative sources (groundwater, storage tanks, bottled water) without extended outage.
  • Medium: Groundwater sources (wells, aquifers) near Bozeman and Idaho Falls are protected from ashfall surface contamination and can supply 10,000–20,000 L/day per location as emergency backup.
  • Low: Water-consumption baseline of 4 L/person/day is adequate for drinking, cooking and hygiene under ashfall conditions. Stress scenarios may exceed 6 L/person/day due to disease or contamination concerns.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), execute a water-convoy exercise from Salt Lake City to Bozeman under ashfall simulation, documenting realistic travel time (target: 18–30 hours). By Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+0), stage 200,000–300,000 liters at Bozeman and 100,000–150,000 liters at Idaho Falls forward depots, with signed 4-hour resupply contracts from Pocatello and Butte suppliers. By Month 1 (2026-11-14), validate that Bozeman and Idaho Falls water systems have documented emergency-isolation and backup-source protocols, and that groundwater or alternative-water sources can supply ≥10,000 L/day as emergency backup.

Notes

  • If ashfall visibility reduction drops below 50 meters and I-15 becomes impassable, ground convoy may be diverted to I-80 (further east) or I-70 (further south), extending travel time to 24–36 hours. Pre-identify alternate routes and test them in the exercise.
  • Forward-depot pre-positioning of water at Bozeman and Idaho Falls (USD 50,000–100,000 initial stocking + 4-hour resupply logistics) is a contingency cost; confirm federal vs. state/local funding split before Month 0 (2026-10-14).
  • Water-contamination risk from ashfall is primarily a turbidity/filtration issue (ash particles block water-treatment filters, not toxicity from ash itself unless heavy metals are present in the ash deposit). Confirm with USGS that Yellowstone ashfall is expected to be basaltic (low metal content) rather than rhyolitic (higher metal and fluorine content).
  • If municipal water intakes are contaminated and groundwater is unavailable, bottled-water shelters will require 2–5 million liters over 10 days (stress scenario). Pre-contract additional supplying capacity (ice-cream trucks, tanker trucks, bulk distributor shipments) as backup to the 12-hour convoy.
  • Power loss at water-pumping and treatment facilities is a secondary risk; coordinate with utility operators to ensure backup generator fuel and UPS systems are in place to keep water flowing during grid outages.

5. Geotechnical Road Hazard Assessment: Gallatin Canyon Single-Lane Clearance Feasibility and South Entrance Bypass Viability

The plan pre-positions two tow/rockfall teams to reach Gallatin Canyon within 15 minutes and sets a 45-minute blockage threshold before diversion. However, no geotechnical data exists to validate clearance feasibility, secondary-slide risk or the time estimates. If Gallatin Canyon clearance actually requires 6–12 hours (as documented in similar volcanic or seismic events), the 15-minute arrival and 45-minute threshold are infeasible. Proceeding without this data risks either (1) committing equipment to a clearance attempt that cannot succeed and exposes crews to secondary-slide hazard, or (2) abandoning the corridor prematurely and overloading surviving exits. This data collection informs the go/no-go decision for single-lane clearance and the loss-of-exit contingency trigger.

Data to Collect

  • Gallatin Canyon slope-stability survey: identification of slide-prone zones, debris-accumulation potential, secondary-slide probability during clearance work, and safe turn-out locations for equipment staging
  • South Entrance landslide-debris quantification: debris volume, slope gradient, ground-water seepage status and secondary-slide triggering mechanisms under continued seismic swarm
  • Time-to-clearance estimates for single-lane opening through Gallatin Canyon blockage under ashfall conditions (reduced visibility, ashfall-dust contamination of equipment, personnel fatigue)
  • Bypass-route options: temporary single-lane track routing around the South Entrance slide, with load-bearing capacity for light-duty vehicles (estimate 500–1,000 vehicles/day max throughput)
  • Seismic-activity triggering criteria for abort: pre-authorized hard thresholds (e.g., M4.0+ event during clearance work, >2 cm slope displacement on incipient-failure zones) that halt work and trigger diversion

Simulation Steps

  • Request a USGS geotechnical field team (Volcano Disaster Assistance Program or Cascades Volcano Observatory) to conduct a rapid survey of Gallatin Canyon (10 km highest-risk section) and the South Entrance landslide 60 days before the eruption window. Deliverables: (1) geotechnical log with slope angles, failure modes and rockfall-size estimates; (2) ground-water seepage assessment; (3) secondary-slide probability if clearance work destabilizes upper slopes; (4) sketches of safe crew-staging areas and equipment-deployment zones.
  • Model debris-removal time using historical slide-clearance data: typical wet-weather debris removal from a 10 m blockage on a two-lane mountain road requires 2–4 hours (estimate) with a mobile wrecker and debris chipper. Under ashfall (visibility <100 meters, ash-coated equipment), add 50% time penalty (3–6 hours estimate per 10 m). If the South Entrance slide or a Gallatin Canyon blockage is >50 m in debris, clearance time exceeds 10–20 hours, violating the 4-hour time-box and 45-minute diversion threshold.
  • Conduct a photogrammetry and ground-penetrating-radar survey of the South Entrance slide to quantify debris volume (estimate: 10,000–100,000 cubic meters, order-of-magnitude), slope stability under seismic swarm loading, and probability of secondary failure if heavy equipment disturbs the slide mass. Compare the debris volume to available clearing equipment capacity (typical debris chipper: 50–200 cubic meters/day); if debris exceeds equipment capacity, single-lane clearance is infeasible.
  • Identify and sketch potential bypass routes around the South Entrance slide or Gallatin Canyon blockage using satellite imagery (Google Earth, USGS topography) and field survey. Design temporary single-lane track segments with grade, turn radius and load-bearing capacity for evacuation vehicles (assume 2,000–3,000 lb single-axle load). Estimate construction/grading time (4–8 hours for a 2–3 mile temporary track) and equipment needed (bulldozer, roller, grader).
  • Model the loss-of-exit scenario: if Gallatin Canyon blockage requires 10+ hours to clear, it exceeds the 4-hour time-box and triggers the 45-minute diversion rule. Divert all traffic to US-89 (North) and US-14/16/20 (East) exits, increasing load on those corridors from 30% and 20% to 50% and 40% (estimate), adding 2–4 hours to transit time for the diverted 50% cohort. Simulate this in a traffic-flow model (CORSIM, SimTraffic) to quantify the cascading delay.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Brief the USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory scientist-in-charge and the USGS Volcano Disaster Assistance Program on the clearance-feasibility question and obtain a written assessment of whether the Gallatin Canyon or South Entrance blockage is clearable within 4 hours given ashfall conditions.
  • Request a professional geotechnical engineer (registered PE in Montana or Wyoming, specializing in slope stability) to review the USGS survey and provide a written opinion on secondary-slide probability during clearance work and the viability of the abort triggers (M4.0+ seismic event, >2 cm slope displacement).
  • Coordinate with the Wyoming and Montana departments of transportation to confirm availability of heavy-equipment crews (dozers, graders, debris chippers) for a 4-hour mobilization and the pre-positioning location (Mammoth, Spanish Creek) that guarantees 15-minute reach to Gallatin Canyon.
  • Consult the FAA (if helicopters will be used for debris removal or surveying) and the Forest Service (if the bypass route crosses National Forest land) to confirm permits and environmental-clearance requirements for emergency access.
  • Execute a site survey and equipment-positioning exercise at Mammoth and Spanish Creek 30 days before the eruption window to confirm 15-minute reach time to Gallatin Canyon under ashfall simulation (fog machines, visibility reduction to 50–100 meters, require spotters and manual communication).

Responsible Parties

  • USGS Volcano Disaster Assistance Program or Cascades Volcano Observatory geotechnician (slope-stability survey and secondary-slide risk assessment)
  • Professional geotechnical engineer (registered PE) (secondary opinion on clearance feasibility and abort triggers)
  • Montana and Wyoming departments of transportation (equipment pre-positioning and heavy-equipment crew availability)
  • NPS Incident Commander or UC Contraflow Operations Manager (go/no-go decision authority for clearance attempts)

Assumptions

  • High: Gallatin Canyon blockage can be cleared to single-lane within 4 hours under ashfall conditions; if clearance requires >6 hours, the 45-minute diversion threshold is infeasible and the corridor should be written off.
  • High: Pre-positioned tow and rockfall teams can reach Gallatin Canyon within 15 minutes from Mammoth or Spanish Creek under ashfall visibility reduction (50–100 meters); if actual reach time is >30 minutes, the threshold should be revised.
  • Medium: Secondary-slide probability during clearance work is <10% if the slope is stable and clearance crews follow geotechnical-spotting protocols; if probability exceeds 20%, clearance should be abandoned as too hazardous to crews.
  • Medium: A temporary bypass route around the South Entrance slide is feasible and can be constructed/graded in 4–8 hours, providing an alternate single-lane exit for light-duty vehicles and emergency traffic.
  • Medium: Hard abort triggers (M4.0+ seismic event, >2 cm slope displacement) are detectable in real time using pre-positioned motion sensors or drone-based monitoring, enabling immediate halt of clearance work before crew entrapment.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month -1.5 (2026-08-29, assuming month-length recalculation for pre-event planning), conduct a full geotechnical survey of Gallatin Canyon (10 km highest-risk section) and the South Entrance slide, documenting debris volume, slope stability and secondary-slide probability. By Month -1 (2026-09-14), obtain written feasibility assessment from professional geotechnical engineer on single-lane clearance time (target: ≤4 hours) and abort triggers. By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), execute a site survey and equipment-positioning exercise at Mammoth and Spanish Creek, validating 15-minute reach time to Gallatin Canyon under ashfall simulation.

Notes

  • If geotechnical survey concludes that clearance is infeasible or exceeds the 4-hour time-box, the plan should explicitly write off Gallatin Canyon as an exit option and reallocate all traffic to US-89 (North, 50%) and US-14/16/20 (East, 50%), abandoning the 50/30/20 three-exit split. This requires revision of the contraflow-operation plan.
  • Secondary-slide risk to crews is the highest safety concern; abort triggers should be conservative and non-negotiable. If M4.0+ seismic activity occurs during work, crews must withdraw immediately and the corridor must be abandoned.
  • The 15-minute reach-time assumption is optimistic for ashfall conditions (visibility <100 meters, ashfall-clogged engine air filters, personnel fatigue). Field-test under ashfall simulation and revise reach-time expectation to 20–30 minutes if data supports it.
  • If bypass routes are identified around Gallatin Canyon or South Entrance, they should be surveyed and graded (within the 4-hour time-box) during the pre-event mobilization phase (T-24 to T+0), not during the evacuation crisis. This reduces the real-time demand on heavy equipment and crew.
  • Environmental permitting for bypass construction on Forest Service or state land must be negotiated and pre-authorized before the eruption window to avoid 48+ hour delays during the 72-hour evacuation.

6. Multi-State Authority Structure and Boundary Coordination Officer Decision Authority Validation

The plan specifies a Boundary Coordination Officer with pre-authorized decision authority, but the Officer's position is not formally created, authority is not delegated by governors in writing and the three state on-scene commanders' acceptance of reduced approval authority is not documented. Without this validation, the Boundary Coordination Officer's reroute decisions will face jurisdictional challenge or delay when implemented during the crisis, potentially halting traffic for 15–45 minutes while approvals cascade through state adjutants general or emergency management chains. This data collection formalizes authority, documents pre-event delegation and validates that multi-state coordination can function under time pressure.

Data to Collect

  • Written pre-event authorization letters from the governors of Montana, Wyoming and Idaho explicitly confirming authorization of Unified Command Zone One and Scenario Beta evacuation orders
  • Signed MOUs among NPS, FEMA, Montana DOT, Wyoming Highway Patrol and Idaho Transportation Department specifying exact boundary-transfer checkpoints (Mammoth on US-89, Gallatin County line on US-191, Cody city limits on US-14/16/20)
  • Written delegation protocol defining that state on-scene commanders (highway patrol, National Guard) have pre-authorized authority to issue temporary reroutes without requesting NPS ranger approval (5-minute reroute window without higher approval)
  • Boundary Coordination Officer position description, decision authority matrix and communications protocol (secure satellite phone/radio links to NPS incident commander, three state commanders, Denver RRCC) with 24/7 availability T-12 h through T+72 h
  • FEMA Region 10 (Seattle) liaison seated at Denver RRCC with documented mutual-aid resource commitments (water, fuel, medical staff, shelter, National Guard personnel) from Idaho State Emergency Management and Pocatello/Boise distribution centers

Simulation Steps

  • Draft a Unified Command authority-delegation document defining: (1) NPS incident commander authority over Zone Zero (park interior) operations until the first park boundary; (2) state on-scene commander authority over post-boundary traffic, shelter assignment and resource requests until formal handoff; (3) Boundary Coordination Officer authority over reroute and shelter decisions at the boundary crossing (specifically, authority to make a traffic-control decision without waiting for higher approval if phone/radio communication is lost >5 minutes). Circulate this draft to NPS headquarters, Montana/Wyoming/Idaho governors' offices, FEMA Region VIII and state emergency management for comment and revision.
  • Develop a multi-state tabletop exercise scenario: at T+3 h, a rockfall blocks Gallatin Canyon, and the Boundary Coordination Officer must decide whether to (1) attempt 15-minute tow-team clearance (per protocol), or (2) divert all traffic to US-89 (North exit) immediately (per loss-of-exit contingency). The diversion decision will increase load on US-89 from 30% to 40%, and the Boundary Coordination Officer must notify MT highway patrol and the state on-scene commander within 5 minutes. Simulate the decision-communication sequence and identify any state-to-federal approval loops that cause delays.
  • Use a Gantt chart or project-management software (Asana, Monday.com) to map out the MOU-signature path: NPS headquarters approval by Week 1, MT/WY/ID governors' offices by Week 2, state DOT legal reviews by Week 3, final signature by Month 1 (2026-11-14). Identify any blocking dependencies (e.g., state attorney-general review) and resolve them early.
  • Conduct a radio-interoperability check among all agencies (NPS, MT/WY/ID highway patrol, National Guard, FEMA, forwad UC): confirm that a single encrypted frequency or secure radio net can link the Boundary Coordination Officer to all three state on-scene commanders and the Denver RRCC simultaneously. Test voice quality, latency and the ability to conference 5+ parties on a single call.
  • Model the FEMA Region 8/10 coordination flow: at T+0, the Boundary Coordination Officer and UC Incident Commander at Denver RRCC activate a call with the FEMA Region 10 (Seattle) administrator and Idaho State Emergency Management Agency. Resource requests from shelters (e.g., 'we need 50,000 gallons of water by Hour 8') should be processed by the Region 10 liaison in <30 minutes and be dispatched to Pocatello or Boise suppliers within 4 hours of the request. Simulate a high-demand scenario (multiple simultaneous water, fuel and personnel requests at Hour 6–8) to test coordination speed.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Request the NPS Incident Commander (or designate) and the governors of Montana, Wyoming and Idaho to formally authorize the Unified Command structure by signing a pre-event Memorandum of Understanding confirming (1) NPS operational authority in Zone Zero, (2) state authority post-boundary, (3) Boundary Coordination Officer pre-authorized decision authority at the boundary crossing.
  • Invite a FEMA regional administrator (Region VIII) and state emergency management directors to review the authority-delegation document and confirm that it does not conflict with Stafford Act procedures, EMAC mutual-aid processes or state emergency-powers laws.
  • Request the Boundary Coordination Officer (named individual or position designation) to conduct a dry-run radio-communication test with all state on-scene commanders and the Denver RRCC 30 days before the eruption window, confirming that the officer can reach all parties simultaneously and that encrypted frequencies are synchronized.
  • Brief the Montana and Wyoming highway-patrol command centers on the pre-authorized reroute protocol, including the 5-minute decision window for traffic-control changes without requesting NPS approval, and confirm that their on-scene commanders understand and accept this delegation.
  • Coordinate a multi-state command-authority exercise involving NPS, FEMA, all three state emergency management agencies and the governors' representatives 60 days before the eruption window (Month -1.5, 2026-08-29), simulating a Scenario Beta trigger at T+12 h and testing the cross-state decision chain (Zone One clearance gate G1 at T+6 h, Zone One evacuation gate G2 at T+24 h, Scenario Beta expansion order).

Responsible Parties

  • NPS Incident Commander (Zone Zero operational authority delegation)
  • Governors of Montana, Wyoming and Idaho (state authority post-boundary and Boundary Coordination Officer pre-authorization)
  • FEMA Region VIII and Region X administrators (Unified Command structure validation)
  • State emergency management directors and highway-patrol commanding officers (on-scene commander authority and reroute protocol acceptance)
  • Boundary Coordination Officer (designated individual with communications validation)

Assumptions

  • High: Governors of Montana, Wyoming and Idaho will sign pre-event MOUs confirming authorization of Unified Command Zone One and Scenario Beta orders by Month 1 (2026-11-14).
  • High: A single Boundary Coordination Officer at the forward UC element can make reroute and shelter-assignment decisions without supervisory approval if higher-authority communication is lost >5 minutes, under pre-authorized Stafford Act emergency delegation.
  • Medium: FEMA Region 10 (Seattle) liaison can be seated at the Denver RRCC from T+0 and coordinate with Idaho resource centers (Boise, Pocatello) with 30-minute response time to mutual-aid requests.
  • Medium: All agencies (NPS, MT/WY/ID highway patrol, National Guard, FEMA) share a common encrypted radio net that allows simultaneous 5+ party conferencing and maintains voice quality under ashfall conditions.
  • Medium: State on-scene commanders (highway patrol, National Guard) will accept pre-authorized decision authority for temporary reroutes issued by the Boundary Coordination Officer without state-level approval delays.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), obtain written pre-event authorization letters from Montana, Wyoming and Idaho governors confirming Unified Command and Boundary Coordination Officer authority. By Month -1 (2026-09-14), execute signed MOUs with state DOTs and highway patrol specifying boundary-transfer checkpoints and pre-authorized reroute protocols. By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), conduct a radio-interoperability test confirming that the Boundary Coordination Officer can reach all three state on-scene commanders and Denver RRCC simultaneously on a secure net. By Month -1.5 (2026-08-29), execute a multi-state command-authority tabletop exercise testing cross-state decision chains and documenting any approval delays or jurisdictional conflicts.

Notes

  • Pre-event MOU signature timelines often exceed 30–60 days due to state attorney-general review, budget office sign-off and legislative coordination requirements. Begin the signature campaign by Month -2 (2026-08-14) or earlier to meet the Month 1 (2026-11-14) hardening deadline.
  • If governors are unwilling to cede operational authority to NPS at the boundary, an alternative structure might be joint NPS-state command at the boundary itself, with a co-located incident commander and state on-scene commander sharing authority. This will slow decisions by ~10–15 minutes per coordination loop; model this delay into the evacuation timeline.
  • Encrypted radio-net sharing (such as P25 digital conventional or trunked systems) requires pre-event frequency coordination through the FCC or state authorities. Request this coordination by Month -2 (2026-08-14) to avoid 30-day delays.
  • The Boundary Coordination Officer's authority to act without supervisory approval if higher communication is lost >5 minutes is an emergency delegation that may require Stafford Act waivers or state governor orders. Confirm legal basis with FEMA counsel by Month -1 (2026-09-14).
  • Multi-state exercises often reveal unforeseen friction between agencies (e.g., state police reluctance to take orders from federal incident commanders, Guard reluctance to operate under NPS authority). Use the Month -1.5 (2026-08-29) tabletop to surface and resolve these cultural or legal conflicts before the 72-hour window.

Summary

The plan aims to evacuate ~35,800 tourists and staff from Yellowstone Zone Zero by T+6 hours and expand to a 100 km Zone One by T+24 hours under a 72-hour, 40% VEI-6+ eruption probability window (Month 0 = 2026-10-14). The six critical data-collection areas focus on: (1) Scenario Beta secondary-stage hub destinations and tiered messaging (resolves the hollow pre-authorization of a 500 km order lacking destinations), (2) Responder relief depth and separate N95 inventory (addresses zero-cushion staffing during peak evacuation), (3) Real-time ashfall monitoring and shelter-relocation protocols (manages forecast uncertainty and mid-operation shelter viability), (4) Water supply-chain validation including forward depots and realistic convoy timelines (closes the T+18–30 h arrival gap), (5) Geotechnical feasibility of single-lane corridor clearance (tests whether Gallatin Canyon and South Entrance are viable exits), and (6) Multi-state authority structure and Boundary Coordination Officer delegation (formalizes NPS-to-governor handoff and pre-authorized decision authority). Each collection area includes simulation steps using standard tools (GIS mapping, traffic models, tabletop exercises, field surveys) and expert validation with USGS, FEMA, state emergency management and professional engineers. Simulation results must be completed by Month 1 (2026-11-14) hardening deadline, with signed MOUs and full-scale exercises by Month 3 (2027-01-14). The priority is validating the three tightest coupling risks: (A) Scenario Beta destinations prevent uncontrolled shadow evacuation that would delay Zone Zero clearing, (B) responder relief depth prevents single-checkpoint failures from cascading, and (C) ashfall monitoring prevents mid-operation shelter placement in heavy ash. Immediate actionable tasks: activate USGS and FEMA hub-feasibility assessments (target Month -1.5 = 2026-08-29 for survey completion), secure governor pre-authorization letters (target Month -0.5 = 2026-09-29 for signature), and deploy PM10 sensors and water-supply contracts (target T+0 = 2026-10-14). All data collection, simulation and expert validation must complete by Month 1 (2026-11-14) to inform Months 2–3 (2026-12-14 to 2027-01-14) multi-state exercises and contingency planning.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • A trigger matrix without explicit numerical thresholds or undefined decision authority creates ambiguity during a high-stress 72-hour window: the Unified Command may hesitate or convene a meeting to reach consensus, delaying the 500 km order by 1–3 hours while evacuees and unordered residents in the 100–500 km ring lack guidance, leading to uncontrolled flight and corridor gridlock that strands Zone Zero tourists.
  • Absence of a written false-trigger procedure leaves the decision-maker exposed to irreversible commitment: if a 500 km order is issued and later revealed to be based on instrument error, the reversal message loses credibility with the public and media, undercutting compliance with future warnings and eroding trust in USGS and FEMA authority.

  • No defined trigger-confirmation protocol or decision latency standard allows confirmation delays of 45 minutes to 2 hours, during which evacuees lack direction and shadow evacuation begins uncontrolled; each hour of delay increases corridor saturation and reduces organized evacuation efficiency by 15–20%.

Worst Case Scenario: Scenario Beta trigger fires, but the pre-authorized USGS trigger matrix is absent or ambiguous, and decision authority is unclear. During that delay, unordered residents in towns 150–300 km from the park (Billings, Bozeman, Idaho Falls, Driggs) observe ashfall intensifying and begin spontaneous mass evacuation without guidance, flooding I-15, I-90 and US-191 with 100,000–200,000 uncoordinated vehicles. The organized Zone Zero evacuation (35,000 tourists) and Zone One residents (5,000–10,000 estimate) become trapped in the chaotic traffic, adding 6–12 hours to their transit times. Ashfall peaks before the majority of evacuees reach safety; respiratory distress cases overwhelm hospitals in Salt Lake City, Denver and Billings, which are already short of N95 masks and generator fuel. An estimated 50–200 preventable deaths occur due to delayed hospital admission, loss of ventilator support, and respiratory injury. Public trust in government eruption-response authority collapses, undermining compliance in future volcanic-risk zones.

Best Case Scenario: The Escalation Trigger and Evacuation Release Doctrine document pre-authorizes a written USGS trigger matrix with explicit numerical thresholds (e.g., combined ULP >5 mm/day + tremor swarms M≥3.5 + SO2 flux ≥10,000 t/day = VEI-7 probable; Unified Command decision authority confirmed in writing). When indicators cross thresholds at Month 0 (2026-10-14) T+48 hours, a USGS volcanologist at the forward UC element confirms the reading within 15 minutes, and the incident commander issues the 500 km Scenario Beta order within 30 minutes. IPAWS disseminates a pre-tested phased message (in English and five languages) reaching 90%+ of target audiences within 15 minutes of issue. Outer-ring residents (100–500 km) understand the tier assignments (shelter-in-place, time-banded, or organized evacuation) and follow published departure windows, avoiding gridlock. The Zone Zero evacuation (35,000) completes within T+8 hours (2 hours better than nominal) because the early Beta order allows forward deployment of secondary-stage buses to Bozeman and Idaho Falls, moving evacuees onward before the shelters reach capacity. Ashfall arrives at T+20 hours, by which time 95%+ of Zone Zero and Zone One populations are in safe, sheltered locations outside the modeled ashfall footprint. Hospital systems receive sufficient notice to relocate fragile patients and pre-stage generator fuel. Scenario Beta secondary-stage hubs are activated on schedule, with pre-arranged shelter capacity, food and water supplies ready. Public trust in government remains high, enabling voluntary cooperation with tier assignments and reducing the unordered evacuation load. Estimated 5–10 lives saved by the 2–4 hour acceleration, and zero authority-confusion incidents.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a full numerical trigger matrix cannot be finalized by Month 0 (2026-10-14) T+3 hours due to USGS data gaps or model uncertainty, pre-authorize a 'provisional trigger' that names one or two high-confidence indicators (e.g., sustained ULP >8 mm/day alone, or tremor swarms M≥4.5 alone) sufficient to issue the 500 km order, with the understanding that a formal comprehensive analysis will follow within 2 hours of the order and may refine or rescind it if early data prove incorrect.
  • Establish a 'trigger-confirmation checkpoint' at T+3 hours where USGS and the Unified Command jointly review available data and issue a written statement: either 'Trigger thresholds pre-authorized as follows [list]' or 'Current data insufficient; provisional single-indicator thresholds active: [list].' Commit to a full review and update by T+6 hours.

  • Draft trigger-matrix alternatives (conservative, moderate, aggressive) and pre-authorize one as the baseline; clearly label the others so that if conditions warrant a revision during the event, the incident commander can issue a written amendment citing the new rationale and authority (e.g., 'Based on updated USGS briefing at T+36h, Unified Command adopts the 'moderate' trigger matrix effective immediately, superseding the baseline matrix from T+0').
  • If multilingual message production is not complete by Month 0 (2026-10-14) T-12 hours, pre-authorize a simple, tested bilingual (English + Spanish) message series and delay the remaining languages (Japanese, German, Mandarin, French) to T+12 hours, when updated IPAWS templates can be disseminated to regional broadcasters; ensure the delayed-language alert carries a timestamp and priority flag so that non-Spanish-speaking audiences understand the message source and freshness.

  • Pre-authorize state on-scene commanders to issue temporary reroutes (max 30 min without supervisory approval) during congestion at the boundary crossing.
  • Document pre-authorized Scenario Beta trigger authority: UC Incident Commander approves and announces the 500 km order within 30 min of USGS trigger confirmation (final trigger values due by T+3h).
  • Obtain written pre-event confirmation from MT, WY and ID governors authorizing the Unified Command orders by Month -1 (2026-09-14); sign full MOUs (EMAC mutual aid, resource requests, authority transfer) by Month 1 (2026-11-14).
  • Schedule multi-state command-authority exercise 60 days before window (Month -1.5, 2026-08-29) testing boundary handoff and escalation under Zone One and Scenario Beta scenarios; document and resolve any jurisdictional conflicts by Month -1 (2026-09-14).

Approval Authorities: UC Incident Commander (FEMA Region VIII), Governors of Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, and Colorado (for forward command resources), NPS Regional Director, State Emergency Management Directors

Essential Information:

  • Define the Unified Command organizational structure: primary seat at FEMA Region VIII RRCC Denver; FEMA Region 10 liaison with direct access to mutual-aid authorities for Idaho resources; forward UC element at Livingston, MT (alternate Bozeman) with NPS incident commander, Boundary Coordination Officer, Contraflow Operations Manager, and Logistics Director co-located.
  • Establish authority transfer protocol at park boundary: NPS incident command authority ends at defined roadside checkpoints (Mammoth on US-89, Gallatin County line on US-191, Cody limits on US-14/16/20); state on-scene commander assumes custody and traffic management on state roads; document which state agency (highway patrol or National Guard) holds primary authority on each corridor.
  • Specify the Boundary Coordination Officer role: real-time voice and data links to NPS incident commander and state on-scene commanders; authority to issue traffic reroutes and initial shelter assignments during the boundary crossing without supervisory approval (max 30 min authority windows); escalation path for decisions exceeding scope.
  • Pre-authorize state on-scene commanders to issue temporary traffic reroutes up to 30 minutes without seeking further approval from NPS or federal supervisors; define reroute scope (lane closures, exit redirections, contraflow reversals) and communication protocol.
  • Document Scenario Beta trigger authority: UC Incident Commander approves and announces the 500 km order within 30 minutes of USGS trigger confirmation; specify that no further approval from governors or federal entities is required once the written trigger matrix thresholds are met.
  • Identify decision authority for resource requests across FEMA Regions VIII and 10: Region 10 liaison owns Idaho mutual-aid requests (fuel, water, medical, personnel); Denver RRCC owns federal asset deployment; define approval latency targets (no approval delays >2 hours for routine requests) and escalation paths for competing demands.
  • Define hourly briefing structure and attendee list for the UC: primary attendees (NPS IC, state on-scene commanders, USGS volcanologist liaison, Boundary Coordination Officer); secondary participants (hospital surge lead, supply chain manager, communications director); cascade briefings to control points at 30-min intervals.
  • Specify inter-agency communication protocols: primary (hourly UC video or voice briefings with shared screen common operating picture); secondary (Boundary Coordinator voice/data links to NPS and state); tertiary (radio nets bridged by Guard signal teams across NPS, state patrol and Guard frequencies); define net discipline (call signs, check-in intervals, traffic priority).
  • Obtain written pre-event confirmation from Montana, Wyoming and Idaho governors authorizing the UC's evacuation orders for Zone One (100 km) and Scenario Beta (500 km); confirm that governors will enforce unified public messaging and will not issue competing shelter-in-place orders.
  • Execute full MOUs covering EMAC mutual aid, authority transfer, resource requests and cost-sharing between the NPS, FEMA Regions VIII and 10, and the three state governments by Month 1 (2026-11-14); include dispute-resolution mechanisms and escalation paths to the governors if authority conflicts emerge.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Authority gaps at the NPS-to-state boundary delay traffic reroutes by 15–45 minutes (estimate), cascading into queues that block 500–1,000 vehicles and extending evacuation by 1–2 hours during peak egress.
  • Conflicting orders from NPS incident command and state on-scene commanders create confusion at traffic checkpoints, causing drivers to ignore guidance, reduce compliance with shelter assignments by 10–20% (estimate), and saturate unplanned routes.
  • Unclear FEMA Region 10 authority leaves Idaho mutual-aid resource requests (fuel, water, medical) unprocessed for 1–2 hours, delaying shelter supply convoys and creating bottlenecks in the east-corridor evacuation.
  • Undefined Scenario Beta trigger authority leaves the 500 km order pending governors' verbal approval or volcanologist consensus, delaying escalation by 2–4 hours past the trigger point and allowing uncontrolled shadow evacuation to begin before official messaging.
  • No pre-authorized reroute authority at the boundary means each traffic decision must bubble up to the UC, adding 30–60 min latency per decision and leaving drivers without real-time guidance during congestion.
  • Absence of written authority-transfer protocol creates turf disputes between NPS rangers and state highway patrol over who owns traffic control on roads crossing the boundary, resulting in fragmented enforcement and reduced throughput.

Worst Case Scenario: Scenario Beta trigger fires at T+36 hours (late Phase 2), but the UC Incident Commander lacks pre-authorized decision authority and must convene the governors and FEMA for verbal approval. The approval loop takes 3–4 hours, during which unconfirmed rumors of a larger eruption spread via media and social networks, triggering uncontrolled shadow evacuation of 100,000+ people in the 100–250 km ring onto I-15, I-80 and I-90. By the time the official 500 km order is announced, these routes are gridlocked with private vehicles, blocking the organized Zone One evacuation of the remaining park visitors and stranding medical transport. The Boundary Coordination Officer at Livingston has no authority to reroute traffic onto secondary roads without state permission, and the state on-scene commanders are overwhelmed by the uncontrolled traffic and unable to respond to real-time requests. Region 10 mutual-aid for Idaho resources is still uncoordinated with the Denver RRCC, and fuel and water convoys from Boise and Pocatello do not arrive for 4–6 hours beyond the target. Hospital patient transfers are delayed 6–8 hours due to gridlock, resulting in 5–10 preventable respiratory-distress deaths and 20–30 cancellations of critical surgeries.

Best Case Scenario: The Unified Command organizational structure is formally activated at T+0 with the UC Incident Commander seated in Denver, FEMA Region 10 liaison already present with pre-authorized access to Idaho mutual-aid authorities, and the forward UC element (NPS IC, Boundary Coordination Officer, Contraflow Operations Manager and Logistics Director) co-located in Livingston, MT. At T+6 hours, the Boundary Coordination Officer executes a pre-authorized reroute within 15 minutes, directing overflow traffic from a Gallatin Canyon bottleneck to the East Entrance, and this decision is implemented at the traffic checkpoint before congestion builds. When Scenario Beta trigger fires at T+45 hours, the pre-authorized trigger matrix allows the UC Incident Commander to announce the 500 km order within 30 minutes without waiting for governor approval, and state on-scene commanders immediately disseminate the order via IPAWS and Guard signal nets. The Region 10 liaison activates pre-signed mutual-aid agreements with Boise and Pocatello, and fuel and water convoys dispatch within 2 hours. The unified, coordinated authority structure enables 98% compliance with the evacuation order and prevents uncontrolled shadow evacuation. Hospital patient transfers proceed on schedule, and no preventable deaths occur due to command delays.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If pre-event MOUs with the three governors cannot be finalized by Month 1 (2026-11-14), activate a standing governor-to-FEMA hotline at T+0 with verbal pre-authorization of the Zone One and Scenario Beta orders, documented in a call log and signed by each governor within 6 hours; this preserves decision authority even if formal MOUs are still in draft.
  • If the Boundary Coordination Officer role cannot be staffed from NPS or state personnel, request a senior National Guard liaison officer assigned to the forward UC element from T+0, pre-authorized to issue reroutes on behalf of both the NPS and state commanders under a jointly-signed delegation of authority.
  • If FEMA Region 10 liaison cannot be seated at the Denver RRCC from T+0 due to staff availability, establish a dedicated voice and data link from the Denver RRCC to the Boise FEMA Region 10 office, with a standing 15-minute call schedule and pre-authorized resource-request authority (no approval delays >30 min for routine mutual aid).
  • If a full multi-state MOU cannot be negotiated by Month 1 (2026-11-14), substitute a simplified 'Emergency Authority Agreement' signed by each governor at T+0, limited to evacuation-phase authority transfer only, and schedule full MOU negotiations for post-event by Month 6 (2027-04-14).
  • If Scenario Beta trigger-matrix thresholds cannot be jointly agreed with USGS by T+3 hours, use a default conservative placeholder (VEI-7 probability at or above 20% in the remaining window, assessed by USGS every 6 hours), with pre-authorized UC authority to order the 500 km expansion if the placeholder is met; refine the final thresholds during Months 1-3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) for use in subsequent years.
  • If the forward UC element cannot be physically located at Livingston, MT due to facility constraints, operate it virtually from Bozeman or Gardner with redundant video/voice links and a rotating daily on-site liaison at each control point to maintain real-time situational awareness of boundary crossing conditions.

Create Document 4: Escalation Trigger Matrix and Scenario Beta Pre-Authorization

Description: Written, pre-authorized threshold-based trigger matrix specifying USGS indicators (uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux, modeled VEI probability in remaining window) that automatically activate Zone One expansion and authorize the Scenario Beta 500 km evacuation order. Secondary Template: Incident Command Decision Authority and Pre-Authorization Document

Steps to Create:

Essential Information:

  • Specify trigger logic: clarify whether ANY single indicator crossing its threshold activates the full 500 km order, or whether multiple indicators must cross simultaneously.
  • Document the pre-authorization mechanism: write the decision authority granting the UC Incident Commander the power to issue the 500 km evacuation order within 30 minutes of trigger confirmation, without requiring further approval from governors, FEMA, or any other authority.
  • Define the communication protocol for hourly indicator updates from USGS to UC from T-12 hours through T+72 hours, including the 15-minute notification window when an indicator crosses a threshold.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • A trigger matrix that lacks specific numerical thresholds or clear trigger logic (e.g., 'ANY indicator' vs. 'ALL indicators') will cause confusion at the moment of decision, delaying the 500 km order by 30 minutes to 2 hours during the critical T+12 to T+36 hour window, leaving millions of outer-ring residents without timely evacuation notice.
  • If the matrix is pre-authorized without a documented interim Scenario Beta second-stage plan and destinations, the UC Incident Commander will issue a 500 km order into a vacuum, triggering chaotic uncontrolled shadow evacuation that saturates I-15, I-90 and US-191, blocking the organized Zone Zero and Zone One evacuations and stranding 5,000–20,000 people in traffic.
  • Vague or undefined communication protocols between USGS and UC (no satellite backup, no redundancy, no 15-minute notification window specified) risk the UC not receiving trigger confirmation promptly, causing decision delays of 1–6 hours and eroding the credibility of the pre-authorization mechanism.
  • Missing written confirmation from USGS on indicator-update frequency, confidence intervals and forecast limitations leaves the UC relying on unvalidated forecasts during the event, risking a trigger that fires on data the USGS later acknowledges as uncertain or incorrect, undermining public trust in the evacuation order.
  • Without signed governor authorization of the pre-authorized trigger and 500 km order, a governor may contest the UC's decision after it is issued, creating jurisdictional conflict and media confusion that reverses public compliance and causes 10,000–50,000 outer-ring residents to ignore or delay evacuation.
  • A trigger matrix that does not specify the communication protocol for disseminating the 500 km order to state governors, the public, and shelter operators will result in some recipients learning of the order via media rather than official channels, causing uncontrolled evacuation movement before the ring-based execution plan can be activated.

Worst Case Scenario: Without a written, clearly specified trigger matrix and pre-authorization mechanism, the UC Incident Commander faces a 15–45 minute delay at the moment of the VEI-7 decision (estimated T+12 to T+24 hours), requiring phone calls to governors, FEMA leadership, and USGS to confirm the indicator values and seek approval for the 500 km order. During this delay, tens of thousands of residents outside the 100 km zone begin uncoordinated evacuation on their own, saturating I-15, I-90 and US-191 with unplanned traffic within 2–4 hours. When the 500 km order is finally issued, it arrives after the shadow evacuation has already jammed the corridors, preventing the organized Zone One and Zone Zero evacuees (35,800 people plus gateway-town residents) from reaching safe zones by T+24 hours. Gridlocked evacuation traffic, amplified by conflicting state-level guidance, results in an estimated 10,000–50,000 people stranded in or near ashfall zones within T+24 to T+48 hours, with 20–100 preventable respiratory-distress and trauma casualties. The cascading failure of the evacuation plan, visible in real-time media coverage, erodes public trust in the Unified Command and triggers a formal inter-state jurisdictional dispute that delays Phase 2 hand-off and second-stage shelter operations by 6–12 additional hours.

Best Case Scenario: A written, pre-authorized trigger matrix with specific USGS thresholds, clear trigger logic (ANY or ALL), and a documented communication protocol enables the UC Incident Commander to issue the Scenario Beta 500 km order within 30 minutes of USGS trigger confirmation, with no delays, disputes, or additional meetings. The order is simultaneously communicated to state governors, FEMA Region 10, the forward element, and public-alert channels (IPAWS, local media) within 45 minutes of confirmation. The pre-positioned interim second-stage plan (ranked hub list, time-banded rings, messaging strategy) activates immediately, directing outer-ring residents to published destinations and time-band windows, preventing uncontrolled shadow evacuation. Well-coordinated ring-based execution (0–100 km organized, 100–250 km time-banded, 250–500 km staged departure) keeps I-15, I-90 and US-191 passable for Zone One and Zone Zero organized evacuations. Signed governor MOUs and EMAC arrangements ensure state-level coordination and messaging discipline. By T+36 hours, the entire 500 km ring is executing with 80–90% public compliance, shelters and hubs are receiving evacuees in an orderly sequence, supply convoys are moving, and secondary-stage medical and logistics operations are activated. The Unified Command maintains credibility and authority throughout, with no jurisdictional reversals or media-driven confusion; estimated cascading-failure risk is reduced from 20–100 casualties to <5.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If USGS cannot confirm final indicator thresholds by T+3 hours due to technical or forecasting-model constraints, substitute a discretionary decision-cell approach: establish a standing volcanologist-and-governor cell that meets at fixed 6-hour intervals (T+0, T+6, T+12, T+18, T+24) with USGS observations presented in real-time, retaining UC authority to issue the 500 km order without additional approval but accepting 6-hour decision latency at each interval. Document this approach in an alternate protocol signed by governors and USGS by Month 1 (2026-11-14).
  • If pre-authorization by governors proves politically infeasible, establish a 'verbal pre-delegation' protocol: governors grant verbal pre-authorization to the UC Incident Commander at T+0 to issue the 500 km order within 30 minutes of a confirmed USGS trigger, documented in a recorded call and confirmed in writing within 24 hours, with the understanding that governors retain the right to dispute the decision after the fact (not ideal, but operationally faster than seeking approval during the event).
  • If USGS forecasting confidence in VEI-7 probability is too low to define a single numerical threshold, use a composite trigger: a combination of at least two indicators (e.g., uplift rate >X mm/day AND gas-emission rate >Y tonnes/day AND seismic magnitude M>5.0 in previous 6 hours) crossing thresholds within a 12-hour window, reducing false-trigger risk while maintaining a defensible, pre-authorized decision rule.
  • If the Scenario Beta second-stage plan cannot be fully developed by T+0, issue an 'Interim Scenario Beta Destinations List' by T+12 hours specifying at least 5 ranked shelter hubs and a time-banded ring-execution schedule, with the full second-stage plan (MOUs, capacity, messaging) to follow by Month 1 (2026-11-14). The interim list is sufficient to activate the pre-authorized 500 km order and prevent vacuum-driven shadow evacuation.
  • If real-time USGS indicator updates cannot be delivered every hour due to satellite or communication failure, establish a 'best-available-data' protocol: the UC proceeds with the most recent USGS observation available (even if >1 hour old) and a stated confidence interval; USGS provides written confirmation of data age and uncertainty at each briefing interval, so UC decisions are made with transparent awareness of data staleness.

Risks of Poor Quality:

Worst Case Scenario: A major rockfall or secondary tremor-induced slide blocks Gallatin Canyon during peak evacuation (T+3 to T+5 hours) when 5,000-8,000 vehicles are queued in the corridor. Tow teams deployed from Mammoth take 20-30 minutes to reach the blockage due to ash or seismic uncertainty. Debris volume exceeds single-lane clearance capacity, and geotechnical assessment takes 45 minutes to 2 hours. With no pre-authorized diversion rule and unclear authority to order reroutes, the forward command delays issuing a diversion order by 30-45 minutes while seeking approval from three agencies. By the time overflow is redirected to US-89 North and US-14/16/20 East, those corridors are already at capacity, creating a bottleneck cascade that extends evacuation by 4-6 hours. An estimated 2,000-4,000 vehicles remain trapped in Gallatin Canyon during ashfall onset (T+6 to T+8 hours), exposing evacuees to 4-8 hours of unforecast heavy ashfall. Respiratory distress among the stranded rises from zero to 50-100 cases, with 5-10 deaths preventable by timely evacuation.

Best Case Scenario: Contraflow is fully operational on all three exits by T+1 hour with clear lane markings, traffic-control posts manned and monitored in real-time. The three-way load split (50/30/20%) evenly distributes traffic, achieving an average throughput of 2,000 vehicles/hour. Geotechnical monitoring detects no incipient slides, and tow teams remain on standby with no blockages requiring deployment. Pre-authorized diversion rules and reroute authority enable the forward command to respond to any minor debris within 5-10 minutes. Zone Zero is declared clear at T+5.5 hours with 98% of 35,800 people confirmed through exit counts, and a final cohort of 200-400 backcountry stragglers under active ranger escort or in designated last-resort shelters. Evacuation peak ends before significant ashfall arrival, limiting respiratory distress to a handful of cases. The plan's success enables confidence in Phase 2 Zone One evacuation by T+24 hours and credibility for the pre-authorized Scenario Beta trigger if escalation indicators cross thresholds.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If staging-lot capacity at West Yellowstone or Gardiner proves insufficient to absorb 660 vehicles/hour without overflow into the interior, stage additional queue-storage on secondary park roads (e.g., Grand Loop Road segments or service roads) within 2-3 km of the exit, with directional signage and ranger escorts to move vehicles forward as primary lots clear.
  • If the South Entrance single-lane clearance attempt is aborted due to seismic activity or slide complexity within the first 2 hours, immediately reclassify it as a loss-of-exit scenario and activate the overflow diversion rule: any remaining southern-sector evacuees shelter in place or are routed northward via Grand Loop Road to Norris, then to the West or North exits—accepting longer interior transit and increased ash exposure for that cohort.
  • If tow and rockfall teams cannot reach a Gallatin Canyon blockage within 15 minutes due to ashfall visibility or tremor-induced road damage, activate an automated 45-minute blockage timer and reroute all arriving traffic immediately to the nearest alternate exit (US-89 North or US-14/16/20 East) without waiting for on-site assessment, trading some efficiency loss for speed and certainty.
  • If real-time queue monitoring and automated reroute authority cannot be established at the forward command by T+0, designate a traffic-control liaison officer at each of the three exits with pre-authorized radio authority to order lane closures or reroutes, reporting status every 15 minutes to the forward command rather than waiting on multistep approval—accepting reduced centralized coordination in exchange for faster local response.
  • If the Boundary Coordination Officer role cannot be filled or cannot communicate reliably with both NPS and state commanders at the corridor crossings, establish a redundant decision protocol: each state highway-patrol on-scene commander is pre-authorized to issue reroutes unilaterally if blockage persists beyond 30 minutes and the UC is unreachable, with a standing order to 'assume control and move traffic' rather than delay for approval.
