Responsible Role Type: Volcanologist & USGS Hazard Forecaster

Steps to Find:

  • Contact USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory (Vancouver, WA office or online portal: https://volcanoes.usgs.gov/observatories/yellowstone/) and request access to real-time monitoring dashboards and weekly eruption-probability briefings.
  • Download monthly USGS Yellowstone monitoring report (published by YVO) covering uplift, seismicity and gas measurements; identify baseline variability and recent deviations.
  • Request any available eruption-scenario modeling or VEI-probability assessments from USGS; clarify which indicators (if any) are established as 'eruption precursors' at Yellowstone vs. other volcanoes.
  • Establish Standing data-sharing agreement with YVO to receive real-time alerts if monitoring parameters exceed established thresholds or if scientists issue any formal eruption forecast.

Access Difficulty: Easy. USGS YVO maintains public real-time seismic and GPS dashboards; scientists are typically available for direct consultation and pre-event coordination calls. Data is non-classified and freely available.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific USGS seismic, GPS, gas-emission and thermal monitoring indicators (uplift rate in mm/year, seismic magnitude thresholds, SO2 flux levels, temperature anomalies) that trigger the pre-authorized escalation from Zone One (100 km) to Scenario Beta (500 km) expansion.
  • Define the baseline normal-range values for each indicator (2020–present historical data) and the threshold values that constitute eruption precursors or VEI-6+ warning signals at Yellowstone Caldera.
  • Quantify the eruption-probability assessment method: how USGS computes or estimates the probability of VEI-6+ eruption within the remaining window (placeholder: VEI-7 probability ≥20%), and what confidence intervals or uncertainty ranges apply.
  • Specify real-time data availability: which monitoring parameters are transmitted to the Unified Command in near-real-time (every 1–6 hours proposed threshold) and which are issued as weekly or formal scientific briefings.
  • List the contact protocols and escalation points: designated USGS liaison officer, YVO scientist on-call during the 72-hour window, and the standing data-sharing agreement that feeds data to the forward command element at Livingston or Bozeman.
  • Document any published USGS Yellowstone eruption-scenario modeling (VEI magnitude distributions, plume height, ashfall footprints, duration estimates) that underpins the shelter-siting strategy and air-quality thresholds in the plan.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague or absent trigger thresholds delay the pre-authorized Scenario Beta order: if USGS indicators lack numerical boundaries, the UC cannot issue the 500 km decision within 30 minutes of the trigger event, slipping decision latency from 30 minutes to 2–4 hours and losing the window for orderly outer-ring evacuation.
  • Baseline-to-anomaly thresholds not established: without historical normal-range data, the UC cannot distinguish between routine monitoring noise and genuine precursor signals, risking either false triggers (premature 500 km expansion straining shelter and road capacity) or missed true precursors (delayed evacuation if a real VEI-6+ sequence begins unrecognized).
  • Eruption-probability methodology not quantified: if USGS cannot express eruption likelihood as a numerical probability or confidence interval, decision-makers cannot calibrate risk thresholds and may anchor on worst-case or dismiss warnings as speculative.
  • Real-time data delivery not specified: if monitoring data is issued only weekly or via email, the UC will lack hourly updates needed to detect rapid escalation and will be forced to make Scenario Beta decisions on stale information, degrading decision quality.
  • USGS liaison role undefined: without a named scientist seated at the forward command or on-call within 15 minutes, gaps in data interpretation could occur during peak decision-making, and conflicting scientific assessments from different USGS offices could confuse the UC.
  • Eruption scenarios not linked to plan triggers: if USGS modeling of ashfall extent, plume height or duration differs from the assumptions in the shelter-siting and air-quality protocols, the plan's protection levels may be inadequate or overstated, affecting shelter placement and supply decisions.

Worst Case Scenario: USGS monitoring data cannot be accessed or interpreted in real-time during the critical first 24 hours of the eruption window. Seismic swarms and uplift accelerate faster than weekly reporting cycles can track; the UC lacks numerical trigger thresholds and cannot authorize the Scenario Beta 500 km order, leaving outer-ring residents (tens of thousands to potentially low hundreds of thousands) without evacuation instructions. Uncontrolled, unguided shadow evacuation begins within 6–12 hours, saturating I-15, I-80 and I-90 with hundreds of thousands of private vehicles. The resulting gridlock prevents the organized evacuation of Zone One (35,800 park evacuees), strands ambulances and hospital transport in traffic, and delays water and fuel convoys beyond 48 hours. An estimated 50–200 preventable deaths result from heat stress, dehydration, respiratory distress and untreated medical emergencies in stalled vehicles. The USGS data gap is the single-point failure that cascades through command, shelter, medical and logistics levers, rendering the entire evacuation plan inoperable.

Best Case Scenario: USGS provides real-time seismic, GPS and gas-emission data to the Unified Command every 1–4 hours, with a named volcanologist seated at the forward element and weekly formal briefings. Trigger thresholds—baseline normal ranges, precursor criteria and the VEI-6+ probability metric—are pre-authorized and embedded in the UC's decision protocol by Month 1 (2026-11-14). When magma signatures cross thresholds at T+3–T+12 hours (within the 72-hour window), the UC issues the Scenario Beta order within 30 minutes, activating the pre-authorized 500 km evacuation rings and secondary-hub destination list. Outer-ring residents receive consistent, credible messages explaining the escalation logic, follow time-banded departure instructions and reach pre-designated secondary hubs (Denver, Cheyenne) via lateral routes. Zone One evacuation completes by T+24 hours; Zone Zero by T+6 hours. Water and fuel convoys arrive on schedule. An estimated 100,000–500,000 additional evacuees beyond Zone One are sheltered safely, ashfall is tracked in real-time and shelter relocations (if needed) occur within 4 hours. Zero preventable deaths attributable to evacuation delays or Scenario Beta decision latency.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If USGS real-time data access is unavailable, establish a standing on-call volcanologist rotation (USGS, university or contracted geophysicist) seated at the forward command 24/7 from T-12 hours onward, with authority to interpret monitoring station data, issue hourly alerts and recommend escalation without waiting for formal USGS briefings.
  • If numerical trigger thresholds cannot be pre-authorized by USGS, use a published precursor framework from a comparable volcano (e.g., Mount St. Helens 1980, Sakurajima, Merapi) to define proxy thresholds—e.g., seismic rate >100 events/day for M>3.0, uplift >10 mm/month, SO2 flux doubling—and apply them as interim decision rules pending USGS endorsement.
  • If real-time data delivery is slow, deploy redundant monitoring equipment (portable seismometers, GPS units, gas samplers) at key locations (Norris, Old Faithful, Mammoth) managed by NPS and National Guard personnel; hourly readings are radioed to the forward command, creating a parallel monitoring net independent of USGS systems.
  • If no USGS liaison is available, designate a UC science advisor (state geologist or academic volcanologist) who is briefed on all monitoring data and authorized to interpret technical assessments, mediate conflicting scientific opinions and advise the UC on escalation decisions in near-real-time.
  • If eruption-scenario modeling is not available from USGS, request the latest peer-reviewed VEI-6 ashfall simulations from academic sources (University of Wyoming, USGS publications) and use them as interim shelter-siting and air-quality assumptions, with explicit disclaimer that actual ashfall may differ.
  • If weekly USGS reporting is the only option, compress it to daily briefings by standing request at T+0, prioritize the specific indicators embedded in the trigger matrix and accept that escalation decisions will be 12–24 hours slower, reducing evacuation lead-time for Scenario Beta.

Find Document 2: NOAA Volcanic Ash Forecast Transport (VAFT) Model Outputs and Wind Forecast Data

ID: 7c60f88d-38a4-4f23-a83c-d28f45f81bfa

Description: Current and historical ashfall-dispersion model output from NOAA's Volcanic Ash Forecast Transport system, showing predicted PM10 concentrations at multiple altitudes and distances from Yellowstone Caldera under various eruption scenarios and wind profiles. Includes 12-hour wind forecasts from Global Forecast System (GFS) and high-resolution local models. Serves as the input for the Shelter Siting Decision Rule (T+6h) and dynamic relocation protocols. Intended audience: Ashfall Forecasting Officer, shelter managers, air-quality specialists. Context: forecast uncertainty is estimated at ±50 km; pre-event access and testing of model output is essential to validating shelter-siting thresholds.

Recency Requirement: Current wind forecasts and VAFT model updates required every 3-6 hours from T-24h through T+72h. Historical ashfall-plume scenarios (e.g., Mount St. Helens 1980, Eyjafjallajökull 2010) useful for model validation and sensitivity analysis.

Responsible Role Type: Ashfall Forecasting and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Officer / Volcanologist & USGS Hazard Forecaster

Steps to Find:

  • Contact NOAA's Hazardous Weather Testbed (Norman, OK) and National Weather Service Forecast Office (Billings or Riverton, WY) to request VAFT model documentation and access to model output.
  • Download high-resolution GFS wind forecasts for the Yellowstone region from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) website or via direct data request.
  • Request any archived ashfall-plume simulations for Yellowstone eruption scenarios (if available) or equivalent documentation from USGS/NOAA describing plume heights, ashfall patterns and concentration profiles for VEI-6 eruptions.
  • Establish pre-event agreement with NOAA to provide 3-hourly VAFT updates and 12-hour wind-forecast products to the forward UC element from T-24h through T+72h, with direct communication to the Ashfall Forecasting Officer.

Access Difficulty: Medium. VAFT model output is available through NOAA, but requires pre-event data-sharing agreements and specific request for Yellowstone-scenario initialization. Wind forecasts are freely available from NCEP.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific ashfall-dispersion thresholds (PM10 concentrations in µg/m³) at which shelter siting becomes untenable and automatic relocation must be triggered at each of the three nominated shelter sites (Bozeman, Idaho Falls, and the third site to be selected at T+6 hours).
  • List the hourly VAFT model output products required from T-24 hours through T+72 hours, including: grid resolution, forecast lead times, PM10/PM2.5 concentration outputs at multiple altitudes, and vertical ash-column height projections.
  • Detail the wind-forecast data inputs that feed the NOAA VAFT model, including GFS grid resolution, update frequency, and any high-resolution local model (NAM, HRRR) data available for Yellowstone-region refinement.
  • Quantify the forecast uncertainty range (currently stated as ±50 km shelter-siting margin) by eruption scenario (VEI-6 vs. VEI-7) and wind-profile class (e.g., winter westerlies, summer ridge circulation).
  • Specify the decision rule linking VAFT model output at T+6 hours to the three ranked shelter sites: which PM10 threshold at each site triggers rejection and escalation to the backup site?
  • Define how historical ashfall case studies (Mount St. Helens 1980, Eyjafjallajökull 2010) inform model validation and sensitivity analysis for Yellowstone-scenario applicability, and list any caveats about model performance under extreme-eruption conditions.
  • Establish the refresh schedule and real-time data handoff: which NWS forecast office (Billings or Riverton) is the primary VAFT output source, what is the communication protocol to the forward UC element Ashfall Forecasting Officer, and what is the fallback if NOAA systems fail?
  • Confirm current access status: can VAFT model output, GFS wind data, and any Yellowstone scenario simulations be downloaded and displayed at a field command post during Month 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) hardening and the actual event, and what pre-event data-sharing agreement must be executed by Month 1 (2026-11-14)?

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Shelter selection at T+6 hours based on inaccurate or outdated ashfall forecasts places 15,000–25,000 evacuees in zones of moderate to heavy ashfall, forcing emergency relocation within 6–12 hours and consuming 3–6 hours of transport, buses and intake capacity during peak operations.
  • VAFT model initialization errors or wind-forecast inconsistencies between GFS and local models lead to conflicting shelter-siting recommendations, causing decision paralysis at the forward UC and delaying shelter assignment by 1–2 hours.
  • Missing or incomplete documentation of forecast uncertainty ranges by eruption scenario and wind profile prevents the Ashfall Forecasting Officer from defending shelter-siting decisions to the UC when actual ashfall diverges from forecast, eroding command credibility.
  • Real-time VAFT output unable to be displayed or updated at the forward UC element due to unclear data-handoff protocols or missing pre-event agreements results in the Ashfall Forecasting Officer relying on manual updates from NOAA via voice-only communication, adding 30–60 minute latency to shelter-siting updates.
  • Forecast model limitations during an unprecedented VEI-7 eruption (ashfall duration, PM10 concentrations, and settling rates potentially far outside historical ranges) not documented in advance leads to public loss of confidence in shelter assignments and triggers unplanned evacuation of shelters.
  • Absence of a fallback ashfall-forecasting method if NOAA systems are ash-contaminated or grid-power-dependent (NCEP, NWS servers) during the event leaves the UC without objective ashfall data for relocation decisions after T+24 hours.

Worst Case Scenario: Pre-event VAFT model access is not established, model output format is unclear, and no data-sharing agreement is in place when Month 0 (2026-10-14) begins. At T+6 hours, the Ashfall Forecasting Officer requests the latest model output but encounters a 2–4 hour NOAA data-processing delay or network outage, forcing shelter-siting decisions to be made on a 12-hour-old forecast. Actual ashfall at T+12 hours diverges sharply from the obsolete forecast, placing 20,000 evacuees in heavy ash (PM10 >200 µg/m³). By T+18 hours, respiratory distress cases at the primary shelter exceed hospital capacity, and the UC orders emergency relocation. The chaotic 6-hour relocation consumes half the available buses, doubles the shelter intake processing time, and strands 500–1,000 evacuees awaiting transport. An estimated 10–20 preventable respiratory-distress hospitalizations and 1–3 deaths occur during the relocation window and its aftermath. Simultaneously, loss of VAFT output after T+24 hours (due to NCEP server failure or ash contamination of local NWS equipment) leaves the UC without an objective basis for further shelter adjustments, forcing decisions based on visual ash depth and evacuation reports alone.

Best Case Scenario: NOAA VAFT model output and GFS wind forecasts are pre-tested and integrated into the forward UC common operating picture by Month 2 (2026-12-14). A signed data-sharing agreement ensures 3-hourly VAFT updates and 12-hour wind-forecast products flow directly to the Ashfall Forecasting Officer from T-24 hours through T+72 hours. At T+6 hours, shelter-siting decisions are made on a current forecast with clearly documented uncertainty bounds (±40 km for VEI-6 scenario under typical wind patterns). Real-time PM10 sensors at each shelter validate forecast accuracy within ±15 µg/m³. When actual ashfall at T+12 hours closely matches the T+6 forecast, evacuee confidence in shelter locations remains high, reducing unplanned departures. A ranked backup shelter 50+ km upwind remains available but is not needed. By T+24 hours, the UC confirms that all three shelters remain suitable under the latest VAFT forecast, eliminating relocation overhead and preserving bus and medical-response capacity for actual emergencies. The Ashfall Forecasting Officer's timely, accurate briefings sustain UC and public trust through the full 72-hour window and any Scenario Beta extension.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If NOAA VAFT model output cannot be accessed in real time during the event, establish a pre-event arrangement with USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory (Vancouver, WA) to provide alternative ashfall-transport calculations (e.g., using ASHFALL or similar operational models) with 1–2 hour update latency via satellite phone to the forward UC.
  • Designate an Ashfall Forecasting Officer with formal training in volcanic ash physics and plume modeling by Month 1 (2026-11-14), who can interpret GFS wind-forecast products directly and make manual ashfall-siting estimates if digital VAFT output is unavailable; pre-produce printed ashfall-scenario lookup tables (plume-height vs. wind-speed vs. PM10 footprint) as hardcopy reference.
  • Establish a 24/7 direct hotline from the forward UC to the NWS Billings (or Riverton) Forecast Office beginning T-24 hours, with a named NWS meteorologist committed to providing 30-minute VAFT briefings by voice even if digital data cannot be transmitted; record briefings for shared-operating-picture documentation.
  • Pre-position a portable weather-radar unit and air-quality monitoring van (equipped with lidar and PM10/PM2.5 sensors) at the forward UC element, capable of observing actual ashfall arrival and fallout patterns in real time; use observed ash depth, visibility and air-quality readings to validate or override VAFT forecasts at T+12, T+18 and T+24 hours.
  • If all external ashfall-forecasting resources are unavailable, activate a conservative fallback rule: at T+6 hours, select shelter sites at the maximum distance (150–200 km) from Yellowstone in all directions (regardless of wind forecast), assume worst-case ashfall footprint extends to all selected sites, and pre-authorize Scenario Beta secondary-hub capacity activation by T+12 hours to begin onward movement of evacuees to sites outside 300 km.
  • Execute an ink-on-paper ashfall-scenario reference manual by Month 1 (2026-11-14), documenting historical case studies (Mount St. Helens, Eyjafjallajökull, Piton de la Fournaise) with ashfall patterns, PM10 concentrations and time-to-arrival charts, cross-referenced to wind-pattern types; print copies for each shelter site and the forward UC so the Ashfall Forecasting Officer can select shelter locations by historical analogy if real-time modeling fails.

Find Document 3: Current Yellowstone National Park Visitor and Staff Census Data

ID: 5bada706-5efa-40fe-848c-e249d21d9790

Description: Current visitor census data for Yellowstone National Park: estimated daily visitor counts by season, lodging occupancy (via Xanterra concession records), campground registrations, backcountry permit issuance rates, and staff employment counts. Provides baseline for the 35,000 tourists and 800 staff estimate in the canonical facts, and enables refinement of shelter-capacity requirements if actual occupancy differs from assumption. Intended audience: Project Manager, shelter planners, population-estimators. Context: the plan assumes 35,800 evacuees for Zone Zero; if actual peak-season occupancy is higher or lower, shelter and corridor capacity calculations must be adjusted.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available year (2024–2025 season data preferred); monthly breakdowns to identify peak occupancy periods and seasonal variation.

Responsible Role Type: Project Manager / Shelter Planner

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Yellowstone National Park Public Affairs office (Mammoth Hot Springs, WY, or online at nps.gov/yell) and request current visitor-use statistics and seasonal occupancy forecasts.
  • Obtain lodging occupancy data from Xanterra Parks and Resorts (concessioner operating all park hotels and campgrounds); request monthly bed-occupancy rates and typical staff counts.
  • Request NPS backcountry permit data: typical number of active permits (by date), geographic distribution of permit holders and average party size.
  • Cross-reference with NPS entrance-fee statistics and vehicle-count data at each of the three main entrances to validate visitor-population estimates.

Access Difficulty: Easy. NPS maintains public visitor-use statistics on its website; Xanterra occupancy data can be requested through official channels (pre-event coordination).

Essential Information:

  • Current visitor census data for Yellowstone National Park: daily visitor counts by season, lodging occupancy rates (Xanterra records), campground registrations, backcountry permit issuance and geographic distribution, and staff employment counts for the most recent full season (2024–2025 preferred).
  • Refinement of the 35,000 tourist + 800 staff baseline: if actual peak-season occupancy differs significantly from 35,800, shelter-capacity and corridor-throughput calculations must be adjusted within the Zone Zero clearance deadline of T+6 hours.
  • Monthly and seasonal occupancy patterns to identify the window of highest concurrent visitor population and determine whether the 35,800 figure represents a reasonable worst-case or a typical peak.
  • Breakdown of visitor origin (domestic vs. international) and estimated share of non-English speakers and mobility-limited visitors to validate the multilingual-alert and assisted-evacuation plans.
  • Lodging and campground distributions across the park (Mammoth, Norris, Canyon, Lake, Old Faithful, West Yellowstone gateway) to tie evacuation corridors to actual visitor clusters and assess whether the three-exit split (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%) matches occupancy distribution.
  • Backcountry permit data: typical number of active permits per day during peak season, geographic spread and average party size, to confirm the 50–100 parties (200–400 people) estimate for the sweep protocol.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Shelter capacity is sized to 35,800 people; if actual peak occupancy is 40,000–50,000, the plan underestimates by 4,000–14,000 evacuees, forcing overcrowding or secondary relocation during the T+6 to T+24 phase and straining water, N95 and fuel supplies by 10–40%.
  • If visitor origin data shows >50% international visitors (vs. the plan's ~40% assumption), multilingual alerts and consular coordination become even more critical, but the plan's five-language coverage may be insufficient for low-incidence populations (e.g., Mandarin, Arabic-speaking visitors).
  • Backcountry permit data uncertainties (actual dispersal, party sizes, compliance with mandatory evacuation orders) directly affect the 'last-person-out' risk; an underestimate of active permits could leave 100–200 unaccounted hikers stranded, requiring secondary extraction during ashfall.
  • If lodging occupancy is concentrated at one gateway (e.g., Old Faithful with 60% of visitors) rather than distributed, the district-to-gate assignment and three-way traffic split become unbalanced, overloading one exit and underutilizing another, extending Zone Zero clearance time.
  • Seasonal variation not captured: if the 72-hour eruption window falls during a low-occupancy season (e.g., late October), the shelter and convoy plans are over-resourced; if during peak summer, they are under-resourced by 20–40%.

Worst Case Scenario: If census data is unavailable or significantly underestimates peak occupancy, the plan may have sized shelters for 35,800 people when actual evacuation demand is 45,000–55,000. A 15,000–20,000 person shortfall in shelter capacity forces either overcrowding with 50–100 additional deaths from dehydration, respiratory distress or medical decompensation, or secondary emergency shelter activation requiring 6–12 additional hours and USD 10–20 million unplanned expenditure. Simultaneously, an underestimate of backcountry permits could leave 200–300 unaccounted hikers, triggering a large-scale SAR operation during ashfall and exposing rescuers to life-threatening conditions. The plan's credibility with public, governors and media collapses if the initial shelter capacity proves demonstrably inadequate within 12 hours of activation.

Best Case Scenario: Current, validated census data confirms the 35,800 baseline as accurate or conservatively high, allowing the plan to size shelters with high confidence and allocate the three-exit split (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%) proportionally to actual lodging and visitor distributions. Backcountry permit data enables a precise sweep strategy and reduces the unaccounted population to <50 people, eliminating last-person-out risk. Visitor-origin and language data refine multilingual alerts to match actual populations, reducing non-compliance and evacuation delays among non-English speakers. Seasonal occupancy patterns identify the time of year when the plan's capacity margins are tightest, enabling prioritized readiness exercises and supply checks for that season.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current season census data (2024–2025) is unavailable, obtain the most recent complete year available (2023–2024) and adjust upward by 2–5% (estimated trend) to account for growth, then conduct a rapid survey of Xanterra lodging managers and NPS entrance rangers during the Month 0 (2026-10-14) preparation phase (T-12 to T-6 hours) to confirm whether occupancy patterns have shifted.
  • If backcountry permit data cannot be obtained from the NPS permit system in time, request Yellowstone ranger district supervisors to provide rapid verbal estimates of active permits during the peak season window and typical party distributions, and increase the sweep reserve from 2–3 last-resort shelters to 4–5 to account for higher uncertainty.
  • If lodging-distribution data is incomplete, assume uniform distribution across gateways and apply a conservative 10% buffer to the smallest exit (East at 7,160 people) to handle route-choice variance and last-minute changes, bringing the East Entrance flow to 7,876 people and reducing the West Entrance from 17,900 to 17,484.
  • If international-visitor origin data shows a significantly higher share (>60%) than the ~40% assumption, engage consular liaison officers 30 days before Month 0 (2026-10-14) to identify additional languages for translation and pre-arrange cultural-liaison volunteers from embassy or community networks in Denver and Salt Lake City.
  • If the eruption window is confirmed to fall outside peak-season months, conduct a sensitivity analysis of the shelter and supply plan under low-occupancy assumptions (e.g., 15,000–20,000 evacuees instead of 35,800) and adjust contingency reserves accordingly, reducing unnecessary pre-positioning cost by USD 5–10 million.

Find Document 4: Zone One Registered Resident Population Census (West Yellowstone, Gardiner, Cody and Surrounding 100 km Radius)

ID: 773771a1-c3cc-4223-9215-45c3086368c1

Responsible Role Type: Project Manager / Emergency Manager (MT, WY counties)

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Madison County, Park County (Montana) and Park County (Wyoming) County Clerk / Emergency Management offices and request current registered resident counts and voter-registration data as proxy for residential population.
  • Download 2020 U.S. Census Bureau data for West Yellowstone city (Madison County, MT), Gardiner census-designated place (Park County, MT) and Cody city (Park County, WY) from census.gov.
  • Request seasonal/transient population estimates from local chambers of commerce (West Yellowstone Chamber, Gardiner Chamber, Cody Chamber) based on hotel and RV-park occupancy data.
  • Coordinate with Montana and Wyoming emergency management to develop a rapid census-update protocol (online survey or phone canvassing) for T+6h status confirmation during the evacuation window.

Access Difficulty: Easy. U.S. Census data is freely available; county population data can be requested from county emergency managers. Seasonal-occupancy estimates require chamber-of-commerce coordination but are typically available.

Essential Information:

  • Registered resident population count for West Yellowstone (Madison County, MT), Gardiner (Park County, MT), Cody (Park County, WY) and the surrounding 100 km radius Zone One area, broken down by permanent residents, seasonal residents, and transient occupants (hotels, RVs, campgrounds).
  • Baseline population figures from the 2020 U.S. Census and 2024–2025 county estimates to serve as the denominator for Zone One evacuation success metric (Gate G2: 95% of registered residents evacuated by T+24 hours).
  • Current hotel, motel, RV park and campground occupancy rates and typical maximum capacity during peak season to estimate transient population at the time of the eruption window.
  • Seasonal resident population counts and arrival/departure patterns to estimate occupancy during the 72-hour decision window (Month 0, October 2026).
  • Census tract-level or neighborhood-scale resident distribution across the three gateway communities to support shelter-capacity allocation and evacuation-traffic routing by district.
  • A rapid census-update protocol or survey mechanism (online form, phone canvassing script, concessioner coordination) that can be executed at T+6 hours to confirm current occupancy and account for visitors who may have left the zone or arrived between the last Census update and the event.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Underestimated Zone One resident population results in undersized shelter capacity, forcing evacuees into overflow sites that lack water, medical triage or reunification services, increasing respiratory distress and missed-reunification incidents by an estimated 10–20%.
  • Outdated or incomplete seasonal-resident counts leave 500–2,000 transient occupants (hotel guests, RV campers) unaccounted for in shelter planning, creating a gap between assumed and actual shelter demand and delaying intake by 2–4 hours.
  • Absence of a T+6 hour census-update protocol means Gate G2 success metric (95% of registered residents out) cannot be verified or defended; incident commander lacks defensible clearance status to begin Zone One Phase 2 closure and perimeter enforcement.
  • Inaccurate district-scale population distribution across West Yellowstone, Gardiner and Cody leads to misallocation of evacuation traffic to the three exits (West, North, East), causing overload at one corridor and underutilization of others, extending peak evacuation time by 1–2 hours.
  • Missing occupancy data for peak-season hotels and RV parks in October 2026 forces shelter-capacity planning to use worst-case estimates (100% occupancy assumed), over-committing shelter space and straining supply convoys, or under-estimates (50% occupancy assumed), leaving 1,000–3,000 evacuees unsheltered.

Worst Case Scenario: Zone One resident population is unquantified at T+0 hours. Shelter capacity planning assumes 25,000–35,000 occupants based on the 2020 Census plus estimates of seasonal residents and tourists. At T+6 hours, when Gate G2 requires confirmation that 95% of registered residents are out, the incident commander cannot verify this metric because no authoritative current census exists. Meanwhile, actual occupancy at gateway communities may be 40,000–45,000 (peak season, 50% above estimate), overwhelming pre-staged shelters designed for 35,800. Unaccounted-for evacuees (5,000–10,000 people) cluster at secondary shelters and lodging outside the plan, creating shadow evacuation that saturates roads to Billings and Salt Lake City and delays organized medical evacuation by 4–6 hours. Two to five preventable deaths occur due to delayed shelter intake and respiratory care.

Best Case Scenario: A current census of West Yellowstone, Gardiner, Cody and surrounding 100 km radius is obtained from county emergency-management offices and the 2020 Census by T+0 hours. Seasonal-occupancy data from chambers of commerce confirm that peak-season (October 2026) transient population adds 3,000–5,000 to the baseline resident count, yielding a Zone One total of 12,000–18,000 registered residents and estimated 17,000–23,000 actual occupants including tourists. Shelter capacity planning is right-sized to 35,800 (Bozeman 15,000, Idaho Falls 10,000, third site 10,800), with no excess or shortage. A T+6 hour census-update protocol (rapid phone survey or online form) confirms that 95% of registered residents have exited, supporting Gate G2 approval. Perimeter enforcement and Scenario Beta escalation proceed without delay. No shelter relocations are needed; all evacuees reach adequate intake and medical triage within 4 hours.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Request emergency Census Bureau recount or American Community Survey extraction for the three gateway towns from the U.S. Census Bureau's emergency-data hotline within 6 hours of declaration, using 2024–2025 population estimates and decay models to project October 2026 occupancy.
  • Engage Montana and Wyoming emergency-management officials to request that county voter-registration offices and property-tax assessor records be searched for registered resident counts at the Zone One addresses within 4 hours of T+0.
  • Coordinate with Xanterra Parks and Resorts (park concessioner) to extract lodge and campground guest manifests from their reservation system at T+0, providing a real-time snapshot of transient occupancy at that moment.
  • Activate local chambers of commerce in West Yellowstone, Gardiner and Cody to conduct a rapid telephone or email survey of major hotels, motels and RV parks at T+0, asking for current occupancy rates and capacity during the peak season.
  • Develop and pre-authorize a simple SMS or online form survey that can be deployed at shelters at T+6 hours (via IPAWS or local radio), asking evacuees to confirm their pre-event residence (Zone One or elsewhere) and provide a count of persons in their household, generating a real-time tally of actual occupancy.
  • Designate a fallback shelter-capacity assumption (worst-case: 50,000 occupants including unplanned shadow evacuees) and pre-authorize activation of 1–2 additional tertiary shelters (e.g., university dormitories or fairground facilities) in Billings or Boise if the T+6 census shows occupancy above 40,000.

Find Document 5: Existing Regional Hospital Bed Capacity, Emergency Department Surge Plans and Current Staffing Rosters

ID: 5107aec8-e81d-4dd8-91f0-21ce7950c3f6

Description: Current bed-capacity inventories, emergency-department surge protocols and staffing rosters for the three designated receiving hospitals (Bozeman Deaconess Medical Center, Livingston HealthCare, Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center, Idaho Falls). Intended audience: Hospital Surge Dispersal Officer, hospital administrators, public health officer. Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025) hospital census data, bed-capacity inventories and staffing rosters.

Responsible Role Type: Public Health & Mass-Casualty Medical Logistics Director / Hospital Administrator

Steps to Find:

  • Contact administrative offices of Bozeman Deaconess Medical Center, Livingston HealthCare and Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center directly and request current bed-capacity inventories, ED surge plans and staffing rosters (may require formal data-sharing agreement and confidentiality assurance).
  • Request any existing hospital emergency operations plans or disaster-response protocols that address mass-casualty surge or infectious-disease isolation.
  • Obtain Ambulance Services and EMS routing data from county EMS coordinators to understand current patient-transport capacity and hospital destination protocols.
  • Coordinate with state health departments (Montana, Wyoming, Idaho) to obtain aggregate hospital-capacity data and mutual-aid surge-capacity estimates from other hospitals in the region.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Hospital bed-capacity and staffing data are sensitive (federal reporting required for Medicare facilities); access requires pre-event formal coordination and confidentiality agreements. State health departments may have aggregate data available.

Essential Information:

  • Obtain current (2024–2025) bed-capacity inventories (ICU, trauma, respiratory beds) from each of the three designated receiving hospitals (Bozeman Deaconess Medical Center, Livingston HealthCare, Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center, Idaho Falls).
  • Document baseline staffing rosters: emergency physicians, respiratory therapists, nurses, and any mass-casualty/disaster-surge expansion protocols currently in place at each facility.
  • Quantify existing emergency-department surge-capacity protocols: maximum additional beds that can be opened, estimated time to activate each surge level, and staffing assumptions for each level.
  • Identify any pre-existing disaster-response plans or pandemic-surge protocols that address respiratory care, isolation capabilities, or mass-casualty triage at each hospital.
  • Confirm current ambulance transport capacity and EMS routing protocols to the three hospitals, including any mutual-aid arrangements with other regional facilities.
  • Identify staffing gaps specific to respiratory-care surge: respiratory therapist availability, ventilator inventory, and any existing agreements for surge staffing from other facilities or traveling providers.
  • Obtain state-level aggregate hospital-capacity data from Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho health departments to identify backup surge hospitals beyond the three named facilities.
  • List any existing memoranda of understanding (MOUs) or mutual-aid agreements between the three hospitals and other regional facilities for patient transfers, staffing, or resource sharing during emergencies.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate bed-capacity data leads to over-estimation of receiving-hospital surge capability, causing dispersal officers to assign more patients to facilities than can realistically be accommodated, resulting in overcrowding, delayed care and preventable patient deterioration.
  • Outdated or incomplete staffing rosters mask actual physician, nurse and respiratory-therapist shortages, leading to assignment of patient loads that exceed available clinical staff and causing care-quality collapse and mortality increases during peak ashfall.
  • Missing existing surge protocols means the plan duplicates or conflicts with hospital internal operations, reducing coordination during the event and delaying activation of additional beds or staff.
  • Lack of clarity on EMS routing and ambulance capacity creates bottlenecks at hospital entrances, backing up emergency transports and leaving patients on stretchers outside overflowing emergency departments for hours.
  • Absence of pre-existing respiratory-therapist or ventilator surge agreements leaves hospitals unable to meet the modeled respiratory-distress surge (estimate: 500–2,000 patients over 72 hours), forcing rationing of ventilators and withholding of care from patients who could otherwise survive.
  • Failure to identify backup hospitals outside the three named facilities leaves the plan with no fallback if one facility loses power, becomes damaged, or is overwhelmed beyond its surge capacity, concentrating all load on the remaining two hospitals.
  • Gaps in state-level mutual-aid arrangements mean hospitals cannot rapidly access surge staffing or equipment from neighboring states, extending patient-care delays and cascading failures across the regional system.

Worst Case Scenario: ">A hospital surge plan based on inaccurate or outdated bed-capacity and staffing data could result in one or more receiving hospitals reaching functional capacity by T+12 to T+18 hours (during peak ashfall), after which new emergency patients cannot be admitted. Ambulances divert to distant facilities 100+ km away, extending transport times to 2–4 hours and leaving severe respiratory-distress and trauma patients untreated for critical periods. If respiratory-therapist shortages prevent full ventilator deployment, 10–20 patients with salvageable acute respiratory distress die due to lack of available mechanical ventilation. A power loss at one hospital coupled with delayed fuel-convoy arrival (due to inaccurate logistics assumptions) extends the outage to 4–6 hours, forcing manual ventilation and cancellation of surgeries, with an additional 5–10 preventable deaths. The cascade of hospital failures erodes public confidence in the medical response, increases uncontrolled flight from shelter to distant hospitals and reduces compliance with evacuation orders, adding 2–4 hours to overall evacuation time. Estimated worst-case: 20–50 preventable hospital deaths, 1,000–3,000 patients in delayed or degraded care, regional medical system destabilization lasting weeks.

Best Case Scenario: ">With accurate, current hospital bed-capacity and staffing data, the Hospital Surge Dispersal Officer can validate and right-size patient-distribution assignments, ensuring each of the three receiving hospitals is loaded to realistic surge capacity without overcrowding. Pre-existing surge protocols and staffing agreements are identified and integrated into the response plan, enabling smooth activation of additional beds and staff within the first 2–4 hours of patient arrival. Backup hospitals outside the three named facilities are confirmed and pre-briefed, providing a fallback if one facility faces capacity or power constraints. Respiratory-therapist and ventilator surge agreements are formalized by Month 1 (2026-11-14), eliminating uncertainty and enabling rapid deployment of travel staff or shared equipment during peak demand. EMS routing is optimized so ambulances reach appropriate receiving hospitals within 45–60 minutes, reducing out-of-hospital time and enabling early intervention. All 500–2,000 modeled respiratory-distress cases receive timely admission and mechanical ventilation; trauma and chronic-disease patients are distributed evenly across the network. Hospital power and life-support systems remain operational throughout the 72-hour event due to pre-positioned fuel reserves and proven generator startup protocols. Estimated best case: zero preventable hospital deaths, all acutely ill patients receive appropriate care within the modeled system capacity, regional medical system maintains public confidence and operational continuity.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Contact hospital chief medical officers and chief nursing officers at each of the three receiving facilities directly by T+6 hours (within the response window) to request immediate bed-capacity and staffing confirmations verbally or via secure email; document in real time rather than rely on pre-event data if current documentation cannot be obtained before Month 0 (2026-10-14).
  • Request aggregate hospital-capacity data from state health departments (Montana, Wyoming, Idaho) and the CMS/Medicare hospital database to estimate surge capacity if individual hospital data-sharing agreements cannot be executed pre-event.
  • Engage a health-system consultant or hospital-capacity modeling firm in Month 1 (2026-11-14) to conduct a rapid audit of the three receiving hospitals and surrounding regional facilities, prioritizing respiratory-care and ICU surge analysis.
  • Establish a standing daily coordination call with hospital administrators at each facility from T+0 through T+72, using real-time occupancy and staffing reports to dynamically adjust patient-distribution assignments and identify bottlenecks in real time.
  • Pre-authorize mutual-aid requests to non-designated regional hospitals (Billings, Bozeman, Salt Lake City) and identify them as secondary dispersal destinations if the three named facilities approach capacity; include telephone and data-exchange pre-agreements.
  • Conduct a Hospital Surge Exercise with the three receiving hospitals and their EMS partners by Month 2 (2026-12-14), simulating a mass-casualty arrival and testing bed-activation, patient-triage and staffing-deployment protocols, with results fed into the final operational plan.
  • Arrange for rotating respiratory-therapy and nursing surge staffing from adjacent health systems or traveling healthcare-provider agencies (e.g., American Red Cross Disaster Health Services, state-level medical reserve corps) with verbal agreements by T+0 and signed contracts by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

Find Document 6: Existing Yellowstone National Park Concessioner Operational Data (Lodging Occupancy, Staff Rosters, Transportation Fleet)

ID: d57f35c4-4e32-43dd-a64b-a8b280ab4b13

Description: Operational data from Xanterra Parks and Resorts (primary NPS concessioner): current guest-room inventory and occupancy forecasts, staff employment rosters (count and job functions), shuttle-bus fleet capacity and scheduling, and visitor-transportation logistics. Serves as input for visitor-needs assessment (language, mobility, vehicle-less populations) and assisted-evacuation planning. Intended audience: Communications Coordinator, visitor-needs planner, transportation logistics officer. Context: concessioners manage ~90% of visitor accommodation and some visitor transport; pre-event data access enables targeted multilingual outreach and transport pre-positioning.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025 season) occupancy forecasts, staff rosters and fleet inventory.

Responsible Role Type: Communications and Public Alerting Coordinator / Shelter Planner

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Xanterra Parks and Resorts operational headquarters (located near Mammoth or in Denver) and request operational data-sharing agreement covering lodging occupancy, staff rosters, guest-contact information and transportation capacity.
  • Request manifests of current guests at each lodge (rooms occupied, check-in/check-out dates, nationality/language preferences if available from reservation systems).
  • Obtain shuttle-bus inventory and capacity: number of buses, typical routes, seating capacity, and driver availability during peak operations.
  • Request any existing concessioner emergency plans or disaster-response protocols.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Concessioner operational data is sensitive (commercially confidential for occupancy and forecasts); requires signed data-sharing agreement with Xanterra and NPS. Pre-event coordination is expected and typically feasible.

Essential Information:

  • Specify the operational data fields required from Xanterra Parks and Resorts: current guest-room occupancy by lodge, staff employment count by job function (drivers, kitchen, housekeeping, management), shuttle-bus fleet inventory (number of buses, seating capacity, current deployment schedule), and any existing concessioner emergency-response protocols or evacuation procedures.
  • Quantify visitor-composition data: percentage of non-English-speaking guests by language group, percentage of guests arriving via tour operator (vehicle-less), percentage with mobility or medical-assistance needs, and typical length of stay by guest type (day-use vs. overnight).
  • Confirm date ranges for occupancy forecasts: peak-season occupancy rates for the months of August–October (the eruption-window months), including weekday versus weekend variation and holiday or event effects that might drive occupancy higher or lower.
  • Obtain staff rosters: employee names, contact information, job titles, shift schedules and languages spoken, so that multilingual volunteers and evacuation-assistance personnel can be pre-identified and pre-briefed before T+0.
  • Detail shuttle-bus operational schedules: typical daily routes (lodge to park attractions, inter-lodge transport, visitor center loops), number of scheduled departures per route, current driver availability and willingness to participate in emergency evacuation, and fuel-consumption rates to estimate contingency fuel needs.
  • Identify any concessioner facilities outside the park that could serve as auxiliary shelter or staging areas (e.g., maintenance yards, storage depots, administrative offices), with capacity and utility-service capability (water, power, sanitation).
  • Request any existing data-sharing agreements or emergency-coordination protocols between Xanterra and NPS, so that data access procedures and approval chains are pre-established by Month 0 (2026-10-14).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate or outdated occupancy data leads to overestimation or underestimation of the 35,000-person evacuation load; if actual occupancy is 20–30% higher or lower than planned, contraflow throughput and shelter capacity calculations are invalidated, forcing real-time capacity revisions during the evacuation peak.
  • Missing or incomplete staff rosters prevent pre-identification of multilingual staff or experienced drivers needed for evacuation shuttles and language support; last-minute staffing recruitment during T+0 to T+12 h is unreliable and leaves non-English-speaking guests without clear guidance.
  • Underestimated non-English-speaking visitor population (if concessioner data shows only 10–15% instead of actual 30–40%) leaves 5,000–10,000 evacuees without multilingual alerts, causing 1–3 hour delays and increased non-compliance with shelter-assignment instructions.
  • Inaccurate shuttle-bus capacity or availability data (if fleet is smaller or less flexible than assumed) strands 500–2,000 vehicle-less guests and forces unplanned secondary-evacuation logistics during peak contraflow congestion.
  • Lack of pre-established data-sharing protocol with Xanterra results in 6–12 hour delays in obtaining operational manifests at T+0, missing the window to pre-brief staff and confirm guest-contact information for targeted multilingual outreach.

Worst Case Scenario: Concessioner operational data is unavailable until T+6 hours or is incomplete (missing staff lists, guest languages, vehicle-less population), forcing real-time guest identification via manual lodge surveys during the evacuation peak. As a result, up to 10,000–15,000 non-English-speaking or vehicle-less guests receive no pre-evacuation briefing, experience delays of 2–4 hours in understanding route instructions or boarding evacuation shuttles, and some become separated from their transportation groups. Approximately 200–500 guests are stranded at lodges or trailheads when shuttles depart without confirmation of occupancy, requiring secondary rescue operations after T+6 h. This gap also prevents pre-identification of multilingual staff and experienced drivers, forcing ad-hoc recruitment of volunteers during the evacuation, reducing the reliability and speed of assisted-evacuation shuttles and multilingual outreach. The combination results in an estimated 2–4 hour delay in Zone Zero clearance and 5–10 preventable casualties among elderly, mobility-limited or medically fragile guests.

Best Case Scenario: Concessioner operational data is obtained by Month 0 (2026-10-14) via a pre-signed data-sharing agreement, providing current occupancy forecasts, complete staff rosters, shuttle-bus schedules and guest-language preferences. This enables pre-production of multilingual briefing materials, pre-identification of 20–50 multilingual staff and experienced drivers, pre-assignment of shuttle buses to lodges, and advance preparation of priority-evacuation staging areas for mobility-limited guests. At T+0, lodge staff can immediately brief guests in their preferred languages using pre-produced materials, and evacuations begin with confirmed transportation arrangements. Vehicle-less guests and those with mobility or medical needs are staged for priority-evacuation shuttles before general traffic departs, reducing bottlenecks. Evacuation of non-English-speaking guests is accelerated to 30–45 minutes per lodge, and Zone Zero clearance is achieved within 5.5 hours, providing a safety margin before ashfall intensity increases. Approximately 99% of 35,800 evacuees depart with clear instructions and assigned transportation, avoiding stranding incidents.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Xanterra data-sharing agreement is not finalized by Month 0 (2026-10-14), request that NPS issue an emergency administrative order for concessioner data access under the Stafford Act declaration at T+0, citing public-safety necessity. Legal authority exists; execution may take 2–4 hours but avoids weeks of negotiation.
  • If current occupancy forecasts are unavailable, use historical occupancy records (prior 2–3 years) for the eruption-window months (August–October) to estimate a probability range (high/medium/low occupancy scenario) and plan shelters for the high-occupancy case (35,000 is the user constraint, so assume peak load).
  • If staff rosters are not provided, establish a concessioner hotline at T+0 with lodging managers at each property, request same-day employee lists by phone, and use volunteer-sign-up forms at each lodge to identify multilingual and evacuation-trained staff in real time.
  • If shuttle-bus capacity is lower than assumed, requisition additional charter buses from regional operators (contract with Greyhound, tour operators) using FEMA emergency-contract vehicles, with 4-hour mobilization clauses in pre-awarded agreements.
  • If guest-language data is absent, produce multilingual briefing materials in the five most common visitor languages (Spanish, Japanese, German, Mandarin, French) at Month 0 (2026-10-14) based on national visitor-pattern benchmarks, and distribute them to all lodges at T-12 hours; follow up with live interpretation at check-in desks if real-time language identification is possible.
  • If concessioner facilities cannot be accessed for secondary staging, designate parks, schools and fairgrounds in West Yellowstone, Gardiner and Cody as auxiliary shelters by Month 0 (2026-10-14), with pre-arranged utility and security access.

Find Document 7: Bottled Water, N95 Respirator, Generator Fuel and Emergency Supply Industry Capacity and Pricing Data

Steps to Find:

  • Contact medical-supply rental companies (emergency shelter equipment, cots, generators) and request rapid-deployment inventory and pricing.
  • Consult Federal Emergency Management documentation on FEMA contract vehicle activation and pre-positioned supply strategies for disasters.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Industry data is commercially sensitive; requires direct corporate inquiry and pre-event negotiations. State emergency management agencies may have supplier contact rosters from prior disaster agreements.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current industry capacity (liters per day, units per month) for bottled-water production and emergency distribution in the Mountain West (Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, Idaho) from major suppliers (Coca-Cola, Nestlé, regional distributors).
  • List maximum emergency-order capacity and lead times (hours to dispatch, days to delivery) for N95 respirators from 3M, Honeywell and medical-supply distributors, specifying stock available for immediate allocation versus manufacturing-lead inventory.
  • Quantify diesel generator fuel distribution capacity across the region: regional storage, tanker-truck availability, wholesale pricing and surge-mobilization timelines from major fuel distributors (Yellowstone Energy, Basin Fuel, regional refineries).
