  • Specify FEMA pre-positioned contract vehicles, surge-activation procedures, vendor rosters and cost-share mechanisms for emergency water, fuel and supply procurement.
  • Compare post-COVID supply-chain disruption recovery status and current pricing against 2024–2025 market benchmarks for each supply category.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate or outdated industry-capacity data leads to overestimation of water-convoy dispatch speed, causing T+12 h dispatch target to become unachievable and convoys arriving T+24–T+36 h instead, leaving shelters with 12–24 hours of inadequate water supply.
  • Underestimated N95 respirator lead times or stock cause initial 100,000-unit allocation to prove insufficient, forcing emergency resupply that arrives too late, leaving shelters and responders without masks during peak ashfall.
  • Inaccurate fuel-distribution capacity or pricing overstates the feasibility of 72-hour generator reserves at three hospitals, risking grid-failure scenarios in which fuel does not arrive within the 4–6 hour window needed to prevent surgical cancellations and ventilator failures.
  • Missing or incomplete FEMA contract-vehicle details prevent verbal activation and 12-hour dispatch, reverting to standard 24–48 hour procurement, delaying all supply arrival by 1–2 days.
  • Omission of regional supplier contact rosters and pre-event pricing locks the plan into worst-case commercial terms at emergency rates, consuming budget contingency without improving actual delivery timelines.

Worst Case Scenario: Industry data is unavailable, severely outdated or commercially withheld, forcing the plan to assume worst-case lead times and capacity constraints at Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+0). Convoys dispatch 12–24 hours late due to unknowable supplier constraints; N95 stock proves insufficient by T+48 h and cannot be rapidly resupplied; hospital fuel reserves fall short of 72-hour needs. Shelters experience water shortages from T+24 to T+36 h affecting 15,000–20,000 evacuees, and respiratory-protection gaps leave thousands unmasked during peak ashfall. These shortfalls force emergency procurement at 2–3x normal cost, consuming the USD 40 million contingency within 24 hours and leaving no reserve for shelter relocation, Scenario Beta hub staging or additional responder calls. The plan's credibility with shelter operators and host communities collapses, reducing voluntary compliance with evacuation and shelter-placement orders by 15–20%.

Best Case Scenario: Current industry capacity and pre-event pricing data are obtained from all major suppliers by Month 1 (2026-11-14), confirming that water convoys can be mobilized within 12 hours from Salt Lake City and arrive at shelters by T+18–T+24 h (within acceptable bounds). N95 manufacturers confirm 200,000–300,000 units available for emergency order, doubling the civilian stock. FEMA contract vehicles include 15–20 pre-authorized fuel and water vendors, enabling verbal activation and guaranteed 12-hour dispatch. Pricing for all supplies is locked in advance at 2024–2025 commercial rates. These confirmations allow the plan's supply-chain milestones to proceed on schedule: forward depots stocked by T-12 h (within the 72-hour window), no bottleneck delays, and USD 15–25 million of the USD 40 million contingency freed for Scenario Beta hub pre-positioning and shelter-relocation reserves.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If industry data cannot be obtained directly due to corporate confidentiality, request aggregate capacity summaries from state emergency management agencies (Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Utah emergency management offices) who maintain standing vendor rosters and post-disaster supplier agreements.
  • If lead-time data is incomplete or dated, conduct a 72-hour pilot water-convoy mobilization from Salt Lake City to Bozeman during Month 2 (2026-12-14) to measure actual dispatch and transit time under realistic ashfall and traffic conditions, using this empirical result instead of industry estimates.
  • If FEMA contract-vehicle details are sparse, escalate to the FEMA Region VIII supply chain coordinator (Denver RRCC) at Month 1 (2026-11-14) to obtain current vendor lists, surge-activation authorities and pre-positioned equipment rosters that already exist in FEMA systems.
  • If hospital fuel and generator capacity cannot be confirmed with precision, conduct a 24-hour power-outage simulation at each receiving hospital (Bozeman, Livingston, Idaho Falls) during Month 2 (2026-12-14), testing actual generator startup, fuel consumption and load-shedding under stress to measure realistic endurance.
  • If commercial pricing is unavailable, use GSA Federal Supply Schedule rates as a floor estimate and confirm with FEMA whether Stafford Act declaration authority allows emergency price adjustments, ensuring budget contingency is sized appropriately.

Find Document 8: FEMA Region 8 and Region 10 Mutual Aid and Emergency Support Function (ESF) Resource Inventories

ID: 425089ab-8957-4fc5-8b04-e28ea2697075

Description: Current mutual-aid rosters and Emergency Support Function resource inventories for FEMA Regions 8 (Denver, covering Colorado, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah, Wyoming) and Region 10 (Seattle, covering Alaska, Idaho, Oregon, Washington). Includes Guard unit locations and availability, pre-positioned supply stocks, medical-surge resources and transportation capacity. Serves as input for responder relief depth, supply-chain and military-asset pre-positioning planning. Intended audience: UC Incident Commander, Region 10 Liaison Officer, logistics directors. Context: the plan assumes access to Guard units and mutual-aid resources; this documentation enables specific asset identification and pre-event commitments.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025) mutual-aid rosters and ESF inventories; any recent updates to unit locations or resource availability.

Responsible Role Type: Regional Emergency Management & Multi-Jurisdiction Coordination Director / FEMA Region 10 Liaison Officer

Steps to Find:

  • Contact FEMA Regional Administrators (Region 8, Denver office and Region 10, Seattle office) and request current mutual-aid rosters and ESF resource inventories.
  • Request National Guard unit rosters and availability: location of Guard units in Colorado, Montana, Wyoming and Idaho; air assets (helicopters, cargo planes) in the region; personnel available for emergency deployment.
  • Request state emergency management agency contact lists for mutual-aid coordination (each state's Emergency Management Division).
  • Obtain EMAC (Emergency Management Assistance Compact) resource lists for the relevant states and neighboring states.

Access Difficulty: Medium. FEMA regional resource data is partially restricted (Guard unit locations may be sensitive); requires pre-event formal coordination with FEMA regional administrators. State emergency management agencies maintain public mutual-aid rosters.

Essential Information:

  • Identify current (2024–2025) mutual-aid rosters and Emergency Support Function resource inventories for FEMA Region 8 (Denver: Colorado, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah, Wyoming) and Region 10 (Seattle: Alaska, Idaho, Oregon, Washington), including specific resource counts and deployment availability.
  • List all National Guard unit locations and personnel availability in Colorado, Montana, Wyoming and Idaho, including active-duty and reserve strength by unit type (infantry, logistics, medical, signal corps, aviation).
  • Quantify air assets available in Region 8 and Region 10: helicopter count and type by location, cargo-aircraft availability, medevac-capable platforms and crew readiness.
  • Detail Emergency Support Function (ESF) resource inventories by function: transportation (buses, trucks), water and sanitation supplies, medical surge capacity (field hospitals, ambulances, personnel), generator fuel and power restoration equipment, communications equipment and personnel.
  • Specify pre-positioned supply stocks in Region 8 and Region 10: bottled water reserves, medical consumables, fuel depots, tents and sheltering materials, and locations where stocks are held.
  • Document mutual-aid activation procedures: which state agencies hold mutual-aid agreements with federal and neighboring-state partners, contact information for duty officers and resource request chains, and response-time estimates for deploying personnel and equipment across state lines.
  • Confirm EMAC (Emergency Management Assistance Compact) participation and current resource commitments by Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Colorado and neighboring states; list any standing requests or conflicts.
  • Identify specific ESF coordinators (primary and backup) for each function in Region 8 and Region 10, with contact information and authority to commit resources during emergency declaration.
  • Provide current assessment of medical-surge capacity: number of field hospital sets deployable, ambulance and transport availability, medical personnel (doctors, nurses, paramedics) and respiratory-support equipment (ventilators, oxygen, CPAP units) not committed to permanent assignments.
  • Specify the Authority and Limitation Statement for FEMA Region 10: under what conditions does a Region 8 incident commander hold authority to request Region 10 resources without separate regional director approval, and what cost-sharing rules apply?

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Resource counts are overstated or unavailable: UC incident commander cannot pre-authorize specific Guard units or mutual-aid assets at T+0, forcing real-time requests that incur 2–4 hour delays and leave the plan dependent on whatever happens to be available rather than committed reserves.
  • Regional mutual-aid procedures are out of date: pre-event coordination calls with state emergency management directors discover that mutual-aid rosters list units since relocated, merged or deactivated, requiring verification and re-coordination during the crisis window.
  • FEMA Region 10 liaison seat at the Unified Command cannot be filled because Seattle regional office has no standing delegation to support Region 8 decisions, forcing ad hoc coordination that delays Idaho-side requests (water convoys, fuel, ambulances) by 1–2 hours.
  • Medical-surge capacity is overstated because field hospitals and ambulance resources are committed to existing state readiness exercises or permanent assignments, leaving the actual available surge much smaller than the inventory lists.
  • Air-asset availability is unclear: Guard helicopter schedules, maintenance status and pilot availability are not documented, so a request for medevac sorties during ashfall meets resistance or discovers assets are unavailable due to competing demands.
  • Fuel depot locations and volumes are not confirmed: convoys dispatched from listed depots in Salt Lake City or Denver discover stocks have been drawn down for other emergencies or depots lack the trucking equipment to load quickly, adding 6–12 hours to delivery.
  • Incomplete contact lists and duty-officer rosters: after-hours mutual-aid requests cannot reach authorized decision-makers, forcing escalation through political channels and consuming 1–2 hours of decision latency at critical moments.
  • Generator fuel pre-positioning agreements with utilities are verbal or expired: hospitals and shelters receive fuel promises that are not honored when the supplier's own grid restoration consumes available stock.
  • Communications equipment (radios, satellites, repeaters) inventories are not interoperable across federal, state and Guard systems, forcing signal-corps teams to spend hours on frequency coordination during the event rather than having it pre-tested.
  • Cost-sharing and reimbursement rules between FEMA regions are ambiguous: disputes over who pays for Region 10 resources requested by Region 8 UC delay reimbursement and discourage mutual aid, reducing the pool of available assets.

Worst Case Scenario: Without current, verified mutual-aid rosters and ESF inventories, the Unified Command cannot pre-authorize specific Guard units, helicopters, medical surge or fuel convoys at T+0, forcing real-time scavenging of resources during the 72-hour evacuation window. A discovery that assumed assets are unavailable, committed elsewhere or incompatible cascades into delays: medical patients are held at shelters 2–4 hours waiting for ambulances that must be summoned ad hoc; water convoys discover depots lack trucking and loading equipment, delaying arrival from T+12 h to T+24+ h; National Guard signal teams discover radios are on incompatible frequencies, forcing 2–4 hours of field coordination when digital comms fail. These delays—multiplied across 35,800 evacuees, 15,000 at shelters, 5–10 hospitals and 10+ control points—extend the evacuation peak by 4–8 hours, overlapping ashfall onset and increasing respiratory casualties by 50–100+ people and stranding 1,000–3,000 evacuees without shelter or water. A regional mutual-aid freeze due to cost-sharing disputes could reduce available personnel and fuel by 30–50%, making the plan execution-impossible. Estimated total impact: failed evacuation, estimated 50–200+ preventable deaths, multi-state incident escalation and international attention on a catastrophic response failure.

Best Case Scenario: Current, verified mutual-aid rosters and ESF inventories enable the Unified Command to seat a FEMA Region 10 liaison at T+0 and pre-authorize specific Guard units (e.g., Colorado 10th Special Forces Group signal platoons, Wyoming Army Guard transportation company, Idaho National Guard medical team) with confirmed personnel counts, equipment and deployment times. Pre-coordinated cost-sharing and mutual-aid agreements remove the need for approval chains, allowing verbal resource requests to move from the forward command to regional duty officers with 30-minute response times. Helicopters, ambulances and fuel convoys are committed in writing 60 days before the event, so requests trigger pre-authorized dispatch rather than ad hoc searches. Medical surge and field hospital availability is confirmed, allowing the plan to size evacuation-shelter medical staffing with confidence. Interoperable communications equipment (radios on pre-coordinated frequencies, satellite terminals tested) is pre-positioned, so signal teams activate systems quickly rather than troubleshooting compatibility. Water and fuel convoys depart on schedule from verified depots with confirmed trucking and loading, arriving at shelters within the T+24 h target. The effect: the plan executes with predictability, responders know their resources are committed, decision latency drops from ad hoc hours to minutes, and the evacuation completes by T+6 h without stranded evacuees or supply shortfalls. Estimated total impact: evacuations complete, water and medical resources sustain shelters, fewer than 10 preventable casualties, confidence in the response and international recognition of effective disaster coordination.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If FEMA Region 8 and Region 10 current rosters cannot be obtained in time: convene an emergency coordination call with the FEMA Regional Administrators and the state Emergency Management Directors (Colorado, Montana, Wyoming, Idaho) at Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 1 week (around 2026-10-21) to collect current unit locations, personnel counts and mutual-aid status verbally; document the call and have each director sign a confirmation memo of their commitments within 48 hours. Use the signed memos as the binding mutual-aid agreement for the plan.
  • If pre-positioned supply-stock locations and volumes cannot be verified: conduct a site survey of all candidate depots (Salt Lake City water distribution centers, Denver fuel terminals, Colorado and Montana Guard armories) by Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 2 weeks (around 2026-10-28), physically verifying inventory on hand, equipment condition and loading capacity; base the plan on observed stocks, not on roster claims.
  • If Region 10 liaison authority and cost-sharing are unclear: request a written legal opinion from FEMA Office of General Counsel by Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 1 week (around 2026-10-21) confirming whether Region 8 UC can unilaterally request Region 10 resources under Stafford Act declaration and what cost-sharing applies; if written opinion is not available, have FEMA Regional Administrators issue a joint memo committing to cost-sharing and mutual aid as of T+0.
  • If National Guard air assets and pilot availability cannot be confirmed: contact the adjutant generals of Colorado, Montana, Wyoming and Idaho by Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 1 week (around 2026-10-21) and request a signed 'Statement of Force Readiness' confirming number of helicopters, pilots and hours available for emergency dispatch; if the statement shows insufficient capacity, request activated federal mobilization (National Guard under Title 10 federal orders) by Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 2 weeks (around 2026-10-28).
  • If ESF medical-surge capacity is overstated or committed: work with state health officers (CO, MT, WY, ID) and the American Hospital Association (Region 8/10 chapters) starting at Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 1 week (around 2026-10-21) to obtain a certified inventory of field hospital sets, ambulances and medical personnel available for emergency deployment; certify that named resources are not committed to other drills or operations until Month 4 (2027-02-14) (after the eruption window).
  • If communications equipment is not interoperable: request that FEMA Region 8 and the National Communications System (NCS) conduct a pre-event frequency-coordination and radio-compatibility exercise at Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 4 weeks (around 2026-11-11), testing all federal, state and Guard radio systems on the named ESF-2 (Communications) channels; document the tested frequencies and create a 'Comms Compatibility Matrix' binding for the event.
  • If mutual-aid activation procedures are unclear or outdated: have the UC Incident Commander request that each state (MT, WY, ID, CO) issue a Governor-signed mutual-aid authorization letter by Month 1 (2026-11-14), pre-authorizing specific resource requests and waiving normal approval chains during the Stafford Act declaration; attach the signed letters to the Unified Command plan as binding commitments.
  • If cost-sharing disputes risk freezing mutual aid: escalate the issue to FEMA Regional Directors (Region 8 and 10) and the Office of the Federal Coordinator for Alaska (responsible for Region 10 disaster response) by Month 0 (2026-10-14) + 2 weeks (around 2026-10-28), and request a written Federal Disaster Cost-Sharing Memorandum of Agreement specifying that all mutual-aid resources requested by the UC are eligible for 100% federal reimbursement under the declaration; have OMB or the White House Counsel sign the MOA if necessary to remove state/federal budget disputes.

Find Document 9: Montana, Wyoming and Idaho Governor Emergency Declaration Authorities and State Emergency Management Plans

ID: 95aae559-8fd0-460b-a695-9a7e484c887e

Description: Current state emergency-management plans, governor emergency-declaration authorities and automatic mutual-aid activation procedures for Montana, Wyoming and Idaho. Includes state-specific evacuation protocols, National Guard mobilization procedures and cost-sharing rules for emergency response. Serves as input for Command Structure and Authority Framework and Stafford Act cost-allocation negotiations. Intended audience: UC Incident Commander, governors' representatives, emergency managers. Context: the plan requires governor pre-authorization (verbal by T+6h, signed by Month 1 = 2026-11-14); this documentation clarifies state-level procedures and legal authorities.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025) state emergency-management plans and governor executive orders governing emergency declarations.

Responsible Role Type: Regional Emergency Management & Multi-Jurisdiction Coordination Director

Steps to Find:

  • Contact State Emergency Management Divisions (Montana Disaster and Emergency Services, Wyoming Emergency Management Agency, Idaho Office of Emergency Management) and request copies of current state emergency-management plans and governor emergency-declaration procedures.
  • Request state-specific evacuation and shelter-operations guidelines.
  • Obtain contact information for each governor's emergency-operations liaison and chief legal counsel (for authority-transfer negotiations).
  • Review state constitutions and statutes governing governor emergency powers and mutual-aid activation (typically available on state legislature websites).

Access Difficulty: Easy. State emergency-management plans are typically public documents or available through formal request. Governor offices maintain public lists of emergency contacts.

Essential Information:

  • Identify each of the three states' (Montana, Wyoming, Idaho) current governor emergency-declaration authorities, including: the legal threshold for declaration, who may issue it, required legislative notification, duration limits, and automatic mutual-aid (EMAC) activation procedures.
  • Detail state-specific evacuation protocols and mandatory procedures for each state: required notification timelines to counties and communities, traffic-control authority delegation (who controls contraflow), shelter-operations responsibility assignment, and cost-sharing rules during declared emergencies.
  • Document National Guard mobilization procedures for each state: who authorizes activation, how many personnel are typically available, restrictions on out-of-state deployment, and cost-reimbursement eligibility under Stafford Act.
  • Specify state-level hazardous-materials and fuel-handling regulations applicable to water convoys and generator fuel delivery during emergency operations.
  • Clarify state authority over evacuation messaging, shelter siting and re-entry perimeter enforcement, and identify any state-imposed constraints on federal NPS incident commander authority at the boundary.
  • List current state emergency-management organizational structure: title and contact information for the emergency-management director, chief legal counsel, and governor's operations liaison for each state.
  • Confirm each state's cost-sharing percentage and reimbursement procedures under the Stafford Act and FEMA regional disaster declarations for evacuation, shelter operations and logistics.
  • Identify any state-level agreements or MOUs already in place with FEMA, neighboring states or federal agencies that may affect mutual-aid activation or resource requests.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Misunderstood or outdated governor emergency-declaration authority leads to delays (15–45 minutes estimated) in issuing formal evacuation orders, as the Unified Command may lack clarity on whether verbal pre-authorization by T+6h is sufficient or if additional state-level approvals are required.
  • Unclear state evacuation protocols and traffic-control authority assignment cause disputes over who controls contraflow checkpoints and reroute decisions during the evacuation peak, resulting in 500–1,000 vehicle delays and reduced corridor throughput.
  • Incomplete or inaccurate National Guard mobilization procedures lead to delays in requesting out-of-region Guard reinforcements if responder staffing falls below 50% at critical checkpoints, extending the gap in coverage by 2–4 hours.
  • Missing state hazmat and fuel-handling regulations force the UC to conduct legal research during the response window, delaying water and fuel convoy dispatch by 6–12 hours and leaving shelters without adequate supply for the first 24 hours.
  • Ambiguity over state authority at the evacuation boundary creates a command gap: unclear who approves shelter assignments and reroutes in the 'transition zone' where traffic crosses from NPS to state control, delaying decisions by 15–45 minutes per reroute.
  • Absent or outdated contact information for state emergency managers and governors' liaisons prevents timely escalation of requests for mutual aid or cost-sharing decisions, stalling resource mobilization by 2–4 hours during the critical T+6 to T+24 window.
  • Unconfirmed cost-sharing percentages and reimbursement procedures lead to disputes over which costs are reimbursable under the Stafford Act, potentially leaving the UC uncertain about budget authority and delaying procurement of critical supplies.
  • Unknown pre-existing state MOUs or agreements may conflict with the UC's planned authority structure, forcing last-minute legal negotiations and creating authority ambiguity at T+0 when the response activates.

Worst Case Scenario: At T+0 hours, the Unified Command activates at the Denver RRCC and issues the verbal evacuation order for Zone One, assuming governors' pre-authorization is already in place. However, upon contact, the governors or their legal counsel challenge the NPS incident commander's authority to direct traffic control and shelter placement in their states, citing state constitutional limits on federal authority or existing state laws that require governor approval for contraflow operations. This dispute delays the issuance of formal evacuation orders by 2–4 hours. Simultaneously, unclear National Guard mobilization procedures prevent rapid deployment of additional traffic-control personnel; the UC cannot confirm whether out-of-state Guard can be deployed without explicit additional authorization from each state adjutant general. By T+6 hours, the West Yellowstone corridor experiences a gridlock backup affecting 5,000–8,000 vehicles, and no Guard reinforcements are available to expand traffic-control coverage. Evacuation time slips to T+8 to T+10 hours, and ashfall onset within this window increases respiratory distress cases by 10–20. Additionally, disputes over cost-sharing and fuel-handling regulations delay water and fuel convoy dispatch from Salt Lake City by 12+ hours, leaving shelters without adequate supply when evacuees arrive by T+8 to T+12 hours. Overall estimated impact: 2–4 hour evacuation delay, 10–20 additional respiratory distress casualties, 1–3 critical supply shortages at shelters, and erosion of public trust due to visible command confusion and inter-state conflict.

Best Case Scenario: The current state emergency-management plans clearly specify that governors' verbal authorization of evacuation orders is valid under each state's declaration authority, and pre-authorized MOUs are already in place confirming federal NPS incident commander authority over contraflow and initial shelter placement until a formal handoff order is issued. National Guard mobilization is streamlined and can proceed with out-of-state deployment via EMAC with a single phone call to each state adjutant general, removing any delay. Cost-sharing is explicitly documented (e.g., 75% federal/25% state), making budget authority clear and allowing the UC to confidently authorize procurement within the USD 200 million envelope. Contact information for state emergency managers and governors' liaisons is current, enabling real-time coordination without research delays. By T+0 hours, the UC confirms verbal authorization with all three governors, activates contraflow without legal disputes, and requests Guard reinforcements immediately; all three state emergency managers are actively coordinated into the response and provide rapid approvals for fuel, water and shelter logistics. Water and fuel convoys dispatch from Salt Lake City by T+12 hours as planned, and shelters are fully staffed and prepared by T+24 hours. The boundary authority transfer occurs smoothly at defined checkpoints, with no command gaps or reroute delays. Evacuation proceeds at planned pace: 98% of Zone Zero cleared by T+6h, 95% of Zone One by T+24h, and Scenario Beta interim destination list issued on schedule.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current state emergency-management plans cannot be obtained or are outdated: Conduct emergency legal briefings with each state's attorney general's office and emergency management director during the first 4 hours of the response (T+0 to T+4h) to clarify authority and cost-sharing verbally and on the record, document the findings in a memo from each governor to the UC, and rely on those memos as the operational authority base for the subsequent 68 hours.
  • If National Guard mobilization procedures are unclear or non-standard: Pre-establish a direct phone line and written standby agreement with each state adjutant general (Army and Air National Guard commanders) before Month 0 (2026-10-14), specifying that out-of-state deployment is pre-authorized under EMAC and requires only a phone request from the UC; test this agreement in a coordination exercise 30 days before T+0.
  • If state cost-sharing percentages are not formally documented: Use the standard Stafford Act cost-share (75% federal/25% state) as the assumed baseline and confirm in writing via each governor's representative at T+6h; if disputes arise later, escalate to FEMA regional administrator for arbitration rather than delay the response.
  • If state emergency-management contact information is incomplete or outdated: Request updated contact rosters from FEMA Region VIII and Region 10 regional liaisons at T-48h before the eruption window; maintain a shared contact list on the UC common operating picture with backup phone, email and satellite phone for each state director.
  • If state traffic-control or hazmat-handling regulations impose constraints that conflict with the UC evacuation plan: Escalate to each governor's legal counsel by T+3h, request a written waiver or emergency order authorizing the necessary contraflow and fuel-handling operations, and proceed under the waiver while the formal legal process continues in parallel.
  • If pre-existing state MOUs are found to conflict with the planned UC authority structure: Convene an emergency legal coordination call with all three governors' representatives and the UC legal counsel at T+0 to T+2h, identify the specific conflicts, and issue a joint written clarification signed by the governors confirming that the UC evacuation plan supersedes any prior conflicting arrangements for the duration of the emergency.
  • If mutual-aid (EMAC) procedures are non-standard or require pre-authorization that is not in place: Use the EMAC duty officer hotline (available 24/7) to request immediate mutual-aid activation for each state, providing verbal authorization from each governor if needed, and follow up with written confirmation within 4 hours; EMAC procedures are designed for this scenario and should not be a bottleneck.

Find Document 10: Current and Historical Seismic and Hydrothermal Hazard Maps for Yellowstone Caldera Region (USGS HazMaps, Slope-Stability Assessments)

ID: f42ce734-7f7e-479a-b1be-9546a9a1567b

Description: Existing USGS hazard maps showing seismic epicenter distributions, slope-stability assessments and hydrothermal-explosion zones within Yellowstone National Park. Includes Gallatin Canyon and US-89 corridor geotechnical surveys (if available) and any documented secondary-slide or hydrothermal-explosion events. Serves as input for Landslide Clearance and Hydrothermal Hazard Road Engineering planning. Intended audience: Geotechnical engineer, transportation planner. Context: the plan assumes Gallatin Canyon and US-89 have secondary-slide risk and the South Entrance has current blockage; this documentation enables specific hazard-zone mapping and equipment pre-positioning.

Recency Requirement: Current (2010–2025) USGS hazard maps and geotechnical assessments for the Yellowstone region.

Responsible Role Type: Transportation Operations & Contraflow Specialist / Geotechnical Engineer

Steps to Find:

  • Contact USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory and Cascades Volcano Observatory and request existing hazard maps for the Yellowstone region (seismic, slope stability, hydrothermal hazards).
  • Download USGS Scientific Investigations Map series (SIM) for Yellowstone region (available on USGS website).
  • Contact Wyoming, Montana and Idaho state geological surveys and request slope-stability assessments or landslide-hazard maps for the Gallatin Canyon and US-89 corridors.
  • Request any NPS maintenance or incident reports documenting prior rockfalls, landslides or hydrothermal explosions on park roads.

Access Difficulty: Easy. USGS hazard maps are publicly available online. State geological surveys maintain geotechnical databases; access may require formal request but is typically available to emergency planners.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific USGS seismic, gas-flux, and uplift-rate thresholds that trigger automatic escalation from Zone Zero to Zone One and from Zone One to the 500 km Scenario Beta radius, with decision latency target (e.g., 'order issued within 30 minutes of threshold crossing').
  • Detail the written trigger-matrix protocol: which agency (USGS, Unified Command, governor) measures each indicator, at what frequency (hourly, continuous), and who has authority to halt or reverse the order if a false positive is detected.
  • List all pre-authorized decision makers and their roles: NPS incident commander, Unified Command at Denver RRCC, FEMA Region 10 liaison, and state governors; specify the chain of command if the primary decision maker is unreachable.
  • Quantify the 'remaining window' reference in the Scenario Beta trigger (e.g., 'probability of VEI-7 within the remaining 48 hours of the 72-hour window'); define how this probability is computed from USGS data in real time.
  • Specify the messaging that accompanies the trigger: what public alert (IPAWS, radio, print) is issued to evacuees and outer-ring residents at the moment the order is given, and in what languages.
  • Define abort and reversal criteria: under what conditions may the Unified Command pause or cancel the Scenario Beta order if indicators drop below thresholds after the order is issued, and who decides.
  • Confirm whether the trigger matrix is finalized and approved by USGS, FEMA, and state governors, or whether it remains a placeholder awaiting technical input by T+3 hours into the event.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or missing thresholds cause 30–90 minute delays in ordering Scenario Beta (estimate), during which uncontrolled shadow evacuation saturates corridors and strands Zone One evacuees.
  • Unclear chain of command or lack of pre-authorization allows one agency to dispute or block the order, splitting evacuation messaging and reducing public compliance by 10–20% (estimate).
  • Triggers based on single indicators (e.g., tremor magnitude alone) may fire on false alarms unrelated to eruption likelihood, eroding public trust and creating a 'boy who cried wolf' scenario that reduces compliance on subsequent escalations.
  • Absence of abort criteria leaves an escalated Scenario Beta order in force indefinitely, keeping millions of people in chaotic evacuation even if USGS downgrades the eruption probability, increasing humanitarian cost and stranding medical response.
  • Multilingual messaging not finalized means non-English speakers do not understand the trigger has fired, missing evacuation windows by 1–4 hours (estimate).
  • Delay in confirming the trigger matrix means the UC operates on a placeholder during the actual event, risking disagreement with USGS volcanologists over indicator interpretation at the moment the order must be issued.

Worst Case Scenario: The Scenario Beta trigger fires (VEI-7 probability crosses a threshold), but the written trigger matrix has not been finalized or pre-authorized. The Unified Command must convene an emergency decision cell to interpret the USGS data and vote on the 500 km order. This process takes 2–4 hours (estimate), during which uncontrolled outer-ring evacuation from Bozeman, Billings and Idaho Falls saturates I-15 and I-90. By the time the order is issued, 50,000–200,000 unplanned evacuees are already on the roads (estimate), gridlock prevents the organized Zone One evacuation of the 35,000 park visitors from reaching the primary shelters by T+24 hours, and secondary rescue of stranded evacuees and medical patients becomes necessary. The absence of second-stage hub destinations compounds the chaos: evacuees fleeing the 500 km ring have no published shelter, driving further uncontrolled dispersal. Final outcome: 4–8 hour evacuation delay, 500–2,000 stranded or injured evacuees, 5–15 preventable deaths in hospital transport delays, and erosion of public trust that undermines future emergency messaging.

Best Case Scenario: The trigger matrix is finalized and pre-authorized by T+0 hours, with USGS committed to hourly updates of the nominated indicators (e.g., uplift rate, gas flux, tremor magnitude) transmitted to the Unified Command. A VEI-7 probability crosses the threshold at T+18 hours. The Unified Command confirms receipt of the USGS data within 10 minutes, issues the 500 km order within 30 minutes (proposed threshold), and IPAWS broadcasts the order in English and five languages within 45 minutes. State governors issue immediate downstream enforcement orders, and the ranked second-stage hub list (Denver, Cheyenne, and three backups outside the 500 km ring) is already pre-authorized, allowing the UC to direct outer-ring evacuees to named destinations. Corridor overflow is diverted to secondary routes before gridlock forms, Zone One evacuees reach primary shelters by T+24 hours, and secondary hubs are staffed and receiving outer-ring evacuees by T+36 hours. Public trust remains intact because the messaging was credible and pre-announced. Outcome: all 35,000 Zone One tourists and 100,000–500,000 additional Beta-ring evacuees reach shelter without major casualties or stranding.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If USGS cannot finalize a quantitative threshold matrix by T+3 hours into the event, adopt a qualitative decision framework: UC meets a standing volcanologist-and-governor cell every 6 hours (at T+6, T+12, T+18, T+24), reviews the latest USGS narrative assessment and gas/seismic plots, and votes on escalation. This delays the order by up to 6 hours but avoids false triggers; couple it with pre-staged second-stage hub messaging so outer-ring residents know what to do when the order comes.
  • Deploy a USGS liaison officer with satellite communication and real-time data-feed equipment to the forward UC element (Livingston) as an alternative to remote indicator transmission; this collocates the volcanologist with the decision maker, reducing latency and interpretation disagreement.
  • Pre-authorize a phased Scenario Beta order: Ring 1 (100–250 km, time-banded evacuation, no new cascade) by T+12 h based on interim thresholds; Ring 2 (250–500 km, staged departure, second-stage hubs activated) by T+24 h only if additional VEI-7 probability increases. This reduces false-alarm risk and buys time to stage second-stage hubs.
  • If public trust erodes after a false escalation, shift messaging from thresholds to scenarios: 'If USGS detects X, the UC will activate pre-authorized evacuation Plan A for Ring 2; residents will have 4 hours' notice.' This frames the order as a pre-planned contingency, not a surprise, and reduces blame on the UC.

Find Document 11: Regional Ground Transportation Network Capacity Data (I-15, I-80, I-90, US-20, US-89, US-14/16/20 Lane Counts, Capacity Analysis)

ID: 20ac35b9-2dc9-4dbb-871c-eeac47d3a083

Description: Detailed highway-capacity data for the primary evacuation routes: Interstate 15 northbound from Salt Lake City to Idaho Falls, Interstate 90 from West Yellowstone/Bozeman to the Livingston area, US-89 from Gardiner to Livingston and I-90, and US-14/16/20 from Cody to Billings and I-90. Includes lane counts, current average daily traffic (ADT), estimated maximum capacity (vehicles per hour per lane), known bottleneck locations (e.g., Gallatin Canyon, mountain passes) and any current or planned construction. Serves as input for contraflow design, throughput validation and evacuation-time estimation. Intended audience: Contraflow Operations Manager, transportation planner. Context: the plan assumes 2,000 vehicles/hour total outbound (660 per exit average), but this must be validated against actual corridor capacity, especially if roads degrade under ashfall or evacuation traffic congestion.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025) highway data: lane counts, construction status, average daily traffic; historical capacity studies from the last 5 years.

Responsible Role Type: Transportation Operations & Contraflow Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Contact state DOT traffic-data offices: Montana DOT (Helena), Wyoming DOT (Cheyenne), Idaho DOT (Boise) and request current ADT data, lane counts and capacity-analysis reports for I-15, I-80, I-90, US-20, US-89 and US-14/16/20.
  • Download highway-capacity manual (HCM) level-of-service analysis from the Transportation Research Board or academic sources; apply to Yellowstone corridor routes to estimate actual evacuation throughput.
  • Request any existing evacuation-routing studies or traffic-modeling reports from state DOT or FHWA for the Yellowstone region.
  • Contact FHWA regional offices and request any regional traffic-capacity data or bottleneck assessments for mountain corridors.

Access Difficulty: Easy. State DOT traffic data is publicly available; historical ADT and capacity analyses can be requested from state DOT planning divisions.

Essential Information:

  • Detailed current lane counts, average daily traffic (ADT) and maximum capacity (vehicles/hour/lane) for I-15 northbound (Salt Lake City to Idaho Falls), I-90 (West Yellowstone/Bozeman to Livingston), US-89 (Gardiner to Livingstone and I-90), and US-14/16/20 (Cody to Billings and I-90).
  • Identification and location of all known bottlenecks: Gallatin Canyon on US-191, Gardiner canyon on US-89, mountain passes on US-14/16/20, and any other choke points with single-lane or reduced-capacity sections.
  • Current construction status, lane closures, or planned maintenance on all three corridors through Month 1 (2026-11-14).
  • Highway-capacity manual (HCM) level-of-service analysis for each corridor at the estimated 2,000 vehicles/hour outbound load (660 vehicles/hour per exit at three-way split) and validated time-to-clearance for the 11,900-vehicle total outbound demand at 3.0 persons/vehicle.
  • Ashfall-degradation impact estimates: how reduced visibility, ash-slicked surfaces, and ash accumulation on shoulders will reduce safe capacity and increase accident rates on each corridor.
  • Historical data on how mountain passes (Gallatin Canyon, Gardiner canyon) have responded to blockages, secondary slides or debris clearance in past events; typical clearance time and equipment requirements.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Corridor capacity overestimated: if actual capacity is 1,500 vehicles/hour instead of 2,000 vehicles/hour, evacuation time extends from 6 hours to 8+ hours, increasing ashfall exposure by 30–50% and stranding 2,000–4,000 vehicles in ash.
  • Bottleneck risk unquantified: if Gallatin Canyon or Gardiner canyon cannot handle the planned load even without blockage, a single-lane cascade under evacuation traffic is certain, not hypothetical.
  • Ashfall-degraded capacity not modeled: if ashfall reduces safe capacity by 30–50% (no data available) and the plan assumes full capacity, peak evacuation will fail to clear Zone Zero by T+6 hours.
  • Clearance timelines not validated: if debris clearance actually requires 6–8 hours instead of the proposed 45-minute diversion threshold, a loss-of-exit event will strand 5,000–10,000 vehicles mid-corridor.
  • Routing decisions made without baseline data: the plan's proposed West 50%, North 30%, East 20% gate-load split has no capacity basis and may exceed one corridor's maximum throughput, forcing traffic onto uncongested lanes.

Worst Case Scenario: Actual corridor capacity is 1,500 vehicles/hour (not validated), and ashfall reduces it by 40% to 900 vehicles/hour. The plan's 11,900-vehicle total load at 2,000 vehicles/hour takes 6 hours under ideal conditions; under realistic ashfall-degraded capacity, it requires 13+ hours. Evacuation extends from the planned T+6 hours to T+13+ hours, with peak outbound traffic occurring at T+6 to T+13, exactly when ashfall intensity is rising. Simultaneous failure of one corridor (blockage in Gallatin Canyon) reduces throughput to 1,200 vehicles/hour across two exits, extending evacuation to 10+ hours and stranding 3,000–5,000 vehicles in moderate to heavy ashfall. Result: 500–1,500 additional respiratory-distress incidents and 10–30 preventable deaths.

Best Case Scenario: Detailed capacity data confirms that all three corridors can sustain 2,000+ vehicles/hour even under ashfall-degraded conditions, and that Gallatin Canyon and Gardiner canyon have sufficient width for rapid debris clearance (15–30 minutes typical). The planned three-way gate split (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%) aligns with each corridor's actual capacity, ensuring balanced load distribution. Evacuation proceeds on schedule, Zone Zero is cleared by T+6 hours with fewer than 500 stranded or delayed evacuees, and the three-exit design proves to be the decisive factor in achieving the T+6 clearance deadline. Credible capacity data also enables the forward command to adjust the gate-load split in real time if one corridor experiences congestion, preventing a bottleneck cascade.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If detailed current capacity data cannot be obtained from state DOTs within T+0 to T+6 hours, request historical evacuation or emergency-response traffic studies from FHWA or academic researchers covering mountain corridors in the western US, and apply those data as proxies for Yellowstone corridors, with a 20% conservative downward adjustment for ashfall.
  • Conduct a rapid (3–5 day) traffic-simulation study using VISSIM or similar software at Month 0 (2026-10-14) based on available ADT data, assuming ashfall reduces visibility to 100 meters and safe speed to 25 mph; iterate the gate-load split until simulated evacuation time reaches T+6 hours or the model identifies the first bottleneck.
  • Activate a dynamic gate-adjustment protocol: measure queue length and exit throughput every 15 minutes from T+0 onward; if one corridor's queue exceeds 500 vehicles or throughput drops below 600 vehicles/hour for >15 minutes, reroute overflow to the least-congested exit within 10 minutes.
  • Request real-time capacity monitoring from state DOTs: ask Montana DOT, Wyoming DOT and Idaho DOT to provide live traffic-speed data from Gallatin Canyon and Gardiner canyon (via road sensors or traffic cameras) during the evacuation window, so the forward command can detect bottlenecks and blockages within 5 minutes and trigger immediate reroutes.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If candidate hubs are inside the 500 km ring or in modeled ashfall zones, Scenario Beta evacuees arriving at those hubs would face unforecast ash exposure, respiratory distress and secondary relocation within 6–12 hours, stranding 10,000–30,000 people and consuming 4–6 additional hours of transport and intake time.
  • If hub shelter capacity is overstated (e.g., listed facilities are unavailable, outdated or inaccessible), the plan cannot absorb the estimated 100,000–500,000 additional Scenario Beta evacuees, forcing uncontrolled camping and overflow into unsafe conditions, increasing respiratory and disease-related casualties by an estimated 20–50 per hub.
  • If Red Cross and Salvation Army coordination is not pre-established, shelters lack trained staff, and intake processing delays by 4–8 hours, evacuees queue at hubs without registration, food or water distribution, increasing dehydration and medical emergencies by 30–50% during the intake window.
  • If hubs lack adequate fuel supply contracts, water treatment and medical-facility bed capacity, the plan's assumptions that evacuees can be moved 'onward' from initial hubs to secondary destinations becomes infeasible, trapping evacuees at overloaded initial sites for 24–48 hours longer than planned.
  • If hub accessibility via lateral routes is poor (e.g., narrow secondary highways, limited fuel stops), transport convoys moving evacuees from primary shelters to secondary hubs face delays of 4–8 hours, reducing throughput and leaving primary shelters saturated beyond design occupancy.

Worst Case Scenario: Scenario Beta trigger fires at T+12 hours. The plan has no verified secondary-hub list: candidate hubs (Denver, Cheyenne, Billings) have not been confirmed as outside the 500 km ring or evaluated for capacity and accessibility. Over the next 12–24 hours, 50,000–200,000 unplanned evacuees from the 100–500 km ring converge on the nearest major towns (Billings, Bozeman, Idaho Falls, Salt Lake City), all of which are inside the Scenario Beta zone or have been overtaxed by primary-stage evacuees. No pre-arranged hub coordination or capacity commitment exists. Evacuees cluster in parking lots, schools and fairgrounds without registration, food service or medical triage. Regional hospitals face a secondary surge of 1,000–3,000 patients with respiratory distress and heat-stress casualties. Without onward-movement routes and host-hub agreements, primary shelters cannot release evacuees to secondary hubs, leaving tens of thousands stranded in ash-exposed zones for 24–48 hours. Estimated casualties: 50–200 preventable respiratory and heat-stress deaths; estimated cost of emergency response: USD 200–500 million in unplanned shelter operations, medical response and evacuation rerouting.

Best Case Scenario: The Residential and Transient Population Data document provides verified current (2024–2025) shelter-facility inventories, lodging capacity and organizational capacity for at least five candidate secondary hubs (Denver, Cheyenne, Billings, Boise, Salt Lake City). Each hub is confirmed outside the 500 km ring with measured distance from Yellowstone. Red Cross and Salvation Army chapters are contacted; pre-event capacity commitments are signed by Month 2 (2026-12-14). A ranking of hubs by distance, capacity and accessibility is published, enabling the Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner to assign evacuation rings (100–250 km, 250–500 km) to specific hubs and pre-position buses and logistical staff. When a Scenario Beta trigger fires, evacuees are directed to named hubs with published shelter addresses, expected arrival times and intake processes. Onward-movement routes via lateral highways are confirmed passable and fuel-stocked. Secondary hubs absorb 100,000–500,000 evacuees over 24–48 hours with minimal additional casualties. Evacuee confidence in the plan increases, reducing shadow evacuation and corridor saturation. Estimated outcome: <10 preventable deaths in secondary-hub operations, USD 50–100 million in planned sheltering costs, and reduced emergency contingency draws.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Contact all state emergency management agencies in Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Colorado and Utah directly; request that each state identify its top three candidate secondary-hub communities and verify their distance from Yellowstone and existing emergency-shelter inventories, then consolidate the state lists into a unified ranked document by T+0 hours.
  • Engage FEMA Regions VIII and X directly to request their existing American Evacuation Preparedness community-shelter databases and regional resource lists; cross-reference those inventories against the candidate hubs to avoid redundant surveying.
  • If facility inventories are incomplete or outdated, conduct rapid phone surveys of city emergency management offices, chambers of commerce and Red Cross chapters in the 3–5 most likely candidate hubs (Billings, Boise, Salt Lake City, Denver, Cheyenne), collecting current-year capacity estimates for gymnasiums, schools and arenas, then publish an interim ranked list by T+12 hours and full details by Month 1 (2026-11-14).
  • If distance verification from Yellowstone Caldera center is uncertain, use USGS geospatial tools and NOAA ashfall-dispersion models to confirm which candidate hubs lie outside the 500 km ring for a representative VEI-7 wind scenario; publish confidence intervals on ashfall risk for each hub.
  • If Red Cross and Salvation Army regional capacity is unavailable, substitute state and local Salvation Army area commanders, county emergency managers and volunteer fire departments as coordination contacts; request mutual-aid letters of intent from each community by Month 1 (2026-11-14), specifying maximum evacuee intake and available facilities.
  • If hub fuel supply or water-treatment capacity is unknown, request pre-event supply audits from the city water authority, municipal utilities and local fuel vendors in each hub, then pre-authorize emergency procurement and delivery contracts with those vendors for the event window, executed by Month 2 (2026-12-14).

Find Document 13: Utility System Infrastructure and Power-Grid Topology for Montana, Wyoming and Idaho (Transmission Lines, Substations, Ash-Flashover Risk Assessment)

ID: 3c23d3db-0621-4b02-9e8f-0775fc3c6de5

Description: Electrical transmission-system maps and substation locations for Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power service territories covering the Yellowstone region and evacuation routes. Includes transmission-line voltages (115–500 kV), substation locations, backup-generator capacity at critical facilities and any existing ash-flashover or secondary-failure risk assessments. Serves as input for grid-resilience planning and load-shedding procedures. Intended audience: Grid Resilience Engineer, utilities coordinators. Context: the plan assumes grid failure from ash flashovers; this data enables specific vulnerability identification and pre-event protective-relay coordination.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025) transmission-system maps, substation listings and protective-relay settings.

Responsible Role Type: Critical Infrastructure & Grid Resilience Engineer

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power operations/planning divisions and request transmission-system maps, substation locations and load-serving areas.
  • Request any existing volcanic-ash risk assessments or secondary-failure analyses from the utilities.
  • Contact WECC (Western Electricity Coordinating Council) and request grid-resilience data or interconnection studies relevant to the Yellowstone region.
  • Request protective-relay coordination diagrams and settings from each utility for substations serving the Yellowstone evacuation region.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Transmission-system maps are commercially sensitive; require formal data-sharing agreements with utilities. Critical-infrastructure protection considerations may limit public disclosure; pre-event coordination with utilities is standard for emergency planning.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the three receiving hospitals (Bozeman Deaconess Medical Center, Livingston HealthCare, Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center) and their current generator fuel capacity, on-site reserves (hours/days) and fuel-port configuration, including number of fueling stations per facility.
  • Quantify the transmission-line voltages, substation locations and load-serving capacity for Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power in the evacuation-corridor and shelter zones (West Yellowstone, Gardiner, Bozeman, Idaho Falls).
  • Detail the existing ash-flashover risk assessments or secondary-failure analyses (if any) conducted by regional utilities; identify any transmission lines or substations with single-point-failure exposure in the Yellowstone region.
  • Specify the protective-relay settings and automatic load-shedding procedures at the two largest substations serving Bozeman and Idaho Falls, including switching timelines and coordination gaps between utilities.
  • Confirm the current status of backup power capacity (mobile generators, voltage regulators, fuel caches) at critical facilities in the shelter zones and estimate pre-event deployment timelines.
  • List the FAA ZLC and ZSE airfield locations with current fuel capacity and helicopter-fuel-cache availability for emergency medevac or supply missions.
  • Document mutual-aid agreements and resource-sharing arrangements between Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power regarding emergency fuel delivery, load shedding and grid restoration.
  • Specify WECC (Western Electricity Coordinating Council) grid-resilience data relevant to the Yellowstone region, including any modeled cascading-failure scenarios or recommendations for protective-relay coordination.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete transmission-system maps or substation data delay identification of critical vulnerabilities, leaving protective-relay coordination unverified and increasing the risk of cascading multi-hospital power loss during ashfall.
  • Absence of ash-flashover risk assessments means utilities have no pre-event load-shedding strategy and cannot stage protective actions (relay adjustments, line de-energization) before failure occurs, resulting in uncontrolled blackouts.
  • Lack of clarity on hospital generator fuel capacity and fueling-port configuration prevents realistic assessment of 4–6 hour outage duration and the need for emergency fuel delivery; overestimating on-site reserves leads to inadequate fuel pre-positioning.
  • Missing utility mutual-aid and emergency-response procedures mean fuel convoys and load-shedding orders cannot be coordinated across utility boundaries, leaving some facilities without power during peak demand.
  • Incomplete airfield fuel-cache data prevents pre-positioning of helicopter fuel for emergency medevac or supply runs, stranding critical patient transfers and shelter resupply if ground routes fail.
  • Failure to coordinate protective relays and control systems across utilities increases the likelihood of malfunction under ashfall stress, accelerating cascading failure timelines.

Worst Case Scenario: A widespread transmission-line flashover event triggered by ashfall ash deposits on insulators occurs within 4 hours of ashfall onset, affecting multiple substations serving Bozeman and Idaho Falls simultaneously. Protective relays malfunction or fail to isolate faulted sections due to ash-clogging or secondary tremor damage, initiating a cascade of failures that blacks out the entire region within 8–12 hours. Hospitals lose grid power before fuel convoys can arrive; generator startup procedures fail due to outdated equipment or maintenance oversights. Three major hospitals operate for 2–4 hours on backup before fuel runs out, forcing cancellation of 15–25 surgeries, loss of ventilator support for 10–15 patients and 5–10 preventable deaths. Shelters lose water pumping and treatment capability, affecting 35,000+ evacuees. The incident commander lacks real-time visibility into grid status and cannot issue load-shedding orders, leaving repair crews without situational awareness. Total impact: regional crisis compounding medical surge and threatening regional continuity of operations.

Best Case Scenario: Utilities provide current transmission-system maps and confirm substation locations, protective-relay settings and mutual-aid procedures. Pre-event coordination identifies two critical substations serving the shelter zones and confirms mobile generator and voltage-regulation equipment can be pre-deployed 48 hours before the eruption window. Each receiving hospital confirms 72-hour on-site fuel reserves and agrees to emergency fuel contracts with local vendors (arrival within 2 hours of request). A 24/7 utility-operations hotline is established with the forward command element, enabling real-time grid monitoring and load-shedding authorization during ashfall. Hospital generator-startup exercises test manual procedures and identify any mechanical failures in advance. Ashfall does cause transmission-line stress, but pre-positioned mobile generators and load shedding prevent cascading failure; hospitals maintain power and medical surge capacity throughout the 72-hour window. Shelf-life and resupply of fuel, water and medical supplies remain uninterrupted. Regional infrastructure resilience is maintained and no preventable deaths occur due to grid failure.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current utility transmission maps are not available due to critical-infrastructure security restrictions, request a summarized vulnerability briefing (substations at highest risk, relay-coordination gaps, single-point failures) from the responsible utility operators rather than full technical documents, then coordinate directly with operations staff during the 72-hour window for real-time load-shedding decisions.
  • If pre-event ash-flashover risk assessments do not exist, commission a rapid ( 30-day) desktop analysis using USGS ash-dispersion models and published literature on volcanic-ash electrical effects, focusing on the two largest substations serving Bozeman and Idaho Falls; use results to justify emergency mobile-generator pre-positioning.
  • If hospital fuel reserves are insufficient (less than 48 hours on-site), establish a fuel-delivery contract with local vendors and pre-stage bottled fuel at each hospital 60 days before the window, then assign a fuel-shortage responder to monitor consumption during the event and trigger emergency dispatch if reserves fall below 24 hours.
  • If utility mutual-aid agreements do not address ash-driven emergencies, draft a simple one-page emergency protocol with the utilities specifying load-shedding triggers (ashfall onset + grid stress indicators), command authority (forward command element voice request triggers action without committee approval) and fuel-convoy priority lanes during evacuation.
  • If airfield fuel caches are not available, pre-authorize helicopter fuel delivery from military sources (Fort Harrison, Helena or Malmstrom AFB, Montana) or civilian aviation fuel suppliers in Billings and pre-position fuel at the nearest forward airfield (Gallatin County or Jackson Hole) 48 hours before the window, then brief medevac units on the fuel location and authorization procedures.

Strengths

  • Clear life-safety mission with hard gates: G1 at T+6 h (at least 98% of 35,800 confirmed out) and G2 at T+24 h (at least 95% of registered Zone One residents out).
  • Three-exit contraflow (West US-20/US-191, North US-89, East US-14/16/20) with fixed district-to-gate split of 50/30/20%, so no vehicle crosses the interior.
  • Unified Command at Denver RRCC with Region 10 liaison from T+0 and a forward element at Livingston, giving corridor visibility and federal resource access.
  • Pre-authorized USGS trigger matrix lets the UC order the 500 km Beta expansion within 30 min without further approval.
  • Layered communications (IPAWS/WEA, Guard signal teams, HAR/VMS, multilingual route cards) and a tiered fuel priority for hospitals, comms and shelter kitchens.
  • Established tools: NIMS/ICS, FEMA contract vehicles, Stafford Act funding with a USD 200 million planning envelope (estimate) and USD 40 million contingency.

Weaknesses

  • No second-stage destinations are confirmed for Scenario Beta; the ring covers millions of people, not quantified, and hubs must lie outside 500 km (Denver, Cheyenne candidates, distance not verified).
  • No pre-event lead time: pre-awarded contracts, MOUs and exercises cannot precede T+0, so readiness actions compress into T+0 to T+12 h and hardening in Months 1-3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14).
  • Thin responder depth: 100-150 rangers (estimate) give about 67-100 concurrent positions, all consumed during T+2 to T+8; responder N95 count is unsized.
  • Water arrival at shelters expected T+18 to T+30 h (estimate) versus the T+24 h target; 12 h dispatch is not delivery.
  • Zone One resident population is unquantified; a census is needed by T+6 h.
  • Shelter sites are chosen only at T+6 h, and Bozeman and Idaho Falls sit near the ash risk; the 100,000 civilian N95 stock may be too small and masks clog quickly.
  • Language and mobility needs have no sizing data; financing split for shelters and hubs is open.

Opportunities

  • Interim ranked hub list (at least 5 hubs outside the ring) by T+12 h, then written plan by Month 1 (2026-11-14), MOUs by Month 2 (2026-12-14) and exercise by Month 3 (2027-01-14), to turn the Beta trigger into an executable order.
  • Ring-based Beta execution (0-100 km organized, 100-250 km time-banded, 250-500 km staged) spreads road load and limits shadow evacuation.
  • Concessioner (Xanterra) buses and manifests raise persons per vehicle and reach vehicle-less and mobility-limited visitors.
  • Lessons from Hurricane Rita, Camp Fire, Mount St. Helens and Eyjafjallajökull on contraflow termini, alert layering, ash logistics and tiered airspace exceptions.
  • Forward depots at Bozeman, Billings and Idaho Falls plus FEMA surge clauses can bring water arrival toward T+24 h.
  • Real-time PM10 sensing and USGS/NOAA plume updates can steer shelter siting and relocation within 4 h.

Threats

  • Gallatin Canyon or Gardiner blockage (rockfall, breakdown, secondary slide) halting a corridor; more than 45 min triggers diversion adding 2-4 h for some.
  • Ash and tremor collapsing cell towers and power, leaving drivers and responders without route guidance.
  • Eruption onset overlapping with the evacuation peak, before Zone Zero is cleared at T+6 h.
  • Authority gaps at the NPS-to-state handoff and FEMA Region 8/10 seam; governors' verbal authorization not yet secured, with a competing shelter-in-place order possible.
  • Shadow evacuation and message reversal (shelter-in-place then Beta) eroding trust and saturating I-90, I-15 and US-191.
  • Ash footprint forecast error placing shelters in heavy ash; hospital and grid failure before fuel arrives.
  • Procurement delays of 24-48 h (estimate) if FEMA verbal activation fails; ash grounding removes medevac unless exceptions are approved.

Recommendations

  • Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+0 to T+12 h): UC seats the Region 10 liaison, obtains verbal governor authorization by T+6 h, and issues the interim ranked hub list (at least 5 outside the ring) by T+12 h. Owner: UC Director, Denver RRCC.
  • T+0 to T+1 h: activate contraflow on all three exits; position at least 2 tow/rockfall teams to reach Gallatin Canyon within 15 min; apply the 45 min diversion rule. Owners: NPS incident commander, MT/WY highway patrol, state DOTs.
  • T+0 to T+12 h: deploy Guard signal teams, HAR/VMS and route cards in English plus 5 languages at every control point and the forward element. Owner: Guard signal lead with FEMA IPAWS.
  • T+0 to T+6 h: activate the 6 h shift and 18 h withdrawal limits, request the 30-50 standby reserve and out-of-region Guard, and size a separate responder N95 stock. Owner: Forward UC logistics chief.
  • By T+12 h: dispatch convoys from forward depots using FEMA surge clauses and a reserved I-15 lane; install PM10 sensors at shelters and set the 4 h relocation rule. Owners: FEMA logistics, Guard, NOAA/USGS liaison.
  • Months 1-3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14): sign MOUs (governors, Region 10, utilities, hubs), finish the written Beta plan, and run full-scale Beta, shift-rotation and water-convoy exercises. Owner: FEMA Region VIII with state emergency managers.

Strategic Objectives

  • Confirm at least 98% of 35,800 people (about 35,084) out through exit counts by T+6 h, with contraflow active on all three corridors by T+1 h.
  • Evacuate at least 95% of registered Zone One residents by T+24 h with the perimeter staffed and the Beta interim hub list issued.
  • Issue an interim list of at least 5 ranked hubs outside the 500 km ring by T+12 h, a written second-stage plan by Month 1 (2026-11-14), signed MOUs by Month 2 (2026-12-14) and a full exercise by Month 3 (2027-01-14).
  • Deliver water to all shelters by T+24 h, targeting about 1.43 million liters for 10 days (estimate), with convoys dispatched by T+12 h.
  • Keep at least 50% responder coverage at every post through T+72 h and relocate any shelter within 4 h of exceedance.

Assumptions

  • Scenario Alpha has a 40% probability within 72 h and T+0 coincides with project start (user constraint).
  • Pre-event contracts and exercises are unavailable; existing FEMA contract vehicles can be activated verbally.
  • The 50/30/20% gate split and 3.0 persons per vehicle hold (estimates).
  • Salt Lake City, Billings, Bozeman, Idaho Falls and probably Boise lie inside the 500 km ring.
  • The cost is fully public; the USD 200 million envelope (estimate) is adequate for the readiness package.

Missing Information

  • Zone One resident population and special-needs registry.
  • Population inside the 500 km ring and capacity of Denver and Cheyenne (distances not verified).
  • Final USGS trigger indicator values (due by T+3 h).
  • Number of Guard signal units, buses, drivers and tow assets available by T+1 h.
  • Responder headcount for N95 sizing and relief depth beyond the rangers.
  • Who finances shelters, hubs and state costs (federal versus state/local).
  • Hourly ash dispersion data and geotechnical status of Gallatin Canyon and the South Entrance slide.
  • Visitor language, mobility and vehicle-less shares.

Questions

  • If the Beta order is issued at T+12 h, where does each ring go, and who owns each destination?
  • What happens to corridor throughput if Gallatin Canyon is blocked for more than 2 h at T+3 h?
  • Which responder posts can be thinned first without breaking the T+6 h gate?
  • How will the public be told that a shelter-in-place instruction is superseded, and through which channel when cell service fails?
  • Which decisions cannot wait for governor MOUs, and what authority covers T+0 to Month 1 (2026-11-14)?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Unified Command Incident Commander

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Unified Command Incident Commander is the central decision authority for the entire 72-hour evacuation response, with continuous operational responsibility from T+0 through T+72 hours. This is a core, uninterrupted leadership role requiring constant presence, direct oversight of the forward element, interface with governors and USGS, and real-time decision authority on life-safety matters. The role cannot be shared or interrupted; continuity and accountability demand a salaried full-time position.

Explanation: The Incident Commander serves as the central decision authority for the entire multi-state evacuation response, operating from the FEMA Region VIII RRCC in Denver with direct oversight of the forward UC element in Livingston/Bozeman. This role is critical for issuing evacuation orders, authorizing the pre-authorized Scenario Beta VEI-7 expansion, managing cross-jurisdiction authority transfers between NPS and state governors, and maintaining a shared common operating picture across all agencies. The IC must interface with USGS volcanologists to interpret eruption triggers, authorize Guard signal deployment, and approve resource requests from shelter, hospital and logistics units.

Consequences: Without a single recognized Incident Commander, authority becomes fragmented across NPS, FEMA, state governors and the Forward UC element. Command gaps delay reroutes by 15–45 minutes, conflict resolution at the park boundary halts traffic, and escalation decisions for Scenario Beta are blocked by jurisdictional disputes or meetings that exceed the 30-minute decision window. Estimated impact: 2–4 hour evacuation delay, 500–2,000 stranded vehicles, 5–10 preventable deaths from exposure or medical transport delay.

People Count: 1

Typical Activities: As the UC Incident Commander, Steele operates from the FEMA Region VIII RRCC in Denver, serving as the central decision authority for the entire 72-hour evacuation response. He issues evacuation orders, authorizes pre-authorized Scenario Beta VEI-7 expansion to 500 km, manages cross-jurisdiction authority transfers between NPS and state governors, and maintains the shared common operating picture across all agencies. Steele conducts hourly briefings with the forward UC element in Livingston, the three state on-scene commanders, USGS volcanologists, NOAA forecasters, hospital surge coordinators, and logistics directors. He approves resource requests from shelter, hospital and logistics units, decides on corridor diversion if blockages persist beyond 45 minutes, and authorizes helicopter medevac exceptions to the FAA airspace grounding. Steele tracks burnout and orders responder relief rotations, reviews ashfall and air-quality sensor data at T+6 h when shelter sites are finalized, and prepares escalation decisions for the Scenario Beta trigger matrix by T+3 h.

Background Story: Dr. Marcus Steele is a veteran incident commander from Denver, Colorado, with 28 years in federal emergency management. He earned his MPA from the University of Colorado and has directed responses to the 2013 Colorado wildfires and 2015 South Carolina floods. Known for decisive leadership and cross-jurisdictional coordination, Steele was selected specifically for the Yellowstone response because of his experience managing multi-state unified commands and his established relationships with governors in the Mountain West. He has worked with USGS on earthquake and volcano monitoring and understands the technical triggers that drive volcanic decisions. Steele is deeply familiar with the Stafford Act, FEMA contract vehicles, and the complexities of handling authority handoffs between federal and state agencies at crisis boundaries.

Equipment Needs: Secure communications suite: dedicated satellite phone, encrypted radio (VHF/UHF), laptop with real-time common operating picture access, backup power systems (generator, UPS). Incident command workspace equipped with 4-6 large displays for data integration from USGS, NOAA, Guard signals and shelter status feeds. Printed contraflow route maps, trigger matrix decision cards, and evacuation-zone boundary markers. Real-time PM10/PM2.5 ashfall data feeds integrated into the command display.

Facility Needs: Primary: FEMA Region VIII RRCC in Denver Federal Center (Lakewood, Colorado) with hardened power, redundant internet and satellite links, secure conference capability for governor calls and USGS coordination. Backup command post at Fort Carson (Colorado Springs) with identical systems. 24/7 staffed operations center with adjacent situation room for briefings. Access to a secure video-teleconference capability linking the forward element in Livingston, state EOCs and USGS/NOAA offices. Proximity to federal emergency-declaration authority and logistics coordination.

2. FEMA Region 10 Liaison Officer

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The FEMA Region 10 Liaison Officer maintains 24/7 coordination with Idaho resources and mutual-aid authorities from T+0 through the entire response window (at least 72 hours, potentially extending to Month 1 = 2026-11-14). This is a continuous, critical interface role bridging regional seams. The liaison must be on-site at the Denver RRCC and available for immediate decision-making and resource requests. Full-time employment ensures sustained availability and organizational commitment.

Explanation: This role represents FEMA Region 10 (Seattle, covering Idaho and parts of the Pacific Northwest) at the Denver RRCC and maintains real-time coordination with Idaho State Emergency Management, Pocatello and Boise water/fuel authorities, and regional mutual-aid resources. The Region 10 Liaison ensures that Idaho's evacuation zone (100–500 km radius, depending on Scenario Beta) is served by pre-coordinated water convoys, medical supplies and shelter capacity from the Pocatello and Boise distribution centers, bridging the gap between Denver RRCC (Region 8) and the Idaho-specific resource network. Critical for pre-event MOUs and T+0 activation of Idaho-based mutual aid.

Consequences: Without dedicated Region 10 coordination, Idaho mutual-aid requests routed through the Denver RRCC experience 1–2 hour delays or are not recognized as priority. Water and fuel convoys from Boise and Pocatello are delayed 12–24 hours, leaving shelters at Idaho Falls with insufficient supply for 1–2 days. Estimated impact: 10–20% of evacuees at Idaho Falls lack adequate water for 12–24 hours, increasing risk of heat stress and secondary health incidents; 5–10 preventable dehydration-related casualties if medical care is delayed.

Access to FEMA contract-vehicle systems and state mutual-aid databases. 24/7 staffed desk with immediate escalation pathways to governors' offices and state emergency managers.

3. Boundary Coordination Officer (Forward Element)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Boundary Coordination Officer operates at the forward element with pre-authorized real-time decision authority for traffic reroutes and shelter assignments during the critical T+0 to T+24 hour phase, and remains in a leadership role through at least T+72 hours. This is a continuous, high-stakes operational post requiring constant presence, uninterrupted attention to the park boundary, and seamless authority handoff protocols. The role cannot be part-time or contract-based without risking command gaps.

Explanation: This role operates at the forward UC element in Livingston or Bozeman, serving as the real-time decision authority for traffic reroutes, initial shelter assignments, and permit/resource requests during the critical park-boundary crossing phase (T+0 to T+24 hours). The Boundary Coordinator holds pre-authorized authority to issue temporary reroutes without supervisory approval, ensuring that contraflow traffic does not stall waiting for NPS or state command approval at the jurisdictional boundary. The role also owns the NPS-to-state authority handoff protocol and maintains direct voice/data links to the NPS incident commander, state highway patrol commanders, and the Denver RRCC.

Consequences: Without a dedicated Boundary Coordinator with pre-authorized decision authority, reroute orders must be approved through chain-of-command calls between the park, the state, and Denver, adding 15–45 minutes of delay per decision. A single reroute delay cascades into a backup of 500–1,000 vehicles at a chokepoint, reducing overall corridor throughput by 10–20% and extending evacuation time by 1–2 hours. Estimated impact: 1,000–2,000 vehicles stranded in ash exposure, 5–10 additional respiratory-distress casualties, USD 50–100 million in indirect response costs.
