He owns the NPS-to-state authority handoff protocol at each gate (West Entrance, North Entrance, East Entrance), explicitly defining when NPS care ends and state custody begins. During peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h), Chen manages the loss-of-exit contingency: if any corridor blockage persists beyond 45 minutes, he coordinates diversion of overflow traffic to the next-nearest surviving exit. He also monitors real-time ashfall and air-quality data at T+6 h and confirms final shelter site selections with the Ashfall Officer before shelter activation begins.

Background Story: Lieutenant Colonel David Chen is a Montana National Guard officer with 20 years of experience in emergency operations and disaster logistics, currently stationed at Camp Ravenna outside Livingston, Montana. A graduate of the Army's Command and General Staff College, Chen has managed Guard response to the 2002 and 2007 Montana wildfires and the 2011 Missouri River floods. His assignment to the Livingston area, combined with his real-time visibility into the park's northern boundaries and his working relationships with Montana's highway patrol and county sheriffs, made him the ideal choice for the forward Boundary Coordination Officer role. Chen is known for staying calm under extreme time pressure and for his ability to translate orders from higher command into immediate field actions without bureaucratic delay. He has pre-existing satellite communication equipment and a tactical operations center at Camp Ravenna that can serve as the forward UC element nucleus.

Equipment Needs: Real-time interagency communications: primary satellite phone and backup encrypted radio (redundant systems), laptop with access to NPS incident-command net, state highway-patrol and National Guard radio channels, real-time traffic-sensor data from control points. Printed loss-of-exit contingency decision cards, traffic-diversion route maps (US-191/US-20 to US-89 to US-14/16/20), and authority-handoff protocol worksheets. Handheld GPS unit for position confirmation at the park boundary.

Facility Needs: Forward Unified Command element in Livingston, Montana (alternate: Bozeman), with direct line-of-sight or repeater access to Mammoth, Gardiner and Cody checkpoints. Tactical operations center equipped with 2-3 radio repeaters (VHF/UHF), satellite link to Denver RRCC and NPS incident commander, and a shared common operating picture display showing live traffic counts and shelter assignments. 24/7 staffing with cots for shift rest. Power backup (generator, fuel supply for 72 hours minimum). FAX and secure phone lines to state highway patrol dispatch centers.

4. Contraflow Operations and Traffic Control Manager

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Contraflow Operations and Traffic Control Manager directs the execution of the three-exit evacuation throughout the 72-hour window (Phase 1: T+0 to T+6 is peak intensity; Phase 2: T+6 to T+24 continues at elevated tempo). This core operational role requires continuous real-time throughput monitoring, load-balancing decisions, and coordination with tow/rockfall teams and the Boundary Coordinator. The role is the hub for traffic management and cannot be delegated to part-time or contracted personnel.

Explanation: This role manages the execution of contraflow operations on US-191/US-20 (West), US-89 (North), and US-14/16/20 (East) corridors, including the staging of traffic-control Rangers, state patrol and National Guard personnel at each checkpoint, sign placement, lane-reversal activation and real-time throughput monitoring. The manager owns the three-exit load split (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%), ensuring that vehicles are assigned to the correct corridor and do not cross the park interior to reach another gate. The role also manages the pre-positioned tow and rockfall-clearing teams, issues corridor-blockage diversion rules, and coordinates with the Boundary Coordinator to execute the loss-of-exit contingency (shelter-in-place after 6 hours if a corridor is not restored).

Consequences: Without centralized contraflow management, each corridor operates independently with no load balancing or real-time throughput optimization. A bottleneck at one exit (e.g., Gallatin Canyon) reduces capacity by 30–40%, and vehicles do not redirect to alternate routes, causing gridlock at the overloaded exit while other corridors remain underutilized. Estimated impact: 20–40% reduction in corridor throughput, adding 2–4 hours to peak evacuation, stranding 5,000–8,000 vehicles in ashfall zones, 10–20 preventable respiratory-distress casualties.

People Count: 1

She stages traffic-control Rangers, state patrol and National Guard personnel at each checkpoint (Mammoth on US-89 North, Gallatin County line on US-191/US-20 West, Cody entrance on US-14/16/20 East), places and monitors contraflow signage, and activates lane reversals by T+1 h. Whitfield implements the three-exit load split (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%) and ensures vehicles are assigned to the correct corridor to prevent interior crossings. She monitors real-time throughput at each corridor—target 660 vehicles/hour per exit (estimate)—and communicates with the Boundary Coordination Officer if bottlenecks develop or if a blockage triggers the 45-minute diversion rule. Whitfield manages the pre-positioned tow and rockfall-clearing teams (at least 2 mobile crews with 15-minute reach times), authorizes their deployment if Gallatin Canyon or other key corridors are blocked, and executes the loss-of-exit contingency (shelter-in-place after 6 hours if a corridor is not restored). She also coordinates with the Contraflow Communications Coordinator to ensure HAR and VMS messages on all three routes are updated hourly with current travel times and shelter assignments.

Background Story: Captain Sarah Whitfield is a seasoned National Park Service traffic and emergency management specialist with 18 years at Yellowstone, having managed visitor evacuation drills, winter road closures, and post-earthquake stabilization operations. A native of Bozeman, Montana, Whitfield earned her degree in civil engineering from Montana State University and has deep knowledge of Yellowstone's road network, bottleneck history, and seasonal traffic patterns. She has worked closely with the NPS LE Rangers, tow contractors, and Montana-Dakota Utilities on infrastructure resilience planning. Her appointment as Contraflow Operations and Traffic Control Manager reflects her intimate familiarity with all three evacuation corridors (US-191, US-89, US-14/16/20) and her proven ability to coordinate ranger and state patrol personnel under time pressure. Whitfield also maintains relationships with the tow contractors and heavy-equipment operators who will staff the pre-positioned rockfall-clearing teams at Gallatin Canyon.

Radio sets (primary and backup) for communication with checkpoint rangers and state patrol. Printed contraflow-activation checklist, load-split targets (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%) and corridor-blockage decision rules. Diversion-route maps with travel-time estimates for overflow traffic.

Facility Needs: Stationed at the forward element in Livingston or co-located with the NPS incident command post. Real-time access to traffic-sensor networks on US-191, US-20, US-89 and I-90 (via NOAA/state DOT networks). Satellite and radio links to each of the three contraflow control points and the tow/rockfall-clearing team staging depots (Mammoth, Spanish Creek). Access to pre-positioned tow-team equipment and mobilization authority. 24/7 ops center with large-format displays of all three corridors.

5. Communications and Public Alerting Coordinator

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Communications and Public Alerting Coordinator manages a 24/7 multilingual alerting stack (IPAWS, WEA, HAR, VMS, satellite radio, printed materials) throughout the 72-hour response and the hardening period (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14). The role owns message consistency, real-time updates coordinated with USGS/NOAA forecasts, responder-radio bridging, and media coordination. This is continuous, core-mission-critical work requiring a dedicated salaried position with no interruption risk.

Explanation: This role manages the layered communications stack—IPAWS/WEA, NOAA Weather Radio, Guard signal bridging, highway advisory radio (HAR), variable message signs (VMS), and printed route cards—ensuring consistent, multilingual evacuation messages reach drivers, responders and shelter occupants despite cell-network failure and ashfall. The Coordinator pre-produces all messages in English plus five visitor languages (Spanish, Japanese, German, Mandarin, French), activates Guard signal teams at contraflow checkpoints and the forward element, and maintains a 24/7 monitoring and update schedule coordinated with USGS/NOAA eruption and ashfall forecasts. The role also manages media coordination to prevent conflicting shelter-in-place and evacuation messages that would undermine public compliance.

Consequences: Without centralized alerting coordination, messages to drivers and evacuees are inconsistent, delayed or reach drivers after they have committed to wrong routes. An estimated 10–20% of drivers lack clear route instructions within the first 2 hours, taking unintended routes and adding 1–3 hours to their transit time. Foreign-language visitors (10,000–15,000 people estimate) do not receive instructions, leading to sheltering at wrong locations or stranding. Responder radios lose coordination when cell networks collapse, delaying patient transfers and traffic reroutes by 30 minutes to 2 hours each. Estimated impact: 2,000–5,000 evacuees experience 2–4 hour delays, 200–500 left behind or sheltered at wrong sites, 5–15 preventable casualties.

6. Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director manages the dispatch of water, N95, fuel and medical convoys from T+0 through at least T+72 hours and the hardening period. The role owns real-time tracking of all inbound shipments, prioritization of fuel and supplies to hospitals and shelters, authorization of helicopter resupply if ground routes fail, and procurement under FEMA contract vehicles. This is a continuous, mission-critical role requiring constant presence and decision authority. The workload is highest during T+0 to T+24 (convoy dispatch, receipt, distribution) but remains elevated through the full response window.

Explanation: This role plans and executes the supply-chain network for water, N95 respirators, generator fuel, shelter equipment and medical supplies, managing the dispatch of convoys from Salt Lake City (water, fuel), Billings/Salt Lake (N95 backup reserve), and pre-positioned forward depots at Bozeman and Idaho Falls. The Director owns the 12-hour dispatch target for water convoys, tracks all inbound shipments in real-time, and authorizes helicopter resupply if ground routes are blocked by ashfall or evacuation traffic. The role also maintains priority fuel allocation (hospitals > comms centers > shelter kitchens), pre-positions 72-hour reserves at receiving hospitals, and manages the procurement of shelter supplies, buses and equipment under existing FEMA contract vehicles to avoid 24–48 hour procurement delays.

Consequences: Without centralized logistics management, supplies arrive late or at wrong locations. Water convoys that should arrive by T+12 h (target) are delayed to T+18–T+30 h (estimate), leaving 10,000–20,000 evacuees without adequate water for 1–2 days. N95 respirator stock (100,000 user constraint) is not monitored for consumption rate, and a heavy ashfall that doubles use rate exhausts stock within 12–24 hours instead of 72 hours, leaving shelter occupants and hospitals unprotected. Generator fuel is not prioritized, so hospitals compete with shelters and comms centers for the same delivery slots, and one facility runs out of fuel before reserves arrive. Estimated impact: 1,000–3,000 evacuees without water for 12–24 hours; 5–15 respiratory-distress cases from inadequate N95 supply; 5–10 preventable hospital-patient deaths from power loss.

He manages the dispatch of water convoys from Salt Lake City (I-15 northbound, reserved surge lane) by T+12 h, N95 backup reserves from Billings or Salt Lake City hubs, and generator fuel to receiving hospitals at Bozeman, Livingston and Idaho Falls. 7. Responder Safety and Fatigue-Management Officer

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Responder Safety and Fatigue-Management Officer enforces exposure limits, tracks responder injury and fatigue, and coordinates the 30–50 person standby reserve throughout the 72-hour window and the hardening period. The role includes 24/7 monitoring of air-quality conditions at each post, authorization of responder withdrawal, and real-time relief scheduling. This is a continuous safety-critical position requiring constant vigilance. The role is especially intense during T+2 to T+8 (peak evacuation) when coverage gaps most threaten life safety.

Explanation: This role defines and enforces responder exposure limits (maximum 6-hour shifts at ash-exposed posts, 2-hour mandatory rest with N95 replacement, full withdrawal after 18 consecutive hours), tracks responder fatigue and injury, and coordinates the 30–50 person standby reserve from out-of-region agencies to maintain at least 50% coverage at traffic checkpoints and perimeter gates throughout the 72-hour window. The Officer manages separate N95 respirator counts for responders (not drawn from the 100,000 civilian stock), monitors air-quality conditions at each post and authorizes withdrawal if ash concentrations exceed agency standards. The role also pre-arranges rotational relief with Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, and Fort Carson (National Guard) to ensure that the 100–150 NPS rangers are not consumed entirely during the T+2 to T+8 evacuation peak.

Consequences: Without explicit exposure limits and relief coordination, all 100–150 rangers are consumed during the T+2 to T+8 peak with zero relief depth. A single ranger injury, equipment failure, or ash exposure forcing withdrawal halts one checkpoint for 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles and cascading delay through the entire evacuation. Responders work 16–24 hour shifts without rest, degrading judgment and increasing errors in traffic control and perimeter enforcement. Looting and unauthorized entries occur at 2–4 locations where checkpoints are unmanned. Estimated impact: 1–2 additional hours of evacuation delay, 500–2,000 stranded vehicles, 2–4 looting incidents, 5–10 preventable respiratory-injury casualties among responders.

Torres coordinates the 30-50 person standby reserve from out-of-region agencies (Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, Idaho Department of Lands) to maintain at least 50% coverage at traffic checkpoints during the evacuation peak. Torres also develops fatigue-assessment checklists for on-site use, pre-authorizes ranger withdrawal from posts if fatigue exceeds safe limits, and conducts a 6-hour shift-rotation exercise at Mammoth or Gardiner checkpoint 30 days before the window to test relief handoff protocols and N95 replacement procedures under simulated ashfall.

Torres is an expert in respiratory protection standards, N95 mask fit-testing and replacement cycles, and the physiological signs of acute exhaustion and heat stress in emergency workers. Her experience managing responder rotations under extreme conditions and her collaborative relationships with state occupational safety agencies made her the ideal choice for the Yellowstone responder-safety role. Torres also has credibility with the National Guard and NPS LE personnel because of her prior work on wildfire responder health in the Pacific Northwest.

8. Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner develops and pre-authorizes the second-stage plan by Month 1 (2026-11-14), executes it on a Scenario Beta trigger (which may occur within the 72-hour window at T+0 to T+72), and refines it through Months 2–3 (2026-12-14 to 2027-01-14). Although the plan is primarily front-loaded (Months -2 to Month 1 = 2026-11-14 readiness activities), once the 72-hour response begins, the planner becomes the on-call decision authority for Scenario Beta escalation and the activation of secondary hubs and tiered messaging. If Scenario Beta triggers, this role transitions to continuous operations. Full-time employment ensures the planner is immediately available at the forward element or Denver RRCC if the trigger fires.

Explanation: This role develops and pre-authorizes the Scenario Beta secondary-stage evacuation plan for a VEI-7 eruption affecting 100,000–500,000+ additional evacuees beyond the initial 100 km zone. The Planner identifies 5–10 ranked shelter hubs outside the 500 km ring (Denver, Cheyenne prioritized; Salt Lake City, Billings and Bozeman excluded as inside-ring), secures signed MOUs from host counties confirming shelter capacity and medical staffing, pre-positions food, water and medical supplies at secondary hubs, coordinates bus fleets and rail corridors to move evacuees from primary shelters to secondary hubs, and develops tiered public messaging differentiating shelter-in-place zones (250–500 km), time-banded evacuation zones (100–250 km), and organized evacuation (Zone One). The role executes this plan on a Scenario Beta trigger, preventing uncontrolled shadow evacuation that would saturate I-15, I-80 and I-90 and strand Zone Zero evacuees.

Consequences: Without a defined Scenario Beta secondary-stage plan, a pre-authorized VEI-7 trigger will activate a 500 km evacuation order affecting tens of thousands to millions of additional people with no published destinations, causing chaotic, uncontrolled flight on all routes away from Yellowstone. I-15, I-80 and I-90 saturate within 2–4 hours of the trigger, preventing the organized Zone One evacuation of 35,800 park visitors and stranding ambulances and medical transport. The evacuation delay cascades by 4–8 additional hours, and uncontrolled evacuees compete with organized evacuees for the same water, fuel and shelter supplies, stranding both groups. Estimated impact: 4–8 hour evacuation delay for Zone Zero, 100,000–500,000 unplanned evacuees stranded without shelter or supplies, 20–50 preventable deaths from exposure, medical neglect or secondary accidents.

9. Ashfall Forecasting and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Officer

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: The Ashfall Forecasting and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Officer maintains continuous ashfall monitoring at the forward command and all three shelter sites from T-12 hours through at least T+72 hours, with special intensity at T+6 hours when shelter sites are selected. The role involves real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensor monitoring, integration of USGS/NOAA forecast updates, and authority to trigger 4-hour shelter relocation if ashfall exceeds thresholds. This is a continuous, life-safety-critical role requiring constant presence at the forward element and shelter sites. The officer must be on-site and available without interruption to detect ashfall escalation and authorize relocation before shelter occupants suffer respiratory distress.

Explanation: This role maintains continuous ashfall and air-quality monitoring at the forward command element and all three shelter sites using real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensors and visual ash-depth markers, integrating updates from NOAA and USGS ashfall models. At T+6 hours when final shelter sites are selected, the Officer updates the selection based on the latest wind and plume forecast (not the T+0 forecast), identifies ranked second and third backup shelter locations 50+ km upwind, and maintains a dynamic 4-hour relocation protocol triggered if actual ashfall exceeds model predictions (threshold: PM10 >100 µg/m³ at primary sites). The Officer also manages the supplemental 100,000 N95 mask reserve at Billings or Salt Lake City and authorizes emergency relocation of 5,000–10,000 evacuees to backup shelters if primary sites fall in heavy ash, preventing shelter occupants from developing respiratory distress.

Consequences: Without dynamic shelter siting and ashfall monitoring, shelter locations are chosen at T+6 h using the T+0 forecast and are never updated. If actual ashfall shifts 50+ km from the forecast or doubles in intensity, 10,000–15,000 evacuees are sheltered in moderate-to-heavy ash for 12–24 hours before a relocation order is issued (if issued at all). The 100,000 N95 mask stock (user constraint) is exhausted within 12–24 hours if ashfall is 2–3 times heavier than forecast, leaving shelters without protection for the remaining 48–60 hours of operation. Relocation of 10,000+ evacuees mid-operation requires 3–6 hours of transport, additional buses and a second intake process, effectively delaying shelter operations by 6–12 hours and stranding evacuees in ashfall during the transition. Estimated impact: 500–2,000 evacuees develop respiratory distress within 6–24 hours; 5–10 die if medical care is delayed; 200–500 stranded during relocation.

At T+6 h when final shelter sites are selected, she updates site selections based on the latest wind and plume forecast (not the T+0 forecast), identifies ranked second and third backup shelter locations 50+ km upwind and confirms their readiness. Background Story: Dr. Susan Kwan is a volcanologist and ashfall-impact specialist with 14 years at the USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory, where she specializes in ash-dispersion modeling, air-quality monitoring and the behavior of volcanic ash in regional water systems. A PhD from Caltech in geology, Kwan has published extensively on the 1980 Mount St. Helens eruption's ashfall impacts and has collaborated with NOAA on volcanic ash advisory (VAAC) protocols. She is deeply familiar with the uncertainty ranges in ashfall forecasts from large eruptions and the practical challenges of sheltering populations in moderate to heavy ash. Her research on N95 mask efficacy in volcanic ash environments and the rate of ash-induced equipment degradation made her the ideal choice for dynamic shelter siting and ashfall monitoring during the Yellowstone response. Kwan maintains real-time connections to NOAA's Hazardous Weather Testbed and the National Weather Service and can access hourly ashfall model updates as they become available.

Equipment Needs: Continuous ashfall monitoring: real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensors and data loggers at forward command and all three shelter sites (estimate: 4-6 sensors minimum). Visual ash-depth measurement stations (scales, photographs) at each location. Laptops with real-time integration of USGS ashfall model outputs, NOAA forecast updates and local air-quality sensor feeds updated hourly. Printed shelter-siting decision cards with PM10 thresholds (relocation trigger >100 µg/m³ at primary sites). Maps showing backup shelter locations 50+ km upwind, confirmed daily from the latest wind forecast. Contact lists for shelter facility managers and logistics director for 4-hour relocation authorization.

Facility Needs: Primary station at the forward element in Livingston (or Bozeman) with continuous access to USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory ashfall models and NOAA Weather Service plume forecasts updated hourly from T-12 h onward. Direct satellite and radio communication with all three active shelter sites and the logistics director. Real-time air-quality data feeds integrated into the forward-element common operating picture. Standby 24/7 for emergency relocation decisions if actual ashfall exceeds model predictions. Coordination capability with secondary-hub facility managers if Scenario Beta triggers and evacuees must be moved onward from primary shelters.

Omissions

1. Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan and Destination List Missing

The plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta VEI-7 trigger ordering immediate 500 km radius evacuation affecting 100,000 to potentially millions of additional people beyond Zone One. No second-stage shelter hubs, host-community MOUs, onward transport routes, or supply-staging depots are defined. If the trigger fires, evacuees from 100–500 km radius will be ordered to leave with no published destinations, causing chaotic uncontrolled flight on I-15, I-80 and I-90 that saturates the very corridors needed for Zone Zero primary evacuation, adding 4–8 hours delay and stranding 35,800 tourists and staff in ashfall zones.

Recommendation: Develop and pre-authorize a written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan by Month 1 (2026-11-14), specifying: (1) five to ten ranked shelter hubs outside the 500 km ring (Denver and Cheyenne prioritized; Salt Lake City, Billings, Bozeman, Idaho Falls excluded as inside-ring) with signed MOUs from host counties confirming shelter capacity; (2) tiered public messaging differentiating shelter-in-place zones (250–500 km, self-supplied), time-banded evacuation zones (100–250 km, pre-assigned by county) and organized evacuation (Zone One); (3) bus fleets and rail corridors moving evacuees from primary shelters to secondary hubs using lateral routes away from I-90; (4) food, water, medical supply pre-positioning at secondary hubs by Month 1 (2026-11-14). Conduct a multi-state Scenario Beta exercise involving sample bus dispatch and shelter intake 30 days before the eruption window (Month 3 = 2027-01-14).

2. Responder Exposure Limits and Relief Depth Undefined; Staffing Insufficient for 72-Hour Operations

The plan assumes 100–150 NPS rangers (estimate) with 1.5 relief ratio per post, leaving approximately 67–100 concurrent positions. At peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h), all ranger hours are consumed with zero relief cushion. A single ranger injury, equipment failure, or weather event at one critical checkpoint (e.g., Gallatin Canyon) halts traffic for 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles and cascading 1–2 hours delay through the entire operation. The plan lists responder exposure limits as a secondary decision but specifies no shift lengths, withdrawal thresholds, or separate N95 inventory for responders (user constraint defines only 100,000 civilian stock).

Recommendation: Define concrete responder exposure limits in writing by Month -1: maximum 6-hour shifts at ash-exposed locations (contraflow checkpoints, perimeter gates), mandatory 2-hour rest with N95 replacement, complete withdrawal after 18 consecutive hours. Count responder N95 respirators separately from the 100,000 civilian stock, with 50% surge buffer (total 150,000–200,000 respirators). Pre-stage a 30–50 person standby reserve from outside the region (Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, Idaho Department of Lands) at a depot outside the ash zone, ready to deploy within 4 hours if coverage falls below 50% at any checkpoint. Pre-authorize the forward command to request additional National Guard without supervisory approval. Conduct a 6-hour shift-rotation exercise at a key control point 30 days before the window, testing relief logistics, N95 replacement and fatigue protocols under simulated ashfall.

3. Ashfall Footprint Uncertainty and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Strategy Lack Real-Time Monitoring and Relocation Protocols

The plan selects final shelter sites at T+6 h from the NOAA/USGS plume forecast but does not specify real-time ashfall monitoring or relocation triggers if actual ashfall diverges from forecast. Volcanic ashfall from a VEI-6 eruption has never been directly observed in North America; grain-size distribution, settling rates and wind variability could shift the modeled footprint by 50–100+ km or intensify by 2–3x. If actual ashfall exceeds forecast by 50 km or doubles in intensity, 10,000–15,000 evacuees will be sheltered in moderate-to-heavy ash (PM10 > 100 µg/m³) for 12–24 hours before a relocation order is issued. The 100,000 N95 mask stock (user constraint) exhausts within 12–24 hours if ashfall is 2–3x heavier, leaving shelters without protection for the remaining 48–60 hours.

Recommendation: Establish continuous ashfall and air-quality monitoring at the forward command and all three shelter sites using real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensors and visual ash-depth markers, updated hourly from T-12 h onward. At T+6 h when final shelter sites are selected, update the selection based on the latest wind and plume forecast (not the T+0 forecast). Maintain a ranked second and third backup shelter for each primary site, located 50+ km upwind (confirmed daily from latest wind forecast), enabling rapid 4-hour relocation if ashfall exceeds thresholds (trigger: PM10 > 100 µg/m³ at primary sites). Pre-stage supplemental 100,000 N95 masks at a secondary hub (Billings or Salt Lake City) with standing agreement for daily resupply if ash consumption exceeds 20% of stock per day. Conduct an air-quality monitoring exercise with NOAA and shelter managers 30 days before the window, testing real-time forecast updates and relocation protocols.

4. Single-Point Road Chokepoint Vulnerability: Gallatin Canyon and Gardiner Lack Viable Bypass and Rapid-Clearance Capacity

The three exit corridors depend on narrow, two-lane mountain passes (Gallatin Canyon on US-191/US-20, Gardiner on US-89, Cody approach on US-14/16/20) with minimal shoulders, documented rockfall and secondary-slide hazard. A single breakdown, rockslide, or tremor-induced slide during peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h) could block an entire contraflow and strand 500–2,000 vehicles within 30 minutes. The plan mentions pre-positioned tow and rescue assets at chokepoints but does not specify equipment count, staging locations, or hard decision rules for diversion if clearance exceeds 45 minutes. The South Entrance remains landslide-blocked, eliminating a potential southern exit.

Recommendation: Pre-position at least two mobile heavy-equipment teams (wreckers, debris chippers, spotters) at Mammoth or Spanish Creek by Month -0.5, with 72-hour fuel and supplies, tasked to reach any Gallatin Canyon blockage within 15 minutes of dispatch. Establish live geotechnical monitoring along Gallatin Canyon and US-89 near Gardiner using motion sensors or drones at identified slide-prone zones, with automatic alerts to the forward command if incipient movement is detected. Conduct a geotechnical survey of the South Entrance landslide 60 days before the window; develop a time-boxed single-lane clearance plan (maximum 4 hours proposed threshold) and a longer-term bypass plan with hard abort triggers (M>4.0 renewed seismic activity, equipment breakdown). Issue written loss-of-exit contingency: if any primary corridor blockage persists beyond 45 minutes and cannot be restored, the forward command will trigger overflow diversion to the nearest surviving exit and issue shelter-in-place orders for queued vehicles in that sector.

5. Cross-Jurisdiction Authority Transfer and Command Gaps: NPS-to-State Handoff and FEMA Region 8/10 Seams Lack Explicit Protocols

The plan specifies authority transfer at the park boundary under written protocol, with NPS incident commander handing responsibility to state governors at defined checkpoints. However, contraflow traffic does not stop at jurisdictional lines; drivers cross from NPS to state control mid-queue, creating windows where no single authority owns traffic-reroute or shelter-assignment decisions. Idaho falls under FEMA Region 10 (Seattle) while Montana and Wyoming fall under Region 8 (Denver); the plan names only the Denver RRCC, leaving Region 10 mutual aid (Boise and Pocatello resources) uncoordinated and potentially delayed 1–2 hours. The plan does not specify written MOUs with the three governors confirming their acceptance of NPS incident command or their agreement to enforce unified messaging.

Recommendation: Establish a dedicated Boundary Coordination Officer at the forward element in Livingston with real-time voice and data links to the NPS incident commander and the three state on-scene commanders. Issue a written protocol specifying that the boundary officer controls traffic reroutes and initial shelter assignments during the corridor crossing, and that NPS care ends at a specific roadside checkpoint where state custody formally begins. Pre-authorize state on-scene commanders to issue temporary reroutes without requesting park ranger approval. Add an explicit FEMA Region 10 liaison call at T+0 hours from the Denver RRCC, with pre-agreed mutual aid arrangements (Boise and Pocatello fuel, water and medical resources) documented in signed MOUs by Month 1 (2026-11-14). Obtain written pre-event confirmation from governors of Montana, Wyoming and Idaho authorizing the Unified Command's Zone One and Scenario Beta orders, and enforce unified public messaging. Conduct a multi-state command-authority exercise 60 days before the window, testing the boundary handoff, Region 8/10 coordination and governor-to-FEMA hotline.

6. Communications Layer Fragility: Ash-Induced Cell-Network Collapse and Tremor Damage Leave IPAWS and Bridge Systems Untested

The plan relies on IPAWS and Wireless Emergency Alerts as the primary public channel, with National Guard signal bridging as the fallback for responder coordination. Ash-induced flashovers on transmission lines, tremor damage to cell towers, and silicate-ash clogging of repeater fans could collapse the local network faster than signal units can deploy. The plan does not specify the number of Guard signal units available, their staging locations, fuel pre-positioning, or testing protocols under simulated ashfall. Printed route cards and highway advisory radio are mentioned as fallbacks but are not pre-produced or validated for clarity and multilingual comprehension.

Recommendation: Deploy National Guard signal corps teams with satellite phones, portable repeaters and generator fuel to each contraflow control point and the forward command element at T-12 h, before ashfall onset. Pre-stage printed route cards and windshield placards at all park entrance stations and lodges by Month -1, in English and five primary visitor languages (Spanish, Japanese, German, Mandarin, French), with simple instructions (e.g., 'North Exit: Follow US-89 to Gardiner, then I-90 to Livingston') and shelter addresses and phone numbers. Activate all available highway advisory radio stations and variable message signs on US-191, US-20, US-89 and I-90 with pre-recorded messages updated hourly from the forward command. Conduct formal radio interoperability testing across all agencies 30 days before the window, confirming frequency coordination, call signs, encryption protocols and on-air checks from each control point. Test satellite and portable-repeater systems under simulated ashfall conditions, measuring radio propagation through ash, equipment overheating and 72-hour fuel adequacy.

7. International and Non-English-Speaking Visitor Notification: Language Access and Mobility-Assistance Gaps Unaddressed

The plan lists international visitor, language and access-needs notification pathways as a low-priority decision. Yellowstone hosted approximately 4 million visitors in 2023, with roughly 40% from outside the USA. During peak season, non-English speakers could comprise 30–40% of the 35,000 visitors in the park (estimate 10,000–15,000 evacuees), many arriving via tour buses or without personal vehicles. The plan does not specify how these populations will receive evacuation instructions, access contraflow lanes, or board priority evacuation shuttles. Visitors without vehicles and unclear instructions could delay departure, cluster at wrong shelters, or become stranded if buses are not pre-allocated.

Recommendation: Pre-produce IPAWS messages, radio broadcasts and digital alerts in five primary visitor languages (Spanish, Japanese, German, Mandarin, French) by Month -1, with simple phased messages validated for comprehension by native speakers. Coordinate with concessioner Xanterra Parks and Resorts to disseminate multilingual briefings to all guest rooms, tour buses and visitor centers at T+0. Pre-identify 20–50 multilingual volunteers from tour operators and position them at major lodges by T+0, with translation materials and communication devices. Establish a dedicated shuttle-bus evacuation plan for tour groups and lodge-based visitors, pre-assigning 4–6 buses per major lodge (estimated 20–30 buses total) with pre-briefed drivers and mobility-assistance attendants. At T-12 h, confirm lodge occupancy and create priority-transport staging areas with medical supplies. Pre-authorize a secondary protocol: if any lodge cannot evacuate within 3 hours, notify the forward command, which will dispatch helicopter support or ground rescue teams from the National Guard.

8. Hospital and Utility Power Grid Failure: No Explicit Fuel Pre-Positioning, Generator Startup Failures, and Cascade-Risk Management

The plan identifies grid failure as a contingency and directs fuel priority to hospitals and communications centers, but does not specify which hospitals are critical receivers, fuel pre-positioning timelines, or how many hospitals have adequate on-site reserves. Regional hospitals typically have 24–48-hour generator fuel on hand (estimate); simultaneous power loss across multiple substations due to ash-induced flashovers could occur within 4–8 hours of ashfall, faster than fuel convoys from distant depots can deliver. Hospitals often have single fueling ports and outdated generators with startup failures during high-stress events; a 4-hour outage before fuel arrives could force cancellation of 10–20 surgeries and loss of ventilator support. The plan does not coordinate with regional power utilities to identify critical transmission lines or single-point failures.

Recommendation: Pre-position 72-hour diesel and propane fuel reserves at the three largest receiving hospitals (Bozeman Deaconess Medical Center, Livingston HealthCare, Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center) by Month -0.5, confirming tank capacity and fueling-port adequacy with each facility. Establish fuel-delivery contracts with local vendors requiring priority dispatch and arrival within 2 hours of a fuel request. Conduct a hospital power-failure exercise at each facility 30 days before the window, testing manual generator startup, fuel-transfer protocols and backup surgical protocols under ash-simulation conditions. Coordinate with Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power 60 days before the window to identify critical transmission lines, substations and protective relays in evacuation and shelter zones. Request pre-deployment of mobile generator units and voltage-regulation equipment at the two largest substations serving Bozeman and Idaho Falls. Establish a 24/7 utility-operations hotline from the forward command to each regional dispatch center, and pre-authorize helicopter fuel caches at forward airfields (Gallatin County, Jackson Hole, Billings) for emergency medical supply delivery if ground routes are blocked.

Potential Improvements

1. Convoy Delivery Timeline Underestimated: Water Arrives Later Than T+12 h Target, Creating Shelter Supply Crisis

The plan states that bottled-water convoys will be 'mobilized within 12 hours' and deployed from Salt Lake City, with an implicit expectation of arrival at Bozeman and Idaho Falls by T+24 h (user constraint). However, the I-15 northbound route from Salt Lake to the shelters is the same corridor that out-of-state evacuees are likely to use if Scenario Beta triggers. Ashfall will degrade road surfaces, reduce visibility and slow all traffic. A realistic estimate under moderate ashfall and evacuation-related congestion is 18–30 hours delivery time (estimate), not 12 hours. If water convoys arrive at T+24 h or later, the shelters must sustain 10,000–20,000 people for 1–2 days on existing, likely inadequate supplies, creating a public-health crisis.

Recommendation: Pre-stage bottled water, N95 respirators and generator fuel at forward depots in Bozeman, Billings and Idaho Falls by Month -0.5, with a minimum of 10 days' supply for the planned shelter capacity (assume 15,000 at Bozeman, 10,000 at Idaho Falls). Establish a dedicated 'supply-surge' lane on I-15 northbound from T+0 to T+24, reserved exclusively for water and fuel convoys, enforced by National Guard escorts. Pre-authorize the forward command to halt non-essential evacuation traffic on I-15 for up to 30 minutes to allow high-priority water convoys to pass if the main route gridlocks. Coordinate with Utah and Wyoming departments of transportation and water authorities to identify additional water sources within 200 miles of the shelters and pre-arrange 24-hour access. Test a water-convoy exercise from Salt Lake City to Bozeman under simulated ashfall and congested-traffic conditions 30 days before the window, measuring actual travel time and identifying chokepoints.

2. Visitor Accountability and Backcountry Evacuation: 200–400 Backcountry Hikers Cannot Be Reliably Evacuated Within T+6 Hours

The plan lists a 'Visitor Headcount Reconciliation and Backcountry Sweep Protocol' but does not specify the number of active backcountry permits, the typical dispersal of permit-holders across 3,500 square miles, or how many ranger-hours and helicopter sorties are required to sweep all trailheads and camps within 6 hours. Yellowstone issues approximately 500–1,000 backcountry permits daily during peak season (estimate); locating and evacuating 300–500 scattered parties requires coordination across multiple ranger districts and helicopter support. If 50–100 backcountry parties (200–400 people estimate) cannot reach main roads within T+6 h, they may become trapped as ashfall intensifies and roads become impassable. On-foot evacuation during heavy ash exposure could require 12–24 additional hours and cause respiratory distress or hypothermia.

Recommendation: At T-24 h, issue an emergency permit cancellation and mandatory evacuation order to all outstanding backcountry permits, instructing holders to exit via designated ranger-escorted routes. Pre-position ranger teams at key backcountry junctions (Norris-to-Canyon trail, Lamar Valley research stations) by T-12 h, with satellite phones and emergency shelter supplies. Establish dynamic backcountry tracking using satellite messenger devices; at T+0, initiate hourly check-ins with all outstanding permit-holders and redirect non-responding parties to ranger-escort meeting points. Designate 2–3 last-resort wilderness shelters in areas outside the modeled ashfall footprint (e.g., South Entrance/Thorofare region), pre-stocked with food, water, first aid and N95 respirators. Coordinate with Wyoming Search and Rescue to stand by for ground-based extraction of stranded parties after the main evacuation window (T+6 h).

3. Public Compliance Risk: Conflicting Evacuation Orders and Shelter-in-Place Messaging Undermine Trust and Corridor Throughput

The plan specifies that outer-zone residents in Bozeman, Billings and Idaho Falls should be told to shelter in place or follow time-banded departure schedules (to prevent shadow evacuation). However, if a Scenario Beta trigger fires, these same populations must then evacuate immediately. This reversal could be perceived as government deception, eroding trust in official channels and causing chaotic, uncontrolled flight. If public trust collapses, uncontrolled evacuation of 50,000–200,000 outer-zone residents could begin within 2–4 hours of a Scenario Beta order, creating gridlock on I-15, I-80 and I-90 that prevents the organized Zone One evacuation and strands primary evacuees 4–8 additional hours in ash exposure.

Recommendation: Develop and pre-authorize an 'Adaptive Messaging Protocol' explaining the rationale for phased evacuation orders: initial shelter-in-place is based on current low-eruption probability; Scenario Beta escalation will be triggered by specific USGS indicators (to be published in advance); outer-zone residents should monitor official channels and expect possible reversal if indicators cross thresholds. Deliver this protocol to media outlets, emergency management offices and community leaders in Zone One communities 60 days before T+0, so the public understands the escalation logic. At T+0, rebroadcast the protocol on IPAWS and local media to reinforce the message. If a Scenario Beta trigger fires, issue separate messaging explaining the new indicator values and stating that the previous shelter-in-place order is superseded, effective immediately. Conduct a messaging credibility exercise with local government and media 60 days before the window, testing message clarity and anticipating public-response scenarios.

4. Procurement and Contracting Lead Times Not Addressed: Emergency Supply Dispatch Delayed 24–48 Hours Without Pre-Event Contracts

The plan assumes water convoys can be 'mobilized within 12 hours,' but sourcing, loading and dispatching a convoy of 20–40 water trucks requires coordination with suppliers, transportation contractors and state agencies. If contracts are not pre-positioned or suppliers are not pre-authorized, typical emergency procurement delays are 24–48 hours (estimate). A 24-hour delay in water-convoy dispatch means the convoy does not arrive at shelters until T+36 h instead of T+12 h, during which shelter occupancy could reach 15,000–20,000 people. Water shortages affecting thousands for 24+ hours increase risk of dehydration, medication non-compliance and secondary health emergencies.

Recommendation: Execute pre-event contracts with bottled-water suppliers, N95 respirator manufacturers, generator-fuel wholesalers and charter-bus operators by Month -1, with explicit 'surge-mobilization' clauses requiring 12-hour dispatch upon verbal activation by the forward command. Identify alternative suppliers (e.g., water distributors in Pocatello, ID and Butte, MT; N95 suppliers in Salt Lake City and Denver) and list them in a standby-supplier roster. Pre-authorize payment via emergency FEMA contract vehicles so suppliers can charge supplies immediately without normal competitive-bidding delays. Establish a procurement checkpoint at the forward command element tasked with tracking all inbound supply shipments and alerting the incident commander if any convoy is delayed more than 4 hours beyond dispatch.

5. FAA Airspace Grounding Coordination Incomplete: Medevac and Reconnaissance Capability Uncertain, Authority Gaps Exist

The plan states that a VEI-6 eruption will trigger grounding of FAA sectors ZLC (Salt Lake) and ZSE (Seattle) to prevent ash-engine encounters. However, the FAA operates independently and may not immediately coordinate grounding with the Unified Command's needs for medevac, reconnaissance or emergency airlift. The incident commander may want exceptions for critical patient transfers that the FAA blocks due to ash-concentration forecasts. Delays in grounding coordination could result in aircraft encountering ash within the first 2–4 hours of ashfall, adding a secondary emergency response load. Alternatively, rigid grounding without medevac exceptions could deny hospitals access to helicopter transport for critical patients, delaying transfers by 4–6 hours and causing preventable deaths.

Recommendation: Establish a pre-event coordination protocol with the FAA Regional Flight Service Stations (Salt Lake City and Seattle centers) and air-operations offices at mountain airports (Gallatin County, Jackson Hole, Billings) at least 60 days before T+0. Define an explicit trigger for airspace grounding (e.g., USGS detection of VEI-6 magma signatures, NOAA forecast of ash concentration >100 µg/m³ in flight corridors) and pre-authorize a narrow set of ash-model-cleared rotary-wing medevac and survey flight corridors below defined ash-concentration limits, approved by the Unified Command. Establish a 24/7 aviation-operations liaison at the forward command element with direct phone lines to the FAA regional desk and the military (Malmstrom AFB, Montana) to coordinate real-time flight requests and ash-model updates. Pre-authorize helicopter fuel caches at forward airfields (Gallatin County, Jackson Hole, Billings) to enable rapid deployment of medevac sorties if airspace restrictions are lifted temporarily.

6. Responder Fatigue Burnout Not Explicitly Tracked: No Fatigue-Assessment Checklists, Withdrawal Authority, or Air-Quality Monitoring at Posts

The plan specifies exposure limits and relief rotations but does not describe operational procedures for identifying responder fatigue, authorizing withdrawal from posts, or monitoring air-quality conditions at each checkpoint to trigger withdrawal thresholds. Responders working 6-hour shifts with 2-hour rest cycles may reach acute fatigue or ash-induced respiratory distress before they self-report. Without a dedicated fatigue-assessment and air-quality monitoring officer, checkpoint staffing decisions are made reactively rather than proactively, risking coverage gaps at the worst moment.

Recommendation: Assign a dedicated Responder Safety and Fatigue-Management Officer with real-time PM10/PM2.5 sensors at each traffic checkpoint and perimeter gate, updated hourly from T+0 through T+72 h. Develop fatigue-assessment checklists for on-site use, with clear withdrawal triggers (e.g., reaction-time degradation, difficulty concentrating, excessive fatigue self-reports). Pre-authorize ranger withdrawal from posts if fatigue exceeds safe limits or if air-quality readings exceed agency respiratory-protection standards. Conduct a 6-hour shift-rotation exercise at a key control point 30 days before the window, testing relief handoff protocols, N95 replacement procedures, fatigue-assessment accuracy and radio communication continuity under simulated ashfall.

7. Exclusion Perimeter and Re-Entry Access Control: Static Checkpoints Consume Guard Personnel Needed for Logistics and Shelter Security

The plan specifies a fixed checkpoint perimeter on all roads out of the evacuation zone to prevent looting and unauthorized entries. However, static checkpoints divert National Guard personnel from logistics convoy escorts and shelter security during the peak evacuation and ashfall phases. A hard perimeter with fully staffed checkpoints at every exit road requires an estimated 50–100 Guard personnel simultaneously, competing with the 30–50 person standby reserve and convoy-escort needs. The plan does not specify the trade-off between perimeter enforcement and other Guard missions.

Recommendation: Develop a tiered perimeter posture: at T+0 to T+24 (peak evacuation and ashfall onset), implement mobile roving patrols and drone surveillance in evacuated communities rather than static checkpoints, consuming fewer personnel while detecting unauthorized entries. Concentrate Guard personnel on logistics convoy escorts and shelter security during this critical phase. At T+24 onward (Phase 2 transition), if ashfall conditions permit, establish more robust static checkpoints. Pre-authorize escorted-return programs in later phases (T+48 h onward) for residents to retrieve documents, medications and animals, with responder escorts and pre-defined access windows. Conduct a perimeter-operations exercise 30 days before the window, testing mobile patrol coordination, drone deployment protocols and escorted-return logistics.

8. Zone One Resident Population Unquantified: Census Data Missing, Evacuation Timing Target May Be Infeasible

The plan specifies that Zone One (100 km radius including West Yellowstone, Gardiner and Cody) must be evacuated by T+24 h, but does not quantify the registered resident population in these communities. Without a population estimate, the plan cannot validate shelter capacity, water supply targets, bus fleet sizing, or overall corridor throughput. A shortfall in any of these could extend the Zone One clearance beyond T+24 h, into the period when ashfall may be intensifying.

Recommendation: Conduct a detailed census of registered Zone One residents (West Yellowstone, Gardiner, Cody and surrounding areas within 100 km) by Month -1, accounting for seasonal variation and summer tourism influx. Cross-reference with hotel and lodge occupancy data from concessioners and local visitor bureaus to estimate transient populations. Update shelter capacity and water-supply targets based on the actual Zone One census. Confirm that the three exit corridors (US-191/US-20 West, US-89 North, US-14/16/20 East) have sufficient throughput capacity to evacuate both Zone Zero (35,800) and Zone One residents within the T+24 h deadline, adjusting load-split percentages if needed. Conduct a full-scale Zone One evacuation drill 60 days before the window, involving local emergency management officials and concessioners.

9. Forward Command Element Location Selection Incomplete: Livingston vs. Bozeman Trade-Offs Not Analyzed

The plan names Livingston as the forward Unified Command element location with Bozeman as an alternate, but does not specify the criteria for choosing between them or document their respective advantages and disadvantages. Livingston is closer to the North Entrance (US-89) and has a preexisting National Guard tactical operations center at Camp Ravenna. Bozeman is larger, has more medical capacity and is the planned shelter site, but is 40+ miles southwest of the park. The choice affects command visibility, response latency, shelter coordination and access to backup facilities.

Recommendation: Analyze Livingston vs. Bozeman by Month -0.5 based on: (1) line-of-sight and satellite/radio coverage to all three exit corridors and shelter sites; (2) proximity to receiving hospitals (Bozeman, Livingston); (3) existing facility capacity (command ops center, power, security); (4) proximity to backup command sites (Fort Carson, Camp Ravenna); (5) local emergency management support and pre-existing coordination. Document the final choice and its rationale in a written decision memo, signed by the UC Incident Commander, by Month -0.5. If Bozeman is selected as the primary, confirm that a secondary command post is maintained at Livingston or another location with direct line-of-sight to the North Entrance corridor.

Critique and recommended actions from domain experts.

1 Expert: Volcanologist & USGS Hazard Forecaster

Knowledge: volcanic hazard assessment, eruption-probability modeling, VEI classifications, ashfall forecasting, USGS monitoring networks

Why: The Scenario Alpha/Beta trigger matrix (Section: Escalation Trigger decision, canonical facts) references a 40% VEI-6+ probability and pre-authorized threshold-based indicators, but the final USGS trigger values are listed as 'due by T+3h' with only a placeholder. This expert must harden the trigger matrix, validate the modeled ashfall footprint upon which shelter siting (T+6h) depends, and confirm the 500 km Scenario Beta ring adequacy.

What: Review and finalize the USGS trigger indicator thresholds (uplift rate, seismic magnitude, gas flux) that activate Zone One and Scenario Beta expansion by T+3h; validate the ashfall dispersion model confidence bounds (currently ±50 km) to certify the shelter-siting rule and real-time monitoring thresholds (50/100 µg/m³ PM10).

Skills: eruption probability estimation, ashfall transport modeling, seismic-swarm interpretation, real-time USGS data integration, multi-agency forecasting protocols

Search: USGS volcanologist eruption forecasting, Yellowstone hazard monitoring, ashfall dispersion modeling, VEI probability assessment

1.1 Primary Actions

  • Halt the plan at its current scope and insert a mandatory pre-authorization gate: do not activate Zone Zero evacuation operations (T+0 onward) until three conditions are met: (1) a written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan with at least five ranked hubs, signed host MOUs and supply pre-positioning schedules is finalized; (2) a Responder Exposure and Relief Protocol with explicit shift limits, a 30–50 person standby reserve and pre-event Guard reinforcement commitments is signed; (3) real-time ashfall monitoring with 4-hour relocation protocols and a supplemental N95 reserve is deployed. These three actions are tightly coupled cascade-failure risks; all must be completed before T+0 or residual risk remains unacceptable.

Shelters in Denver and Cheyenne will be overwhelmed without advance capacity planning, forcing emergency relocations and stranding 200–500 evacuees mid-operation.

1.4.E Root Cause

The plan was written under the constraint that pre-event lead times are unavailable and execution must begin at T+0. The decision to pre-authorize the 500 km trigger (user constraint) was made before a destination plan existed, creating a temporal mismatch: the trigger is ready to fire, but the execution plan does not exist. This is a process gap, not an operational oversight.

The 1.5 relief ratio is a standard assumption, but it is inadequate for a 72-hour sustained operation with zero pre-event lead time for recruiting or training reinforcements.

1.6.A Issue - Shelter siting based on a single T+6 forecast update ignores ashfall forecast uncertainty of ±50 km and masks clog rate

The plan selects final shelter sites at T+6 hours from the latest NOAA/USGS plume forecast. Ashfall modeling uncertainty is typically ±50 km or larger, and volcanic-ash forecasts from an unprecedented VEI-6 event have no ground-truth calibration. If actual ashfall diverges from the forecast by 50 km southward or doubles in intensity, shelter sites (e.g., Bozeman, Idaho Falls) could be placed in moderate-to-heavy ash within 4–6 hours of occupancy. The plan pre-stages only 100,000 N95 masks for 35,800 evacuees; assuming a 70% occupancy rate (25,060 people), masks clog after 6–8 hours in heavy ashfall and require replacement cycles not detailed in the plan. No real-time monitoring or relocation protocol exists.

Develop a ranked three-shelter backup system for each primary site by Month -1 (2026-09-14), identifying second and third locations 50+ km upwind with pre-authorized 4-hour relocation protocols. Without relocation protocols and standby facilities, 200–500 people will be stranded or delayed by 4–8 hours. Mask clogging without replacement logistics will leave evacuees unprotected for 6–12 hours, causing respiratory distress in 500–1,000 people and forcing 100–200 hospital transfers, overwhelming receiving facilities.

1.6.E Root Cause

Ashfall forecasting for a VEI-6 event is unprecedented; model uncertainty ranges widely and is often not disclosed. The plan assumes a single forecast update at T+6 hours is sufficient for a 24-hour shelter occupancy. N95 clog rates in heavy ash (6–8 hours) are documented in industrial and wildfire contexts, but the plan does not specify replacement cycles or a supplemental reserve, treating the 100,000 stock as static.

The plan did not allocate real-time PM10 monitoring or relocation protocols, treating shelter sites as fixed once selected. This underestimates both forecast error and the need for adaptive management during the operation.

Canonical facts propose 6-hour shifts, 2-hour rest, and 18-hour withdrawal limits, plus a 30–50 'standby reserve' from out-of-region. However: (1) all 67–100 ranger positions are consumed during T+2 to T+8 peak evacuation with zero cushion for injury, equipment failure, or scope creep; (2) responder N95s are 'counted separately, not drawn from the 100,000 civilian stock' (proposed threshold), but no responder headcount exists to size this separate stock; (3) a single traffic incident at Gallatin Canyon or a ranger injury during peak hours cannot be absorbed without halting one checkpoint, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles and cascading 2–4 hours delay. The 30–50 reserve exists only if it can be deployed within 4 hours; no mutual-aid agreement or pre-positioning is documented.

8.5.B Tags

  • responder-capacity-thinness
  • N95-sizing-opaque
  • single-point-staff-failure
  • relief-availability-unconfirmed

8.5.C Mitigation

By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29, before T+0), secure written pre-event mutual-aid commitments from Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wyoming Game and Fish, Idaho Department of Lands and Fort Carson (Colorado National Guard) for 50–100 out-of-region traffic-control and patrol personnel, pre-positioned at Billings or Cheyenne with 4-hour deployment authorization. Size responder N95s from confirmed responder headcount (rangers, highway patrol, Guard, utility crews estimated 300–500 total); estimate 2–3 respirators per responder over 72 hours = 600–1,500 total responder N95s. Pre-stage this stock separately at the forward command depot with dedicated replacement logistics. By Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+6 hours), assess actual ranger availability and request additional Guard personnel if coverage at any checkpoint drops below 50%. Test shift-rotation and relief handoff at Gardiner checkpoint (Month -0.5, 6-hour exercise) to confirm 4-hour reserve-deployment time.

8.5.D Consequence

If responder depth is not increased and confirmed, peak-hour traffic control will fail. A single breakdown at Gallatin Canyon or ranger injury at T+4 hours cannot be absorbed. One checkpoint halts for 2–4 hours, queuing 500–2,000 vehicles in ash, adding 2–4 hours to their exit time and increasing respiratory-distress cases by 30%. Stranded vehicles may attempt uncontrolled departures on secondary roads, risking 5–10 additional collisions. Responder N95 supply exhaustion at T+36–48 hours forces withdrawal of traffic-control staff, leaving checkpoints unmanned and allowing looting in evacuated towns. Preventable respiratory deaths among responders increase 10–15%.

8.5.E Root Cause

Responder staffing was dimensioned against the 35,800-person Zone Zero evacuation in isolation, without modeling peak concurrent demand across traffic control, perimeter patrols, backcountry sweeps, medical transport, and comms maintenance. The 1.5 relief ratio is typical for planned operations, not crisis response with ash exposure and injury risk. Responder N95 sizing was deferred ('counted separately') without defining the responder population. No pre-event mutual-aid agreements or forward pre-positioning exist; the standby reserve is aspirational and depends on T+0 decisions and verbal authorization.

8.6.A Issue - Shelter siting at T+6 hours based on a single plume forecast with ±50 km uncertainty and inadequate real-time monitoring enables shelter placement in heavy ashfall

The plan chooses final shelter sites at T+6 hours using the latest NOAA/USGS plume forecast and proposes a 4-hour relocation rule if conditions worsen. However: (1) ashfall forecast uncertainty for a VEI-6 event is ±50 km or greater (unvalidated, never directly observed in North America); (2) PM10 sensors are 'at forward element and every shelter' (proposed threshold) but no sensor deployment timeline or communication protocol is documented; (3) a single forecast update at T+6 hours provides one snapshot; no continuous 4-hourly updates are guaranteed; (4) if actual ashfall exceeds forecast by 50 km or doubles in intensity, 10,000–15,000 evacuees sheltered at Bozeman or Idaho Falls sit in moderate-to-heavy ash (PM10 > 500 µg/m³ estimate), consuming N95s 3–5x faster than model estimates. A 4-hour relocation of 10,000 people requires ~20–30 buses and 4–6 hours actual transport time, not 4 hours decision-to-arrival. Shelters could be placed in the plume.

8.6.B Tags

  • forecast-uncertainty-underestimated
  • shelter-siting-brittle
  • real-time-monitoring-sparse
  • N95-consumption-underestimated
  • relocation-latency-optimistic

8.6.C Mitigation

By Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+0), deploy continuous PM10/PM2.5 sensors at Bozeman, Idaho Falls and the forward command with automated hourly data feeds to the forward command and USGS/NOAA. Set thresholds: >50 µg/m³ triggers immediate forecast update; >100 µg/m³ triggers shelter-suitability review. By Month -0.5 (2026-09-29), develop ranked three-shelter backup system for each primary site, identifying second and third locations 50+ km upwind of each primary, confirmed daily from 00:00 UTC wind forecast. Pre-authorize rapid occupancy-transfer protocols (4-hour decision-to-notification maximum). By Month 0 (2026-10-14) (T+6 hours), stage a supplemental 100,000 N95s at Billings or Salt Lake City hub with 8-hour ground-convoy or helicopter-transport agreement. Conduct an air-quality and shelter-siting exercise 30 days before eruption window (Month -0.5, 2026-09-29) simulating ashfall 50 km south of forecast, testing relocation decision and bus dispatch for 5,000–10,000 evacuees within 4 hours.

8.6.D Consequence

If shelter sites are placed 50 km downwind of forecast and ashfall exceeds model predictions, 10,000–15,000 evacuees shelter in moderate-to-heavy ash (PM10 > 500 µg/m³ estimate) with inadequate N95 supplies. Daily N95 consumption 3–5x exceeds model; stock depletes within 12–24 hours instead of 10 days. Respiratory distress cases increase 50–100% at receiving hospitals. A 4-hour relocation decision-to-movement window is unachievable; actual bus dispatch and transport require 6–12 hours, stranding evacuees in ash. 200–500 people cannot reach a second shelter before N95 supply fails. Pneumonia and acute respiratory failure cases increase 20–30%; preventable deaths increase 5–10 over baseline.

8.6.E Root Cause

Shelter siting was treated as a T+6-hour tactical decision, not a strategic design. The plan inherited plume-forecast uncertainty from NOAA/USGS without quantifying forecast error (±50 km is a reasonable estimate but unvalidated). PM10 sensors and continuous monitoring were specified as 'proposed thresholds' but no deployment authority, cost or timeline was documented. Real-time relocation was assumed to fit within 4 hours; actual bus dispatch and transit (6–12 hours estimated) makes this infeasible. The 100,000 N95 civilian stock was not stress-tested against 3–5x consumption in heavy ashfall. Backups and upwind sites were mentioned but not pre-surveyed or pre-authorized for rapid occupancy.
