Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Scenario Beta has no executable destinations, risking cascade failure of Zone Zero evacuation: a pre-authorized VEI-7 trigger will order millions to evacuate with no published shelter hubs, causing uncontrolled shadow evacuation on I-15/I-80/I-90 that saturates the same corridors needed for the 35,800-person Zone Zero clearance, adding an estimated 4–8 hours of delay and stranding 5,000–20,000 people in ashfall zones. The interim hub list is due T+12 hours, the written plan by Month 1 (2026-11-14), and signed MOUs by Month 2 (2026-12-14)—all post-event deadlines with no buffer for discovery of hub capacity shortfalls or distance mismatches (Denver and Cheyenne distances unverified).

  2. Responder staffing has zero relief depth and will collapse under the first incident: 100–150 rangers at 1.5 relief ratio yields only 67–100 concurrent positions, all consumed during the T+2 to T+8 evacuation peak, leaving no margin for injury, equipment failure or respiratory exposure. A single vehicle breakdown or traffic incident at Gallatin Canyon lasting 30+ minutes will halt a checkpoint for 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles and cascading 1–3 hours of additional delay through the entire operation. The 30–50 standby reserve is not pre-positioned, pre-authorized or tied to a Guard reinforcement commitment.

  3. Shelter siting at T+6 hours based on a single forecast with ±50 km uncertainty and no real-time monitoring creates high risk of placing 10,000–15,000 evacuees in heavy ashfall: if actual ashfall diverges 50 km from forecast or doubles in intensity, Bozeman or Idaho Falls shelters become untenable within 12–24 hours, requiring emergency relocation of 10,000–15,000 people (order within 4 h of exceedance, move and occupy about 8 h)—impossible without pre-authorized backup sites 50+ km upwind, pre-staged buses and protocols. PM10 sensors and relocation protocols are proposed but no deployment timeline exists; real-time response to forecast error is unvalidated.

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Positive: Pre-authorized Scenario Beta trigger eliminates decision delays and enables rapid 500 km evacuation order within 30 minutes, saving an estimated 2–4 hours of decision latency versus discretionary approval chains. This coupled with a written trigger matrix published in advance (due T+3 h) restores public trust by making escalation criteria transparent. Interaction: Fast triggering only succeeds if second-stage hubs are named and MOUs signed by Month 2 (2026-12-14); without them, the speed advantage evaporates into uncontrolled shadow evacuation. Recommendation: Prioritize signed hub MOUs (5–10 hubs outside 500 km ring) as a blocking dependency for trigger pre-authorization; do not finalize the trigger matrix without simultaneous hub validation.

  2. Negative: Real-time ashfall monitoring and 4-hour shelter relocation protocols depend on PM10 sensors, NOAA VAFT updates every 3 hours, and pre-positioned buses—all requiring T+0 deployment and Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) hardening exercises costing an estimated USD 5–8 million (sensors, exercises, backup shelters). Failure to deploy results in 10,000–15,000 evacuees sheltered in heavy ashfall, overwhelming hospitals with 50–100 additional respiratory cases and consuming USD 20–50 million in emergency relocation and medical surge. Interaction: Ashfall relocations divert buses from primary evacuation, cascading 6–12 hours delay to Zone One clearance and potentially extending overlap with peak ashfall. Recommendation: Treat ashfall monitoring as a pre-T+0 capital investment (not a post-event decision); validate sensor reliability and NOAA forecast latency in a Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) exercise (simulated ashfall, 4-hour relocation drill).

  3. Negative: Responder staffing at 100–150 rangers with zero relief depth and a 30–50 standby reserve that is not pre-positioned or pre-authorized costs an estimated USD 3–5 million and remains opaque until Month 1 (2026-11-14). A single incident (vehicle breakdown, ranger injury, respiratory exposure) during peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h) will halt a checkpoint for 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles and adding USD 50–100 million in indirect response costs and 5–10 preventable deaths. Interaction: Staffing shortfall cascades into longer evacuation time, increasing ashfall overlap; shortage also prevents real-time shelter relocation (buses and crews unavailable). Recommendation: Pre-authorize and seat the 30–50 standby reserve (deployable within 4 h) at T+0 at Billings or Cheyenne; sign Guard reinforcement commitment within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14); conduct a 6-hour shift-rotation exercise at Gardiner checkpoint within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) to validate 4-hour reserve deployment time.

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Use existing FEMA contract vehicles with verbal activation at T+0 and 12-hour dispatch clauses for water, fuel and N95 convoys, hardening contracts by Month 1 (2026-11-14); expected impact: eliminates 24–48 hour procurement delays, dispatching convoys by T+12 h with arrival T+24 h target (T+18–30 h estimate) versus T+36–72 h, saving USD 50–100 million in emergency-response overhead and preventing water-rationing crises affecting 10,000–20,000 evacuees. Priority: CRITICAL (blocking dependency for Phase 2 shelter operations). Implementation: activate existing contract vehicles verbally at T+0 h and finalize contract terms and vendor sign-off in Month 1 (2026-11-14); establish procurement checkpoint at forward command to track in-flight shipments and enforce 4-hour delay escalation.

  2. Secure written governor authorization letters from Montana, Wyoming and Idaho confirming UC authority over Zone One and Scenario Beta orders by T+6 h (verbal); execute signed MOUs and EMAC mutual-aid arrangements by Month 1 (2026-11-14); expected impact: prevents jurisdictional disputes that delay reroutes by 15–45 minutes per decision, saving an estimated 2–4 hours of total evacuation time and reducing authority-gap risk by 80–90%. Priority: CRITICAL (foundation for Boundary Coordination Officer authority). Implementation: distribute draft authorization package at T+0; schedule governor briefing calls by T+3 h; obtain verbal confirmation by T+6 h; assign legal counsel to lead MOU negotiation with state attorneys general from T+0; target all signatures by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

  3. Conduct geotechnical survey of Gallatin Canyon and South Entrance slide within Month 1 (2026-11-14); develop time-boxed single-lane clearance plan and hard abort triggers; expected impact: quantifies secondary-slide risk (if >20%, write off South Entrance clearance entirely), preventing crews from expending 6–12 hours on infeasible work and freeing heavy equipment for maintaining open corridors, saving USD 5–10 million in wasted clearing effort and 2–4 hours evacuation delay. Priority: HIGH (gates corridor management decisions). Implementation: engage USGS Volcano Disaster Assistance Program at T+0; deliver geotechnical report and bypass options within Month 1 (2026-11-14); pre-position tow teams at Mammoth and Spanish Creek by T+12 h with documented abort triggers (M>4.0 seismic event, >2 cm slope displacement, 30-minute equipment breakdown).

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Financing split for second-stage hubs and shelter sites remains open; if states/host communities refuse cost-sharing, federal envelope absorbs USD 20–40 million, which is a financing question only, since Beta hub pre-positioning sits inside the readiness package and is not counted again against the USD 30–35 million free contingency, so the buffer is preserved for for supply-chain disruptions or responder reinforcement surge (Likelihood: High). Hub pre-positioning and shelter setup are within the USD 200 million envelope only if cost-sharing is confirmed by Month 1 (2026-11-14); without pre-event clarity, negotiations cascade into Months 2–3 (2026-12-14 to 2027-01-14), delaying hub readiness and forcing makeshift shelter capacity at Scenario Beta trigger. Interaction: Financing delay compounds Scenario Beta hollowness: no hubs ready, no pre-positioned supplies, uncontrolled shadow evacuation. Recommendation: Resolve federal vs. state/local/host-community cost split by Month 1 (2026-11-14) via FEMA-governor MOU negotiations; document explicit cost-allocation line items and pre-approve state legislative authority for matching funds. Contingency: If states decline cost-share, hubs remain in the readiness package inside the USD 160 million base; shelter relocation (USD 5–10 million) stays the only identified draw on the USD 40 million contingency.

  2. FEMA Region 10 (Idaho) liaison seat at Denver RRCC from T+0 is a single point of failure for Idaho mutual aid; no written pre-authorization or resource-commitment MOU exists between FEMA Region 10 and Pocatello/Boise suppliers (Likelihood: Medium). If the Region 10 liaison is unavailable or communications with Idaho resources are delayed, water and fuel convoys experience 2–6 hour dispatch delays, pushing arrival at Idaho Falls shelter from T+24 h to T+30–36 h, leaving 10,000 evacuees on water rationing for 1–2 additional days and increasing dehydration/medical emergency risk by 20–30%. Interaction: Region 10 coordination failure cascades into shelter water-supply crisis, triggering early relocation or public-health incident. Recommendation: Execute a signed FEMA Region 8/10 coordination MOU by Month 1 (2026-11-14), with a verbal liaison seat at T+0, pre-authorizing Idaho mutual-aid resource commitments (100,000+ gallons water, 50,000 gallons fuel, portable generators) and naming Idaho State Emergency Management liaison with 24/7 availability; conduct a 2-hour tabletop Region 10 activation drill within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) to test dispatch speed. Contingency: Pre-position a 100,000-liter supplemental water reserve at Pocatello or Boise by T+12 h; if Region 10 liaison is unavailable, activate backup ground-convoy dispatch from Salt Lake City to Idaho Falls on parallel route (US-89 south via Arizona, estimated 36–48 h).

  3. Zone One resident population remains unquantified; census is not scheduled until T+6 h, leaving no time to pre-stage shelter capacity or transport before evacuees arrive (Likelihood: High). If Zone One population exceeds the census estimate by 20–30% (plausible during peak tourism season), shelter capacity shortfall of 5,000–10,000 people forces overflow to unsecured secondary venues or out-of-state hubs, delaying shelter registration by 4–6 hours and increasing family-reunification failure rate by 15–25%. Interaction: Population underestimate cascades into shelter-capacity crisis, which forces emergency Scenario Beta hub activation even if trigger has not fired, consuming contingency supplies and creating false alarm messaging credibility loss. Recommendation: Conduct Zone One resident and transient-visitor census by T+6 h (estimate), coordinate with concessioners (Xanterra manifests) and county visitor bureaus to obtain hotel/lodge/campground occupancy estimates; pre-stage to the canonical 35,800 and seek a proxy Zone One estimate by T+6 h. Contingency: If the census shows population materially above planned capacity, size and activate third-site shelter expansion and request additional buses from FEMA contract vehicle pool after the census; if capacity still insufficient, issue tiered public messaging advising outer-zone residents to self-supply lodging (hotels in non-evacuation zones) to reduce shelter load.

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Assumption: NOAA/USGS ashfall forecasts are accurate within ±50 km and can be updated every 3 hours with reliable PM10 concentration outputs. If forecast error exceeds ±50 km or updates become unavailable, shelter sites chosen at T+6 h will be placed in heavy ashfall; relocation of 10,000–15,000 evacuees within the 8 h move-and-occupy window is unvalidated, stranding 200–500 people in moderate-to-heavy ash (PM10 > 100 µg/m³, suitability review threshold) for 6–12 hours and increasing respiratory hospitalizations by 50–100% (cost impact: USD 20–50 million emergency relocation + medical surge). Interaction: Forecast failure cascades into early N95 depletion (consumption 3–5x model estimate), forcing rationing and protective-equipment shortages for responders. Recommendation: Validate NOAA VAFT model skill for Yellowstone by T+12 h through USGS consultation; deploy PM10 sensors at all shelters by T+0 with independent satellite uplink (not cell-dependent); conduct a Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) shelter-relocation exercise (simulated 50 km forecast error, 4-hour bus dispatch) to expose real relocation latency and adjust decision rules accordingly.

  2. Assumption: Three receiving hospitals (Bozeman Deaconess, Livingston HealthCare, Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center) have adequate generator fuel reserves (72 hours on-site) and can sustain continuous operations during 4–8 hour grid outages caused by ash-induced transmission-line flashovers. If generators lack fuel or fail to start under stress, hospitals lose power within 4–6 hours, forcing manual ventilation of 10–20 critical patients and canceling 10–20 surgeries; estimated cost: USD 50–100 million in emergency generator mobilization and 5–15 preventable hospital-related deaths. Interaction: Hospital power failure disables wound-transfer coordination, stranding ambulances en route and cascading medical transport delays by 2–4 hours. Recommendation: Pre-position 72-hour fuel reserves at all three hospitals by T+12 h, validate generator operability and cross-train responders on fuel-transfer procedures at Month 0 (2026-10-14); coordinate with utilities (Montana-Dakota, Pacific Power, Idaho Power) to pre-authorize emergency load-shedding sequences by Month 0 (2026-10-14) to prevent cascading blackout across the region.

  3. Assumption: Scenario Beta secondary-stage hubs (Denver, Cheyenne) lie outside the 500 km ring, have committed shelter capacity for 100,000–500,000 additional evacuees, and can be activated and supplied within 24–36 hours of trigger without requiring post-event MOU negotiations. If hubs are inside the ring, lack capacity commitment, or require state legislative approval to activate, Scenario Beta trigger becomes unexecutable; uncontrolled evacuation of 100,000+ unordered residents saturates I-15/I-80/I-90, preventing Zone Zero clearance and extending evacuation delay by 4–8 hours (cost impact: USD 200–500 million in cascade-failure response and 20–50 preventable deaths). Interaction: Hub validation failure directly undermines the pre-authorized trigger's credibility; if hubs cannot receive evacuees, published trigger matrix becomes hollow and erodes public trust in escalation messaging. Recommendation: Verify Denver and Cheyenne distances from Yellowstone center and distance from ashfall plume by T+12 h (desktop check); obtain written capacity confirmation (beds, kitchens, medical triage) from host counties by Month 1 (2026-11-14); execute signed MOUs documenting pre-authorization to activate within 24 h of UC request by Month 2 (2026-12-14); conduct a full multi-state Beta hub activation tabletop (including sample bus routing and intake registration) by Month 3 (2027-01-14).

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. KPI 1: Evacuation Throughput and Gate Clearance — Target: Gate G1 (T+6 h) ≥98% of 35,800 (at least 35,084 persons); Gate G2 (T+24 h) ≥95% of registered Zone One residents cleared; corridor blockage duration <45 minutes. Success metric: exit counts reconciled against lodging manifests and permits by T+6 h and T+24 h gates. If achieved, confirms contraflow design (about 660 veh/h per exit as fleet average; West requires about 994 veh/h, about 1,190 from T+1) and responder staffing are adequate. Interaction: Blockage delays compound ashfall overlap; shortfalls indicate tow-team positioning or diversion rules require revision. Monitoring: Track hourly vehicle counts at all three gates starting T+1 h; trigger real-time reroute if any exit cumulative count falls >10% below the load-split target; compare exit manifests with backcountry sweep status at T+5 h decision checkpoint.

  2. KPI 2: Shelter Occupancy and Relocation Readiness — Target: Primary shelters (Bozeman, Idaho Falls, third site) reach full planned capacity (15,000, 10,000, 10,800 estimate) by T+12 h with <2-hour intake processing; relocation order issued within 4 hours of an exceedance (200 µg/m³ or a failed suitability review at 100 µg/m³, proposed threshold). Success metric: <5% shelter-intake processing errors; zero evacuees left unplaced; sheltered exposure above 200 µg/m³ is minimized, with completion time set (estimate) after the relocation drill. Interaction: Relocation latency directly reduces responder relief-rotation time available elsewhere. Forecast error cascades into overflow; backup-site readiness is the containment lever. Monitoring: Deploy PM10 sensors at T+0 with hourly reporting to forward UC; establish shelter-occupancy dashboard updated every 2 hours; execute relocation drill (sample 1,000 evacuees moved to backup sites) within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) to validate the 4 h detection-to-order step, set move and occupy times (8 h stop rule) and identify bottlenecks.

  3. KPI 3: Supply-Chain Continuity and Responder Availability — Target: Water convoy arrival by T+24 h (or T+18–30 h via forward depots T+12 h); N95 consumption ≤20% of daily stock; responder coverage ≥50% at all traffic-control and perimeter posts through T+72 h; zero responder entrapment or respiratory-injury casualties. Success metric: all three receiving hospitals maintain generator fuel >24 hours on-site; fuel resupply convoys dispatched within 4 hours of low-fuel alert. Interaction: Supply failure cascades into shelter rations and responder withdrawal, which collapses traffic throughput and evacuation timeline. Low coverage (<50%) at one post halts a corridor 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 evacuees. Monitoring: Establish 24/7 logistics checkpoint at forward command tracking water/fuel/N95 inventory in-flight and on-site; activate backup suppliers if convoy is delayed >4 hours beyond T+12 h dispatch; flag responder staffing falls below 50% coverage at any post within 30 minutes and request standby reserve deployment.

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary Objectives: Report documents a 72-hour Yellowstone evacuation plan for 35,800 Zone Zero evacuees (T+0 to T+6 h) and 100 km Zone One residents (T+6 to T+24 h), with pre-authorized Scenario Beta expansion to 500 km if USGS triggers fire. Intended audience: FEMA Regions VIII and X, state governors (MT, WY, ID), NPS, and multi-state UC stakeholders. Key decisions to be informed: (1) pre-authorization of UC trigger matrix and 500 km evacuation order within 30 minutes; (2) NPS-to-state boundary handoff and Boundary Coordination Officer authority; (3) Scenario Beta second-stage hub naming and signed MOUs by Month 2 (2026-12-14).

  2. Deliverables: Written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan naming 5–10 ranked hubs outside 500 km ring with signed host MOUs by Month 2 (2026-12-14); interim ranked hub list by T+12 h; signed governor authorization and EMAC mutual-aid MOUs by Month 1 (2026-11-14); responder exposure limits and 30–50 standby reserve deployed by T+0; PM10 sensors and 4-hour relocation protocols at shelters by T+0; three full-scale exercises (Scenario Beta routing, shift rotation, water convoy) by Month 3 (2027-01-14); post-event after-action report and institutional-memory capture.

  3. Version 2 Differences: Version 1 treated Scenario Beta as a pre-authorized trigger with no executable second-stage plan; Version 2 must require signed hub MOUs and supply pre-positioning as blocking dependencies before trigger pre-authorization is finalized. Version 1 left responder staffing at 1.5 relief ratio with zero contingency; Version 2 must specify concrete 6-hour shift limits, separate N95 inventory sizing and 30–50 standby reserve pre-positioning by T+0. Version 1 deferred all ashfall monitoring and shelter relocation to post-event; Version 2 must mandate PM10 sensor deployment and real-time monitoring from T+0 to enable 4-hour relocation protocols.

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Zone One resident population census is not quantified; baseline estimate lacks source and seasonal variation unknown. Critical because shelter capacity pre-staging (Bozeman 15,000, Idaho Falls 10,000 estimate) depends on it; if actual population is 20–30% higher during peak tourism, shelter shortfall of 5,000–10,000 forces overflow to unsecured secondary venues, delaying intake 4–6 hours and increasing registration failures by 15–25%. Recommendation: Execute census by T+6 h via concessioner manifests and county visitor-bureau surveys; validate against lodging occupancy and campground permits; pre-stage to the canonical 35,800 and size any added capacity after the census, seeking a proxy Zone One estimate (county, lodging manifests) by T+6 h.

  2. Scenario Beta hub distances from Yellowstone center to Denver and Cheyenne are not verified; canonical facts note 'distances not verified' yet designation assumes these hubs lie outside the 500 km ring. Critical because if either hub is actually inside the ring or ashfall reaches it under different wind scenarios, Scenario Beta destinations become untenable within 12–24 hours of occupancy, forcing emergency secondary relocations and cascading shelter crisis. Consequence: if relocation needed mid-operation, USD 20–50 million emergency transport cost and 4–8 hour evacuation delay. Recommendation: Map exact distances using geographic center of Yellowstone Caldera; model ashfall plume reach to each hub under USGS ensemble forecasts (10–20 wind/emissions scenarios); confirm final hub selection by Month 1 (2026-11-14) with ashfall survivability assessment.

  3. Water convoy realistic arrival time is T+18–30 h (estimate), not the T+12 h dispatch target; forward-depot pre-staging at Bozeman and Idaho Falls (quantity 200,000–300,000 liters estimate) is not specified with contract timelines or supplier naming. Critical because shelters must sustain 25,000–35,000 people with adequate water from T+6 h onward; if convoys arrive T+30 h and forward depots are not staged by T+0, shelters face 18–24 hour water rationing, increasing dehydration risk in 20–30% of occupants and forcing 100–200 emergency hospital transfers for electrolyte imbalance. Recommendation: Stock forward depots by T+12 h and finalize water-supply contracts naming delivery timelines and depot locations in Month 1 (2026-11-14); conduct a Salt Lake City to Bozeman convoy exercise under ashfall simulation and I-15 congestion conditions within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) to measure realistic travel time; keep the T+24 h arrival target (realistic T+18–30 h, estimate) with explicit backup supplier activation if arrival is delayed >4 hours.

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. FEMA Region 10 and Idaho mutual-aid resource pre-authorization: Does Idaho State Emergency Management Agency confirm written commitment to dispatch 100,000+ gallons bottled water, 50,000 gallons fuel, and portable generators within 6 hours of UC request? Critical because Idaho Falls shelter (10,000 occupants) depends on Pocatello/Boise suppliers if Salt Lake City convoy is delayed; unconfirmed commitment risks 12–24 hour supply shortage affecting 10,000 evacuees and stranding USD 10–20 million in contingency. Recommendation: Obtain signed FEMA Region 10 MOU and Idaho State Emergency Management commitment by Month 1 (2026-11-14); conduct a 2-hour tabletop Region 10 activation drill within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) testing dispatch authorization and supply-order fulfillment; document backup supplier names and contact authority for fallback activation if primary commitment fails.

  2. Scenario Beta hub financing ownership and host-community pre-acceptance: Do Denver, Cheyenne, and any secondary hub counties formally accept the role of secondary shelter sites and agree to pre-position supplies (food, water, medical) on 48–72 hour notice without requiring post-event legislative approval or cost-reimbursement disputes? Critical because unsigned host MOUs leave hub pre-positioning undefined and delay activation beyond T+12 h interim list; cost uncertainty (federal vs. state vs. local share) defers spending decisions into Months 2–3 (2026-12-14 to 2027-01-14), delaying supply staging; hub pre-positioning stays inside the readiness package and is not a contingency draw. Recommendation: Initiate host-county outreach by Month 0 (2026-10-14); obtain written capacity confirmation and pre-acceptance letters by Month 1 (2026-11-14); execute fully signed MOUs with explicit federal cost-share percentages and supply pre-positioning schedules by Month 2 (2026-12-14).

  3. Contraflow corridor engineering validation and tow-team positioning: Can tow and rockfall teams realistically reach any Gallatin Canyon blockage within 15 minutes and clear single-lane debris within 4 hours under ashfall conditions, or must the 45-minute blockage diversion threshold be revised based on geotechnical feasibility? Critical because if clearance time exceeds 4 hours or secondary-slide risk during work exceeds 20%, tow-team deployment becomes a liability (crews entrapped), not an asset; diversion rule then becomes the only viable option, reducing effective exit capacity by 20–30% and cascading 3–6 hours evacuation delay. Recommendation: Deliver geotechnical survey of Gallatin Canyon (debris volume, slope stability, secondary-slide probability) by Month 1 (2026-11-14); execute tow-team mobilization and diversion exercise at Mammoth staging depot within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14); validate 15-minute reach time and 4-hour clearance window under ashfall simulation; revise corridor management strategy and loss-of-exit contingency if empirical findings contradict assumptions.

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. Assumption: 660 vehicles/hour per-exit throughput (3.0 persons/vehicle average, ~2,000 vehicles/hour total) is achievable on narrow two-lane mountain corridors (US-191, US-89, US-14/16/20) under ashfall visibility reduction (<100 meters) and evacuation-traffic chaos. If actual throughput drops 20–30% due to ashfall speed reduction (10 mph safe speed vs. 60 mph assumed) or staging-lot bottlenecks, evacuation extends from T+6 h to T+8–10 h, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles in peak ashfall and increasing respiratory-injury hospitalizations by 40–60% (cost impact: USD 20–50 million emergency medical surge). Version 1 assumed baseline traffic-engineering; Version 2 requires geotechnical and staging-capacity validation. Interaction: Reduced throughput cascades into responder fatigue (shifts lengthened 2–3 hours beyond 6 h limit) and shelter intake backlog. Recommendation: Validate contraflow termini capacity and throughput by measuring parking-lot staging dimensions, turn-pocket geometry and queue-storage length at Mammoth, Gardiner and West Yellowstone by Month 0 (2026-10-14); conduct a mock contraflow exercise under simulated ashfall conditions within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) to measure actual vehicle speeds and identify any lot-saturation chokepoints.

  2. Assumption: Scenario Beta secondary-stage hubs outside the 500 km ring (Denver, Cheyenne candidates) are survivable under ashfall and have zero ashfall overlap under any USGS ensemble forecast scenario. If modeling reveals that either hub experiences measurable ashfall (>50 µg/m³) under 10–20% of wind/emission scenarios, hub survivability assumption fails; designation as 'safe' destination becomes probabilistic, not deterministic. Consequence: evacuees routed to hubs may face unprotected ashfall within 12–24 hours of arrival, forcing emergency secondary relocation to tertiary hubs and cascading USD 50–100 million in unplanned transport (cost impact: 2–4 hour additional delay and 10–20 preventable respiratory deaths). Interaction: Hub ashfall risk compounds Scenario Beta triggering: if trigger fires and hubs are not ash-safe, the pre-authorized 500 km order becomes unexecutable. Recommendation: Run USGS ashfall ensemble forecasts (10–20 wind/emissions combinations) to all candidate hubs (Denver, Cheyenne, Albuquerque, Las Vegas) by Month 0 (2026-10-14); confirm zero ashfall above 20 µg/m³ for each hub in >90% of scenarios; designate only validated ash-safe hubs as Scenario Beta destinations in final MOU by Month 2 (2026-12-14).

  3. Assumption: Bottled-water supply chain from Salt Lake City, Pocatello and Butte can deliver water to shelters by T+24 h target (realistic T+18–30 h, estimate) via forward depots (T+12 h); the 1.43 million liters is the 10-day supply target without ashfall-road closures or evacuation-traffic congestion blocking I-15 and I-90 corridors. If ashfall visibility falls below 50 meters or I-15 congestion from unordered evacuees reaches 40%+ by Hour 8–12, convoy speeds drop from 60 mph to 10–15 mph and arrival time extends to T+36–48 h. Consequence: shelters must ration water for 18–24 hours; 10,000–20,000 evacuees experience dehydration risk and 5–10 preventable electrolyte-imbalance deaths (cost impact: USD 10–20 million emergency relocation and medical response). Version 1 assumed 12 h dispatch = T+24 h arrival; Version 2 must account for realistic ashfall delays. Interaction: Water shortage cascades into shelter-intake crisis and early Scenario Beta activation if Zone One population exceeds estimates. Recommendation: Conduct a water-convoy exercise from Salt Lake City to Bozeman under simulated ashfall (fog machines reducing visibility to 50–100 meters) and I-15 saturation (25–40% traffic) within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14); measure actual transit time; if arrival is after T+30 h, pre-stage 300,000+ liters at forward depots by T+0 instead of relying on convoy arrival by T+24 h.

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Federal vs. state/local/host-community cost-share for shelter sites and Scenario Beta secondary hubs is unresolved; decision required by Month 0 (2026-10-14) to unlock spending authority. If states/host communities refuse cost-sharing, federal envelope absorbs USD 20–40 million (estimated Beta hub pre-positioning), but Beta hub pre-positioning is already inside the readiness package (USD 47.5–87 million within the USD 160 million base) and is not counted again; free contingency stays at USD 30–35 million. Recommendation: Obtain written cost-allocation confirmation from FEMA, Montana, Wyoming and Idaho emergency management by Month 0 (2026-10-14) documenting federal percentage, state match and host-community in-kind contributions; embed allocations in signed MOUs by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

  2. Water convoy pre-award contract language must specify 12-hour dispatch and 4-hour resupply-cycle performance targets; unclear if FEMA contract vehicles already include bottled-water and fuel convoy capacity or if new blanket purchase agreements are required. If existing contracts lack surge clauses, procurement delays revert to 24–48 hours, pushing water arrival to T+36–48 h instead of T+24 h and creating USD 10–20 million emergency replacement cost for supplemental depots and helicopter resupply. Recommendation: Audit current FEMA contract vehicle roster for water, fuel and N95 capacity by T+12 h; use existing FEMA vehicles with verbal activation at T+0 and dispatch by T+12 h; issue RFP for missing surge-capacity gaps with 12-hour dispatch performance targets as a separate Month 1 (2026-11-14) hardening item.

  3. Budget contingency allocation for Scenario Beta execution is ambiguous; if Beta trigger fires, does the USD 40 million contingency activate for second-stage hub supplies (food, water, medical) or is that cost absorbed by host communities or a separate federal appropriation? If contingency were consumed for other unfunded items, no reserve would remain for shelter relocation, hospital surge or supply-chain failures, forcing choices between competing priorities and risking USD 50–100 million emergency response cost overruns. Recommendation: Define explicit contingency-allocation tiers in the budget envelope by Month 0 (2026-10-14): shelter relocation USD 5–10 million (estimate) as the only identified contingency draw; Beta hub pre-positioning stays in the readiness package, and hub activation operating costs are a separate, unfunded item pending a Beta-specific appropriation or host in-kind contributions by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

Review 12: Role Definitions

  1. Boundary Coordination Officer (Forward UC Element): Requires explicit job description, interagency authority matrix, and 24/7 succession plan. Why essential: Officer holds pre-authorized decision authority over traffic reroutes and shelter assignments at NPS-to-state boundary during T+0 to T+24 h peak evacuation; if authority limits are undefined or succession is absent, reroute decisions cascade to higher command, adding 15–45 min delay per decision (estimated 2–4 h total evacuation delay and 500–2,000 stranded vehicles). Recommendation: Draft written Officer position description by T+0 specifying decision authority (reroutes without supervisory approval if comms lost >5 min), communications protocols (dedicated satellite phone to NPS incident commander, three state on-scene commanders, Denver RRCC), and succession roster (named primary, alternate, backup); confirm 24/7 availability and seat Officer at forward element at T+0.

  2. FEMA Region 10 Liaison (Denver RRCC Seat): Explicit mandate, resource-commitment authority, and 24/7 dispatch protocol for Idaho mutual aid required. Why essential: Liaison coordinates water, fuel and generator convoys from Pocatello and Boise for Idaho Falls shelter (10,000 occupants); if role lacks written authority to activate pre-authorized mutual-aid resources or liaison is unavailable, Idaho resource dispatch is delayed 6–12 h, pushing water arrival from T+24 h to T+30–36 h and leaving evacuees on ration for 1–2 days (estimated 10–20% dehydration-risk exposure, USD 10–20 million emergency resupply cost). Recommendation: Document Region 10 Liaison responsibilities in signed FEMA Region 8/10 MOU by Month 1 (2026-11-14); seat liaison at T+0; confirm 24/7 availability and pre-authorized dispatch authority for minimum 100,000 gallons water, 50,000 gallons fuel and portable generators on UC request; conduct activation drill at Month 0 (2026-10-14).

  3. Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Hub Activator (Multi-State Coordination Role): Clarity on who authorizes hub occupancy, supply routing and time-banded evacuation schedules across Colorado, Wyoming, Idaho and Utah required. Why essential: If Scenario Beta triggers at T+12 h, interim hub list must be transmitted to evacuees with published occupancy assignments within 30 min; if no single named authority owns hub activation and supply coordination across state lines, decisions delay 2–4 h per hub or contradict each other, causing evacuees to queue at wrong destinations and stranding 10,000–20,000 people (estimated USD 50–100 million emergency reroute cost and 4–8 h additional delay). Recommendation: Designate a named Deputy UC (or FEMA Region 8 officer) as Scenario Beta Hub Activator by Month 1 (2026-11-14); grant explicit authority to issue hub-activation orders via IPAWS/WEA and coordinate with state emergency managers; pre-authorize pre-positioning of supplies at each hub by Month 2 (2026-12-14); test activation authority in a full multi-state tabletop exercise by Month 3 (2027-01-14).

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. Scenario Beta interim hub list (T+12 h) precedes signed host MOUs (Month 2 = 2026-12-14): If hubs cannot be named and published by T+12 h due to incomplete distance verification or capacity confirmation delays, Scenario Beta trigger becomes unexecutable at T+12–24 h, forcing uncontrolled outer-zone evacuation (estimated 50,000–200,000 additional evacuees) onto I-15/I-80/I-90, saturating primary Zone Zero corridors and delaying 35,800 park evacuees 4–8 additional hours. Interaction: Uncontrolled flight cascades into water/shelter shortages and extends ashfall overlap by 20–40%. Recommendation: Initiate hub distance verification and capacity surveys from T+0; obtain interim capacity confirmations (unsigned) from all 5–10 candidates by T+0 h to enable T+12 h interim list issuance; defer final signed MOUs to Month 2 (2026-12-14) without blocking interim publication.

  2. Responder exposure limits and standby reserve deployment must be confirmed and pre-positioned before T+0, but formal deployment authorization from state adjutants general may not arrive until T+24–48 h: If standby reserve is not seated at forward depot by T+12 h, a checkpoint incident at T+3–6 h cannot be covered within 4 h, halting one corridor and stranding 500–2,000 vehicles. Interaction: Staffing failure cascades into longer evacuation, increasing ashfall overlap and preventing real-time shelter relocation due to lack of available buses/crews. Recommendation: Secure written pre-event Guard reinforcement commitments from all three state adjutants general by Month 1 (2026-11-14), pre-positioning standby personnel at designated depots by T+12 h under a Stafford Act emergency-delegation clause (verbal activation authority at T+0, not subject to 24–48 h state approval delays).

  3. Water convoy dispatch T+12 h to shelters by T+24 h assumes realistic 12–30 h travel time (estimate) and no I-15 congestion from shadow evacuation; if Scenario Beta triggers before water arrives (T+12–18 h range), secondary hub activation will consume buses, extending water-transport logistics and cascading arrival to T+30–48 h. Interaction: Delayed water arrival leaves first 10,000 Zone Zero evacuees at Bozeman/Idaho Falls with 18–24 h ration shortfall; early Beta trigger also pulls forward-depot stock into secondary hubs. Recommendation: Pre-stage forward depots (Bozeman, Idaho Falls) with 200,000–300,000 liters by T+0 (not relying on Salt Lake City convoy for T+24 h arrival); sign all water-supply contracts with 4-hour resupply clauses and secondary-source names (Pocatello, Butte) by T+0 to enable rapid convoy re-dispatch if Scenario Beta consumes primary supply ahead of schedule.

Review 14: Financial Strategy

  1. Post-event cost-share and federal vs. state/local expense attribution for recovery and Phase 3 re-entry unspecified: if FEMA covers 100% of Scenario Alpha response but states claim 25–50% cost-share for Scenario Beta secondary hubs (estimated USD 20–40 million), the question is who finances these items; Beta hub pre-positioning is inside the readiness package and is not a second draw on the USD 200 million envelope. Interaction: Unresolved attribution delays federal reimbursement claims (12–24 months post-event), forcing state/local budget gaps and straining partner agencies' willingness to participate in future operations. Recommendation: Obtain written FEMA pre-event guidance on cost-share percentages for multi-state Scenario Beta operations by Month 1 (2026-11-14); embed federal reimbursement triggers and cost-allocation rules in signed MOUs with all states and host hubs; clarify whether pre-event hardening (readiness package, exercises) is 100% federally funded or requires state match.

  2. Long-term institutional sustainability: no budget line for annual maintenance, refreshment or re-validation of MOUs (currently estimated at USD 2–5 million/year for Months 4–60 = 2027-02-14 to 2031-10-14 and beyond); if Scenario Alpha does not occur, readiness assets (sensors, contracts, pre-positioned supplies) must be rotated, tested and renewed through ongoing appropriations. Interaction: Budget uncertainty for months 4–60 (2027-02-14 to 2031-10-14) leaves the plan at risk of lapsing if annual funding is not secured post-Month 3 (2027-01-14); standby responder contracts and pre-positioned supplies degrade without refreshment. Recommendation: Establish a dedicated Yellowstone Evacuation Readiness Fund with annual Congressional appropriation (proposed USD 2–5 million/year) by Month 2 (2026-12-14); include line items for equipment rotation, MOU renewal (every 2 years), responder reserve retainer and full-scale exercises every 18 months.

  3. Break-even or cost-avoidance threshold not quantified: no analysis of whether USD 200 million pre-event investment avoids more expensive post-event emergency response or whether a scaled-down readiness posture would reduce cost while accepting higher mortality/morbidity risk. Interaction: Without explicit cost-benefit analysis, decision-makers cannot justify the readiness budget to legislatures or compare it against alternative mitigation (e.g., pre-event visitor restrictions, park closure during eruption window). Recommendation: Commission a formal cost-benefit analysis by Month 2 (2026-12-14) comparing: (1) full readiness plan (USD 200 million pre-event) vs. baseline response (USD 500–800 million post-event emergency cost estimate + 20–50 preventable deaths); (2) scaled-down readiness (USD 100 million, forgoing Beta hubs and some supply pre-positioning) vs. full plan; publish findings to justify budget request and communicate risk-mitigation value to stakeholders and Congress.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Clear, measurable milestones with executive visibility and accountability: Gate G1 (T+6 h, ≥98% evacuation) and Gate G2 (T+24 h, ≥95% Zone One clearance) provide objective success criteria that sustain stakeholder confidence. If milestones slip (actual clearance <95% at T+24 h), motivation falters because ambiguity spreads about whether the plan is viable; estimated cost: USD 50–100 million in extended operations and 5–10 additional deaths from ashfall overlap. Interaction: Gate slippage cascades into Scenario Beta credibility loss (if Beta triggers before Zone One clears, public trust in escalation messaging collapses). Recommendation: Publish monthly progress reports (Months 1–3, 2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) documenting readiness checkpoints (MOUs signed, exercises completed, sensors deployed) with explicit red/yellow/green status; brief governors and FEMA administrators monthly to sustain political commitment.

  2. Tangible pre-event hardening wins (signed MOUs, completed exercises, equipment deployed) by Month 1 (2026-11-14): if Month 1 (2026-11-14) deadline passes with unsigned hub MOUs or unexecuted shift-rotation exercises, urgency erodes and follow-on activities drift. Consequence: Scenario Beta plan remains hollow through T+0; if trigger fires and interim hub list cannot be published by T+12 h, uncontrolled shadow evacuation cascades (estimated 4–8 h evacuation delay and 5,000–20,000 stranded evacuees). Interaction: Unmet Month 1 (2026-11-14) targets signal that the plan is underfunded or politically unsustainable, undermining responder recruitment and multi-state partner engagement. Recommendation: Establish a Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) Readiness Steering Committee (NPS, FEMA, governors, UC leadership) with monthly executive-level reviews; publish signed MOUs within 30 days of Month 1 (2026-11-14) and exercise completion dates within 60 days; tie responder recruitment and supply contracts to visible progress milestones.

  3. Sustained federal funding commitment through the 72-hour window and post-event cost-share clarity (federal vs. state/local/host): if appropriation lapses or cost-attribution disputes surface in Months 1–2 (2026-11-14 to 2026-12-14), stakeholders question whether readiness is credible. Consequence: state/local partners withdraw, supply contracts are delayed or cancelled, and responder reserve recruitment stalls; estimated cost: USD 50–100 million in emergency procurement premiums and 1–3 month plan readiness delays. Interaction: Funding uncertainty compounds Scenario Beta hub validation (if hubs cannot confirm pre-positioning costs are federally covered, they refuse to participate). Recommendation: Secure written FEMA pre-event guidance on cost-share percentages by Month 1 (2026-11-14); embed reimbursement triggers in all MOUs; obtain Congressional pre-appropriation of the USD 200 million envelope by Month 0 (2026-10-14) start and confirm no rescission risk through Month 3 (2027-01-14).

Review 16: Automation Opportunities

  1. Real-time evacuation-gate vehicle counting via automated traffic sensors and RFID windshield tags: Deploy sensors at all three exit checkpoints (Mammoth, Gardiner, West Yellowstone, Cody) at T+0 with real-time dashboard integration to forward UC. Expected savings: eliminates 30–60 minute manual gate-count reconciliation cycles (currently required at T+3, T+5.5, T+6 h decision points), enabling Gate G1 assessment 30 min earlier and accelerating any reroute decisions by 15–30 min per incident. Cost to deploy: USD 0.5–1 million (sensors, dashboard). Interaction: Faster gate-count feedback cascades into quicker diversion decisions if corridor blockages occur, reducing stranded-vehicle exposure by 200–500 people per incident. Recommendation: Procure RFID tag stock and deploy sensors by T+12 h; pre-stage tag distribution at all park entrance stations; test sensor accuracy and tag-reader latency in a Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) contraflow exercise.

  2. Pre-programmed IPAWS/WEA alert templates and automated dispatch routing by shelter-intake status: Develop and pre-code all Zone One and Scenario Beta evacuation messages (English + five languages) with geographic targeting and time-triggered release logic by T+0. Expected savings: eliminates 15–30 min messaging delays at each decision point (T+0 public alert, T+6 h shelter-assignment broadcast, T+12 h Scenario Beta interim hub list), reducing driver uncertainty and uncontrolled departures by 10–20%. Cost to implement: USD 0.2–0.5 million (message development, IPAWS technical setup, testing). Interaction: Faster alert dispatch reduces shadow evacuation of outer-zone residents, preserving I-15/I-80/I-90 corridor capacity for primary evacuees. Recommendation: Finalize all message templates and geographic-targeting logic by T+0; conduct a Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) full-cascade alert exercise (deploy all messages within 5 min of each trigger point); validate message clarity with native speakers (3–5 per language) by Month 0 (2026-10-14).

  3. Automated supply-chain inventory tracking and resupply-trigger algorithms: Deploy GPS-tracked convoy monitoring and automated alerts to forward UC when water/fuel/N95 inventory at shelters falls below consumption-rate thresholds (e.g., 20% of stock per day triggers backup-supplier activation). Expected savings: eliminates 4–8 h manual inventory audits and decision delays, enabling 4-hour resupply cycles versus current 8–12 h estimated lag. Cost to implement: USD 2–3 million (GPS/IoT sensors on trucks, inventory-management software, contracted monitoring staff). Interaction: Automated triggers accelerate N95 and fuel resupply before stock-outs cascade into respiratory-protection shortages or generator fuel failures, reducing emergency convoy surges and USD 20–50 million unplanned logistics costs. Recommendation: Select and pre-deploy inventory-tracking platform by T+12 h; test sensor-to-alert latency under ashfall simulation within Months 1–3 (2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14); pre-authorize backup suppliers to activate within 2 h of automated alert (not waiting for human decision).

Q1: What is the 'Scenario Beta' escalation trigger, and why does the plan pre-authorize it without a defined second-stage destination list?

A1: Scenario Beta is a pre-authorized order to expand evacuation from Zone One (100 km) to a 500 km radius affecting millions of people, triggered by USGS indicators (e.g., VEI-7 probability ≥20% remaining). The UC can issue this order within 30 minutes without further approval. However, no second-stage shelter hubs, host-community MOUs or supply pre-positioning exist yet. This creates a critical gap: the trigger is authorized but unexecutable, risking uncontrolled shadow evacuation that saturates I-15/I-80/I-90 and delays the primary 35,800-person Zone Zero evacuation by 4–8 hours.

Q2: Why does the plan state that water convoys will arrive by T+24 hours when realistic estimates are T+18–30 hours, and how does this gap affect shelter operations?

A2: The plan targets water dispatch by T+12 h from Salt Lake City, expecting arrival by T+24 h. However, ashfall reduces I-15 visibility to 50–100 meters, safe convoy speed drops to 10–15 mph, and evacuation-traffic congestion of 25–40% delays all northbound traffic. Realistic arrival is T+18–30 h. This 6–30 hour gap forces shelters to sustain 25,000–35,000 evacuees on rationing for 1–2 days, increasing dehydration risk and secondary health emergencies. The plan mitigates this by pre-staging forward depots at Bozeman and Idaho Falls by T+0, but depot capacity (200,000–300,000 liters estimate) and resupply schedules are not specified in detail.

Q3: What does 'responder exposure limits and relief rotation regime' mean, and why is the plan's specification of 100–150 rangers at 1.5 relief ratio insufficient?

A3: Responder exposure limits define maximum shift length (proposed: 6 hours at ash-exposed posts), mandatory rest cycles (proposed: 2-hour rest with N95 replacement), and full withdrawal thresholds (proposed: 18 consecutive hours). At 1.5 relief ratio, 100–150 rangers yield only 67–100 concurrent positions, all consumed during peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h) with zero cushion. A single traffic incident or ranger injury lasting 30+ minutes will halt a checkpoint for 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles in ash. The plan proposes a 30–50 person standby reserve from out-of-region agencies, but it is not pre-positioned or pre-authorized, creating a single-point staffing failure.

Q4: How does the plan select final shelter sites at T+6 hours, and what risks does ashfall forecast uncertainty (±50 km) create for evacuation safety?

A4: At T+6 h, shelter sites are chosen from the latest NOAA/USGS plume forecast. The plan specifies PM10 thresholds (>50 µg/m³ triggers forecast update; >100 µg/m³ triggers shelter-suitability review) and proposes ranked backup shelters 50+ km upwind. However, ashfall forecast uncertainty for a VEI-6 event is ±50 km or greater (unvalidated, never directly observed in North America). If actual ashfall diverges 50 km from forecast or doubles in intensity, 10,000–15,000 evacuees will be sheltered in moderate-to-heavy ash within 12–24 hours, requiring emergency relocation. The plan proposes a 4-hour relocation protocol, but actual bus dispatch and transport require 6–12 hours, stranding 200–500 people in ash if conditions worsen.

Q5: What is the relationship between the pre-authorized Scenario Beta trigger and the three-exit contraflow design, and why do they create a cascade-failure risk if Scenario Beta fires during Zone Zero or Zone One evacuation?

A5: The plan's three-exit contraflow (West 50%, North 30%, East 20%) is designed to clear 35,800 Zone Zero evacuees by T+6 h and Zone One residents by T+24 h. Scenario Beta (500 km radius) is pre-authorized to trigger at T+12–24 h, ordering millions in outer zones to evacuate. If Scenario Beta fires before Zone One clearance (likely at T+12–24 h range), outer-zone residents (Bozeman, Billings, Idaho Falls) will attempt uncontrolled self-evacuation on the same I-15/I-80/I-90 corridors needed by Zone Zero and Zone One evacuees. This shadow evacuation of 50,000–200,000 unordered people saturates the corridors, reducing organized evacuation throughput by 30–50%, adding 4–8 hours to total evacuation time and stranding 5,000–20,000 people in ashfall zones.

Q6: The plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta 500 km evacuation order affecting 'millions of people' without quantifying the actual population in that ring or confirming that published destinations can absorb them. What are the ethical implications of issuing an evacuation order without knowing whether shelter exists for the evacuees?

A6: Scenario Beta pre-authorization prioritizes decision speed (30-minute trigger) over execution readiness, raising a core ethical tension: the UC can order millions to flee without confirmed shelter destinations, forcing evacuees into uncontrolled flight and potential stranding in ashfall zones. This violates the principle of duty of care—government cannot ethically order evacuation if it has not verified that refuge exists. The risk of false escalation (trigger fires but Beta destinations are overwhelmed or unreachable) also erodes public trust and may cause non-compliance with future orders, indirectly harming evacuees who ignore warnings. Mitigation requires signed hub MOUs and published destination lists by T+12 h, but this depends on post-event negotiation, not pre-event certainty.

Q7: The plan uses 'shelter-in-place' messaging in outer zones (250–500 km ring) early in the 72-hour window but then may reverse this order if Scenario Beta triggers. How does the plan protect against loss of public trust and non-compliance if escalation appears to reverse earlier guidance?

A7: The plan acknowledges this risk under 'Shadow Evacuation Suppression and Public Compliance Dynamics': early shelter-in-place messaging (if Beta does not trigger) is designed to prevent uncontrolled shadow evacuation, but if Beta later triggers and evacuees are told to leave, the reversal may be perceived as deception or government incompetence. Proposed mitigation is an 'Adaptive Messaging Protocol' published pre-event explaining that escalation logic is transparent (specific USGS thresholds trigger the reversal). However, the plan does not specify how to communicate this reversal credibly during the chaos of ashfall or confirm that local media and trusted voices will support the message. If compliance drops 20–40% due to trust loss, uncontrolled evacuation consumes the same corridors needed for organized Zone One clearance, cascading 4–8 hours of additional delay.

Q8: The plan prioritizes responder safety through exposure limits (6-hour shifts, 18-hour withdrawal) and separate N95 respirator stock, but these protections compete with evacuation throughput during the T+2 to T+8 peak. How does the plan balance responder protection against the risk that strict limits reduce traffic-control coverage and delay civilian evacuation?

A8: Responder exposure limits are ethically justified: responders should not sacrifice their health or lives for the response. However, enforcing 6-hour shifts and full withdrawal after 18 hours reduces concurrent traffic-control positions from the estimated 100–150 rangers to 67–100 during peak evacuation, with zero relief depth. A strict interpretation leaves checkpoints unmanned during critical hours, halting corridors and stranding 500–2,000 evacuees per incident. The plan proposes a 30–50 standby reserve to fill gaps, but if not pre-positioned and pre-authorized, the reserve is unavailable when needed. This creates a trilemma: (1) enforce limits and accept traffic delays that trap evacuees in ash, (2) waive limits and expose responders to preventable injury, or (3) invest heavily in pre-positioned relief to avoid choosing between the two. The plan implicitly assumes option 3 is feasible, but responder N95 stock is 'counted separately' without explicit sizing, and the standby reserve is not pre-authorized.

Q9: The plan pre-stages 100,000 civilian N95 respirators (user constraint) for 35,800 evacuees (about 2.8 masks per person over 10 days) but does not account for responder consumption or replacement cycles if ashfall is 2–3 times heavier than forecast. How does the plan handle N95 shortages if forecast error occurs, and what are the ethical implications of inadequate respiratory protection?

A9: The 100,000 civilian stock assumes ~2.8 masks per person for 10-day shelter occupancy and approximately 1-mask-per-person-per-day consumption in moderate ashfall. If ashfall is 2–3 times heavier than forecast, consumption rises to 2–3 masks per person per day, exhausting stock within 12–24 hours instead of 10 days. The plan proposes a supplemental 100,000 N95 reserve at Billings or Salt Lake City with 8-hour transport agreement, but deployment depends on real-time PM10 monitoring (not pre-deployed sensors) and rapid recognition of consumption surge. If the surge is not detected or transport is delayed, evacuees will lack respiratory protection during heavy ashfall, increasing respiratory-distress hospitalizations by 50–100% and preventable deaths by 5–10. Ethically, this represents a choice to accept mortality risk rather than pre-stage larger N95 reserves (estimated USD 5–10 million additional cost).

Q10: The plan specifies pre-authorized evacuation orders and trigger matrices published in advance to prevent hindsight blame on decision-makers, but this transparency also reveals the thresholds that enable judicial or political challenge post-event. How does pre-publishing USGS triggers affect legal liability if evacuation proves to have been unnecessary or if the triggers are deemed to have been too conservative or too aggressive?

A10: Publishing a pre-authorized trigger matrix (USGS indicators, thresholds, decision timeline) in advance protects decision-makers from hindsight blame by showing that escalation was rule-based, not arbitrary. However, it also creates a fixed target for post-event legal and political challenge: if the trigger fires and Scenario Beta evacuation occurs but the eruption does not materialize, evacuees or host communities may sue FEMA, USGS or the UC for 'unnecessary' evacuation, citing the published thresholds as evidence of over-caution. Conversely, if thresholds prove too aggressive (i.e., the trigger does not fire but a VEI-6 eruption occurs), beneficiaries of the timely evacuation may sue for claiming the thresholds were too conservative. This liability ambiguity is partially resolved by pre-event publication (demonstrating deliberation) and USGS science-based justification, but it is not eliminated. The plan does not address legal-defense strategy, post-event liability apportionment, or how to prove that triggers were 'correct' given the irreducible uncertainty of eruption forecasting.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

Assumptions to Kill

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

ID Assumption Validation Method Failure Trigger
A1 Hubs outside the 500 km ring (Denver, Cheyenne) exist with enough verified capacity and will accept evacuees on short notice; distances and capacity are not verified. Measure distances from the caldera to Denver and Cheyenne, and request written capacity and acceptance statements from both emergency managers within 7 days. Either hub lies inside 500 km, or combined confirmed capacity is below 50,000 beds, or neither commits to accept evacuees without legislative approval.
A2 Contracts, vendors and convoys can be activated verbally at T+0 and deliver water, fuel and N95 stock within the 12 h dispatch and T+24 h arrival targets without pre-awarded contracts. Audit existing FEMA contract vehicles for surge clauses and run a dry-run verbal activation with three vendors, timing dispatch. Any vendor needs more than 12 h to dispatch, or existing vehicles lack surge capacity, or Salt Lake City to Bozeman arrival falls after T+30 h (transit over 18 h) in the dry run (estimate).
A3 The public and outer-zone residents will follow staged instructions, and trust holds if shelter-in-place guidance is superseded by a 500 km order, so shadow evacuation stays manageable. Run a message-comprehension and compliance-intent pilot with 1,000 residents in Bozeman, Gardiner and Cody, using the reversal message sequence. Stated compliance with time-banded departure is below 70%, or recall of assignment logic is below 80%.
A4 Gallatin Canyon and Gardiner corridors can sustain about 660 vehicles/hour per exit as a fleet average only (estimate), with the West exit needing about 994 vehicles/hour (about 1,190 from T+1) (estimate) under ashfall and tremor, and blockages clear within the 45-minute diversion threshold (proposed threshold). Commission a rapid geotechnical and staging-lot survey of Gallatin Canyon, Mammoth and West Yellowstone, and time a tow-team dispatch drill to the canyon. Measured West throughput is below about 994 vehicles/hour (estimate), or North falls below about 600 vehicles/hour (about 716 from T+1) or East below about 400 vehicles/hour (estimate), tow reach time exceeds 15 minutes (proposed threshold), or clearance of a typical blockage exceeds 4 hours.
A5 Guard signal teams, IPAWS/WEA, HAR/VMS and satellite links will keep drivers and responders connected through ashfall and tremor from T+0, with interoperable radio nets across NPS, state patrol and Guard. Run an interoperability and ash-degradation test of Guard repeaters, satellite phones and HAR/VMS at three control points, confirming Guard signal unit count. Any agency pair cannot hold a two-way net at a control point, fewer than 4 signal teams are available by T+1 h, or message delivery to test drivers falls below 90%.
A6 Responder staffing of 100-150 NPS rangers (estimate) plus patrol and Guard, with a 30-50 person standby reserve deployable within 4 h (proposed threshold), can hold 6 h shift limits at every post through T+72 h. Obtain written headcounts by unit from NPS, state patrol and Guard, and obtain written commitments and mobilization times from the standby reserve agencies. Confirmed concurrent positions fall below 67, reserve commitments cover fewer than 30 people, or reserve mobilization time exceeds 4 h.
A7 The USD 200 million planning envelope (estimate) and USD 30-35 million free contingency (estimate) cover shelters, hubs and state costs, and the federal versus state/local/host split gets settled before spending is needed. Obtain written cost-share positions from FEMA and the MT, WY and ID emergency management agencies, and reconcile the readiness package (USD 47.5-87 million, estimate) against the base. Any state or host community declines cost-sharing, or unfunded items push committed draws above the USD 40 million contingency.
A8 Bozeman, Idaho Falls and the third site can be stocked and staffed, with a relocation order issued within 4 h (proposed threshold) of a PM10 exceedance, with buses, drivers and backups 50+ km upwind available when needed. Run a relocation drill of 1,000 volunteers from one shelter to a surveyed backup, timing decision, notification, bus dispatch and intake, and confirm bus and driver counts. Detection-to-order exceeds 4 h, completion of relocation (time to be set after the drill) (estimate) exceeds 8 h (estimate), or fewer than 20 buses are confirmed for relocation.
A9 Visitors, including non-English speakers, vehicle-less and mobility-limited guests, will reach the three exits and follow fixed district-to-gate assignments so that 98% of 35,800 are confirmed out by T+6 h. Obtain concessioner manifests and run a lodge-level sampling of language, vehicle and mobility shares, plus a gate-assignment comprehension test using route cards in six languages. Vehicle-less or mobility-limited visitors exceed the confirmed bus and shuttle capacity, or gate-assignment comprehension in the test is below 90%.

Failure Scenarios and Mitigation Plans

Each scenario below links to a root-cause assumption and includes a detailed failure story, early warning signs, measurable tripwires, a response playbook, and a stop rule to guide decision-making.

Summary of Failure Modes

Failure Modes

FM1 - The Verbal Order That Never Rolled

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A2
  • Owner: Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Plan relies on verbal FEMA activation and 12 h dispatch clauses with no pre-awarded contracts.
  • Procurement runs 24-48 h (estimate) and vendors lack surge capacity.
  • Convoys leave after T+36 h, well past the T+12 h dispatch target; shelters ration water for 12-24 h.
  • Hub and shelter financing split is unresolved, freezing spending.
  • Contingency drained by relocation and resupply.
Early Warning Signs
  • Any vendor quotes dispatch lead time above 12 h
  • FEMA contract audit finds no surge clause for water, fuel or N95
  • Federal versus state cost-share unresolved at Month 1 (2026-11-14)
Tripwires
  • Convoy not dispatched by T+12 h
  • Shelter water stock below 24 h of supply at T+18 h
  • Vendor dispatch quote above 12 h
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Activate backup vendors in Pocatello and Butte and release forward-depot water to shelters immediately.
  • Assess: Audit inventory, consumption rate and convoy positions at each shelter within 2 hours.
  • Respond: Shift to helicopter resupply and tanker fills, and renegotiate contracts with fixed dispatch penalties.

STOP RULE: If no signed surge-dispatch contract covers water and fuel by Month 1 (2026-11-14), halt shelter activation planning and escalate to a federal pre-positioning mandate.

FM2 - The Ring With No Landing

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A1
  • Owner: Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 20/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Beta order is pre-authorized but second-stage hubs are unverified.
  • Denver or Cheyenne distance or capacity falls short.
  • Bus, rail and supply routing to hubs undefined.
  • Evacuees saturate I-15, I-80 and I-90, blocking Zone Zero exits.
  • Delay of 4-8 h (estimate) overlaps ashfall.
Early Warning Signs
  • Hub distance check places a candidate inside 500 km
  • Fewer than 5 hubs with written capacity by T+12 h
  • Interstate traffic above 25% saturation before Beta order
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 5 hubs confirmed at T+12 h
  • Confirmed hub capacity below 250,000 beds
  • Interstate saturation at or above 40% by T+10 h
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Hold the 500 km order's outer rings in later time bands and publish the interim hub list at once.
  • Assess: Verify hub distances, capacity and ash exposure and count evacuees already moving on interstates.
  • Respond: Add only hubs verified outside the 500 km ring (distance and ash exposure), pre-position supplies and run bus shuttles on lateral routes.

STOP RULE: If fewer than 5 verified hubs with signed MOUs exist by Month 2 (2026-12-14), suspend automatic 500 km authority and revert to a staged decision cell.

FM3 - The Reversal That Broke Trust

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A3
  • Owner: Communications and Public Alerting Coordinator
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Outer-zone residents told to shelter in place, then ordered out under Beta.
  • Reversal read as deception; compliance falls 20-40% (estimate).
  • 50,000-200,000 (estimate) residents flee unassigned.
  • Corridors clog; governors' competing orders amplify confusion.
  • Cell failure removes the corrective channel.
Early Warning Signs
  • Pilot stated compliance below 70%
  • Radio call-in complaints on shelter-in-place messaging rising
  • Governor offices issue differing statements
Tripwires
  • Stated compliance below 70% in pilot
  • Corridor traffic exceeds plan by 20% within 2 h of order
  • Message recall below 80%
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Issue one unified superseding message across IPAWS, HAR and trusted radio with governor co-signatures.
  • Assess: Measure traffic counts and call volume against time-band targets within 1 hour.
  • Respond: Release time bands by county, use secondary routes and publish the indicator values that triggered escalation.

STOP RULE: If pilot compliance stays below 70% after two message revisions, abandon shelter-in-place messaging and use time-banded departures only.

FM4 - The Roster That Ran Dry

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A6
  • Owner: Responder Safety and Fatigue-Management Officer
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Rangers and patrol fill every post during T+2 to T+8 with no relief depth.
  • Reserve commitments are unsigned; Guard activation waits on state approvals.
  • Shift limits force post withdrawals; a checkpoint goes dark.
  • Overtime and reserve call-ups draw on the contingency.
  • Gate G1 slips past T+6 h.
Early Warning Signs
  • Confirmed headcount below 67 concurrent positions
  • Reserve commitment letters cover fewer than 30 people
  • Any post under 50% coverage for 30 minutes
Tripwires
  • Coverage below 50% at any post for 30 minutes
  • Reserve not on site within 4 h of request
  • More than 3 responders withdrawn for exposure in one shift
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Consolidate thin posts and request out-of-region Guard immediately.
  • Assess: Count staffed positions, hours on shift and N95 stock per post within 1 hour.
  • Respond: Rotate the standby reserve in and re-tier posts by mission criticality.

STOP RULE: If confirmed responder headcount is below 67 concurrent positions at T+0, treat Gate G1 as slipped and escalate to a different decision (two exits is not a G1-compliant fallback) until reserves are seated.

FM5 - The Canyon That Closed

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A4
  • Owner: Contraflow Operations and Traffic Control Manager
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 15/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • A rockfall or breakdown in Gallatin Canyon blocks the West exit at peak.
  • Tow teams cannot reach the site through queued vehicles in ash.
  • Secondary slide endangers crews; clearance exceeds 4 hours.
  • Diversion overloads US-89 and US-14/16/20, adding 2-4 h transit.
  • Zone Zero clearance misses T+6 h.
Early Warning Signs
  • Slope displacement alerts on canyon sensors
  • Tow dispatch drill exceeds 15 minutes
  • Queue length at West gate above staging capacity
Tripwires
  • Blockage lasts more than 45 minutes
  • Any M4.0+ event during clearance work
  • West exit throughput below about 994 vehicles/hour (estimate; about 1,190 from T+1) for 60 minutes
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Halt inbound queueing and divert overflow to the nearest surviving exit.
  • Assess: Survey blockage, slope movement and queue length with drones within 30 minutes.
  • Respond: Apply the 6 h loss-of-exit rule, rebalance gate split and open bypass track if certified.

STOP RULE: If the West exit is not restorable within 6 hours, shelter in place queued vehicles and cancel single-lane clearance attempts.

FM6 - The Silent Drivers

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A5
  • Owner: Communications and Public Alerting Coordinator
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Cell towers and power fail; WEA and IPAWS stop reaching drivers.
  • Guard nets do not interoperate; reroute orders stall at boundaries.
  • Drivers and visitors without English rely on rumor and crowd cues.
  • Wrong-exit choices unbalance the gate split and fuel shadow flight.
  • Public trust in official channels drops.
Early Warning Signs
  • Interoperability test fails for any agency pair
  • Fewer than 4 Guard signal teams confirmed
  • Test driver message receipt below 90%
Tripwires
  • Message receipt below 90% in drill
  • Gate load deviates more than 10% from split
  • Control point out of contact for 15 minutes
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Switch to printed route cards, HAR and runners at every control point.
  • Assess: Check link status, driver receipt and gate counts within 1 hour.
  • Respond: Redeploy signal teams, restore nets and reissue consistent multilingual instructions.

STOP RULE: If interoperable nets are not confirmed at all three gates by T+1 h, delay contraflow release and run staged departures by printed card.

FM7 - The Envelope That Split Three Ways

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A7
  • Owner: FEMA Region VIII Finance and Grants Lead
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Cost-share for shelters, hubs and state costs stays open.
  • States and hosts withhold commitments pending reimbursement terms.
  • Hub pre-positioning and shelter stocking stall.
  • Relocation and resupply draws consume the USD 40 million contingency (estimate).
  • Plan runs short of money at the Scenario Beta trigger.

  • No written cost-share by Month 1 (2026-11-14)
  • Host MOU drafts returned with reimbursement conditions
  • Committed draws above 50% of contingency before T+24 h
Tripwires
  • Free contingency below USD 20 million (estimate)
  • Fewer than 3 states signed on cost-share by Month 1 (2026-11-14)
  • Any hub MOU unsigned at Month 2 (2026-12-14)

  • Assess: Reconcile committed, obligated and unfunded items by line within 24 hours.
  • Respond: Seek a federal cost-share declaration and re-sequence hub pre-positioning by ring priority.

STOP RULE: If no cost-share agreement covers Beta hubs by Month 2 (2026-12-14), cancel hub-dependent automatic Beta authority and pivot to a staged decision cell.

FM8 - The Shelter Under the Plume

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A8
  • Owner: Ashfall Forecasting and Dynamic Shelter-Siting Officer
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 15/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Ash arrives heavier or farther south than the T+6 h forecast.
  • PM10 exceedance detected late; decision slips.
  • Buses and drivers already consumed by the evacuation.
  • Backup sites lack water, power or registration capacity.
  • N95 stock clogs faster than planned.
Early Warning Signs
  • PM10 above 50 ug/m3 at a shelter (forecast update); above 100 ug/m3 (shelter-suitability review)
  • Sensor feed latency above 2 h (estimate)
  • Fewer than 20 buses held in reserve
Tripwires
  • PM10 above 200 ug/m3 at a primary site or a failed suitability review (relocation-order exceedance, proposed threshold)
  • Relocation order not issued within 4 h of exceedance (proposed threshold)
