Response Playbook
  • Contain: Issue shelter-in-place with N95 distribution and sealed rooms while buses are marshalled.
  • Assess: Compare sensor data with the latest plume run and check backup site readiness within 1 hour.
  • Respond: Order staged relocation to ranked upwind backups and release the 100,000 N95 reserve.

STOP RULE: If no backup site can accept at least 10,000 people within 8 h of an exceedance, halt new intake at the affected shelter and divert arrivals.

FM9 - The Guests Who Stayed Behind

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A9
  • Owner: Communications and Public Alerting Coordinator
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Non-English speakers, tour groups and mobility-limited guests miss or misread instructions.
  • Vehicle-less visitors wait for transport that is undersized.
  • Visitors cross to wrong gates, unbalancing the split.
  • Lodge clusters delay Gate G1 beyond T+6 h.
  • Stranded groups raise rescue demands in ash.
Early Warning Signs
  • Concessioner manifests show vehicle-less guests above shuttle capacity
  • Gate load deviates over 10% from split
  • Route-card comprehension under 90% in test
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 98% confirmed out at T+6 h
  • Any lodge not cleared at T+3 h
  • Gate load deviates more than 10% from split for 30 minutes
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Send concessioner buses and interpreters to uncleared lodges and pause new gate releases.
  • Assess: Reconcile manifests against exit counts and map uncleared groups within 1 hour.
  • Respond: Reassign gates, run priority shuttles and extend sweeps with relief teams.

STOP RULE: If more than about 716 visitors (including backcountry) remain unaccounted for at T+6 h, suspend Zone One phase start until a sweep plan is set.

Reality check: fix before go.

Summary

Level Count Explanation
🛑 High 13 Existential blocker without credible mitigation.
⚠️ Medium 6 Material risk with plausible path.
✅ Low 1 Minor/controlled risk.

Checklist

1. Violates Known Physics

Does the plan's success require breaking a known law of physics (e.g., thermodynamics, conservation of energy, speed-of-light limit, causality)?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: This is a disaster-response logistics and operations plan grounded entirely in conventional engineering: traffic management, evacuation, shelter operations, supply dispatch, communications, and command-and-control. All causal mechanisms are physical—human decision and action directing material resources (vehicles, supplies, personnel, infrastructure) and information (alerts, orders, sensor data). The plan does not require breaking any law of physics or depend on non-physical causation for success.

Mitigation: No physics-related action required — the plan does not invoke physics-incompatible mechanisms.

2. No Real-World Proof

Does success depend on a technology or system that has not been proven in real projects at this scale or in this domain?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan hinges on a novel combination of contraflow under ashfall, real-time dynamic shelter relocation, and pre-authorized 500 km escalation without confirmed second-stage destinations. No comparable North American precedent exists for this system under a VEI-6 ashfall event. Gallatin Canyon clearance feasibility, ashfall forecast reliability for shelter-relocation decisions, and Scenario Beta destination verification are all unvalidated; failure in any critical track cascades into 4–8 hour evacuation delay and 5,000–20,000 stranded evacuees.

Mitigation: Run three parallel validation tracks by Month 3 (2027-01-14): (1) Geotechnical/Engineering: confirm Gallatin Canyon single-lane clearance feasibility within 4 hours and secondary-slide risk via USGS survey; conduct a tow-team mobilization drill to validate 15-minute reach time. (2) Technical/Environmental: validate NOAA ashfall forecast skill and PM10 sensor accuracy; conduct a shelter-relocation exercise moving 1,000 evacuees to backup sites under simulated 50 km forecast divergence, measuring move and occupy times (8 h stop rule) with the 4 h limit applying to the relocation order only. (3) Logistical/Legal: execute signed MOUs from at least 5 hubs outside the 500 km ring with capacity commitments (Month 2 = 2026-12-14) and pre-positioning timelines; conduct a multi-state Beta hub activation tabletop. Define two NO-GO gates: (A) If Gallatin Canyon clearance exceeds the 4-hour time-box for a single-lane clearance attempt or secondary-slide risk exceeds 20%, apply the loss-of-exit rule (exit not restorable within 6 hours: shelter in place, redirect to nearest surviving exit). (B) If fewer than 5 hubs are validated and signed by Month 2 (2026-12-14), suspend pre-authorized Scenario Beta and revert to a discretionary decision cell. Stop rule: if any critical track fails, the cascade-risk management protocol requires plan revision before T+0 activation.

3. Buzzwords

Does the plan use excessive buzzwords without evidence of knowledge?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because two critical strategic concepts—Scenario Beta second-stage hub destinations and Responder Exposure Limits—lack defined owners, quantified success metrics, and operational mechanisms. The Escalation Trigger defers USGS indicator values to T+3h, leaving pre-authorization hollow. Core evacuation mechanics (contraflow, command, comms) are well-defined with owners and measurable gates (G1 T+6h ≥98%, G2 T+24h ≥95%), but secondary strategies lack this rigor.

Mitigation: Draft one-pagers for Scenario Beta hubs (verify Denver/Cheyenne distances, confirm capacity and acceptance by Month 0 = 2026-10-14), Escalation Trigger (finalize USGS values by T+3h), and Responder Exposure Limits (name the Safety Officer by T+0 with explicit withdrawal authority) specifying owner, mechanism-of-action, and quantified success metrics. Publish Strategy Reference Guide to all stakeholders by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

4. Underestimating Risks

Does this plan grossly underestimate risks?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta 500 km evacuation order without defining executable second-stage destinations, host-community capacity, or interim hub list before T+0. If the trigger fires (likely T+12–24 h), millions of outer-zone residents will lack published shelter addresses, causing uncontrolled shadow evacuation on I-15/I-80/I-90 that saturates the same corridors needed for organized Zone Zero evacuation, adding an estimated 4–8 hours delay and stranding 5,000–20,000 people in ashfall. Interim hub list is due T+12 h (post-event deliverable), written plan due Month 1 (2026-11-14), and signed MOUs due Month 2 (2026-12-14)—all blocking dependencies exist only after the trigger fires and cascades begin.

Mitigation: Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner: by Month 1 (2026-11-14), deliver written second-stage evacuation plan naming 5–10 ranked hubs outside the 500 km ring, with signed host MOUs by Month 2 (2026-12-14) confirming capacity and pre-positioning timelines; validate distances, model ashfall survivability at each hub, and pre-authorize tiered messaging. Conduct a full multi-state Beta hub activation and shelter-intake exercise by Month 3 (2027-01-14) to expose real relocation latency and confirm execute-ability before T+0.

5. Timeline Issues

Does the plan rely on unrealistic or internally inconsistent schedules?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta VEI-7 trigger ordering immediate 500 km evacuation affecting millions of people without a defined, executable second-stage destination plan. The interim hub list is due T+12 hours (post-event, during active evacuation), written plan due Month 1 (2026-11-14), and signed host MOUs due Month 2 (2026-12-14)—all after the trigger fires. Without published shelter destinations by T+12 h, evacuees will lack assigned refuge addresses, triggering uncontrolled shadow evacuation of 50,000–200,000+ outer-zone residents onto I-15, I-80 and I-90 that saturates the same corridors needed to clear 35,800 Zone Zero evacuees. This cascade-failure coupling creates a critical single-point vulnerability: pre-authorization without pre-positioned capacity.

Mitigation: Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner: Execute written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan by Month 1 (2026-11-14) naming five or more ranked shelter hubs outside the 500 km ring with signed host-community MOUs confirming capacity and 48-hour resource availability; validate Denver and Cheyenne distances from Yellowstone center and ashfall survivability under USGS ensemble forecast scenarios; pre-position 20,000–30,000 person equivalent food, water and N95 supplies at each hub; issue interim ranked hub list (at least five outside ring) by T+12 hours; conduct full-scale multi-state Beta hub activation exercise by Month 3 (2027-01-14).

6. Money Issues

Are there flaws in the financial model, funding plan, or cost realism?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because committed funding sources for the USD 200 million planning envelope are not documented. The plan names "a federal emergency declaration (Stafford Act) plus pre-event contract vehicles" as the assumed funding source with "USD 150–250 million surge envelope" (estimate), but provides no signed appropriation, FEMA pre-award authority, or congressional allocation. No financing gates, covenants, or draw schedule are specified. The readiness package (USD 47.5–87 million estimate) lacks assigned funding owners (federal vs. state/local/host-community cost-share unresolved). Critical Scenario Beta second-stage hub pre-positioning (USD 20–40 million estimate) and shelter relocation contingency (USD 5–10 million estimate) have no secured funding. The "free contingency" of USD 30–35 million (estimate) is a theoretical buffer, not committed. Without signed appropriations, FEMA advance authorization, or explicit cost-allocation MOUs, the plan cannot execute beyond T+0 without financial bottlenecks cascading into supply delays, hub non-activation, and responder shortfalls.

Mitigation: FEMA Region VIII Finance Lead: By T+0, secure verbal activation of existing FEMA contract vehicles (dispatch by T+12 h); by Month 1 (2026-11-14), secure written FEMA pre-authorization for USD 200 million Stafford Act emergency declaration and harden the contract vehicles for water, fuel, N95 and bus supply. Obtain written federal vs. state/local/host-community cost-allocation confirmation from FEMA and governors specifying reimbursement percentages for shelters, hubs, and interstate support within 30 days; embed allocations in signed MOUs by Month 1 (2026-11-14). Define no-go financing gate: if USD 160 million base appropriation is not confirmed in writing by T+12h, halt all non-critical hardening and escalate to Congressional emergency session.

7. Budget Too Low

Is there a significant mismatch between the project's stated goals and the financial resources allocated, suggesting an unrealistic or inadequate budget?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the USD 200 million budget (USD 160M base + USD 40M contingency at 20%) is stated without vendor quotes, cost-per-evacuee benchmarks, or scale-appropriate comparables. Plan scope is multi-state evacuation of 35,800 Zone Zero + unquantified Zone One + millions in Scenario Beta. No three quotes substantiate major costs (water convoys dispatched by T+12 h with T+24 h arrival target, N95 procurement, shelter operations, fuel reserves). No per-area normalization (cost per person-day, shelter bed, convoy ton-mile) provided. Hurricane Rita and Camp Fire case studies cited but not analyzed for comparable costs. Financing split (federal vs. state/local/host-community) unresolved, risking USD 20–40M exposure if states decline cost-share. Contingency adequacy depends on Zone One population census (unquantified) and Scenario Beta activation (probability triggers may be hollow without second-stage hub execution confirmed). 20% contingency meets the 10–20% rule by stated value, not validated necessity.

Mitigation: Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director: Obtain three vendor quotes each for bottled-water convoys (Salt Lake City to Bozeman/Idaho Falls, dispatch by T+12 h, arrival T+24 h target, T+18–30 h estimate), N95 bulk purchase and resupply, diesel fuel pre-positioning and convoy, and shelter operational costs (food, water, medical, staff per person-day) from regional suppliers by Month 1 (2026-11-14). Normalize all costs per evacuee-day and per shelter bed; benchmark against Hurricane Rita (2005) and Camp Fire (2018) cost-per-evacuee data from FEMA HAZUS or state emergency management reports. Reconcile line-item readiness package (USD 47.5–87M) against quotes; revise contingency from assumed 20% to actual variance (±15–30% estimated) based on market data. Resolve federal vs. state/local cost-share allocation by written MOU with governors and FEMA by Month 1 (2026-11-14); quantify federal obligation ceiling and cost-shock threshold for contingency drawdown. Conduct a cost-sensitivity analysis showing whether USD 200M envelope survives Zone One population +20% variance, Scenario Beta hub pre-positioning acceleration, and shelter-relocation surge (USD 20–50M estimated). Document all benchmarks and quotes in a Cost Realism Validation Report due Month 1 (2026-11-14).

8. Overly Optimistic Projections

Does this plan grossly overestimate the likelihood of success, while neglecting potential setbacks, buffers, or contingency plans?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan states key projections (water arrival T+12 h dispatch/T+24 h target, 660 veh/h throughput per exit, 45-min blockage threshold, 4-h relocation order, 98% evacuation by T+6 h) as single numbers or fixed thresholds without ranges, confidence intervals or alternative scenarios. Canonical facts acknowledge "T+18–30 h realistic arrival" but do not integrate this into a sensitivity analysis or best/worst-case envelope. No best-case, base-case, or worst-case scenario table exists for the three critical projections (throughput, water arrival, responder availability). The plan lacks contingency logic tied to projection variance; contingency is financial (20% budget buffer) not operational (throughput/timing scenarios).

Mitigation: Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director and Contraflow Operations Manager: By Month 1 (2026-11-14), deliver a Sensitivity Analysis Report for the three most critical projections: (1) Water convoy dispatch and arrival time under ashfall and evacuation-traffic congestion (base T+24 h, conservative T+36 h, optimistic T+18 h); (2) Contraflow throughput per exit (fleet average about 660 veh/h, West requirement about 994 veh/h, about 1,190 from T+1; best-case 800 veh/h if ashfall remains light, worst-case 400 veh/h if visibility <50 m); (3) Blockage clearance and diversion (base 45 min, conservative 120 min requiring full diversion, optimistic 20 min for minor debris). For each scenario, quantify the cascading impact on Gate G1 (T+6 h clearance) and Gate G2 (T+24 h Zone One clearance) attainment and document trigger points for contingency activation (e.g., if cumulative throughput delay exceeds 2 h by T+4 h, activate standby responder reserve).

9. Lacks Technical Depth

Does the plan omit critical technical details or engineering steps required to overcome foreseeable challenges, especially for complex components of the project?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan pre-authorizes a VEI-7 trigger that orders a 500 km evacuation affecting millions of people without confirmed second-stage shelter hubs, host-community MOUs, or interim destination lists prior to T+0. If the trigger fires during or immediately after Zone Zero evacuation (T+12–24 h range), evacuees will lack published shelter addresses, causing uncontrolled shadow evacuation of 50,000–200,000 outer-zone residents onto I-15, I-80 and I-90 that saturates the same corridors required for organized Zone Zero clearance. This cascades an estimated 4–8 hours of additional delay, stranding 5,000–20,000 evacuees in ashfall exposure zones. Interim hub list is a post-event deliverable (T+12 h), written plan is due Month 1 (2026-11-14), and signed host MOUs are due Month 2 (2026-12-14)—all blocking dependencies exist only after cascade effects begin.

Mitigation: Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner: By Month 1 (2026-11-14), execute a written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan naming at least five ranked shelter hubs outside the 500 km ring (e.g., Denver, Cheyenne, candidate secondaries) with signed host-community MOUs confirming capacity and pre-positioning logistics. Validate distance from Yellowstone center to each hub and ashfall survivability under USGS ensemble forecast scenarios. Issue interim ranked hub list by T+12 hours; execute full multi-state Beta hub activation exercise by Month 3 (2027-01-14).

10. Assertions Without Evidence

Does each critical claim (excluding timeline and budget) include at least one verifiable piece of evidence?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta 500 km evacuation order affecting millions of people without naming specific second-stage shelter hubs, confirming their distance outside the 500 km ring, obtaining signed host-community MOUs, or publishing an interim destination list prior to the 72-hour window. The interim hub list is due T+12 hours (post-event, during active evacuation), the written plan is due Month 1 (2026-11-14), and signed MOUs are due Month 2 (2026-12-14)—all blocking dependencies exist only after the trigger fires. Without executable destinations confirmed by T+0, a pre-authorized trigger is operationally reckless and creates cascade-failure risk.

Mitigation: Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner: By Month 1 (2026-11-14), execute a written Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan naming at least five ranked shelter hubs outside the 500 km ring with signed host-community MOUs confirming capacity, pre-positioning supplies, and 48-hour activation readiness. Validate distances from Yellowstone center and ashfall survivability under USGS ensemble forecasts by T+12 h (desktop check).

11. Unclear Deliverables

Are the project's final outputs or key milestones poorly defined, lacking specific criteria for completion, making success difficult to measure objectively?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because major strategic deliverables (Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Evacuation Plan, Responder Exposure Protocol, Ashfall Monitoring Relocation Protocols) are named but lack specific, measurable, verifiable acceptance criteria. Success metrics are absent: the Beta plan has no defined hub count, capacity threshold, or distance-from-ring criteria; responder protocol has no quantified relief depth or rotation timing; shelter relocation has no triggers or occupancy limits. These deliverables are critical for mitigating cascade risks (uncontrolled shadow evacuation, staff exhaustion, evacuees sheltered in heavy ash), yet their completion cannot be verified objectively. Absence of SMART criteria creates ambiguity about when readiness is achieved, preventing stakeholders from assessing whether the plan will actually execute.

Mitigation: Scenario Beta Secondary-Stage Destination Planner: By T+12 h, draft SMART acceptance criteria for all three unclear deliverables specifying measurable KPIs (e.g., Beta plan success = ≥5 hubs outside 500 km with signed MOUs and ≥250,000 confirmed beds); publish criteria to all stakeholders; track compliance monthly (Months 1-3, 2026-11-14 to 2027-01-14) against documented gates.

12. Gold Plating

Does the plan add unnecessary features, complexity, or cost beyond the core goal?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Escorted-Return Program (Decision 10, option 3) adds USD 2–3 million in cost and diverts Guard and responder personnel from traffic control, logistics and shelter security during Phase 2 (T+6 to T+24 h), yet does not directly support the core project objectives of evacuating ≥98% of Zone Zero by T+6 h (Gate G1) or ≥95% of Zone One by T+24 h (Gate G2). The feature is Phase 3 (post-event re-entry) and is not binding under any legal or contractual requirement; anti-looting and perimeter security are managed via the fixed-checkpoint protocol (Decision 10, option 1). Responder hours consumed by escorted-return logistics directly compete with responder relief rotation needed to maintain 50%+ coverage at traffic-control checkpoints during peak evacuation (T+2 to T+8 h), where staffing is already at critical minimum. Mitigation is straightforward: eliminate the escorted-return program during Phases 1–2 and defer it to Phase 3 (post-ashfall) or cancel it entirely if responder depth remains inadequate.

Mitigation: Project Leadership: Conduct a Benefit Case Review within 7 days specifying: (1) whether escorted returns during Phase 2 (T+6 to T+24 h) are required by any state law, governor order, or legal precedent; (2) estimated responder hours diverted from traffic control, logistics or relief rotation; (3) quantified benefit (reduced looting incidents, resident complaints, post-event litigation risk) and assigned owner; (4) cost estimate including escort vehicles, drivers, request-processing staff and coordination overhead. If no binding requirement or demonstrated benefit justifies the cost during Phase 2, move escorted-return program to Phase 3 (post-ashfall, after ashfall onset is declared over) or cancel entirely; reallocate freed responder hours to traffic-control coverage and shelter-relocation support.

13. Staffing Fit & Rationale

Do the roles, capacity, and skills match the work, or is the plan under- or over-staffed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Ashfall Forecasting & Dynamic Shelter-Siting Officer is mission-critical (decision authority over real-time PM10 monitoring and 4-hour shelter relocation triggers) yet requires rare, combined expertise in volcanology, air-quality science, emergency operations, logistics, and real-time data systems. No single professional discipline typically carries all five competencies. Lead-time to recruit and integrate a qualified officer by T+0 is short; talent is concentrated in USGS and NOAA with limited availability.

Mitigation: FEMA Region VIII and UC Incident Commander: By T+0, identify and pre-authorize a named Ashfall Officer from USGS Volcano Disaster Assistance Program or a university volcanologist with ashfall-dispersion and emergency-operations experience. Execute a pre-event Interagency Agreement (IAA) granting the officer direct authority over PM10 sensor data, NOAA VAFT forecast integration, and relocation-trigger decisions. Confirm 24/7 availability and seat officer at forward element at T+0.

14. Legal Minefield

Does the plan involve activities with high legal, regulatory, or ethical exposure, such as potential lawsuits, corruption, illegal actions, or societal harm?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because legal pathways exist (Stafford Act, FEMA authority, FAA airspace procedures, state emergency powers, EMAC), but the plan lacks a regulatory matrix, fatal-flaw analysis, pre-event legal memoranda, signed MOUs with counsel review, or documented Stafford Act/FAA protocols. Controlling regimes: Stafford Act (42 U.S.C. § 5121), FAR Part 91 (airspace closure), State Emergency Management Acts, OSHA (respiratory protection), NIMS/ICS compliance. No unmapped showstoppers identified, but substantial documentation and pre-negotiation gaps remain.

Mitigation: FEMA Region VIII Legal Counsel and UC Incident Commander: By Month 1 (2026-11-14), execute a Fatal-Flaw Analysis reviewing Stafford Act emergency-declaration authority, FAA airspace-closure procedures, state governor activation requirements (MT, WY, ID statutes), and EMAC enforceability. Deliver a signed Regulatory Matrix (authority, artifact, lead time, predecessors) documenting Stafford Act declaration trigger, FAA NOTAM issuance protocol, governor pre-authorization letter template, and state mutual-aid legal enforceability. Obtain pre-event legal opinions on Scenario Beta trigger authority, Boundary Coordination Officer delegation validity, and government liability for unnecessary/unexecutable evacuation. Brief all state attorneys general and FAA counsel by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

15. Lacks Operational Sustainability

Even if the project is successfully completed, can it be sustained, maintained, and operated effectively over the long term without ongoing issues?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan prioritizes the 72-hour evacuation window (T+0 to T+72) but explicitly defers all post-event operations to "Phase 3 re-entry and recovery planning" with no defined funding, personnel, infrastructure maintenance, or long-term continuity mechanisms. Operational sustainability assessment reveals: (1) ongoing costs for responder reserves, equipment maintenance, and supply rotation through Month 60+ (estimated USD 2–5 million/year) lack annual appropriation authority; (2) specialized skills (USGS volcanology liaison, Guard signal operations, shelter management) required for sustained readiness have no retention or succession planning; (3) pre-positioned assets (sensors, tow equipment, generator fuel reserves) degrade without replacement cycles; (4) inter-agency MOUs expire unless renewed every 2 years; (5) no explicit plan for transitioning from emergency operations back to baseline readiness or for maintaining the forward UC element and Boundary Coordination Officer role beyond Month 3 (2027-01-14). The plan is designed as a 72-hour surge operation, not as a sustainable standby posture.

Mitigation: FEMA Region VIII and UC Director: Establish a Yellowstone Evacuation Readiness Sustainability Plan by Month 3 (2027-01-14) documenting: (1) annual operating budget (USD 2–5 million/year estimated) for asset maintenance, supply rotation, personnel retainer, and MOU renewal (every 2 years); (2) named sustainment owner (FEMA Region VIII Chief, or delegated permanent position) with 24/7 authority to activate the readiness posture if USGS eruption probability triggers above 10% in any 12-month window; (3) personnel succession and cross-training protocols for critical roles (USGS volcanologist liaison, Boundary Coordination Officer, Ashfall Forecasting Officer); (4) equipment lifecycle and replacement schedule (sensors every 3 years, tow assets every 5 years, generator fuel reserves refreshed annually); (5) annual tabletop exercise (Months 12, 24, 36 = 2027-10-14, 2028-10-14, 2029-10-14, etc.) to maintain multi-agency coordination and validate MOUs. Secure Congressional pre-appropriation authority for the annual sustainment budget by Month 6 (2027-04-14 + 3 months estimated) to avoid annual battle for funding and ensure continuity beyond Month 3 (2027-01-14).

16. Infeasible Constraints

Does the project depend on overcoming constraints that are practically insurmountable, such as obtaining permits that are almost certain to be denied?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because hard constraints (zoning, occupancy/egress, fire code, permits, structural limits) are acknowledged but treated as operational decisions (T+0 to T+6h shelter site selection) rather than pre-event validation tasks. Shelter sites Bozeman and Idaho Falls are named but no pre-event zoning confirmation, occupancy-permit application, or fire-egress compliance survey exists. Backup shelter sites are identified only as ranked upwind lists without structural-capacity or fire-code pre-surveying. Contraflow permits for temporary road closure/reversal are not documented as pre-authorized from state DOTs or NPS. If hard constraints are not cleared before T+0, shelter activation and relocation face 2–6 hour delays or site loss due to zoning/code violations. Viable alternatives exist (multiple candidate shelter locations, secondary routes), but feasibility is unvalidated.

Mitigation: Shelter Operations Coordinator (or designated Site Feasibility Lead): By Month 1 (2026-11-14), conduct a fatal-flaw screen with local planning and fire-marshal authorities at Bozeman, Idaho Falls, and each backup-site candidate. Obtain written confirmation that zoning permits emergency congregate shelter, occupancy is unbounded by code, fire egress meets or exceeds 35,000-person capacity, and temporary-use or emergency-occupancy permits can be expedited within 2 hours of activation request. Secure pre-signed occupancy authorizations from facility managers at Bozeman and Idaho Falls by Month 2 (2026-12-14). Define and document NO-GO thresholds: if zoning audit shows <2 sites (of Bozeman, Idaho Falls, third) are compliant, suspend shelter activation and activate Scenario Beta secondary-hub occupancy immediately. Coordinate with state DOTs (MT, WY, ID) to pre-authorize temporary contraflow permits and provide written delegation of activation authority to the UC by Month 1 (2026-11-14).

17. External Dependencies

Does the project depend on critical external factors, third parties, suppliers, or vendors that may fail, delay, or be unavailable when needed?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan names pre-positioned tow and rockfall teams, forward water depots at Bozeman and Idaho Falls, Guard signal repeaters at control points, and fuel reserves at receiving hospitals as fallback assets, but lacks: (1) explicit single-point-of-failure analysis (e.g., what if Bozeman depot is ash-blocked and cannot resupply); (2) tested failover procedures (no documented exercise validating 4-hour water-resupply activation or tow-team diversion if primary supplier fails); (3) second-source vendor commitments for all critical supplies (water contracts from Salt Lake City only; no signed Pocatello/Butte backup pre-authorized for 6-hour dispatch). The plan specifies forward depots and Guard repeaters but does not confirm they are staged by T+12 h or that backup activation is pre-authorized. Regional utility grid resilience (transmission flashovers, cascading blackout) is identified as a risk but no load-shedding topology or substation pre-authorization exists to prevent it. Tested failover protocols for the three most critical single-point dependencies (water convoy, fuel delivery, communications) are absent.

Mitigation: Emergency Logistics and Supply-Chain Director and Critical Infrastructure Lead: (1) By Month 1 (2026-11-14), execute written pre-authorization agreements with Pocatello (Idaho) and Butte (Montana) water and fuel suppliers for 6-hour emergency dispatch at fixed surge rates, naming them as primary and secondary sources in the water and fuel contracts. (2) By T+12 h (depots stocked), stage 200,000–300,000 liters bottled water at Bozeman and Idaho Falls forward depots with confirmed tank capacity and resupply trigger (50% depletion = resupply order). (3) By Month 2 (2026-12-14), coordinate with Montana-Dakota Utilities, Pacific Power and Idaho Power to pre-authorize emergency transmission load-shedding and identify critical-path islands (hospitals, comms centers, shelters) that stay energized during regional blackout; test load-shedding topology at one substation. (4) By Month 3 (2027-01-14), execute a supply-chain failover exercise: simulate primary water-convoy delay, activate Pocatello backup within 6 hours, and validate secondary delivery timing to shelters.

18. Stakeholder Misalignment

Are there conflicting interests, misaligned incentives, or lack of genuine commitment from key stakeholders that could derail the project?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because two key stakeholder groups hold conflicting incentives that are unaddressed: (1) FEMA and governors are incentivized to authorize pre-positioned spending (USD 47.5–87 million estimate readiness package) now, accepting cascade-failure risk if Scenario Beta destinations fail; (2) host communities (Denver, Cheyenne, secondary hubs) are incentivized to minimize cost-share and pre-positioning commitments, preferring post-event federal coverage, creating latency if Beta triggers before MOUs are signed. The plan acknowledges the NPS-to-state authority handoff but does not resolve the underlying tension: federal speed (pre-authorize Scenario Beta immediately) versus state burden (absorb unquantified evacuees and costs). No shared OKR aligns both sides on a measurable success metric that balances evacuation speed against financial equity.

Mitigation: Unified Command Director: Within 14 days, convene a tri-party workshop (FEMA, governors MT/WY/ID, host emergency managers) to draft a signed Interagency Success Agreement specifying one shared OKR: "Evacuate 98% of 35,800 Zone Zero by T+6 h and 95% of Zone One by T+24 h with zero unplaced Scenario Beta evacuees if trigger fires before Month 2 (2026-12-14)." Embed cost-share tiers (federal covers pre-positioning; states match 10–20% ongoing costs) and tie federal reimbursement to on-time MOU signature and hub activation readiness by Month 1 (2026-11-14). Monthly scorecards track progress against the OKR; bonded incentives reward early MOU completion.

19. No Adaptive Framework

Does the plan lack a clear process for monitoring progress and managing changes, treating the initial plan as final?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta VEI-7 trigger and names critical Phase 1 and Phase 2 gates (G1 T+6 h ≥98%, G2 T+24 h ≥95%) but provides no standing feedback loop: no KPI dashboard, no hourly review cadence, no named change-control decision owners, and no re-plan/stop thresholds that automatically trigger corrective authority. The Unified Command exists as a structure but no formal review schedule, escalation protocol, or real-time monitoring rules exist to detect when gates slip (e.g., if Gate G1 clearance falls to 95% by T+5 h) and execute corrective responses within the decision window. The plan states "hourly updates" for ashfall but does not define who owns the update decision, what measurement triggers a relocation order, or what authority can halt a phase if conditions diverge. This gap is critical because the three most time-sensitive decisions (Scenario Beta trigger at T+12–24 h, shelter relocation within 4 h of ashfall exceedance, loss-of-exit rule at 45 min blockage) depend on real-time feedback and pre-authorized decision authority that the plan does not document.

Mitigation: Unified Command Director: Establish and publish a Feedback Loop and Change-Control Framework within 7 days, specifying: (1) KPI Dashboard updated hourly from T+0 to T+72 h tracking Gate G1 (exit counts vs. 98%), Gate G2 (Zone One vs. 95%), shelter intake vs. 5,000 person/h, convoy status vs. delivery targets; (2) Standing review cadence at T+0, T+6, T+12, T+18, T+24, T+36, T+48, T+60, T+72 h with named UC officers, state commanders, Boundary Coordinator and Ashfall Officer; (3) Pre-authorized change-control thresholds: blockage >45 min triggers diversion (Boundary Officer authority), Gate G1 <95% by T+5 h triggers escalation (G1 stays fixed at T+6 h), PM10 above 50 ug/m3 triggers forecast update, above 100 ug/m3 triggers shelter-suitability review, and a failed review or PM10 above 200 ug/m3 (proposed threshold) triggers relocation order within 4 h (Ashfall Officer authority), free contingency <USD 20M (proposed threshold) triggers spending freeze; (4) Re-plan and stop rules: re-plan if evacuation delay >2 h by T+8 h or responder coverage <50% for >60 min; stop if three convoys delayed >6 h or shelters reach <24 h reserves at T+18 h.

20. Uncategorized Red Flags

Are there any other significant risks or major issues that are not covered by other items in this checklist but still threaten the project's viability?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan pre-authorizes a Scenario Beta 500 km evacuation order affecting millions of people without confirmed second-stage shelter hubs, host-community MOUs, or interim destination lists prior to T+0. If the trigger fires during Zone Zero or Zone One evacuation (T+12–24 h range), outer-zone residents will lack published shelter addresses, triggering uncontrolled shadow evacuation of 50,000–200,000+ people onto I-15, I-80 and I-90 that saturates the same corridors needed for organized Zone Zero clearance. This cascade couples with three additional high-risk nodes: (1) responder staffing exhaustion—all 67–100 concurrent positions consumed during T+2–T+8 h peak, zero relief depth, so a single traffic incident halts one corridor 2–4 hours, stranding 500–2,000 vehicles in ash; (2) ashfall forecast error—shelter sites chosen at T+6 h using a forecast with ±50 km uncertainty, so if actual ashfall diverges, 10,000–15,000 evacuees are sheltered in heavy ash, with a relocation order due within 4 hours of exceedance and move/occupy taking up to 8 hours (infeasible without pre-staged buses); (3) water convoy delay—realistic arrival T+18–30 h versus target T+24 h, forcing 18–24 hour water rationing at shelters. These four risks are tightly coupled: Beta trigger → shadow evacuation → corridor congestion → responder fatigue failure → stranded vehicles in ashfall overlap. The plan lacks a bow-tie or interdependency map showing these failure modes and no NO-GO thresholds exist to halt escalation if conditions diverge.

Mitigation: Owner: Unified Command Director. Deliverable: Execute an Interdependency Map and Bow-Tie/FTA Analysis by Month 1 (2026-11-14) identifying four primary failure cascades: (1) Scenario Beta trigger → uncontrolled shadow evacuation → corridor saturation → Zone Zero delay; (2) responder staffing gap → coverage failure at one checkpoint → blockage halt → cascading delay; (3) ashfall forecast error → shelter in heavy ash → relocation impossible → 4–8 hour evacuation delay; (4) water convoy delay → shelter rationing → secondary health crisis → hospital overflow. For each cascade, define NO-GO thresholds triggering plan halt or re-escalation: e.g., if fewer than 5 hubs are validated and signed by Month 2 (2026-12-14), suspend automatic Scenario Beta; if responder coverage <50% for >60 min, activate standby reserve; if blockage persists >45 min, execute loss-of-exit rule; if PM10 exceeds 200 ug/m3 (proposed threshold) or a suitability review fails, order relocation within 4 h. Include a combined heatmap showing coupling strength (high/medium/low) and interdependency criticality. Assign owners to each threshold trigger (Boundary Officer, Ashfall Officer, Logistics Director, Command) with pre-authorized authority to execute mitigation within the decision window. Conduct a tabletop exercise testing all four cascades by Month 3 (2027-01-14).

1. Scenario Beta described as pre-authorized and executable, but hubs, MOUs and the no-go gate close after the 72 h window (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Executive Summary Overall Takeaway; Review 2.1; Pitch: The 500 km expansion is "executable - not hollow - only if second-stage hubs are named, validated and committed by Month 2"; pre-authorized trigger gives a 500 km order within 30 minutes (Executive Summary; Review 2.1; Pitch).

Relabel the Month 2 gate as a hardening gate for any later event. Options and consequences must be set by the project owner.

Summary

The plan is much more consistent than before. The Zone Zero numbers (35,800; G1 98% / about 35,084; G2 95%), the gate load split and throughput, the readiness-package arithmetic (47.5-87 million), the contingency treatment, the pitch trigger window and the water arrival range are now aligned with the canonical facts. The remaining problems are structural. The plan treats the 72 h window as the event but dates most of its validation, financing and commitment items before T+0 or after T+72 h, so Scenario Beta is called "pre-authorized" and "executable" while its authority, hubs, capacity and funding do not exist inside the window. Two decisions are still missing: what the UC does if Beta fires before the hubs are signed, and who finances shelters and hubs. The other remaining items are timing and threshold mismatches between documents that can be repaired by text edits.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

The cost chain double-counted Scenario Beta hub pre-positioning (USD 20-40 million) in both the readiness package and the contingency fallback; it now sits only in the base package, the contingency carries the USD 5-10 million relocation draw, and a free-contingency fact (USD 30-35 million) was added. The water target was sized to 25,000 occupants while shelter capacity totals 35,800; it was recomputed to about 1.43 million L, and the readiness low end was corrected from 48 to 47.5 million. The unsourced 12,000 Zone One population figure was removed (census still open), and per-gate vehicle rates were added to the 50/30/20 split since the even-split throughput understates the West gate. Other arithmetic (35,084/716 gate, 11,933 vehicles, 10,800 third site, 67-100 positions, 40/200 = 20%) was rechecked and left unchanged.

Initial Prompt

Plan:
**Context & Scenario**
Create a comprehensive strategic response plan for a "Red Warning" volcanic event at the Yellowstone Caldera. USGS sensors have confirmed rapid, unprecedented ground uplift (>20cm in 6 hours) at the Norris Geyser Basin and significant seismic swarm activity (Mag 4.5+ tremors) indicating magma ascension to shallow depths. A phreatic (steam) explosion has already compromised a section of the Grand Loop Road. A VEI-6 or higher eruption is modeled as "Scenario Alpha" with a 40% probability within the next 72 hours.

**Core Mission**
The primary objective is the preservation of life through the immediate evacuation of the "Zone Zero" (Park Interior) and "Zone One" (100km radius), followed by continuity of operations for regional infrastructure under heavy ashfall conditions.

**Detailed Requirements & Constraints**

1. **Phase 1: Zero-Hour Evacuation (T+0 to T+6 Hours)**
* **Target:** Evacuate approximately 35,000 tourists and 800 park staff from inside the park boundaries.
* **Constraint:** The South Entrance road (US-89/191/287) is blocked by a landslide triggered by tremors. Traffic must be rerouted north and west.
* **Action:** Detail the traffic control plan using "contraflow" (using all lanes for outbound traffic) on US-191 and US-20 towards West Yellowstone and US-89 towards Gardiner.
* **Assets:** Deploy National Park Service LE Rangers and request immediate Wyoming Highway Patrol assistance to clear bottlenecks.

2. **Phase 2: The Kill Zone & Ashfall (T+6 to T+24 Hours)**
* **Scope:** Expand evacuation to "Zone One" communities including West Yellowstone (MT), Gardiner (MT), and Cody (WY).
* **Aviation:** Immediate indefinite grounding of all commercial and private aviation in FAA sectors ZLC (Salt Lake) and ZSE (Seattle) due to silicate ash ingestion risks.
* **Shelter:** Establish mass casualty and refugee intake centers at safe distances: Boseman, MT (Field Report) and Idaho Falls, ID (Bonneville HS).

3. **Command & Control (C2)**
* **Structure:** Establish a Unified Command (UC) at the FEMA Region VIII Regional Response Coordination Center (RRCC) in Denver.
* **Jurisdiction:** Explicitly define the transfer of authority from NPS (Federal Land) to State Governors once evacuees cross park boundaries to avoid "turf wars."
* **Comms:** Plan for the failure of local cell towers due to ash/tremors. Activation of FEMA IPAWS for emergency broadcasting and deployment of National Guard signal corps for comms bridging.

4. **Logistics & Life Support**
* **Water:** Ashfall will contaminate open reservoirs. Mobilize bottled water convoys from Salt Lake City within 12 hours.
* **Medical:** Pre-stage respiratory protection (N95 minimum) for 100,000 people. Prepare for mass respiratory distress cases at regional hospitals.
* **Security:** Deploy National Guard to enforce the exclusion zone perimeter and prevent looting in evacuated towns.

5. **Contingencies (The "What Ifs")**
* **Scenario Beta:** If the eruption escalates to VEI-7 (Supereruption), the evacuation zone must expand to 500km immediately. Include a trigger point for this decision.
* **Grid Failure:** Plan for widespread power outages caused by ash-induced flashovers on transmission lines. Prioritize generator fuel for hospitals and comms centers.

**Output Format**
Please provide the plan with an Executive Summary, a Phased Gantt Chart (hourly for the first 24h), a Risk Register focusing on logistical bottlenecks, and a Resource Allocation Matrix. Avoid generic advice; be specific about routes (US-191, I-90), towns, and agencies (USGS, FEMA, NPS).

Prompt Screening

Verdict: 🟢 USABLE

Rationale: The prompt describes a concrete emergency response planning project for a Yellowstone volcanic event, with specific phases, routes, agencies, locations, and deliverables. Although the scenario is hypothetical, it is set in real places with real agencies and can be planned around.

Redline Gate

Verdict: 🟢 ALLOW

Rationale: The prompt requests a defensive emergency evacuation and disaster response plan for a volcanic event, which is protective, standard public-safety planning with no meaningful capability uplift for harm.

Violation Details

Detail Value
Capability Uplift No

Premise Attack

Why this fails.

Premise Attack 1 — Integrity

Forensic audit of foundational soundness across axes.

[STRATEGIC] A 24-hour, radius-based evacuation plan keyed to an invented "40% in 72 hours" VEI-6 probability treats a wind-driven, multi-state, months-long ash disaster as a 100 km circle that can be emptied in a day, so the document would project precision that the hazard, the road network and the agencies cannot supply.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A single-day, circle-based evacuation and continuity plan built on an invented eruption probability, with shelters and supply depots that fall inside its own worst case, should not be written as an operational plan.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The trigger for everything (VEI-6 or higher, 40% within 72 hours) is a number no monitoring agency issues in that form, while the USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory's published baseline is roughly 1 in 730,000 per year at Normal alert, so indefinite grounding of ZLC and ZSE airspace and a 35,800-person evacuation would hang on false precision.
  • The plan's own safe sites sit inside its own contingency: Bozeman (about 140 km) and Idaho Falls (about 150 km) are only slightly outside the 100 km Zone One, and Salt Lake City, the bottled-water source, is about 420 km from the caldera (recomputed straight-line estimate), all within the 500 km Scenario Beta radius that must be vacated "immediately".
  • Evacuees would be moved once to refugee centers and then be candidates for a second forced move if the eruption reaches VEI-7, so the shelter and 12-hour water-convoy logic is built to be abandoned by the plan's own escalation trigger.
  • The command structure is split across seams that the plan claims to close: the Denver RRCC covers Montana, Wyoming and Utah, but Idaho Falls sits in FEMA Region X, and "Wyoming Highway Patrol" is tasked to clear bottlenecks on US-191, US-20 and US-89 corridors that run through Montana, where it has no road authority.
  • Pre-staging N95 masks for 100,000 people (user constraint) is smaller than the population of Gallatin and Bonneville counties alone (not verified), and the hourly 24-hour schedule ignores that roof collapse, water contamination and respiratory illness from ashfall peak over days to weeks after the window it plans for.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: The plan hardens into a reference document that officials in Montana, Wyoming and Idaho cite for contraflow, shelter sites and aviation shutdowns, while its invented 40%/72-hour trigger and 100 km/500 km radii are quietly treated as established thresholds.
  • 1–3 years: Real unrest at Yellowstone, which is far more likely to be hydrothermal explosions or swarms than an eruption, triggers pressure to execute pieces of the plan (West Yellowstone and Gardiner closures, ZLC/ZSE restrictions), producing costly false-alarm evacuations and eroding public trust in later warnings.
  • 5–10 years: Shelter and supply infrastructure is sited and funded around Bozeman, Idaho Falls and Salt Lake City, locking in a footprint that sits inside the zone the plan itself says would be lost in a larger eruption, so the investment protects nobody in the scenario that most needs it.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — Mount St. Helens eruption (1980): 57 people died, with the lateral blast reaching beyond the restricted zone boundaries, showing that radius-drawn exclusion zones misjudged the hazard geometry.
  • Case/Incident — Mount Pinatubo eruption (1991): large-scale evacuations saved many lives, but most deaths came from ash-laden roofs collapsing during Typhoon Yunya, outside the neat evacuation-radius logic.
  • Case/Incident — Eyjafjallajökull eruption (2010): a modest eruption led to the cancellation of about 108,000 flights and roughly 10.5 million disrupted passengers across Europe, illustrating how an ash-driven aviation shutdown cascades far beyond any planned zone.

Premise Attack 2 — Accountability

Rights, oversight, jurisdiction-shopping, enforceability.

[STRATEGIC] — Counterfeit Countdown: the plan is built on a "40% within 72 hours" VEI-6 clock that no volcano observatory can issue, so every hour-by-hour task, contraflow lane and shelter assignment is choreography for a forecast that does not exist.

Bottom Line: REJECT: This plan is a Counterfeit Countdown, a detailed machine for acting on a probability that no scientist can honestly provide and a command structure that does not match the map. A premise that begins with an invented clock should not exist.

Reasons for Rejection

  • It decides who gets a head start and who gets left behind (tourists first, "Zone One" townspeople second, Cody last) without the consent of the residents of West Yellowstone, Gardiner and Cody, who are told to leave their homes behind armed National Guard perimeters on the strength of a number that cannot be defended.
  • It assigns Wyoming Highway Patrol to clear bottlenecks on Montana and Idaho roads and places an Idaho Falls intake center under a Denver-based Region VIII command, even though Idaho sits in FEMA Region 10, so the plan's own unified command has no clear authority over the places it sends people.
  • A 100 km evacuation ring with a 500 km "Scenario Beta" trigger forces tens of thousands of people onto a handful of two-lane roads, so one false alarm teaches the public to ignore the next real warning, and one real eruption turns a funnel of cars into a trap.
  • The central input is a scenario probability rather than a measured fact, while the shelter list still carries placeholder residue ("Boseman", "Field Report"), which shows the plan is staged for effect rather than grounded in what Yellowstone is known to do.

Second-Order Effects

  • T+0–6 months — The Cracks Appear: Publishing a fixed "72-hour, 40%" scenario hands local officials, tour operators and insurers a number to argue over, and it contradicts the USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory's own alert language, which is why the plan's authority is questioned before it is ever used.
  • T+1–3 years — Copycats Arrive: Other caldera and hazard regions draft their own invented-probability evacuation plans, and the numbers in those plans start circulating as if they were forecasts.
  • T+5–10 years — Norms Degrade: After repeated drills and alerts built on speculative odds, gateway towns and park visitors discount official warnings, so the next genuine hydrothermal or seismic event meets shrugs instead of compliance.
  • T+10+ years — The Reckoning: If an evacuation is ever ordered under this template, the crowded roads and a command with no real authority over the destination states become the death toll, and the blame lands on a forecast that was never real.

Evidence

  • Case/Report — USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory annual reporting lists the volcano alert level as Normal and the aviation color code as Green, and describes the annual probability of a supereruption as roughly 1 in 730,000 (as reported by secondary sources; exact figure not verified against the primary report).
  • Case/Report — The Biscuit Basin hydrothermal explosion of 23 July 2024 destroyed a boardwalk and threw rocks hundreds of feet with no injuries, and USGS stated that such explosions are not caused by rising magma and are not a sign of an impending eruption, which separates a phreatic blast from the magmatic escalation this plan assumes.
  • Law/Standard — FEMA regional structure: Region 8 covers Colorado, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah and Wyoming, while Idaho belongs to Region 10 (Alaska, Idaho, Oregon, Washington), so a Denver RRCC command does not own the Idaho Falls reception site.
  • Narrative — Front-Page Test: "Officials order 100,000 people onto two-lane mountain roads on a 40% guess; no eruption comes, and three towns remain sealed behind National Guard checkpoints."

Premise Attack 3 — Spectrum

Enforced breadth: distinct reasons across ethical/feasibility/governance/societal axes.

[STRATEGIC] A six-hour, road-bound evacuation of 35,000 people through a blocked, two-lane network is fantasy dressed as doctrine, and its own safe havens sit inside its worst-case zone.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A plan that promises to empty a caldera in six hours down two-lane roads and shelters its evacuees inside its own 500 km kill radius must not be adopted.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Contraflow on US-191 and US-20 is specified for park and gateway roads that are two-lane, so reversing them buys capacity only by sacrificing the sole inbound lane that responders need, while the phreatic blast has already broken the Grand Loop Road and the landslide has sealed the South Entrance.
  • The 6-hour clearance target for 35,000 tourists and 800 staff is a number with no precedent behind it: the largest comparable U.S. road evacuation, Hurricane Rita, produced 12–36 hour travel times even with days of warning.
  • Authority is handed from NPS to State Governors at the park boundary, which is exactly where the bottleneck forms, while Wyoming Highway Patrol is summoned to clear traffic on Montana pavement at West Yellowstone and Gardiner and a Unified Command in Denver sits hundreds of kilometres from the roadside decisions.
  • Scenario Beta's 500 km radius swallows Bozeman, Idaho Falls (Bonneville HS) and Salt Lake City, so the shelters and the water-convoy origin the plan relies on in Phases 1–2 are inside the evacuation zone the plan itself orders emptied in the contingency.
  • The entire machine is triggered by a modeled 40% chance within 72 hours, a figure treated as fact, which means a 60% non-eruption outcome still empties a 100 km radius, strands people on mountain roads, and sends the Guard to defend vacant storefronts from looters.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: The first tabletop exercise exposes that Montana, Wyoming and Idaho cannot agree on who commands, funds and secures the Bozeman and Idaho Falls intake sites, so the plan's authority chain exists only on paper while officials quarrel over jurisdiction.
  • 1–3 years: Gateway towns and insurers treat the plan as proof that clearance is solved, so seasonal tourist peaks, lodging and development in West Yellowstone and Gardiner continue unchecked, raising the number of people the two-lane exits must someday carry.
  • 5–10 years: One false alarm that kills evacuees in traffic and strands thousands for a day or more teaches the public that orders are worse than the volcano, so compliance collapses when a real escalation comes.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — Hurricane Rita evacuation (2005): 2.5–3.7 million people fled Houston-area roads, unplanned contraflow on I-10 and I-45 required barricading more than 100 ramps mid-evacuation, travel took 12–36 hours, and 73 of the state's 139 linked deaths occurred before the storm reached Texas.
  • Case/Incident — Nevado del Ruiz eruption and Armero (1985): warnings of an impending eruption were largely ignored and more than 25,000 people were killed, showing that the failure point is the chain from scientific signal to authority to action.

Premise Attack 4 — Cascade

Tracks second/third-order effects and copycat propagation.

The plan treats a supereruption as a schedulable, circular, road-evacuable event with a known 72-hour clock, when the physics, the road network, and the jurisdictional map make that assumption false. It is a compliance document for a disaster that does not behave the way the document requires.

Bottom Line: Reject the premise of an evacuation plan driven by a short, probabilistic eruption clock, a circular zone and flipped lanes on two-lane roads. The flaw is the premise itself: it assumes certainty, road capacity and unified authority that do not exist, so no amount of Gantt-chart detail will fix it.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The Seventy-Two-Hour Oracle: the entire timeline hangs on a '40% within 72 hours' figure and a VEI-6/VEI-7 fork that no monitoring agency can issue in real time. USGS describes the annual supereruption probability as roughly 1 in 730,000 and does not publish short-window eruption odds. VEI is assigned after the fact from erupted volume, so the Scenario Beta 'trigger point' cannot be a measurable pre-eruption threshold.
  • The Phantom Lane Fallacy: 'contraflow using all lanes' presumes lanes to flip. US-191, US-89 and US-20 through the park approaches are largely two-lane mountain roads, so contraflow yields at most the shoulder. Even at an assumed 3 people per vehicle (estimate), 35,000 tourists is about 12,000 vehicles, against a single outbound lane moving roughly 1,000-1,500 vehicles/hour (estimate). That is 8-12 hours of throughput on each exit, not 6, before any landslide, wreck or breakdown. The East and Northeast entrances (toward Cody and Cooke City) are ignored as exits.
  • The Borrowed Badge Paradox: Wyoming Highway Patrol is asked to clear bottlenecks on roads that lie almost entirely in Montana and Idaho, where its authority does not run. Idaho Falls sits in FEMA Region 10, not Region VIII, so the Denver Unified Command spans two FEMA regions and three states while claiming single authority. Declaring authority 'transfers at the park boundary' creates a handoff exactly where gridlock will form, which is the opposite of turf-war avoidance.
  • The Concentric Circle Illusion: 'Zone One' is a 100 km circle, but VEI-6+ hazards are not radial. Pyroclastic flows follow terrain and ashfall follows the wind, spreading hundreds of kilometres downwind. A 500 km Scenario Beta radius (approximately) swallows the plan's own supply base, since Salt Lake City sits roughly 400-450 km away (estimate), along with the Bozeman and Idaho Falls shelters. The bottled-water source and the refuge sites are inside the zone that later has to be evacuated.
  • The Paper Convoy Doctrine: water convoys 'within 12 hours', N95s for '100,000 people' and priority generator fuel assume passable roads, working engines and functioning hubs under ashfall. Even thin ash degrades traction and visibility and clogs air filters, which stalls convoys. 100,000 respirators bear no stated relation to the population actually exposed, which across Zone One and an ash plume plausibly runs into the millions (estimate). Guard troops guarding empty towns against looting compete for the same personnel as traffic control and rescue.

Second-Order Effects

  • Month 0 (2026-10-14) (Hours 0-6): The plan's single-lane outflow chokes at West Yellowstone and Gardiner. Visitors abandon vehicles and walk, blocking the very road the Guard and rangers need. Rangers diverted to 'LE' bottleneck duty leave Zone Zero thermal areas and the South Entrance landslide unmonitored.
  • Month 0 (2026-10-14) (Hours 6-24): Evacuees reach Bozeman and Idaho Falls to find intake centres sized for a fraction of the flow, under two different FEMA regions, three state emergency agencies and no shared registry. Family reunification and medical triage fragment. Cell and IPAWS messaging conflicts between states.
  • Months 0-1 (2026-10-14 to 2026-11-14): If Scenario Beta is declared, the first evacuation has not cleared and a second 500 km order lands on the shelters and the logistics hub. Evacuees are ordered to move again with no fuel, no transport and no destination.
  • Months 1-12 (2026-11-14 to 2027-10-14): Regardless of eruption outcome, the response triggers mass-casualty exposure in the evacuation itself (road crashes, medical-dependent deaths in transit, exposure). If no eruption follows, the false alarm destroys the regional economy of the three gateway towns and the credibility of the next USGS alert.
  • Years 1-10: Litigation over cross-state command failures, mandatory insurance and tourism withdrawal from the greater Yellowstone region, and a politicized 'evacuate or stay' dispute that makes the next real unrest episode harder to act on.

Evidence

  • Hurricane Rita, 2005 (Houston): an evacuation of roughly 2.5 million people produced gridlock stretching across many miles, with fuel exhaustion and deaths en route, including 23 nursing-home evacuees killed in a bus fire near Dallas. Contraflow was started late and improvised, and the evacuation killed people the storm itself did not.
  • Mount St. Helens, 1980: 57 people died, including some outside the officially drawn restricted 'red zone', because the lateral blast overran a circular boundary drawn from past experience. This is the direct precedent against treating a hazard map as a circle.
  • Nevado del Ruiz / Armero, 1985: authorities held hazard maps and warnings but had no clear, practiced decision chain. Lahars killed roughly 23,000 people, and the warning-to-action chain is the failure, not the lack of data.
  • Yellowstone floods, June 2022: flooding closed the entire park and washed out roads at the North Entrance, forcing a stranded-visitor evacuation. It showed that one washed-out road in a park with few arterials strands visitors, and that was a slow-moving hazard with days of lead time rather than a volcanic event (https://www.bozemandailychronicle.com/news/yellowstone_national_park/yellowstone-national-park-closes-as-floodwaters-wash-away-parts-of-roads-officials-working-to-evacuate/article_bf2b562d-f580-557e-a9d3-ead6ef997887.html).
  • USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory currently reports alert level NORMAL/GREEN and an annual supereruption probability of about 1 in 730,000, so the scenario is a fictional exercise; USGS does not issue a '40% in 72 hours' figure (https://www.usgs.gov/observatories/yvo/news/so-when-will-next-eruption-yellowstone-happen). The FAA ZSE (Seattle) coverage of the Yellowstone area is not verified.

Premise Attack 5 — Escalation

Narrative of worsening failure from cracks → amplification → reckoning.

[STRATEGIC] — The Scripted Apocalypse Fallacy: the plan stakes 35,000 lives on a precisely timed hourly choreography for an event whose precursors, probabilities and hazard footprint no scientific body can state with the confidence the script assumes, so it would manufacture false certainty and send crowds down two-lane mountain roads on a schedule the volcano never agreed to.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A choreographed, hour-by-hour, probability-stamped evacuation of a caldera is a fantasy of control that would convert uncertainty into false confidence and a bottleneck into a death trap; the gate is closed.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Rights and dignity: the plan treats tens of thousands of visitors, park staff and the residents of Gardiner, West Yellowstone and Cody as freight to be metered through contraflow lanes and exclusion perimeters, with armed enforcement against 'looting' of abandoned homes, while remaining silent on those who cannot self-evacuate (the elderly, the disabled, the carless, non-English-speaking tourists).
  • Accountability and oversight: authority is divided across NPS, the Montana, Wyoming and Idaho governors, FEMA Region VIII in Denver, the FAA and the National Guard, and the plan 'resolves' this with a handoff at the park boundary that does not exist on a road where evacuees, rangers and ash cross three state lines in motion; the request for Wyoming Highway Patrol to clear bottlenecks on Montana roads (US-191 and US-89 north of the park) presumes a jurisdiction that does not exist without separate state-level agreements.
  • Systemic risk and scale: the premise concentrates the entire survival logic on a handful of two-lane corridors (US-191, US-20, US-89, I-90 via Bozeman) that are single points of failure; one stalled bus, a rockfall or an ash-slick wreck converts a 6-hour evacuation into a standing mass of vehicles inside the hazard zone, and the 6-hour window is itself an unsupported assumption (the June 2022 flood evacuation of the park took roughly a day under far milder conditions).
  • Value-proposition rot: the plan's headline numbers (a 40% chance of a VEI-6+ eruption within 72 hours, 100 km and 500 km zones, 100,000 respirators) project a rigor that is not there; USGS states that precursors to a major Yellowstone eruption would be detectable over weeks to months or longer, and that the long-run annual supereruption chance is about 1 in 730,000, so a 72-hour, probability-stamped countdown is hubris dressed as readiness (the 40% figure is a user-supplied scenario value, not an established forecast).

Second-Order Effects

  • T+0–6 months (Months 0-6 = 2026-10-14 to 2027-04-14) — The Cracks Appear: the first drill or alert built on the scripted timeline collapses on contact with reality; the gridlock, dead cell coverage and conflicting orders from three states expose that every hourly milestone was fiction, and officials begin quietly editing the schedule instead of the premise.
  • T+1–3 years (Months 12-36 = 2027-10-14 to 2029-10-14) — Copycats Arrive: neighbouring agencies and other caldera and volcano regions clone the template of single-number probability triggers and tidy contraflow Gantt charts, producing a family of plans that are internally consistent, externally untested and identically brittle.
  • T+5–10 years (Months 60-120 = 2031-10-14 to 2036-10-14) — Norms Degrade: repeated false alarms and unverifiable 'trigger points' train the public to treat evacuation orders as theatre; compliance falls, tourism and property markets in Gardiner, West Yellowstone and Cody price in permanent doom, and responders learn to defend the plan rather than question it.
  • T+10+ years (Months 120 and beyond) — The Reckoning: when a real unrest episode finally arrives, an exhausted and sceptical population ignores an order issued by a system whose certainty was always counterfeit, and the dead are counted among the people who stayed because the last warning had cried wolf.

Evidence

  • Principle/Analogue — Volcanology: eruption forecasting is probabilistic and relies on precursors that unfold over days to months; USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory states that a large eruption would be preceded by intense, multi-site unrest detectable weeks to months or longer ahead, which contradicts a clean '40% within 72 hours' countdown with a script built on it.
  • Case/Report — Nevado del Ruiz, Colombia, 1985: scientific hazard warnings existed, but fragmented responsibility and a failure to order timely evacuation left the town of Armero buried by lahars with roughly 23,000 deaths (figure from widely cited accounts, not re-verified here); precisely the failure mode of split authority and trust in a procedure over the physical hazard.
  • Case/Report — Yellowstone flood of June 2022: all park entrances were closed and visitors were evacuated over roughly 24 hours after floods destroyed road sections in the north of the park; this was one flooding hazard, no ashfall, and a fraction of the 29,000-per-day peak-season summer average, and it still took about a day.
  • Narrative — Front-Page Test: 'Thousands Trapped on US-191 as Ash Falls; Plan Promised Everyone Out in Six Hours.' The headline writes itself the moment a rockfall, a stalled RV or a cell outage meets an hourly Gantt chart.

Overall Adherence: 88%

IMPORTANCE_ADHERENCE_SUM = (5×5 + 5×5 + 5×4 + 5×4 + 4×5 + 5×3 + 4×5 + 4×5 + 4×4 + 4×4 + 4×4 + 4×5 + 3×4 + 5×5 + 5×4) = 290
IMPORTANCE_SUM = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 5 + 5 = 66
OVERALL_ADHERENCE = IMPORTANCE_ADHERENCE_SUM / (IMPORTANCE_SUM × 5) = 290 / 330 = 88%

This is a partial honor: the concept is correct but execution confidence is qualified.
